articles.title: Black Friday Amazon : cet écran QD-OLED 240 Hz de Lenovo passe à 329,99€
articles.text:
Le Black Friday d’Amazon touche aussi les moniteurs OLED, alors que GTA VI sort le 19 novembre sur PS5 et Xbox Series. Le Lenovo Legion 27Q-10 OLED y passe à 329,99 €, soit 59,01 € sous son plus bas des 30 derniers jours, mais ses 240 Hz profitent surtout aux joueurs sur PC.
Amazon met plusieurs écrans OLED en promotion pour le Black Friday, dont ce Lenovo. Le Lenovo Legion 27Q-10 OLED est un moniteur de 27 pouces à dalle QD-OLED, en définition 2 560 × 1 440 pixels et 240 Hz. Amazon l’affiche à 329,99 € contre 479 € de prix conseillé, soit 31 % de remise affichée.
Cette remise se lit autrement face à l’historique : son plus bas des 30 derniers jours était de 389 €, ce qui ramène l’écart réel à 59,01 €, soit 15 %. L’écran vise les joueurs sur PC qui veulent passer à l’OLED sans y consacrer 500 €.
Le Lenovo Legion 27Q-10 OLED est à 329,99 € chez Amazon, contre 479 € de prix conseillé affiché par le marchand, qui présente l’offre comme limitée dans le temps.
Pourquoi choisir le Lenovo Legion 27Q-10 OLED ?
- Des noirs profonds : La dalle QD-OLED offre le contraste et la réactivité propres à l’OLED, avec un temps de réponse annoncé à 0,03 ms, ce qui se remarque dans les jeux sombres et rapides.
- Du 240 Hz en QHD : Le QHD est nettement plus facile à exploiter à haute fréquence que la 4K, et le FreeSync Premium annoncé limite les déchirures d’image.
- Une surface mate : La fiche indique un traitement anti-reflet et une finition mate, utiles dans une pièce éclairée où une dalle brillante renvoie les lumières.
Du jeu rapide sur PC à GTA VI sur console : ce que change l’écran
Sur PC, le couple QHD et 240 Hz vise les jeux d’action et les titres compétitifs, où la réactivité de l’OLED se ressent d’abord. Les noirs profonds profitent aussi aux films regardés dans une pièce tamisée, et la certification Eyesafe annoncée concerne ceux qui passent de longues heures devant l’écran. Le réglage en inclinaison permet d’ajuster la position selon le bureau.
GTA VI sort le 19 novembre sur PS5 et Xbox Series, et nous rapportions fin août qu’un vidéaste évoquait une cible de 30 images par seconde sur ces consoles, sans confirmation de Rockstar. Si l’écran doit surtout servir à ce jeu sur console, les 240 Hz resteront donc inexploités et seule l’image de l’OLED justifie l’achat. Il trouve mieux sa place chez les joueurs sur PC, dont la carte graphique peut soutenir une cadence élevée en 2 560 × 1 440 pixels.
Face au marché : un QD-OLED abordable, mais pas le seul
Dans notre comparatif des meilleurs écrans PC gamer, l’AOC Q27G4ZD, noté 7/10, illustre l’accès plus abordable au QD-OLED : même diagonale de 27 pouces et même définition QHD, mais 280 Hz, deux HDMI 2.1 et un hub USB à quatre ports. Nous lui reprochons une dalle très brillante, parfois réfléchissante, là où le Lenovo annonce une surface mate. La fiche Amazon du Lenovo ne précise ni la version de ses ports HDMI ni la présence d’un hub USB, deux points à vérifier si vous visez une console. C’est donc la pièce où l’écran sera installé, plus que la fréquence, qui doit trancher entre les deux.
✅ Les points forts
- Dalle QD-OLED de 27 pouces en 2 560 × 1 440 pixels
- 240 Hz, 0,03 ms annoncé et FreeSync Premium
- Surface mate avec traitement anti-reflet
- Deux ports HDMI et un DisplayPort
- 329,99 €, contre 389 € au plus bas des 30 derniers jours
❌ Les limites
- Aucun port USB-C sur cette version
- Luminosité annoncée à 400 nits, à surveiller dans une pièce très lumineuse
- Remise réelle de 15 % seulement face au plus bas des 30 derniers jours
- Aucun test Clubic de ce modèle et 17 avis seulement sur Amazon
Au moment de notre relevé, Amazon indiquait l’écran en stock à 329,99 € : prix et disponibilité peuvent changer avant la fin de l’offre.
À 329,99 €, le Lenovo Legion 27Q-10 OLED place une dalle QD-OLED de 27 pouces à 240 Hz sous la barre des 330 €. Le chiffre de 31 % se lit face à un prix conseillé : contre le plus bas récent d’Amazon, à 389 €, l’économie est de 59,01 €. L’offre intéresse surtout les joueurs sur PC en QHD, qui profiteront à la fois de l’OLED et des 240 Hz, et ceux qui veulent une surface mate dans une pièce lumineuse.
Elle convainc moins si l’écran sert surtout à GTA VI sur console, ou si un USB-C est nécessaire pour un ordinateur portable : la même fiche Amazon propose alors une version avec USB-C à 407,46 €. Faute de test Clubic de ce modèle, les caractéristiques citées viennent de la fiche du marchand et non de nos mesures. Dans le doute, confrontez ces points à votre usage réel, car ce sont eux, plus que la remise affichée, qui décideront de votre satisfaction.

articles.title: Anthropic buscará una valuación de 1,3 billones de dólares en su salida a bolsa
articles.text:
Anthropic fijó en 1,33 billones de dólares la valuación con la que saldrá a bolsa, una cifra que representa una rebaja significativa frente a las expectativas de 2 billones de dólares que manejaban los inversores hace apenas un mes, y que refleja la presión ejercida por la caída brusca de las acciones tecnológicas que sacudió los mercados la semana pasada.
La empresa creadora de Claude, el asistente de inteligencia artificial, presentó el martes una actualización de su prospecto ante la Comisión de Valores y Bolsa (SEC) en la que informó que ofrecerá 825 millones de acciones a un precio de entre $ 70 y $ 78 por título. Al precio medio de ese rango, Anthropic captaría más de $ 61.000 millones en su debut bursátil, previsto para antes de que termine noviembre, según informó el Wall Street Journal.
La caída del Nasdaq recortó en cientos de miles de millones la valuación esperada
La oferta pública inicial llega en un clima de marcada incertidumbre. El jueves pasado, el índice Nasdaq 100 se desplomó un 6,4%, borrando 2,3 billones de dólares en valor de mercado en una sola jornada —la mayor pérdida en un único día registrada hasta ahora—, lo que forzó a los potenciales inversores a revisar a la baja sus estimaciones para la empresa. Semanas antes, varios de ellos habían comunicado a los bancos encargados de la operación que consideraban justo un valor de entre 1,4 y 1,5 billones de dólares; ese techo se recortó aún más tras el derrumbe bursátil, según Bloomberg. Algunos compradores llegaron a plantear cifras cercanas a 1,1 billones.
Stephan Kemper, director de inversiones de BNP Paribas Wealth Management Alemania, estimó que las valuaciones deberían ubicarse “al menos en el extremo inferior del rango rumoreado de 1,5 a 2 billones, quizás entre un 10% y un 15% por debajo de eso”. Michael Alfaro, director de inversiones del fondo de cobertura Gallo Partners, había señalado antes del desplome que Anthropic necesitaba apuntar a una valuación de entre 1,3 y 1,4 billones “para construir un libro de calidad”, en declaraciones recogidas por Bloomberg.
Además del IPO, la empresa planea levantar hasta 26.000 millones de dólares de inversores estratégicos.
El prospecto reveló que, en paralelo a la oferta pública, Anthropic tiene previsto captar hasta USD 26.000 millones adicionales de inversores institucionales de peso, entre ellos Google y AMD. Esta vía de financiamiento complementa la salida a bolsa y apunta a consolidar la base de capital de la compañía antes de que sus acciones comiencen a cotizar.
Los ejecutivos de Anthropic sostuvieron reuniones con banqueros de Goldman Sachs y Morgan Stanley en los últimos días para definir el rango de valuación. La ecuación es delicada: fijar un precio demasiado alto podría desalentar la demanda y hundir el papel en sus primeras jornadas, mientras que un precio excesivamente conservador abriría a la empresa y a sus asesores a críticas por haber dejado miles de millones sobre la mesa.
El IPO de Anthropic se perfila como un termómetro del apetito inversor por la inteligencia artificial
La operación es observada con atención por el mercado como un indicador del estado de ánimo de los inversores frente al sector de la inteligencia artificial. La última valuación privada de Anthropic —de 965.000 millones de dólares, obtenida en su ronda Serie H de mayo pasado— ya quedó por debajo de cualquiera de los rangos que se discuten hoy para el IPO, lo que implica que incluso en el escenario más conservador la empresa debutaría en bolsa con una prima sobre su precio privado más reciente.
El Nasdaq compuesto recuperó parte del terreno perdido el lunes, cuando cerró con un alza del 2,7%, aunque la volatilidad en el sector tecnológico sigue siendo el telón de fondo de una operación que el mercado seguirá de cerca.

articles.title: OpenAI wants more data centers, but even ChatGPT might struggle to sell that idea to the American public right now
articles.text:
OpenAI wants to build more AI data centers — but Americans are increasingly saying no
OpenAI is going for a charm offensive and promising transparency but faces stiff opposition to its plans
OpenAI wants to build more enormous data centers to power ChatGPT and its increasingly ambitious AI systems. Unfortunately, Americans are becoming considerably less enthusiastic about having those facilities built in their neighborhoods.
Following a midterm election in which opposition to data centers became a significant political issue, OpenAI promised in a new announcement to be more transparent and listen more carefully to the communities expected to host them.
Under its new community infrastructure commitments, OpenAI says it will provide more information about construction plans and their environmental effects. The company is also moving away from requiring public officials to sign non-disclosure agreements during negotiations, with limited exceptions for sensitive information. It's a notable change for an industry that has often approached local development as though the promise of technological progress should be enough to overcome almost any objection.
The timing of the announcement is notable as it comes after the Nov. 3 U.S. elections, which saw the resounding victory of almost every effort to restrict or forbid new data centers and the defeat of many of their political advocates. Across the country, communities have been questioning the electricity demands of AI infrastructure and whether the economic benefits justify the disruption.
The sweetness-and-light approach differs from the inevitability many AI companies have promoted around the technology. Given the origin of the new message, it wouldn't be surprising if some of the pro-data center efforts were drafted or tested with AI assistance. ChatGPT might be helping persuade Americans to welcome more infrastructure for itself.
Data center resistance
To encourage acceptance, AI companies have couched data centers as essential investments in America's technological future and promised new jobs and tax revenue.
But those living near a proposed site have their own calculations regarding how much energy, water, and other resources the data centers consume. That might mean higher bills or a strain on the local infrastructure that could lead to its failure or necessitate expensive upgrades. The possibility of paying more for electricity so a technology company can operate a profitable AI service isn't an especially compelling sales pitch. And whether the long-term economic benefits will match the promises made during development remains uncertain.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Those concerns have helped turn data center construction into a political issue that crosses traditional party lines. Communities that disagree about plenty of other subjects can find common ground in opposing a massive industrial facility near their homes. The technology industry is discovering that local opposition doesn't disappear simply because a project involves artificial intelligence.
The midterm results have made that lesson harder to ignore. Candidates and local campaigns challenging data center expansion found receptive audiences among voters worried about infrastructure costs and environmental effects.
ChatGPT tries to win over the neighborhood
OpenAI's response promises a more cooperative approach. The company says its new framework will involve communities earlier in the development process and provide clearer information about the consequences of proposed facilities. It also intends to establish local agreements that address concerns and make commitments more transparent. The company even promises to cover all electricity and infrastructure costs for the facilities it owns and operates.
The decision to reduce the use of non-disclosure agreements is probably essential in the current political climate. Suspicious residents are demanding to know what representatives are negotiating on their behalf, particularly when those decisions could affect local finances and infrastructure for years. The company has highlighted local investments tied to existing developments, though that may not convince every community that a massive data center is a good neighbor.
The company's new approach also has the unmistakable feel of a marketing campaign. OpenAI needs more computing capacity, and growing public opposition threatens to make it slower and more expensive to obtain. Americans are becoming increasingly willing to challenge the assumption that every new AI facility represents progress worth welcoming. If OpenAI wants to keep expanding, it will need to offer something more convincing than polished promises, whether a human or a chatbot helped write them.

articles.title: Microsoft Developer Builds a GPU Task Manager to Show Which Apps Are Eating Your VRAM
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 10th 2026
Microsoft Developer Builds a GPU Task Manager to Show Which Apps Are Eating Your VRAM
Anyone wondering what is filling up their GPU's VRAM can now try gputaskman, a free, open-source tool from Microsoft VP Scott Hanselman. It runs in a terminal window with an htop-style layout and lists every process using the GPU with its memory footprint, engine activity, and loaded runtime, such as CUDA or Vulkan. A panel up top tracks utilization, clocks, temperature, and power. Hanselman shared the project on X last week and asked for pull requests.
Task Manager has shown GPU usage since 2017, and it will happily tell you that 15 GB of video memory is in use. It just won't say what is using it. gputaskman goes after that gap with a heavy focus on local AI. Its model inspector can identify the LLM a process has loaded and report its quantization, weights, and estimated KV cache cost, while Ollama and LM Studio users also get context size and proper model names. Hanselman calls it early, experimental software, and the AI breakdowns are estimates for now.On Windows, only NVIDIA and AMD GPUs are supported currently, and Intel support is limited to native Linux as of v0.3.5. There's also a native Windows ARM64 build, though it's unclear whether anyone has tested it on RTX Spark machines like the Surface Laptop Ultra. When a user said they want this detail in the built-in Task Manager, Hanselman replied "step one...;)", which is a hint at best. The portable Windows builds are also unsigned.

articles.title: C’est officiel, garder son vieux compteur électrique n’est plus un droit : ce qui attend les derniers foyers sans Linky
articles.text:
Refus du compteur Linky : ce que change la décision de la justice européenne et combien vous allez payer
La Cour de justice de l’Union européenne vient de trancher : aucun abonné ne peut exiger de conserver son vieux compteur électrique face à sa décriée déclinaison connectée, le Linky.
Les réfractaires au Linky vont devoir se faire une raison : le boîtier connecté d’Enedis devra tôt ou tard arriver chez eux. L’Union européenne vient en effet de juger qu’un gestionnaire de réseau n’est pas obligé d’accepter la demande d’un abonné voulant garder son ancien compteur électrique. Si l’affaire a débuté en Autriche, la jurisprudence de cet arrêt concerne désormais tous les États membres, forçant ainsi les derniers foyers français non équipés à rentrer dans le rang.
La fin du prétendu droit de refus et une addition salée pour les réfractaires au Linky
Tout est parti de Basse-Autriche, où l’abonnée Roswitha Vizvary refusait que le gestionnaire du réseau électrique local, Netz Niederösterreich, remplace son vieux compteur électrique périmé depuis fin 2023. Invoquant des craintes pour ses données personnelles et les ondes électromagnétiques du nouveau modèle connecté, elle a saisi la justice jusqu’au renvoi du dossier C-468/24 devant la Cour de justice de l’Union européenne (CJUE).
Rendue le 5 novembre 2026, la décision de justice estime en effet que l’appareil appartient exclusivement au distributeur d’électricité et que les textes européens ne garantissent aucun droit à conserver un ancien boîtier. Cela “siffle la fin du match sur le prétendu droit à s’opposer à Linky” d’après l’avocat Alexandre Archambault, étant donné que la France fait face à de multiples contestations similaires menées par des collectifs d’opposants.
Comptabilisant déjà plus de 38,06 millions d’unités installées fin juin 2025 (95,64 % du parc), Enedis voit ainsi sa position confortée vis-à-vis des pénalités fixées par la Commission de régulation de l’énergie (CRE) depuis le 1er août 2025. Si un particulier peut interdire l’accès à son domicile lorsque le compteur est situé à l’intérieur, il n’échappe donc toujours pas aux frais de relève résiduelle. Portés à 40,08 € hors taxes par an au 1er août 2026 (6,68 € tous les deux mois), ces frais grimpent jusqu’à 65,70 € hors taxes (75,60 € TTC) par an si l’abonné ne transmet aucun relevé d’index sur douze mois.
Alors que Bruxelles vise 50 % de clients équipés d’un compteur intelligent en 2030 et 75 % en 2033, l’avocat autrichien Gottfried Forsthuber déplore un jugement qui “prend la protection des données beaucoup trop à la légère”. Les opposants craignent en effet que des relevés fréquents ne trahissent la vie privée du foyer (heures de lever et de coucher, absences, nombre d’occupants…), étant donné que la CJUE autorise malgré tout leur envoi automatique en jugeant que le RGPD suffit à les encadrer.
En France, suite aux interventions de la Commission nationale de l’informatique et des libertés (CNIL), les citoyens peuvent toujours refuser que leur fournisseur collecte le détail de leur consommation toutes les demi-heures, une option qui nécessite leur accord explicite et reste désactivable à tout moment depuis leur espace client.

articles.title: Adobe ouvre enfin Photoshop et Premiere à ChatGPT et Claude, et ça change tout
articles.text:
Présenté à l’Adobe Max 2026, Creative Cloud MCP permettra à des assistants et agents IA compatibles d’intervenir dans vos projets Photoshop ou Premiere. Vous pourrez ensuite, si besoin, ajuster leurs modifications directement dans les logiciels d’Adobe.
Il a suffi d’une consigne pour synchroniser trois caméras et une piste son dans Premiere. La démonstration, présentée lors du prébrief de l’événement annuel Adobe Max 2026, donne une idée du travail que l’éditeur entend confier à son Creative Agent. Mais Adobe veut aussi ouvrir ses logiciels créatifs aux assistants d’autres éditeurs de LLM. C’est le rôle de Creative Cloud MCP, une passerelle qui permettra aux IA tierces d’intervenir dans Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere ou, encore, After Effects.
L’agent intervient, le fichier reste éditable
Le MCP, pour Model Context Protocol, permet à un assistant IA d’appeler les fonctions d’un autre logiciel. Adobe propose déjà des connecteurs qui donnent accès à certains de ses outils depuis ChatGPT, Claude ou Gemini. Avec Creative Cloud MCP, l’agent pourra solliciter les applications installées sur l’ordinateur de l’utilisateur et modifier directement le fichier de travail dans son format d’origine.
Après une retouche dans Photoshop, le graphiste pourra rouvrir son projet et ajuster lui-même un calque. Même principe dans Illustrator, où les éléments vectoriels resteront modifiables, ou dans Premiere, où le monteur pourra déplacer une coupe dans sa séquence.
De même, si l’agent est aussi connecté à Google Drive et à Slack, il pourra récupérer un brief dans Google Docs, modifier le projet avec les outils d’Adobe, puis partager le résultat avec l’équipe dans Slack. Le géant des logiciels de création doit toutefois encore préciser si l’IA traitera la consigne en local ou à distance, et quelles données du projet elle recevra.
- Suite créative très complète
- Logiciels Adobe professionnels
- Intégration entre les applications
Dans Premiere, une consigne peut resservir d’un montage à l’autre
En parallèle, Adobe étend en version beta son propre Creative Agent à Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects et Frame.io. Dans la démonstration de Premiere à laquelle nous avons pu assister, l’assistant a calé les rushes de trois caméras sur une piste audio enregistrée à part, puis préparé un clip multicaméra. Le monteur pouvait ainsi passer d’un angle à l’autre sans avoir à refaire la synchronisation.
La fonction prend un autre intérêt quand plusieurs personnes travaillent sur les mêmes projets. L’équipe peut ainsi consigner sa méthode de travail dans un fichier Markdown, un document texte avec une mise en forme légère, puis le partager entre monteurs. Adobe appelle ça des skills. L’assistant IA peut y retrouver les règles de nommage des rushes, leur rangement ou, encore, les étapes de préparation d’un montage multicaméra.

Il est surtout le modèle de milieu de gamme le mieux équipé pour l'intelligence artificielle, mais aussi le plus généreux en mises à jour. Si les Pixel “a” sont de moins en moins compacts, cette itération a le mérite de n'être ni trop lourde ni trop encombrante, et s'avère assez équilibrée pour satisfaire le plus grand nombre.

articles.title: Seagate FireCuda Forge external HDD review: Is this the best portable hard drive ever?
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
It took me a while to get my head around how tiered storage worked, with initial benchmarks showing the speed of the SSD, which acts as an access point to the internal HDD's vast storage. Pushing the system by switching between large projects showed those limits. However, overall performance for quickly offloading files and editing small to medium-sized video projects is impressive.
Reasons to buy
- + Fast transfers
- + Large-capacity drive
- + Easy to use
Reasons to avoid
- - Self-installation of the SSD
- - Not bus-powered
- - Relatively large physical size
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Seagate FireCuda Forge: 30-second review
Storage Capacity: 8TB / 20TB HDD
Storage Technology: Seagate Alkemi dynamic tiered storage
HDD Form Factor: 3.5-inch
SSD Type: M.2 2280 NVMe (user-installed, not included)
SSD Interface: PCIe Gen 3 or newer
Maximum Sequential :Read Speed: 2,500MB/s, Write Speed: 2,000MB/s
Computer Interface: USB4 (USB-C)
Operating System Compatibility: Windows 11, macOS 26 or later
Power: External AC power adapter
Dimensions: 240.3 × 146.8 × 65.2mm
Weight: 1.919kg (20TB), 1.845kg (8TB)
Warranty: 2 years (UK and Europe)
Seagate has approached the latest iteration of its FireCuda Forge external HDD in an interesting new way for this drive format. Essentially, it combines the speed of an SSD and the storage capacity of an HDD in one device. While this has been done before, as it works as tiered or cached storage, this is usually seen in enterprise level hardware.
This works by having your main HDD, which in this case is a large 20TB drive, and then having a smaller but faster SSD. When you plug in the drive, instead of seeing the two as you would expect, you see only one.
As you copy files to the drive, the system uses the SSD to speed up transfers, while Seagate's Alkemi technology automatically prioritises frequently accessed files on the SSD and keeps less frequently accessed files on the HDD.
Getting started with the drive does require you to insert an SSD of your choice, as the main unit arrives with just the 20TB HDD installed, so you’ll need to purchase an SSD as well, which is something to consider when you look at the cost. Seagate supplied a 2TB PCIe 5.0 SSD, but the specifications show a 1TB limit. Another key factor is that the SSD should include DRAM cache.
Installing the SSD is easy enough, and once it's installed, I was able to plug the drive into the USB4 port of the GMKtec EVO-X5 Pro. Unlike the FireCuda X Vault that I looked at recently, which is bus-powered, the Forge requires its own power supply.
Initial tests showed this drive’s potential, and while the interface is USB4 and the M.2 SSD inside is the latest PCIe 5.0, the speed tests hovered around 2,000MB/s for both read and write.
This is far in excess of any HDD I have used in the past and showed that, while I could only see the single drive, the SSD was doing its job and enabling these much faster transfer rates.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
As the test progressed, I started to see exactly what this drive was about, how it would fit into workflows and its limitations. The SSD enables fast transfers to and from the HDD. However, this is tiered storage with the clever Seagate Alkemi technology managing the data, so frequently accessed files are prioritised on the SSD, while less frequently accessed files are stored on the HDD. This meant that for a 4TB Premiere Pro project, opening up the initial project was admittedly fast, and then editing the file proved to be a fluid process. When I switched to the same edit on an older 5TB HDD I often use for editing, the editing was still smooth, but there were also slowdowns, especially during timeline rendering.
By the end of the test, the most notable advantage of the Forge was its backup speed compared with a standard HDD. Files could be transferred at near 2,000MB/s compared to the usual 200MB/s. Even as a working drive, it performed faster, and the workflow felt more fluid than I expected for a drive that uses an HDD for most of its capacity.
Seagate FireCuda Forge: Price & availability
The FireCuda pricing has yet to be officially announced but is expected to be around the £900 mark for the 20TB and then an addition £100 for the 1TB SSD.
- Score: N/A
Seagate FireCuda Forge: Design & build
The design and build of the FireCuda Forge reflects what I saw with the FireCuda X Vault earlier in the year. There are differences, but essentially, there’s no mistaking the similarities of this external hard drive family.
The overall look and design are solid, and the build quality and materials are exceptionally high. It’s not metal, but the plastics are well finished, and it felt solid enough as I unpacked it and set it on the worktop.
One of the first points that I noted about the drive is that it requires its own power source, and a power brick is included in the box along with a USB4 cable. Before plugging everything in, the drive needs an SSD installed, and the instructions state it has a 1TB limit. However, Seagate also included a 2TB FireCuda PCIe 5.0 module which seemed to work fine.
This is installed into the side of the unit, with four hex screws on the base holding the cover in place. Once you pull it free, you can access the SSD slot on the side of the machine. While Seagate includes a hex key in the box, you'll need to provide a cross-head screwdriver to install the SSD.
After installation, the drive can be plugged in and is ready to go, with the internal HDD being pre-formatted to the NTFS file system. According to the instructions, you can reformat the drive for macOS if needed, but either way, once connected, it’s ready to go. The drive officially supports Windows 11 and macOS 26 or later. Since it arrives formatted to NTFS, you'll need to reformat it to a Mac-compatible file system if you want normal read-and-write access on macOS.
In this test, I connected the drive to the GMKtec EVO-X5 Pro and then transferred data from an existing video project from a 5TB LaCie Tough Pro drive with an HDD inside and a 4TB LaCie Rugged SSD Pro5. I connected both to the other USB4 port on the mini PC, but not at the same time.
Aesthetically, the exterior casing is beautifully designed and features an LED light at the top. It also acts as a status light, showing the drive's basic activity, which is extremely useful.
Connections to the drive are limited, with a power socket for the AC adapter and a USB4 port for the data connection to the machine.
In terms of size, it includes a 3.5-inch drive inside that, like the SSD, is replaceable if you need more capacity or want to replace it in the future. The overall dimensions are 240.3 × 146.8 × 65.2mm, and it weighs in at 1.92kg.
- Design & build: 4.5/5
Seagate FireCuda Forge: Features
From the start, the tiered storage makes this drive far more than most, combining the best features of both SSD and HDD into one. The off-the-shelf unit arrives with a 20TB 3.5-inch HDD installed, but you can replace it later if you want. As well as this 20TB version, a smaller 8TB option is also available; aside from the capacity difference, the drive is also marginally lighter at 1.845kg.
However, while the drive arrives with a ready-to-go HDD installed, before the drive is recognised by the system, be that PC or Mac, it does need an NVMe M.2 2280 SSD to be installed, and this is not provided. The SSD you install must be PCIe Gen 3 or newer, with a maximum supported capacity of 1TB and minimum rated read and write speeds of 2,400MB/s and 2,000MB/s respectively. Seagate also recommends an SSD with DRAM cache.
The surprise here is that once the two drives, the pre-installed HDD and self-installed SSD, are fitted, you would normally expect them to appear as separate drives on the desktop or in the file manager when plugged in. However, because of the system's tiered design, those two drives combine into a single drive.
Seagate's Alkemi technology automatically manages the storage using dynamic tiering to organise data between the HDD and SSD. Essentially, those files being accessed by the user are made accessible on the SSD, speeding up the response time.
Seagate highlights maximum transfer rates of up to 2,500MB/s, but, as ever, this depends entirely on your configuration. Write speeds are also quoted at a very respectable 2,000MB/s.
Although the drive has only one data connection, it uses USB4, which proved to be compatible with Thunderbolt 3, 4, and 5.
- Features: 4.5/5
Seagate FireCuda Forge: Performance
All benchmarks run on GMKtec EVO-X5 Pro
CrystalDiskMark 8 Sequential Read: 2,248.52 MB/s
CrystalDiskMark 8 Sequential Write: 1,726.77 MB/s
ATTO Disk Benchmark Read: 2,320 MB/s
ATTO Disk Benchmark Write: 1,610 MB/s
AS SSD Benchmark Sequential Read: 1,855 MB/s
AS SSD Benchmark Sequential Write: 1,380.33 MB/s
AJA System Test Read: 1,721 MB/s
AJA System Test Write: 1,153 MB/s
Unlike most external drives, getting started with the FireCuda Forge wasn’t as simple as unboxing and plugging it in. While the drive comes with a large 20TB HDD, this cannot be accessed until an SSD has also been installed. The SSD, unlike the HDD, isn't included, so you'll also need to factor in the additional cost of a 1TB module. For a premium option, the FireCuda X1070 1TB SSD costs £179, though that is direct from Seagate, and I have found it elsewhere for much less.
Seagate officially supports SSDs up to 1TB. However, during testing, I installed the supplied 2TB FireCuda X1070 SSD and found that it worked.
Installing the SSD is relatively simple, with the four screws on the base of the machine being removed before the entire base and side cover are removed as one piece. This reveals the HDD, which you can replace later if needed. On the side of the unit is the slot for the SSD, which can be placed in and screwed into place. A small screw is provided in the box, but you’ll need to provide your own small cross-head screwdriver.
Seagate has also included two large thermal pads that stick to the back of the SSD module. Once everything is installed, the base can be reattached and screwed into place. Then attach the USB4 cable, which, at 50 cm, gives a good length between the machine and the drive. Then connect the power, and after a few seconds, the drive mounts. The initial mount took around 10 seconds, which I found to be about average throughout the test.
I started by running the benchmarks, and the initial results were exceptional for a drive of this type and showed how the SSD came into play with standard transfers.
Copying the files from the first external drive over to the HDD, it was obvious that the speed was being limited by the older drive, and any advantage that the drive should have had due to that SSD was being wasted on the slower technology being used at the other end.
However, as I switched to the small 4TB Thunderbolt 5 SSD, the speeds ramped up, and the transfer rate of the real-world files reflected some of the faster transfer speeds that were highlighted in the benchmarks.
Compared with my usual archival storage, there’s really no comparison to be had, and after a video shoot, connecting up the OWC CFexpress Type B card reader and transferring just over 1TB of data to the drive happened in around 12 minutes. Testing this with a more standard HDD, that same data took around 1 hour and 20 minutes, so a significant difference when you’re backing up the files after a shoot.
In the standard backup-and-transfer process, the drive is significantly faster than a standard HDD. However, this isn’t always the case.
The SSD is limited to 1TB, and as I increased the amount of data being copied to the drive, I noticed a slowdown. When I copied the 1.2TB of data over, the system appeared able to maintain high transfer speeds by managing the data between the SSD and HDD, despite the SSD's 1TB capacity limit. However, when I transferred 4TB from an external SSD to the drive, the first part of the transfer was at a similar speed before it started to slow. It was still significantly faster than a traditional HDD, however.
I then used the FireCuda Forge as a working drive, and the potential here really impressed me. Most of my video edits are around the five-minute mark, so are under or close to 1TB. Compared to editing from a standard fast HDD over USB4, which is possible, but where there are often some slight delays as timelines render, here it was the same as editing on a straight SSD.
Again, there is that 1TB limit, and when I opened an old project that I have had timeline rendering issues with in the past, I found that combination of speed and capacity was extremely useful. I can't see exactly what the unit is doing, but it appeared to transfer the data in use onto the SSD when needed, giving the speed you would expect from the format. However, reaching for clips and footage that hadn't been used until then caused a brief slowdown. Once loaded, the speed was again far faster than you would expect compared with files on a standard HDD.
Since I pulled the files from an HDD, I did a quick side-by-side comparison, and the difference in speed and workflow was notable. So while the drive might not hold the entire project, it still sped up the process, and no doubt having additional storage that can hold several video projects at once will be beneficial, with transfer rates that far exceed a standard large-capacity drive.
The final test was two-tiered. The first was storing game files for Steam, and the second was storing the LLMs for Lemonade. On the game front, while the drive can store the files, load times were much longer than when they were stored on the local SSD. However, once loaded, speeds were good, so if your internal drive is limited, then this is a good way to offload the files.
Using the drive to store the LLMs proved to be a good use, especially right now, when I seem to swap and change between models to get the results I want. While it's not as fast as the internal SSD, the convenience of all that space was definitely beneficial, although model load times were slower.
The major benefit of this drive is speedy file offloads. If you’re downloading to the drive from other fast SSDs, memory cards and other media, and you need it to do so at speed, which many photographers and videographers do, then this is a great solution.
For most other users, while the initial speed is beneficial, that data still has to be copied to or from a more traditional HDD at some point, and that can slow the progress. However, it only became an issue when I pushed the system well beyond what I would realistically do. Otherwise, this HDD can provide the speed of an external SSD with the capacity of an HDD.
- Performance: 4.5/5
Should you buy the Seagate FireCuda Forge?
This is the first tiered storage drive I have used, and the test results are impressive. It did take me a while to get my head around the workings of the drive: the fact that the drive featured two internal drives, the 20TB HDD and a smaller 2TB SSD (limited to 1TB), yet they both appear as one and not in a RAID configuration.
Having to supply your own SSD is a bit odd, but given the memory cost and the size limit, it probably makes sense. I have several old 1TB SSDs with DRAM cache that would have done the job, so this step was probably added to keep the drive cost down.
While official pricing has yet to be announced, the FireCuda Forge will need to justify its cost compared with a standard 20TB external HDD, with Seagate's own 20TB Expansion desktop drive costing around £300 at the time of writing. However, what you do get with the FireCuda Forge is a far more capable drive, with transfer rates much closer to an external SSD, yet with the capacity of an HDD. Whether that justifies the additional cost will depend on the final pricing.
There are limits to this speed. However, for the most part in this test, the drive acted like a huge 20TB SSD. The slower HDD speeds only kicked in when I accessed multiple files that exceeded the 1TB limit, such as switching from one Premiere Pro project to another.
In real-world use, you’re unlikely to notice much difference between this and a smaller, fast SSD, and Seagate really seems to have got that balance right. The one time I did experience a slowdown was when copying 4TB of video data from a Thunderbolt 5 drive. Still, even then, it had such a head start on a standard drive that, again, the FireCuda Forge still provides far greater performance.
If you’re in the market for a large-capacity, fast-transfer external drive without upgrading your network or looking at NAS solutions, the FireCuda Forge is an impressive option, although its overall value will depend on the final price.
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Row 0 - Cell 1 | Row 0 - Cell 2 | 
| Value | To be confirmed once pricing is available | n/a | 
| Design | he design breaks from the small black box that is so familiar with most external drives, and that’s a welcome change. | 4.5 | 
| Features | The features of this drive are hidden. Essentially, you see only a single drive, but behind the scenes is technology that blends speed with capacity. | 4.5 | 
| Performance | The speed boost that this provides when downloading files is huge, and video editing from the drive sees an overall pickup compared with using standard HDDs. | 4.5 | 
| Total | I'd recommend this drive if you want a fast desktop drive for backups and working on small to mid-sized creative projects. | 4.5 | 
Buy it if...
You need a large-capacity drive.
The 20TB storage is incredibly useful if you regularly need to offload files. The transfer speeds are SSD-comparable, while the storage is huge.
You edit video locally.
The storage size and SSD speed make a great solution for desktop video editing. There is some initial slowdown, but as you edit, instead of the usual HDD slowdown, things just get faster.
Don't buy it if...
You need maximum speed.
While the speed is impressive, you do notice a slowdown when copying more than 1TB of data to the internal drive. However, that slowdown is still faster than a standard HDD.
You need to switch between large video projects.
Each time you switch video projects, the file manager needs to organise the data to be accessed. While this is fast, if you push the system, you will start to see HDD slowdown, but only if you’re really trying.
For more storage options, we've tested the best portable SSDs around.
Alastair is a photographer, filmmaker and tech writer who has been working in the publishing industry since the late 1990s. For more than 25 years he has covered photography, video and technology across Future's photography, technology and gaming brands. He runs a photography and video production company and lectures in TV and film. He can usually be found testing mini PCs or prototyping and prop building with the aid of 3D printing.

articles.title: AI operations expand to Kubernetes upgrades as teams shrink - SiliconANGLE AI operations take on Kubernetes upgrades as IT teams do more with less - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI operations take on Kubernetes upgrades as IT teams do more with less
AI operations are moving out of the slide deck and into the platform itself. Hiring freezes and smaller teams are colliding with growing workloads, so enterprises now expect the infrastructure layer to investigate, plan and help fix problems.
Kubernetes platforms are among the first places that shift is landing. Red Hat Inc. launched OpenShift 5 this week, the platform’s first major version in seven years, with Model Context Protocol servers, guardrails and agent skills built into the stack. Customers’ expectations of the platform have changed enough to justify a new version number, according to Mike Barrett (pictured, left), vice president and general manager of hybrid platforms at Red Hat.
“We started putting in guardrails. We started putting in agent skills, and now you can really have an agentic experience with the platform,” Barrett said. “The platform itself can actually do things for you. It can notice what’s running.”
Barrett and Ju Lim (pictured, right), senior manager of product management at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how OpenShift 5 builds AI into upgrades, troubleshooting and day-to-day operations. (* Disclosure below.)
From weeks of planning to one click
On paper, upgrades look like routine, predictable work. In practice, a single cluster can run hundreds of applications, each with its own dependencies, release notes and Kubernetes version requirements. OpenShift 5 uses AI to sort through all of that and produce an upgrade plan, Barrett explained.
“We have customers that sometimes plan this out in weeks and months,” Lim said. “Now, through what Mike was just saying, we have a way where, through a single click, you can actually generate an AI plan that actually does all that risk analysis and assessment for you.”
Troubleshooting gets the same treatment. OpenShift 5 pulls in telemetry, logs and Kubernetes resource metadata to investigate problems and suggest fixes, according to Lim. Every action is opt-in, and a human operator stays in control. Fully autonomous troubleshooting and agentic updates remain in technology preview, according to Virtualization Review. Red Hat’s own site reliability engineering team offers an early test case.
“We run OpenShift as a managed service, and they’re seeing anywhere between an 8x and 10x time improvement to find the root cause of issues,” Barrett said.
Security is adding urgency. A surge of software vulnerabilities and exploits has cut the time between disclosure and attack from days to hours, according to Barrett. Customers want help moving older applications faster, and running existing virtual machines in Kubernetes clusters is part of Red Hat’s answer.
“We felt that really emphasized a number change,” Barrett said. “How people want to work with the platform is completely different now, and so we needed a major number.”

articles.title: España llega tarde al DAB+ pero llega: el estándar digital de radio que Europa lleva usando una década empieza su despliegue
articles.text:
El Gobierno ha aprobado un real decreto que agrupa una serie de medidas de impulso para la tecnología de radio digital DAB+ (Digital Audio Broadcasting Plus). Con él se da el espaldarazo definitivo para arrancar la radio digital terrestre en España, un proyecto que llevaba décadas en el cajón y no termina de desplegarse.
En este sentido, España llega con mucho retraso con respecto a otros países del viejo continente como Noruega, que preparaba el apagón de su FM para 2017, mientras aquí la radio digital seguía en pruebas. Con el nuevo decreto del Gobierno, se establecen normas y plazos, aunque se deja en el tintero fijar alguna fecha para que el dial de la FM deje de sonar.
Qué cambia con el decreto. El Real Decreto 958/2026, publicado en el BOE no parte de cero ya que recoge parte del plan técnico ya previsto en 1999 y seguirá vigente aplicando ciertas modificaciones necesarias para impulsar la implantación de este nuevo estándar para la radio digital en España.
Uno de los objetivos de la nueva normativa es hacer que DAB+ gane en cobertura de servicio. Esta tecnología permite agrupar varias emisoras en un mismo bloque de frecuencias de emisión, por lo que no es necesaria una frecuencia específica para cada emisora de FM. Con la publicación del nuevo decreto se amplía el área de cobertura de esas emisiones para que la señal de radio digital llegue a más poblaciones de las que la reciben en la actualidad.
Más lugares para escuchar la radio. Como ente público, el decreto pone a RTVE al frente de la expansión de la cobertura de radio digital ampliando las exigencias que tenía hasta ahora. El decreto le exige cubrir el 50% de la población a los 6 meses de entrar en vigor. 18 meses más tarde la exigencia sube hasta el 70% de cobertura del territorio, llegar al 50% de cada capital de provincia, así como de las autopistas y autovías.
En 30 meses, la exigencia vuelve a subir y la señal de radio digital debe llegar al 80% de la población, incluidas el 70 % de las ciudades de más de 25.000 habitantes y el 70% de la red de autopistas y autovías. La entrada en vigor llega tres meses después de la publicación
Solo RTVE está obligada a cumplir los plazos. La corporación pública es la única obligada a cumplir estos plazos y porcentajes de cobertura. Las emisoras privadas con licencia estatal (SER, COPE, Onda Cero) también tienen la obligación de adoptar esta tecnología, aunque no con los mismos requisitos que debe cumplir el ente público. Para las emisoras de ámbito autonómico y local su adopción en este primer despliegue tiene un carácter voluntario. Posteriormente, cada comunidad autónoma determinará la fecha a partir de la cual todas las emisiones de su ámbito territorial deberán realizarse exclusivamente mediante DAB+.
Eso condiciona que, al menos en los primeros meses del despliegue de la señal DAB+, algunas emisoras que emiten en FM, pueden no estar disponibles en el nuevo formato digital. En cualquier caso, la implantación de este sistema de radio digital no implica un apagón inmediato en la señal de radio FM, que asume su propio calendario.
Pero qué es DAB+. Por establecer un paralelismo, el sistema DAB+ es el equivalente al TDT de la TV, pero aplicado al ámbito de la emisión de señal de audio. Este sistema digital aporta una sustancial mejora en la calidad de sonido eliminando las interferencias y ese característico crepitar cuando la recepción de la onda FM no era buena. Con el sistema digital, mientras se tiene cobertura, el sonido es totalmente nítido, aunque puede registrar cortes cuando se pierde la cobertura. Algo similar a lo que sucede con la cobertura móvil. El sistema no requiere conexión WiFi o bluetooth. Lo único que necesita es que el dispositivo receptor sea compatible con esta tecnología.
La tecnología DAB+ permite el sonido multicanal o envolvente, un formato de audio más avanzado que el sonido estéreo. También posibilita la incorporación de nuevas funcionalidades, como el Sistema de Alerta Automática de Seguridad (ASA, por sus siglas en inglés), que permite enviar avisos urgentes a las zonas afectadas por inundaciones, incendios o accidentes graves.
Además, junto a la señal se transmiten indicaciones e información adicional en forma de texto e imágenes que después se muestran en las pantallas de los receptores de radio. Por ejemplo, puedes ver la portada del disco o del programa que estás escuchando, o el nombre de la canción que está sonando.
España llega tarde. Europa lleva años de ventaja en la implantación de la radio digital. España se quedó en la fase de ensayos de esta tecnología, aunque RTVE lleva desde 2024 emitiendo en este formato. Sin hoja de ruta ni incentivos, las empresas privadas no tuvieron motivos para mover ficha y migrar sus emisoras a este formato.
Países como Suiza o Noruega sí fijaron calendario y llevan casi una década emitiendo en formato digital. La normativa europea también ha tomado medidas para cimentar la expansión de esta tecnología, y desde 2020 es obligatorio que los sistemas de entretenimiento a bordo de todos vehículos nuevos sean compatibles con DAB+.
¿Necesitas un nuevo dispositivo para DAB+? La respuesta rápida es: depende. El dispositivo debe ser compatible con el estándar DAB+, por lo que será necesario mirar la compatibilidad de cada dispositivo. Los receptores más modernos, sistemas de audio e incluso altavoces Bluetooth pueden tener esa compatibilidad, por lo que no necesitas un nuevo dispositivo para escuchar la radio en formato digital. Para aquellos con compatibilidad con DAB (sin el añadido Plus), conviene consultar con cada fabricante si su capacidad queda ampliada también a DAB+.
Los dispositivos receptores de radio FM más antiguos, que no cuenten con soporte para esta tecnología no podrán decodificar la señal digital y, por tanto, no podrán usar esta tecnología.
En Xataka | En el caos del apagón eléctrico, lo que me salvó fue algo que los móviles desterraron: la radio FM

articles.title: De la simple idée à la vidéo montée... La métamorphose impressionnante d'Adobe Firefly
articles.text:
À l’occasion de l’événement Adobe Max 2026, Firefly se dote de nouveaux outils pour créer des visuels, monter des vidéos et les adapter aux réseaux sociaux. Son assistant IA peut prendre en charge plusieurs étapes à partir d’une seule consigne.
Une photo vous plaît pour sa lumière, une affiche pour ses couleurs. Vous pouvez les épingler dans Firefly Boards, un tableau où rassembler les images qui vous inspirent. L’éditeur vidéo de Firefly prend ensuite le relais pour animer une image, ajouter une voix et monter les plans.
Du tableau d’inspiration au montage vidéo
Creative Agent, l’assistant d’Adobe, arrive dans Firefly Boards et dans d’autres espaces d’édition. Vous pouvez lui décrire en langage courant les étapes que vous souhaitez lui confier. Pour générer des images, des vidéos ou des voix, Firefly donne accès aux modèles d’Adobe et à ceux de partenaires comme Google, OpenAI, Runway et ElevenLabs.
Avec le mode Plan, vous pouvez relire et modifier les étapes proposées par l’assistant avant de les valider. Vous pouvez aussi choisir le modèle d’IA pour la session ou laisser Firefly le sélectionner selon le résultat recherché.
Lors d’une démonstration devant la presse, Adobe a utilisé ElevenLabs pour générer la voix off d’une publicité qui présentait une barquette à emporter comme un produit de luxe. L’assistant a ensuite demandé quelles plateformes viser, puis préparé quatorze versions du film pour les réseaux sociaux.
Dans l’éditeur vidéo, Firefly peut repérer les changements de plan ou baisser automatiquement la musique quand quelqu’un parle. Si vous avez déjà placé une image fixe dans le montage, elle peut aussi servir à générer un plan vidéo.
Côté visuels, de nouvelles commandes permettent de retoucher un objet, de modifier un texte ou de changer l’éclairage. Le nouvel espace Firefly Design permet, lui, de travailler à plusieurs sur une même création, qu’il s’agisse de retoucher une photo, de dessiner des formes vectorielles que l’on peut agrandir sans les pixelliser, ou d’ajouter de l’animation et de la 3D.
- Génération multimédia centralisée
- Retouche générative intégrée
- Applications web et mobiles
Les tâches que Firefly peut répéter d’un projet à l’autre
Pour créer une miniature, il suffit de charger la vidéo et de choisir l’image qui servira de point de départ. Firefly génère ensuite le visuel au format souhaité. Ainsi, si vous répétez régulièrement toute une suite d’étapes, Firefly Graph permet de les assembler dans l’ordre voulu, puis de relancer le même enchaînement sur un autre projet. L’outil est d’ores et déjà disponible en bêta publique.
Firefly Builder, en bêta privée, sert à un autre usage. Vous décrivez le site ou l’application que vous avez en tête et l’outil en produit une maquette interactive qui reprend les couleurs et le style de votre marque.
Adobe a aussi donné un aperçu d’agents qui, dès le début de l’année prochaine, pourraient travailler en arrière-plan pour ranger les fichiers, vérifier la qualité des contenus ou préparer des versions pour plusieurs canaux. Dans l’un des exemples, un restaurateur fournit ses menus et ses images à un agent, qui lui soumet chaque semaine des brouillons de publications. Le restaurateur choisit ensuite ce qui sera diffusé, sans se prendre la tête et tout en restant créatif.

articles.title: Sega newsletter data breach sees 2.2 million email addresses exposed — gaming giant says it is investigating, but user financial data not affected
articles.text:
Sega newsletter data breach sees 2.2 million email addresses exposed — gaming giant says it is investigating, but user financial data not affected
SEGA breach is part of a much larger supply chain attack
- Sega disclosed a third-party breach that exposed nearly 2.2 million customer email addresses through a marketing service provider
- Around 92,000 additional records related to email distribution were also compromised in the incident
- Sega and its provider warned users about phishing risks, though no misuse of the leaked data has been confirmed
Gaming giant Sega has disclosed suffering a third-party cybersecurity incident that exposed email addresses of almost 2.2 million people, as well as other details of at least 92,000.
The company is now investigating deeper, to confirm the details of the leaked information.
What happened
Sega is one of many Japanese companies using the services of Arara, a technology firm providing digital marketing and customer engagement services.
One of its services is called Arara Message, an email distribution platform that businesses can use to send newsletters and other communications to millions of people. This also means Arara was managing contact information on behalf of those organizations, including email addresses, names, and often phone numbers and membership details.
In early November 2026, Arara reported its email distribution infrastructure suffering a compromise. Apparently, a combination of a web server vulnerability and “other system weaknesses” allowed unidentified threat actors to access 97 servers that stored data of up to 380 corporate customers.
The attackers accessed (and most likely exfiltrated) more than 81 million email addresses, together with people’s names, dates of birth, phone numbers, postal addresses, and membership numbers. Not every customer had all of this data exposed - it varied from person to person.
In a subsequent report, Arara added that the attackers compromised a separate environment containing additional 3.38 million email addresses and more than 400,000 customer records containing PII. They ended up sending more than seven million phishing emails spoofing various credit card companies, forcing the company to temporarily shut down the service on October 31 2026.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Many large organizations had their newsletter contacts exposed. Asoview reported approximately 15.82 million records, while electronics retailer Bic Camera reported 15.2 million. Fast-food chain MOS Burger disclosed the exposure of some 7.5 million email addresses, while cinema operator Shochiku Multiplex Theaters 3.3 million.
Sega under fire again
Among them were also video game giant Sega and its subsidiary Sega Fave, who disclosed approximately 2.2 million affected email addresses.
“Sega Corporation uses Arara Corporation's distribution system to distribute certain email newsletters related to products and services of our company and its group company, Sega Fave Corporation. It has recently been discovered that Arara Inc. was subjected to unauthorized access by a third party, and the email addresses of customers used to distribute the email newsletter were leaked externally,” the company said in a short announcement.
The company said that as of November 9, it can confirm 2,196,044 emails as compromised, together with 92,273 other items “related to distribution”.
Information that has not been leaked at this time include customer names, dates of birth, gender, addresses, phone numbers, credit card information, and login passwords.
“At this time, no misuse of the leaked information related to this case has been confirmed,” Sega said. “The email address registered with the "SEGA Account" uses a different distribution system and is therefore excluded from the leaked information.”
This is Sega’s second major cybersecurity incident this month after its Sega Fave arcade game network services were recently brought offline and are, according to BleepingComputer, still unavailable as the company works on maintenance and safety checks.
On November 2, Sega Fave said an unidentified threat actor accessed its servers supporting its ALL.Net and Aime arcade gaming network services but later stressed that these two incidents were unrelated. Online gameplay, Sega Lucky Kuji Online, and new Sega ID registrations, were all brought offline for investigation.
So far, no threat actors claimed responsibility for the breach. Both Sega and Arara warned their users about possible phishing emails and urged them not to click on any links or download attachments from emails claiming to come from the companies.

articles.title: Madrid se está convirtiendo en el nuevo Los Ángeles y por el camino se ha quedado con sus atascos permanentes
articles.text:
"A estas horas se tarda solo seis minutos menos en ir en coche de Leganés a la Estación de Chamartín que de Burgos a Bilbao. Madrid ha colapsado"
Dos oraciones, un tweet y 6.000 me gusta. Podríamos achacar la captura de pantalla a un día convulso en la ciudad, con huelga en Cercanías y la amenaza de lluvia, que siempre complica el tránsito madrileño. Pero el problema va mucho más allá de lo puntual.
En unos años, Madrid se ha convertido en una ciudad con un atasco perenne por las mañanas. En una charla distendida, un amigo me aseguraba que está tardando todos los días unas dos horas de Fuenlabrada a Alcobendas para ir a trabajar. Por un caso cercano sé que recorrer apenas doce kilómetros puede llevar una hora en coche, en función de si hay o no colegio, si se ha cerrado un nuevo paso en la A-5, si dos personas han chocado o vaya usted a saber qué cosa. Lo que es irremediable es el resultado: atasco, atasco y atasco día sí y día también.
La experiencia no es nueva ni mucho menos y eso, probablemente es lo más preocupante. En 2018, los madrileños se pasaban atascados 42 horas al año, según el informe del INRIX Global Traffic Scorecard que analiza el tiempo perdido en las grandes ciudades del mundo cada año. Ese mismo informe apunta ahora a que el tiempo perdido ha aumentado a 50 horas. Y aunque estamos muy lejos de los grandes horrores del tráfico mundial (Estambul, Ciudad de México o Chicago duplican esta cifra), el estado del tráfico va cada vez a peor.
Un cúmulo de causas y un atasco constante
En 2019, en plena campaña contra Madrid Central (la primera ZBE madrileña que restringía el tráfico a algunos coches en el corazón de la ciudad), Isabel Díaz Ayuso, ahora presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid y entonces candidata al puesto, sentenciaba que "los atascos son una seña de identidad de Madrid". Se refería a los atascos de madrugada pero dan una idea de cómo la ciudad ha asumido vivir atascado como una realidad más del día a día.
"¿Qué a mí me gustan los atascos? Evidentemente no, pero forma parte de la vida de Madrid", dejaba claro Díaz Ayuso. En eso estarán de acuerdo quienes tienen que malgastar horas a diario en las circunvalaciones madrileñas. Y es que, como decíamos, la situación ha ido a peor.
En 2021, el fin generalizado al teletrabajo tras la pandemia devolvió los atascos a las calles y las carreteras cada mañana. Un martes cualquiera de octubre de ese año, El Mundo recogía que la ciudad había colapsado como consecuencia de las obras, la vuelta al trabajo y un accidente. En El País se recogía que habían bajado un millón los trayectos en la capital pero que los coches eran exactamente los mismos.
Las causas son múltiples. Entre las temporales, un buen listado de obras: A-5, Parque Ventas, Conde de Casal, Madrid Nuevo Norte... con complicaciones puntuales que agravan todavía más la situación como una huelga de Cercanías, la próxima huelga general o cierres de vías por las propias obras, como la A-5.
Hay afectaciones que deberían ser puntuales pero que se han convertido en atemporales. El servicio de Cercanías en Madrid vive entre retrasos y averías todas las mañanas. El servicio de Metro se está ampliando pero las nuevas líneas llegan cuando la ciudad lleva viviendo un atasco mañanero constante durante más de un lustro.
Y un cinturón de ciudades dormitorio que no dejan de crecer sin una infraestructura que lo sostenga. La carretera A-42 es un buen ejemplo de esto. La carretera se ha convertido en una ratonera, con un atasco constante todas las mañanas mientras una de pago discurre a su lado completamente vacía. El aumento de vecinos en los pueblos del sur de Madrid (y norte de la provincia de Toledo) no ha sido correspondido con un servicio público a la altura.
El caso del sur madrileño es uno más en una región que ha crecido el año pasado el doble de lo que lo ha hecho el resto de comunidades autónomas de España. La ciudad, convertida en un agujero negro de atracción de inversiones necesita más y más trabajadores que, a su vez, no se pueden permitir una vivienda en la ciudad o, al menos, con un transporte público realmente eficiente.
El urbanismo de la ciudad ha creado un flujo de movimientos evidente: buena parte de los trabajadores que buscan vivienda asequible pasan la noche en el sur de la ciudad (y de la región) pero tienen que trabajar en el norte de la misma. Todo ello se agudiza con un planteamiento que ha priorizado los PAUs alrededor de la ciudad, espacios cochistas de baja densidad poblacional donde el transporte público es mucho menos eficiente. Y los últimos proyectos aprobados no difieren mucho de todo esto.
La situación empieza a ser tan insostenible que Valladolid está ganando trabajadores madrileños, aprovechando la conexión con la ciudad. No es el único caso, Segovia o Toledo ya hace tiempo que se convirtieron, en parte, en ciudades dormitorio de la ciudad. Y el problema, como nos señalara el ingeniero César Franco en una entrevista a Xataka es que las infraestructuras se conciben en un contexto social y económico que cuando luego quieren ser una realidad es completamente diferente porque se tarda una, dos y hasta tres décadas en sacar los proyectos adelante.

articles.title: Repositionner la lumière ou effacer un intrus en vidéo : Adobe frappe très fort
articles.text:
Les nouveautés d’Adobe Max 2026 touchent autant à la retouche photo qu’au montage vidéo. Photoshop permet désormais de reprendre l’éclairage sur un calque, Premiere affine ses réglages de couleur et de son, et InDesign ouvre ses maquettes à la coédition.
Vous avez bouclé le tournage et c’est au montage que vous repérez la voiture qui traverse votre meilleur plan. Premiere pourra bientôt l’effacer directement dans la séquence, sans vous obliger à retourner sur place pour shooter un nouveau plan. Photoshop pour sa part s’attaque à un autre regret de fin de séance des photographes. Vous auriez préféré placer une lumière derrière votre sujet ? Bonne nouvelle : vous pourrez maintenant le faire une fois les projecteurs rangés et votre mannequin rentré chez lui.
Dans Photoshop, la lumière devient un réglage comme les autres
Dans la nouvelle version de Photoshop, Relight sort de bêta et permet d’ajouter jusqu’à trois sources lumineuses à une photo. On peut déplacer chacune d’elles et régler leur taille, leur couleur et leur intensité. Lors d'un pré-brief à la presse, l’éditeur a ainsi fait l'impressionnante démonstration de faire varier l’ambiance d’un portrait en déplaçant une lumière verte autour d’un sportif. Et, en plus, l’éclairage reste sur un calque séparé, ce qui permet d’en atténuer l’effet plus tard sans avoir à refaire les autres retouches.
Generative Restyle, désormais lui aussi en version stable, part d’une consigne écrite. On peut demander à Photoshop de donner à une photo la lumière d’une fin de journée, puis doser l’effet au curseur sur un calque dédié. L’outil Supprimer s’intéresse de son côté à ce qu’un objet laisse derrière lui, comme une ombre ou un reflet qui trahirait la retouche. Photoshop teste aussi une fonction capable de transformer les inscriptions intégrées à une image en calques de texte éditables. De quoi corriger une affiche quand il ne vous reste qu’une image du résultat.
Quant à Lightroom, le logiciel de développement photo d'Adobe intègre Glow pour adoucir et diffuser la lumière ainsi qu’un outil pour corriger les petites imperfections. Open Eyes, conçu pour rattraper une photo prise au moment où quelqu’un cligne des yeux, reste quant à lui en version bêta.
Premiere reprend la couleur et le son dans la séquence
Color Mode quitte la bêta dans Premiere 27.0. Cet espace consacré à l’étalonnage, le travail sur les couleurs et le contraste, permet d’appliquer un style à un clip ou à une séquence entière, puis de l’ajuster. On peut aussi regrouper plusieurs plans qui tirent sur le bleu pour les réchauffer ensemble. Côté son, les nouveaux outils peuvent isoler des voix qui se chevauchent ou séparer les sources d’une même prise pour régler leurs niveaux individuellement.
Premiere étend aussi la génération d’images, de musique et d’ambiances sonores directement dans la timeline. À partir d’un plan muet, Adobe a montré comment le logiciel pouvait produire quatre pistes audio que le monteur peut ensuite mixer séparément.
Quant à la voiture indésirable à effacer dans un plan, c’est Generative Remove qui s’en charge dans Premiere Beta. Le monteur délimite l’objet à effacer avec un masque. Le logiciel suit ensuite l’objet d’une image à l’autre et reconstitue la partie du décor qu’il cachait. Une fonction qui va changer la vie de bon nombre de monteurs.
- Suite créative très complète
- Logiciels Adobe professionnels
- Intégration entre les applications
InDesign permet de travailler à plusieurs sur la même maquette
Avec la coédition en temps réel, qui arrive en bêta dans InDesign, un maquettiste pourra reprendre la mise en page d’une brochure pendant qu’un collègue corrige ses légendes dans le même document. Quand une correction rallonge ou raccourcit un passage, Flex Layout adapte automatiquement la taille du bloc de texte. Adobe ajoute aussi des outils pour suggérer des reformulations et repérer des erreurs courantes de rédaction ou d’accessibilité.
Dans Illustrator, l’outil Dégradé de formes, qui crée une transition progressive entre deux objets, gagne un panneau de réglages qui reste accessible pendant le travail. On peut modifier la transition et voir le résultat évoluer directement sur le plan de travail. Adobe renouvelle aussi les bibliothèques de pinceaux, de styles graphiques, de motifs et de dégradés.
Avec le vibe coding, on voit arriver des clones de Photoshop ou de Premiere. Mais évolueront-ils aussi vite que les originaux ?

articles.title: AI agent security sees Red Hat layer masked keys and sandboxes - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Non-deterministic agents break the rules traditional software security was built on
AI agent security has become the critical gating factor for enterprises that want autonomous software doing real work.
Unlike chatbots that answer questions, agents take actions, and every tool or credential they touch widens the potential damage. To that end, Red Hat Inc. has spent the past year building guardrails for that shift, including a sandbox for OpenClaw agents. The complexity lies in the fact that agents break the assumptions traditional software security was built on, according to Joe Fernandes (pictured, right), vice president and general manager of Red Hat AI at Red Hat.
“For forever, we’ve been building software, but that software is deterministic. It does what we program it to do,” Fernandes said. “Agents are different. They’re non-deterministic; you’re giving them a goal. You don’t know what actions they’re going to take to get to that goal.”
Fernandes and Jessica Forrester (left), senior distinguished engineer and chief architect of Red Hat AI at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Red Hat is building layered security for autonomous AI agents through sandboxing, identity management, access controls and enterprise-scale agent management. (* Disclosure below.)
Building AI agent security in layers
Red Hat learned lessons through its own engineering teams. When it first built an agentic software development life cycle, it handed agents prefetched data and let them touch nothing else, Forrester explained. OpenShell, the open-source agent runtime Nvidia Corp. launched in March with Red Hat as a founding member, let the company loosen that grip safely. The two companies have since expanded their partnership around securing autonomous agents. One approach from Red Hat involves giving agents access to the tools they need while keeping sensitive credentials out of reach.
“With OpenShell, your agent doesn’t ever get any real keys to anything. It gets masked on the way in and then swapped on the way out,” Forrester said. “If something convinces it to give away its keys, it’s not actually giving any real keys away. That really helps you have a little bit more faith in what’s happening inside that agent box.”
OpenShell can also run agents in Kata Containers with their own kernels, inside full virtual machines on OpenShift Virtualization and behind network egress controls, Forrester noted. Red Hat has also detailed kernel-level agent isolation in its platform. Identity comes next, with every agent assigned its own identity and the narrowest set of permissions, Fernandes added.
“It’ll integrate with different identity systems to basically allow you to assign agent identity,” he said. “Then you can authorize what that agent can do — and more importantly, what it can’t.”
Red Hat is now looking beyond individual agents. It is working with OpenAI Group PBC on OpenClaw Enterprise, a project for managing thousands of personal agents at scale, while OpenShell is available in preview in Red Hat AI. For enterprises still weighing AI agent security, the project’s maturity is the moment to watch, Fernandes explained.
“We’re really now approaching that stable milestone,” Fernandes said. “That’s when we feel like, ‘Okay, we’re comfortable enough. We can actually rely on this for enterprise production.'”
Stay tuned for the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA.

articles.title: Otto Introduces Otto One: the Personal AI Computer for Autonomous Agents
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 10th 2026
Otto Introduces Otto One: the Personal AI Computer for Autonomous Agents
Otto, the company building the operating system for the agentic era, today introduces Otto One, the first purpose-built agent computer: a compact, screenless computer designed for an AI agent to live and work on. Running on Otto OS, its proprietary software layer, Otto One lets people deploy, direct and monitor autonomous agents from a phone or desktop while the device works continuously in the background, even when the user closes their laptop or walks away.
AI agents are finally capable of taking on a persistent role in people's lives. The real opportunity is not a better inbox assistant; it is an agent that can keep a household organized, manage a budget and taxes, coordinate care and appointments, and keep a business moving. To do that well, it needs usable context and the authority to act across the financial, personal and work systems that make up a life.Today, that leaves people with a difficult choice. They can place an agent inside a cloud service they do not control or try to assemble one themselves on a phone, laptop or repurposed mini PC. The local route is still a project, involving a server to configure, models and integrations to wire together, credentials to manage and a system to keep running. That complexity is the symptom of software built for a human at a keyboard, not an agent working continuously on someone else's behalf.
Otto offers an alternative. Your agent lives on a dedicated, always-on computer that sits under your control. It can keep working after you close your laptop or put down your phone, while its memory, credentials and context have a home on hardware you own. This matters when the agent is trusted with intimate access, because everything it learns about the user stays there.
For fifty years, computers have been designed around a human sitting in front of a screen. Otto One has no keyboard, mouse or monitor. Plug it in, pair it with the Otto app and talk to your agent from anywhere. Otto flips that relationship: the agent operates the computer; the person tells it what to do, sets its boundaries and decides when it needs their approval. Otto OS provides the persistent environment and controls that make that relationship practical.
Otto is preconfigured and secure, but not locked down. The platform is designed to support major AI models and open-source agent frameworks as they evolve, giving users flexibility across providers rather than tying them to a single AI lab. Otto's gateway manages model access, token usage and per-agent limits while the core agent environment remains under the user's control.
Otto gives agents a full working environment: a browser, file system, applications, APIs and system tools, alongside preconfigured connections to more than 2,000 services. Those include Gmail, Google Calendar and Drive, Slack, Discord, WhatsApp, Telegram, Notion, Microsoft 365, GitHub and more. From there, agents can conduct research, keep work organized, prepare outreach, monitor competitor pricing and carry out work across the tools people already use, without asking users to wire together integrations themselves.
Otto is the control plane for your agents. From any authorized phone or desktop, users can connect to services, grant permissions, observe their work and pause, stop or delete tasks. They can also set approval requirements, ongoing application permissions, token and usage limits, spending controls and alerts.
Jake Trefethen, co-founder and CEO of Otto"The computer was designed for a person to sit in front of it. Otto is the first computer designed so nobody has to. This is the most intimate computer ever built. It holds your credentials, your correspondence, your files, everything you'd hand a chief of staff. Something so personal shouldn't be rented from someone else's data center."
Quinn Finney, co-founder and CTO of Otto"Everyone is building agents that can act, what people aren't thinking about is building the part that decides what they're allowed to do, what they're allowed to spend and what needs your sign-off first. That's why we've built Otto OS. The agent is the worker. Otto OS is everything a worker needs to be trusted with the job, and Otto One is the first machine it runs on."
The agent's home is Otto One, not Otto's servers. The agent, its memory, chat history, automations and actions run on the device. Conversations between your phone and your Otto are end-to-end encrypted with the same protocol family behind the messaging app Signal (X3DH + Double Ratchet); Otto's servers relay ciphertext they cannot read. Keys you add yourself never leave the device, and unpairing erases the owner's data in one stroke. Some functions still require the cloud: model processing, notifications (delivered as sealed previews), signed software updates, billing and certain third-party integrations, where credentials are held by the integration provider. Users who bring their own API keys send requests straight from Otto to their chosen model provider.
Otto sold 15,000 branded units directly to consumers in its first six months, generating $9 million in booked revenue, with more than 1,000 units already shipped. Otto has reached approximately $750,000 in weekly booked volume, equivalent to a $39 million annualized revenue run rate, without institutional venture funding. The company is in active conversations with more than 25 distributors about retail distribution across Europe, Asia-Pacific, Australia, New Zealand and Mexico, alongside early discussions with enterprise customers.
Otto is launching Otto Pro, a line designed to run supported AI models directly on the device, with optional access to cloud models through the same Otto apps. Introduced to its early customer community in response to growing demand for local inference, Pro gives users dedicated compute for their agents without requiring them to assemble and configure a local AI setup.
Powered by an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 processor, Otto Pro comes in three configurations: 32 GB of DDR5 memory with a 512 GB SSD; 64 GB with a 1 TB SSD; and 96 GB with a 2 TB SSD. Presales open November 10, with the first units expected to ship in Q1 2027.
Otto One is designed as an accessible entry point to local agents, purpose-built for always-on agent work and priced to make ownership practical. It is fanless and silent, 4.4 by 4.4 by 1.5 inches (112 by 112 by 38 mm), and available in two configurations: 8 GB of memory with 256 GB of storage, and 16 GB of memory with 512 GB of storage. The hardware is owned outright with no hardware subscription. Customers can reserve a unit with a $20 fully refundable deposit, with the balance charged before shipment; customers who pay in full at the time of reservation receive a 20% discount. Model usage is available on a pay-as-you-go basis through the Otto app, or users can bring their own API keys to use supported AI models for a flat monthly fee.
