articles.title: AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ deep dive and benchmarking – 9686F outclasses Nvidia’s Vera, dual EPYC 9996 with 1,024 threads delivers up to 93% performance gain gen-on-gen
articles.text:
AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ deep dive and benchmarking – 9686F outclasses Nvidia’s Vera, dual EPYC 9996 with 1,024 threads delivers up to 93% performance gain gen-on-gen
Our first look at Zen 6, both under the hood and in real-world applications.
AMD’s EPYC ‘Venice’ CPUs are the first to debut the new Zen 6 architecture, and we’ve been testing two chips from the range over the past several weeks to see how they compare to Nvidia’s Vera, and more broadly, how the Zen 6 architecture departs from Zen 5 ahead of the expected consumer-focused Olympic Ridge launch next year. Zen 5 was a ground-up redesign of AMD’s storied Zen core, and Zen 6 takes that foundation and expands it in just about every regard.
Zen 6 uses TSMC’s N2P node, but it also comes with significant architectural changes under the hood. Within the core, a redesigned vector engine pushes AMD’s SIMD performance even higher, and it now natively supports half-precision FP16 instructions alongside full, 32-bit precision. It also splits integer schedulers within the execution engine, allowing for more instructions in flight through the core.
Across the die, AMD made other significant changes. The single IOD of previous generations is now split across two IODs, giving the SP7 platform access to 16 memory channels (though at the cost of PCIe 6.0 lanes compared to the previous generation and SP8 platform).
The CCDs have been upgraded, too, for the first time since Zen 3. A standard Zen 6 CCD can now scale up to 12 cores, while a Zen 6c packs 32 cores. With Zen 5 and 5c, CCDs topped out at eight cores and 16 cores, respectively. For the Zen 6c CCD, AMD also doubled the amount of shared L3 per core, which effectively quadruples the L3 compared to Zen 5c, since the CCD packs twice the number of cores.
Interestingly, Zen 6 is neither a marginal optimization to Zen 5, nor a complete architecture redesign. Stepping back, it looks like AMD pushes as many dials as it has access to to their highest level, and that holds up looking at performance.
The 256-core EPYC 9996 delivers 1,024 threads in a 2P configuration, which came out 93% ahead of the 768-thread 2P EPYC 9965 server we tested in SPEC CPU 2026’s intrate throughput test. The frequency-optimized EPYC 9686F excels elsewhere, notably in scientific computing and HPC workloads, and it serves as AMD’s competitor to Vera, at least before the LPDDR-based Verano platform arrives from AMD next year.
AMD says it believes Venice is fundamentally a generation ahead of the competition, which would be a worthless line if it wasn’t backed up by data. Intel’s Granite Rapids-AP is rarely in the conversation, and although Vera maintains some competitive positions, Venice is often ahead — sometimes orders of magnitude ahead.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Intel’s Diamond Rapids is set to launch next year, which should help balance the scales. But AMD has set an incredibly high bar with Venice, one that it will likely extend even higher for some workloads with the arrival of Venice-X and Verano next year.
There’s a lot to get to here. We have a full deep dive into the Zen 6 microarchitecture, a broader look at the chip itself, the platform(s) AMD is pushing out this generation, and of course, more than 100 benchmarks covering everything from Python performance to HPC.
AMD Zen 6 microarchitecture breakdown
AMD Zen 6 microarchitecture breakdown
The headline for Zen 6 is a 27% average IPC uplift over Zen 5 in enterprise, cloud, and AI workloads. The debut of this new microarchitecture is focused on the data center, so you shouldn’t take that 27% IPC improvement as broadly applicable to all workloads. Additionally, AMD arrived at that number by comparing fixed-frequency Zen 5 to Zen 6c with 16 cores. As we’ll get into in the next section, a Zen 6c CCD can comfortably fit 16 Zen 6c cores with room to spare, while 16 Zen 5 cores are split across two CCDs.
The compute die is built on TSMC’s N2P node, which is an already optimized version of N2 that comes with a 5% performance improvement. Compared to N3E (Zen 5 used N4P), N2P offers an 18% speed improvement at iso-power, or a 36% reduction in power at the same speed.
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Speed Improvement (v. N3E) | Power Improvement (v. N3E) | Density (v. N3E) | 
| TSMC N2P | +18% (iso-power) | -36% (iso-speed) | +15% | 
AMD described Zen 5 as a ground-up redesign when the microarchitecture first broke cover in mid-2024, characterized by a wider execution engine capable of dispatching and returning eight instructions per cycle, a wider frontend to feed it, full AVX-512 support, and doubled bandwidth between the L2 and L1 cache. Zen 6 is a continuation of the redesign we saw on Zen 5. It carries many of the same characteristics, as well as the same general topology, just enhanced in a number of ways.
As we go through the breakdown, keep in mind that Zen 6 and Zen 6c use the same microarchitecture. Zen 6c is just a space-optimized design that consumes less power, clocks lower, and, obviously, takes up less die space than a full Zen 6 core. But, the company uses the same microarchitecture inside the core, unlike Intel’s E-cores, which use a different microarchitecture than the P-cores.
Starting with the frontend, it’s largely unchanged from Zen 5, short of a few notable improvements. You get the same dual 4-wide decode pipes and 8-dispatch, but AMD has improved the BPU and op cache. For the BPU, it has a 64-entry Return Address Stack, up from 52 on Zen 5. AMD also increased the op cache size back up to 6.75K entries from 6K on Zen 5 (Zen 4 also had a 6.75K-entry op cache). This larger cache can serve up to 18 micro-ops per cycle, up from 12 on Zen 5.
AMD split the integer schedulers for Zen 6 (Zen 5 had a unified scheduler), now offering higher capacity, with 96 shared ALU/AGU and 48 dedicated ALU entries, compared to an 88 / 56 split for ALU/AGU on Zen 5. AMD also expanded the general-purpose registers to a 352-entry physical register file, up from 240 on Zen 5.
The vector execution engine is also improved, following on the heels of a true 512-bit register in Zen 5. Zen 6 carries forward that 512-bit data path and adds some additional improvements. Notably, the engine now supports half-precision AVX-512 FP16 instructions, which needed to be converted in Zen 5’s vector execution engine. Also notable is the FP load/store bandwidth. Zen 5 supports two loads of any size, but Zen 6 supports either two 512-bit loads or four 256-bit loads. Store bandwidth is unchanged, at one 512-bit store or two 256-bit stores.
Zen 6 carries forward the 48 KB 12-way L1 data cache from Zen 5, along with 1 MB 16-way private L2. The shared L3 is treated as victim cache for the L2, as is the case in Zen 5. However, AMD increased the in-flight window compared to Zen 5, with an 80-entry load queue and 128-entry store queue.
AMD Zen 6 and Zen 6c CCD and platform breakdown
AMD Zen 6 and Zen 6c CCD and platform breakdown
Perhaps the biggest change going from Zen 5 to Zen 6 comes in the density of the CCD. Zen 6 offers up to 12 cores per CCD, up from 8 on Zen 5, while Zen 6c scales up to 32, double that of Zen 5c. Elsewhere, the updated CCDs either match or improve on Zen 5/5c CCDs.
For Zen 6, AMD retained the 4 MB of L3 cache per core, increasing the total cache to 48 MB to accommodate the new 12-core limit. The maximum frequency of a standard Zen 6 CCD has increased from 5 GHz on Zen 5 to 5.3 GHz on Zen 6. Keep in mind these clocks are in the context of Venice; we expect higher maximum boost clocks on consumer Olympic Ridge.
Zen 6c has more enhancements. AMD doubled the amount of L3 per core from 2 MB to 4 MB, matching the normal Zen 6 CCD. And, with double the L3 per core and double the number of cores, the Zen 6c CCD has a total of 128 MB of L3, quadruple that of a Zen 5c CCD. For Zen 6c, the maximum frequency is also up, going from 3.7 GHz on Zen 5c to 4.1 GHz on Zen 6c.
Across both, AMD claims a “large core IPC uplift,” as well as improved power and SMT efficiency. We haven’t seen an overall IPC claim yet, though the numbers referenced above put Venice at about a 27% advantage over Turin in enterprise, cloud, and AI workloads.
In the context of Venice, AMD can fit up to eight CCDs on a chip, coming out to 256 cores in total for Zen 6c, and 96 cores total for regular Zen 6 for SP7 platforms (the initial lineup for Venice). AMD is moving past the SP5 socket available to Genoa and Turin CPUs for SP7, which is a slightly larger socket at 76 x 80 mm (SP5 is ~72 x 75 mm).
The topology of the chip is largely intact from Turin, short of the dual IO dies that characterize Venice. The two IODs live in the middle of the chip, flanked by Zen 6 CCDs. The second IOD is what gives SP7 chips access to 16 channels of memory per socket (8 channels per IOD), supporting up to 12,800 MT/s speeds using MRDIMMs in a 1DPC configuration. With RDIMMs, AMD supports up to 8,000 MT/s. The platform supports up to 8 TB of memory per socket, and AMD claims bandwidth of up to 1.6 TB/s per socket (1 TB/s per socket with RDIMMs).
Also on the IOD, there’s the hardware root-of-trust, as well as AMD’s confidential computing extensions, including execution encryption, memory integrity, and trusted I/O. New to the platform is PCIe 6.0 at speeds up to 64 Gbps per lane. A 1P SP7 configuration has access to 96 PCIe 6.0 lanes, while a 2P platform has up to 128. Each configuration also comes with “bonus” PCIe 4.0 lanes, either 8 for 1P configs or 16 for 2P.
Two 64G SerDes interfaces bring the PCIe lanes into the IOD, one of which is used to link the chips in a 2P configuration. That second interface can still optionally handle an additional 12 PCIe 6.0 lanes, giving the “up to” 128 2P lanes number. The bonus lanes run through a smaller 16G SerDes interface.
Platforms with the SP8 socket trade memory channels for PCIe lanes. The SP8 socket is smaller at 62.5 x 80 mm, and the platform supports eight memory channels instead of 16, though with the same support for up to 12,800 MT/s MRDIMMs. Memory bandwidth drops to 819 GB/s for MRDIMMs and 512 GB/s for RDIMMs at the maximum supported transfer rate.
However, SP8 chips have access to 64 PCIe 6.0 lanes per IOD, for a total of 128 lanes in a socket (plus the additional eight PCIe 4.0 bonus lanes). Just like SP7, some of those lanes are shared in a 2P configuration, dropping the total to 192 PCIe 6.0 lanes in 2P SP8 servers, with 16 additional PCIe 4.0 lanes. Both platforms support CXL 3.1.
AMD also provided a platform breakdown for its upcoming Verano range, which uses the Zen 6 microarchitecture on an LPDDR5X-based platform, leveraging replaceable SOCAMM2 DIMMs.
UPP, UBPS, and FAST in Zen 6 ‘Venice’ CPUs
UPP, UBPS, and FAST in Zen 6 ‘Venice’ CPUs
AMD has added a few quality-of-life features to Venice CPUs that should make them easier to manage when actually deployed. First is UPP, or Unified Power Provisioning, which is a power management feature that takes into account total platform power, allocating it as needed to different components, depending on the workload. With it, AMD says it’s able to deliver a power consumption of 830W on 16 servers to 706W on 18 servers, or a decrease in provisioned power by 15%, while increasing the number of servers per rack.
Also dealing with power is UBPS, or Utilization Based Power Scaling. It’s a dynamic power scaling feature that aligns with whatever workload is running on the server, which AMD says “helps close the gap between provisioned and consumed power.” Like UPP, UBPS is concerned with platform power, not just the power consumption of the CPU.
The most interesting addition is FAST, or Frequency Adaptive Spectrum Technology. The feature takes in telemetry from the platform and policies set in firmware to adjust the frequency within set power and thermal limits. It sounds a little more involved than a simple Precision Boost Overdrive for the data center, however.
AMD described FAST to us as allowing for two performance tiers within one socket. As an example, AMD pointed to a 96-core Venice CPU, saying FAST allows 32 of those cores to run in a “premium” category, with a base clock of 3.65 GHz and a max clock of 5 GHz, while a “batch” category with 64 cores runs at 2 GHz with a 2.4 GHz max. AMD described it as multiple commercial SKUs within a single socket.
Preliminary MEXT support, claims of 95% performance at 50% DRAM capacity
Venice marks the point when AMD will start offering MEXT on its EPYC platforms. AMD aquired MEXT earlier this year, and it has used the feature internally. With HPE, AMD is rolling out “MEXT ready” platforms, which will, eventually, have access to MEXT licenses. The technology is interesting, especially given how constrained memory is right now.
The general concept of MEXT is using flash as DRAM. Even the fastest flash is orders of magnitude slower than DRAM, but MEXT attempts to take advantage of DRAM access patterns to expose more memory to the system without it actually being there. Pages that haven’t been accessed in several minutes are offloaded to flash storage, and an AI model predicts pages that are needed. Then, those pages are loaded back into memory as you need them.
Conceptually, it sounds too good to be true. AMD pointed out that MEXT is using a transformer-based LLM, and effectively, LLMs are predicting what words go next when generating text. Here, AMD says the bar isn’t even that high. As long as the model can stream the correct pages in, and do so fast enough to cover the flash latency, the order of them doesn’t matter.
MEXT is delivered through a Linux kernel module, and AMD has bold claims about its capabilities. The company has deployed the software internally on 145 servers, which it expects to expand to over 2,000 servers next year. Currently, AMD is using it for critical EDA workflows, such as Synopsis PrimeTime. The company says that it’s able to maintain 95% of the application’s performance on Venice with just 50% of the system DRAM. Going down as low as 25%, the company claims the app maintains 80% of its performance.
We’ll have more on MEXT shortly. The feature is exclusive to EPYC CPUs, and AMD was clear that it only applies to certain workloads right now. There are likely applications where you won’t be able to cut the DRAM capacity of a server, or where you’ll need to use a more conservative cut of 25% or less.
AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ test configurations
AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ test configurations
AMD gave us access to two Zen 6 Venice systems for the purpose of testing, both of which were dual-socket servers. For the first system, we tested the dense EPYC 9996, which is AMD’s high-core-count design, packing 256 cores and 512 threads per socket, for a total of 512 cores and 1024 threads across a 2P system. It’s a peak throughput SKU, designed to handle heavily concurrent workloads.
On the other end of the spectrum, we have the EPYC 9686F, which is still a high core count CPU in its own right, with 96 cores and 192 threads, giving a 2P system 192 cores and 384 threads. The “F” suffix for AMD’s data center CPUs notes a high-frequency SKU, designed to push performance up in more demanding applications, as opposed to the dense, frontend-focused EPYC 9996.
| Chip | Cores / Threads | Base / Boost Clock (GHz) | L3 Cache | TDP | 
| Epyc 9996 | 256 / 512 | 2.55 / 4.1 | 1024 MB | 600W | 
| Epyc 9966 | 192 / 384 | 2.9 / 4 | 768 MB | 600W | 
| Epyc 9846 | 168 / 336 | 2.85 / 3.7 | 768 MB | 500W | 
| Epyc 9756 | 128 / 256 | 3.15 / 4 | 512 MB | 500W | 
| Epyc 9G76 | 96 / 192 | 3.4 / 4.8 | 384 MB | 500W | 
| Epyc 9656 | 96 / 192 | 3.05 / 3.7 | 512 MB | 400W | 
| Epyc 9686F | 96 / 192 | 3.4 / 5 | 384 MB | 500W | 
| Epyc 9556 | 64 / 128 | 2.75 / 4.3 | 384 MB | 300W | 
| Epyc 9586F | 64 / 128 | 3.75 / 5 | 384 MB | 500W | 
Both chips use AMD’s SP7 socket, which is geared toward data centers, with higher core count SKUs. The upcoming SP8 socket is focused on enterprise customers, with smaller core counts and support for fewer memory channels.
Although the EPYC 9996 is a dense design with the Zen 6c core, it comes with a fairly high boost clock of 4.1 GHz, though a much lower 2.55 GHz base clock, which it will likely be running closer to in real deployments. It comes with a massive 1,024 MB pool of L3 for the chip, as well as a 600W rated TDP, though it can be manually adjusted between 400W and 600W.
The EPYC 9686F proves out AMD’s claims about Venice, serving as one of two chips in the SP7 lineup to boost up to 5 GHz. It has a lower 500W TDP, though it can again run between 400W and 600W. This is the SKU AMD has heavily referenced in its published Venice benchmarks as a “96-core HF” model.
It’s an interesting model, perhaps more so than the EPYC 9996. It’s in direct competition with Nvidia’s Vera CPU, not only based on core count, but also on performance. These two chips trade blows in several benchmarks, and it’s clear that AMD is pushing this SKU as its “agentic CPU” of the Venice lineup, similar to how Nvidia has positioned Vera.
| Test Platform | Memory | Tested Processors | 
| 2P AMD Nigeria reference platform | 32 x 64 GB (2TB) SK hynix DDR5-12800 ECC MRDIMM | AMD EPYC 9996, EPYC 9686F | 
| 2P AMD Volcano reference platform | 24 x 64 GB (1.5 TB) SK hynix DDR5-6000 ECC RDIMM | AMD EPYC 9965, EPYC 9755 | 
| 2P Supermicro SYS-222HA | 24 x 64GB (1.5 TB) Micron DDR5-8800 ECC MRDIMM | Intel Xeon 6980P | 
| 2P Nvidia MGX Vera reference platform | 16 x 96 GB (1.5 TB) Samsung LPDDR5-9600 ECC SOCAMM2 | Nvidia Vera | 
You can see the platforms we tested above. The Nigeria reference platform we tested these Zen 6 chips on came with top-end DDR5-12800 MRDIMMs, arranged to fully saturate the 16-channel memory with 32 sticks. This massive jump in memory support is a critical aspect of Venice, particularly for the hotly contested EPYC 9686F and its all-important matchup against Vera.
Vera’s use of LPDDR5 SOCAMM2 memory allows for higher transfer rates than standard RDIMMs in a field-replaceable package, though through a relatively tame eight-channel setup. Vera can get away with 8-channel memory, however, with its topology allowing for massive data movement across the chip. AMD’s distributed design necessitates a bigger memory configuration, with double the channels and access to even higher transfer rates through the use of MRDIMMs.
AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ 9996 and 9686F SPEC estimates
Starting off our benchmarks is SPEC CPU 2026, the de facto industry benchmark for server CPU performance. As usual with SPEC runs, the numbers below are “estimates.” We gathered the numbers from real SPEC runs, but we haven’t reported them to the SPEC committee, so they remain “estimates.”
For the throughput benchmark suites, intrate and fprate, we ran a number of copies for each application equal to the thread count of the chip. All of our tests were run on Ubuntu Server 26.04 with Linux Kernel 7.0, and we used GCC 15.2 for all but the Venice chips. GCC 16 brings official support for Zen 6, which we used here. However, we did regression testing against GCC 15 and found only minor differences, and nothing that would change our standings.
Using GCC 16 was important to keep our optimization flags equal. We used common GCC flags, including fast link-time optimization and march/mcpu flags to expose the correct processor instruction support. We also used the open-source jemalloc memory allocator across all tested systems.

The overall intrate scores set the tone, particularly for the EPYC 9996. It has access to 1,024 threads in a 2P configuration, multiplying the clear speed improvements in Zen 6 broadly across more threads compared to last-gen’s top-end EPYC 9965. The 9996 scored a massive 93% higher in this test, though that number requires some context.
Both throughput benchmarks in SPEC reward not only how much work is done, but also how quickly it’s done. With access to a much larger thread pool and improvements in Zen 6 broadly, there’s that multiplicative effect when looking at pure throughput. A 2P EPYC 9996 system is 93% faster than a 2P EPYC 9965 system in this benchmark, but not broadly across the board.
The EPYC 9686F provides some context, which is still good news for AMD, just not on the level of doubling the performance of the previous generation. We unfortunately didn’t have access to a 9575F for a closer gen-on-gen comparison, but the EPYC 9755 is a decent proxy, with its 128 cores and relatively high 4.1 GHz boost clock. Compared with that CPU, the EPYC 9686F in a 2P configuration is 19% ahead — not too shabby considering the thread disadvantage.
Critically for AMD, the EPYC 9686F is also 17% ahead of Nvidia’s Vera CPU. Vera punches far above its weight class compared to the x86 competition, as evidenced by its matchup against the 9755 and Intel’s flagship Granite Rapids-AP 6980P.

Flipping over to float performance, AMD did a lot of work on the vector engine in Zen 6, and it shows up in fprate. The differences between the EPYC 9996 and 9686F are smaller, though not in a way where both chips are hamstrung. Rather, the EPYC 9696F is able to push up closer to the 9996, leaving both Zen 6 chips running circles around the field.
AMD more than doubled the score with its Zen 6 chips compared to our Zen 5 touchpoints, which is a massive achievement. The EPYC 9686F excels even more over Vera in fprate with a 40% lead, despite only a minor bump in core count (88 on Vera to 96 on the 9686F). Intel’s Granite Rapids-AP isn’t in the conversation here for raw performance; though, apparently the range is still in high-enough demand that Intel has increased production in the tight CPU environment we’re currently experiencing.

These throughput benchmarks are most representative of how these CPUs will actually be deployed, running multiple copies of applications under high concurrency. However, SPEC CPU also includes its speed suite, which looks at application performance when you can dedicate the whole chip to running just that one application, more along the lines of a client CPU benchmark.
The EPYC 9686F naturally looks better here with its blistering 5 GHz boost clock. In the integer suite, the frequency-optimized chip is 21% ahead of Vera, both in a 2P configuration. The 9996 still holds up, only falling short of the 9686F, despite much more inter-CCD communication.
SPEC shows the various improvements in Zen 6 showing up in a compounding fashion. There’s the new microarchitecture with an optimized vector path, but also more cores per CCD. And also support for higher memory speeds, as well as more memory channels. In isolation, any of these improvements are solid (if rote) for typical gen-on-gen improvements. Add them up in a workload that can take advantage of all of those improvements, however, and Zen 6 is blistering.
AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ 9996 and 9686F Python and memory benchmarks
Two of the biggest performance vectors in the agentic era are memory performance and Python performance, at least at the moment. Agentic frameworks are largely defined by Python between LangGraph and CrewAI, though alternative frameworks written in TypeScript and Rust have started to appear as well. Regardless, Python remains important for agentic CPUs right now.
Similarly, memory bandwidth is important for certain types of agents, particularly those that need to query large databases, regardless of if they’re a traditional relational database written in SQL or a non-relational database.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Starting with the industry-standard STREAM benchmark, AMD is ahead of Nvidia’s Vera by between 11% and 19%, depending on the test. However, this was with the OpenMP “true” policy for process binding, which binds processes to the thread they’re placed on to avoid them jumping around and skewing the results. Vera performs well, even with this policy, but its mesh cache and monolithic design allow it to realize big performance gains with the “spread” policy.
This policy also binds processes, but it distributes them across the chip as far away from each other as possible. AMD chips don’t see an improvement with the spread policy, and Intel’s Granite Rapids-AP sees a slight regression. Vera, however, remains on top of the pile, with a clear victory margin with the policy applied.

In the tried-and-true MBW benchmark, the pair of 9996s claim a small lead over Vera, with a small array size of just 128 MB, but Vera jumps into first place when the array size increases. AMD has certainly tightened up the memory matchup against Vera with 16 channels and support for 12,800 MT/s MRDIMMs, but Vera’s topology and already competitive memory subsystem still wins the day.
The clear differences in memory performance flatten off as we flip to Python, which is a much more hotly-contested area of performance. Starting with a broad overview, we have PyBench. Across the suite, the EPYC 9686F was 32% faster than Vera, while the EPYC 9996 naturally claims a smaller 14% lead with its relatively limited boost clocks. For gen-on-gen comparisons, the EPYC 9996 is an impressive 24% ahead of the EPYC, while the 9686F claims a lead of 35% over the 9755 – though, no small part of that advantage is the 900 MHz higher boost clock that the 9686F has access to.

PyPerformance allows us to go more granular into specific Python applications and functions, but a similar pattern appears. The rankings of other CPUs change, but across the vast majority of tests, the EPYC 9686F leads by a clear margin. It makes sense, too, given that Python heavily leans on a single thread at stock.
There are some exceptions, notably the networkx benchmark, where the throughput-optimized 9996 tops the charts, matching Nvidia’s Vera. Despite how impressive Nvidia’s chip is, considering the company’s infancy in data center CPUs and the chip’s tame spec sheet, Venice shows that the CPU game is AMD’s to win (or lose).
AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ 9996 and 9686F compression and rendering benchmarks
Breaking out of the agentic bubble, AMD has continually proven itself as the leading force in general-purpose data center applications, and that trend continues with Venice. As with all of the workloads here, they can touch on agentic AI depending on what the agent is set up to do; database performance, for example, is important if an agent is often querying a database. However, we’re going to keep our analysis at a high level here, as EPYC CPUs will be deployed for a broad range of workloads, some portion of which won’t come remotely close to agentic AI.

Starting with compression performance, AMD generally sits at the top of the charts for compression and decompression speeds, which is the case here with zstd and 7-Zip. In zstd, Vera claims an early lead at the lowest compression level. However, its poor decompression performance shows up even at level 3, and AMD takes over with a clear victory at the compression level 19, with Vera falling even further behind in decompression performance.
The long mode results are especially interesting. Although the rankings don’t change, Vera’s performance in these sustained compression workloads gets worse, while AMD is able to hang onto much more of its performance. Vera and the EPCY 9686F are within noise of each other in the level 3 compression test, and Vera falls to the bottom of the rankings when looking at decompression.
7-Zip has been, for years now, AMD’s game. The charts really speak for themselves here; we’re dealing in multiplicative factors compared to Vera, not to mention the weak competition from Intel’s Granite Rapids-AP. AMD is always strong in 7-Zip, which is compounding here considering the already high base level of performance we see out of Zen 6 across a wide range of workloads.

Onto rendering, Blender shows big gen-on-gen gains for Venice, with the EPYC 9996 offering somewhere between a 30% and 40% improvement over the EPYC 9965 depending on the scene. This is true even in demanding scenes like Barbershop, where render time can be expressed as minutes instead of seconds for many chips. The EPYC 9996 completed the render 35% faster than the EPYC 9965. The EPYC 9686F was able to match the dense EPYC 9965, despite packing half of the cores. Vera isn’t included in our Blender results because a native Arm version isn’t available.
Vera retains a top position in C-Ray, both at 4K and 1080p, though a dual EPYC 9996 configuration is within spitting distance. The script flips in OSPRay, with AMD pulling off clear leads in real-time ambient occlusion, scientific visualization, and path tracing. There are some massive jumps, with the EPYC 9996 nearly tripling the performance of the Xeon 6980P and Vera in the ambient occlusion and scientific visualization tests.
The reworked vector engine in Venice shows up even more clearly in the dim_512 tests, which further stress both the vector engine and memory bandwidth of the platform.
AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ 9996 and 9686F Java and database benchmarks
We run three Java suites to measure the ever-important programming language that shows up everywhere from scientific computing to database workloads. Starting on the former end, Java SciMark shows the EPYC 9686F in a clear lead over the competition, with a massive 92% lead over Vera in the composite score. For an apples-to-apples gen-on-gen increase, the EPYC 9996 managed a respectable 24% jump over the EPYC 9965.

Java SciMark provides a nice overview of some critical functions, such as Monte Carlo risk analysis that’s applicable to financial institutions. DaCapo and Renaissance are much wider suites measuring a range of Java-based applications. Many of these tests are highly specific, so the rankings jump around, depending on what the workload stresses. We can see a bit of that with Java SciMark, as well, with Vera claiming the top slot in FFTs. Venice, however, remains ahead.

In large column-based database workloads like Clickhouse, Venice also looks impressive, though not from the jump. Vera maintains its performance from a cold cache, while none of the x86 competition reach steady performance until the cache is warm. The reason should be obvious given Vera’s topology and its distributed mesh, which allows it to jump straight to its peak performance, even when the cache is cold.
Once it’s warm, the 9686F jumps into the lead. There’s a regression in performance going from the 9965 to the 9996, which makes sense for Clickhouse, as larger core counts can create issues in cache coherency.
To look at NoSQL performance, we have simdjson, which leverages SIMD instructions for JSON parsing, as the name implies. Once again, the vector engine in Venice shines, regardless of the workload you look at.
AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ 9996 and 9686F HPC and compilation benchmarks
View Original

Vera showed strong compilation performance against AMD’s Turin chips, but Team Red leapfrogs that performance with Venice. Starting with LLVM, the frequency-optimized 9686F earns a top slot with makefiles, while the EPYC 9996 tops with Ninja. The drop is around 19% gen-on-gen, aligning with the performance we’ve seen with other workloads.
In PHP, where Vera is more competitive, the EPYC 9686F squeezes out the most marginal of victories, but perhaps most telling is the 9996, which is in the upper tier of chips, despite how dense it is. Building applications, the Godot game engine and ImageMagick once again show both Venice chips on the top of the stack, outclassing the performance of Vera, which previously held a top slot in ImageMagick, and only fell slightly behind the 9755 in Godot.
View Original

The 9686F shows large performance jumps in HPC workloads, which AMD says is the target of these lower-core, frequency-optimized SKUs. In CloverLeaf, the EPYC 9686F is more than twice as fast as Vera, and it’s nearly twice as fast with FFTE. In Octave, Vera retains its top position, but both Venice chips are only slightly behind.
Although not traditional HPC, the heavily threaded number crunching behind the scenes in the Stockfish chess engine allows the 1,024 threads in a 2P EPYC 9996 server to outclass the 9965 by nearly 50%. Primesieve shows similarly large leaps, with the EPYC 9996 calculating some 37 billion prime numbers in less than half a second.
More to come
More to come
AMD already had a strong position in the newly reinvigorated CPU market with Turin. The unique topology and strong focus of Vera has allowed Nvidia to make inroads in certain workloads, but even looking at two SKUs from AMD’s broad Venice lineup, it’s clear that AMD is able to push performance much higher across the board. In some cases, that’s by orders of magnitude gen-on-gen.
There isn’t one area of Zen 6, or the SoCs available with Venice broadly, that totally accounts for the performance increase. It’s small advantages throughout the design, pushing an already strong vector engine further, vastly increasing CCD density, and giving memory bandwidth a boon between support for 12,800 MT/s MRDIMMs and 16-channel memory courtesy of the dual IODs.
But the story AMD has been trying to tell, and the one that’s difficult to ignore in the current market of a one-size-fits-all approach we’ve seen from Nvidia and Arm, is that Venice is available in a broad range of different configurations. We tested two chips on SP7, but the enterprise-focused SP8 socket is arriving within the next few months. And next year, AMD is pushing out Venice-X with 3D V-Cache for HPC workloads, as well as Verano, which looks like AMD’s take on Vera with its field-replaceable SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X memory.
Even without those chips, the two SP7 chips we tested already give AMD a leading position among current data center CPUs. Intel’s Diamond Rapids could change that story come next year, but the EPYC 9686F provides top-tier performance with HPC and AI host node performance, while the EPYC 9996 provides unmatched throughput.

articles.title: Claude Code a transmis les adresses mail de ses utilisateurs à des sites web sans leur accord, Anthropic présente ses excuses
articles.text:
L’assistant de programmation d’Anthropic a transmis des adresses mail personnelles à des services externes, sans l’autorisation des utilisateurs concernés. Alertée depuis plusieurs mois sur l’utilisation de ces données, l’entreprise a reconnu le problème et commencé à déployer des correctifs.
Neuf requêtes envoyées au site de la Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), le régulateur américain des marchés financiers, et un détail qui n’aurait jamais dû s’y trouver : l’adresse mail personnelle du développeur à l’origine des recherches. Ce dernier n’avait pourtant jamais demandé à Claude Code de la communiquer. L’assistant disposait même d’instructions lui interdisant explicitement de transmettre cette information à un service tiers. Il l’a fait malgré tout, comme le rapporte Cyberattaque.org, qui s’appuie sur les historiques publiés fin octobre sur le dépôt GitHub officiel du logiciel. Et ce développeur est loin d’être le seul concerné.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Une adresse personnelle transformée en coordonnées de contact
Pour comprendre comment Claude Code en est arrivé là, il faut revenir sur une fonctionnalité développée par Anthropic pour faciliter l’attribution du code. Lorsqu’il génère un fichier, l’assistant peut y insérer des commentaires précisant l’identité de son auteur, à l’aide d’une mention « @author ». Comme il lui arrivait d’inventer des noms, Anthropic avait décidé de lui communiquer automatiquement l’adresse mail associée au compte connecté. Cette information, intégrée au contexte du modèle sous une rubrique « userEmail », lui restait accessible pendant toutes ses autres tâches.
Or, Claude Code peut aussi exécuter des commandes, télécharger des fichiers et consulter des ressources sur Internet. Quand un site exige des logiciels automatisés qu’ils fournissent une adresse de contact, l'assistant peut alors reprendre celle de son utilisateur, sans solliciter son accord. L’information se retrouve dans l’en-tête HTTP « User-Agent » des requêtes exécutées avec l’outil curl, normalement destiné à identifier le programme à l’origine d'une connexion. Elle est ainsi transmise au serveur distant, qui peut en conserver une trace dans ses journaux techniques.
Les historiques publiés sur GitHub montrent que ces divulgations se sont répétées. Fin octobre, un développeur a ainsi rapporté avoir retrouvé quinze transmissions de son adresse personnelle dans quatre projets différents, entre août et octobre 2026. Les requêtes visaient notamment des services américains de données financières et statistiques, dont le Bureau of Labor Statistics, l’organisme chargé des statistiques du travail. Au cours d'une même opération, Claude Code aurait communiqué six fois cette information sans jamais en avertir son utilisateur.
Des alertes dès avril, une correction toujours attendue
Les premiers avertissements concernant l’utilisation de données personnelles par Claude Code remontent pourtant au printemps. Dès le 19 avril 2026, un développeur signalait en effet sur GitHub que l’assistant réutilisait des informations présentes dans son contexte pour générer du contenu. D’autres utilisateurs avaient ensuite constaté que leur adresse mail était systématiquement communiquée au modèle, sans possibilité de désactiver cette fonctionnalité.
Pour contenir les risques de nouvelles divulgations, Anthropic a donc déployé une première protection dans la version 2.1.317 de Claude Code, publiée le 3 novembre. Baptisé « cc-plugin-privacy » et activé par défaut, ce module cherche à intercepter les commandes susceptibles de transmettre l’adresse personnelle de l’utilisateur à un service extérieur.
Mais moins d’une semaine plus tard, deux nouveaux témoignages sont venus jeter de l’huile sur le feu. Le premier, publié le 5 novembre, accusait Claude Code d’avoir transmis son adresse personnelle à plusieurs sites Internet et affirmait recevoir désormais des dizaines de courriels frauduleux chaque jour. Le second, daté du 9 novembre, remettait en question l’efficacité de la protection. Son auteur avait constaté qu’une commande contenant son adresse mail dans un en-tête User-Agent pouvait être exécutée malgré l’activation du module. L’essai visait une adresse locale et n’a entraîné aucune transmission vers Internet, mais le filtre n’avait pas bloqué la commande.
Entre ces deux signalements, Anthropic a fini par sortir du bois par la voix de Lydia Hallie, membre de l’équipe Claude Code, qui a reconnu sur Hacker News que l’ajout automatique des adresses mail au contexte du modèle avait rendu ces divulgations possibles. Elle a présenté ses excuses pour ce problème qui aurait dû être détecté plus tôt, admis les limites du premier correctif et annoncé qu’Anthropic allait s’attaquer directement à la cause des divulgations en supprimant l’adresse mail du contexte fourni au modèle. Claude Code ne pourrait alors plus récupérer automatiquement cette information pour l’intégrer à ses requêtes.
Anthropic n'a cependant pas encore confirmé le déploiement de cette modification : la dernière version du logiciel, estampillée 2.1.322 et publiée le 10 novembre, n’en fait aucune mention dans son journal des changements.

articles.title: Arm Expands Its Portfolio with New Arm Cortex-M42 Processors
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 10th 2026
Arm Expands Its Portfolio with New Arm Cortex-M42 Processors
Innovation across the semiconductor industry continues to accelerate, driven by growing demand for AI, more capable intelligent connected devices, and specialized computing across industries. As applications become increasingly diverse, silicon partners need access to a broad portfolio of advanced, power-efficient compute technologies to meet different performance, power and cost requirements. 
Through Arm Flexible Access and Arm Total Access, Arm provides that choice, giving silicon partners access to a wide range of technologies to develop differentiated products and bring them to market faster. Today, Arm is expanding both portfolios with the new Arm Cortex-M42 processor, bringing efficient AI compute capabilities to more intelligent devices.Evolving Cortex-M-based designs to bring advanced AI capabilities to more endpoints 
Cortex-M42 combines Arm Helium technology with a compact, AHB-based design, making it easier for silicon partners to upgrade existing Arm Cortex-M4 and Cortex-M33-based microcontrollers (MCUs) while introducing more advanced machine learning (ML) and digital signal processing (DSP) capabilities. This supports a wide range of cost- and area-sensitive applications, from audio processing and keyword spotting in wearables to sensor analysis, condition monitoring and signal processing in connectivity and industrial controllers. 
These capabilities are also relevant to physical AI, where intelligent machines rely on distributed embedded processing for sensing, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance and control. For example, Cortex-M42 could enable local signal processing and condition monitoring of robotic motors and joints, helping identify abnormal behavior or signs of equipment wear without performing safety-critical motion-control functions. 
Built on the Armv8.1-M architecture, Cortex-M42 delivers up to 3x the vector compute capability and 2x the vector power efficiency of Cortex-M33, while Arm Custom Instructions provide additional flexibility to optimize processors for specific workloads. The addition builds on the continued expansion of the Arm Flexible Access portfolio, including Arm Cortex-M52, Arm Cortex-M55, Arm Cortex-M85, Arm Ethos-U85 NPU, Arm Corstone-320 reference design platform and the Armv9 Edge AI platform, providing partners with a broader range of compute options for intelligent devices. 
Accelerating silicon innovation
As of November 2026, Arm Flexible Access has 319 active members and has enabled more than 500 unique tape-outs. Arm Total Access continues to grow, with 60 partners to date and more than 600 projects undertaken through the program since launch. 
Arm Flexible Access offers low or no-cost access to a broad portfolio of Arm processor designs, development tools, and technical resources to explore and develop new products before committing to a final design. Arm Total Access supports established semiconductor companies, OEMs, ODMs and system integrators as they develop, commercialize and scale their products across a wider range of applications and performance points. 
Across both programs, partners are using the Arm compute platform to bring differentiated silicon to market, based on a common compute foundation and software ecosystem. 
Recent partner tape-outs include:
- EnSilica, using Arm Cortex processors and Ethos NPUs to develop custom ASICs across communications, satellite, automotive and industrial markets.
- Nordic Semiconductor, building on Cortex-M33 in its nRF54LM20B for low-power wireless and connected devices.
- Synaptics, combining the Cortex-M52 and Arm Ethos-U55 in its SRW1500 series to support AI processing in embedded devices, while its Astra SR80 series uses Cortex-M33 for energy-efficient connected applications.
As AI moves into more of the devices and systems we rely on every day, the need for efficient, scalable compute continues to grow. By expanding access to technologies like Cortex-M42, Arm is helping more silicon innovators bring intelligence closer to where it's needed, accelerating the next generation of intelligent, connected devices.

articles.title: ViewFinity S7 é o novo monitor 4K de 32” da Samsung; veja preço no Brasil • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
ViewFinity S7 é o novo monitor 4K de 32” da Samsung; veja preço no Brasil
Marca sul-coreana expandiu linha de monitores voltada para a produtividade no Brasil. Além de 4K, ViewFinity S7 traz HDR10 e recursos de proteção ocular.
A Samsung já havia lançado os monitores ViewFinity S5, S6, S8 e S9 no Brasil. Faltava o ViewFinity S7 de 32 polegadas. Bom, não mais. O modelo, que conta com resolução 4K e HDR10, chega oficialmente ao país com preço sugerido de R$ 1.729. O anúncio foi feito nesta terça-feira (10/11), em São Paulo (SP).
Ninguém vai te impedir de usar um monitor da linha Samsung ViewFinity para jogar ou assistir a um filme, por exemplo. Mas o foco da linha está na produtividade, isto é, em usuários que precisam de telas mais caprichadas, por assim dizer, para trabalhar ou estudar.
Para tanto, o Samsung ViewFinity S7 traz recursos como o já mencionado HDR10, que realça determinados elementos e permite uma visualização mais detalhada de objetos sob sombra.
Outro recurso digno de nota é o Eye Saver Mode, que reduz a exposição à luz azul de modo a diminuir o desconforto visual, sendo útil principalmente para quem passa muito tempo diante da tela.
A Samsung também chama a atenção para o Flicker Free, modo que reduz a cintilação da tela, novamente diminuindo o desconforto visual após longos períodos na frente do monitor.
Sobre a tela em si, estamos falando de um painel VA LCD que, além das 32 polegadas e da resolução 4K, tem ângulo de visão de 178 graus. Porém, a taxa de atualização é de 60 Hz e o brilho típico alcança 300 nits.
No quesito conectividade, o Samsung ViewFinity S7 oferece uma porta HDMI 2.0, uma porta DisplayPort 1.2, além de uma conexão para fones de ouvido. Não há portas USB.
Em linhas gerais, o S7 não é o monitor mais avançado da família Samsung ViewFinity, mas pode atender a quem precisa de uma tela generosa, tanto no tamanho quanto na resolução.
A Samsung atende aos usuários que precisam de recursos mais específicos com os demais modelos da família ViewFinity. Por exemplo:
O ViewFinity S7 de 32 polegadas já está à venda no Brasil. No site da Samsung, o monitor de vídeo tem preço oficial de R$ 1.729. Mas quem fizer a compra até 17 de novembro de 2026 usando o cupom ViewFinity26 pagará R$ 1.639 pelo modelo.

articles.title: Scandale chez Nvidia : Trump défend Jensen Huang, Pékin dément et le FBI s'en mêle… les dernières infos
articles.text:
Jensen Huang, le directeur de Nvidia, a avoué avoir eu une relation extraconjugale avec Alice Huang, dirigeante de l’entreprise singapourienne Megaspeed. Seulement voilà, outre les problèmes d’ordre intime, les autorités américaines semblent être persuadées qu’Alice Huang est une espionne au service de la Chine. Son objectif aurait donc été de séduire le dirigeant de Nvidia pour ensuite dérober des secrets commerciaux de l’entreprise et les transmettre à la Chine. Une histoire digne d’un film d’espionnage qui n’est pas sans rappeler les récentes affaires d’espionnage dont s’accusent mutuellement Apple et OpenAI. Quoi qu’il en soit, Donald Trump assure que le dirigeant de Nvidia ne savait rien de la véritable identité d’Alice Huang. Le FBI vient par ailleurs d’ouvrir une enquête. Quant à la Chine, elle nie toute implication dans cette affaire.
Selon Trump, Jensen Huang ignorait la véritable identité d’Alice Huang
Lors d’une conférence de presse, Donald Trump a déclaré : « Je lui ai parlé aujourd’hui [à Jensen Huang], et il a dit qu’il n’avait absolument aucune idée que la personne en question était une espionne… Je le crois vraiment ». Il faut dire que les deux hommes affichent une certaine complicité depuis maintenant un moment. Si le géant Nvidia investit ses milliards de dollars un peu partout, il a aussi financé la nouvelle salle de bal de la Maison Blanche à hauteur de 25 millions de dollars. En septembre dernier, en pleine conférence, Jensen Huang avait même reçu un appel, non pas d’Alice Huang, mais de Donald Trump qui voulait affirmer une nouvelle fois sa volonté de ne pas freiner la course au développement de l’intelligence artificielle. Bref, Donald Trump a Jensen Huang de son côté, et il n’est donc pas étonnant qu’il protège ce dernier dans cette affaire d’espionnage.
Mais depuis quand Donald Trump est-il au courant qu’Alice Huang est potentiellement une espionne au service de la Chine ? Le président américain se montre très vague à ce propos : « Je vérifierai certainement auprès des services de renseignement. Cela a peut-être été mentionné. En tout cas, cela ne m’a pas particulièrement marqué ».
La Chine nie toute implication
Le ministère chinois des Affaires étrangères a démenti toute implication dans cette affaire. Guo Jiakun, porte-parole du ministère, a déclaré à des journalistes : « L’accusation d’espionnage par la Chine est totalement infondée et vise à discréditer la Chine ». Notons au passage que Donald Trump se rendra en Chine les 18 et 19 novembre prochain, à l’occasion du sommet des dirigeants de l’APEC, organisé à Shenzhen. Donald Trump rencontrera Xi Jinping, mais il a d’ores et déjà annoncé qu’il ne comptait pas aborder cette affaire d’espionnage avec le président chinois.
Le FBI s’empare de l’affaire
Le conseil d’administration de Nvidia a annoncé le lancement en interne d’une enquête pour déterminer si son dirigeant a bel et bien été victime d’espionnage. De son côté, Donald Trump a confirmé que le FBI « examinait » le dossier de Jensen Huang, mais sans donner plus de précisions. Par ailleurs, il faut aussi noter que les démocrates, qui ont remporté la majorité des sièges au Sénat et à la Chambre des représentants lors des élections de mi-mandat, pourraient demander des comptes à Jensen Huang, un proche de Donald Trump. Une affaire de relation extraconjugale se transforme donc en véritable crise qui implique la Chine et les États-Unis, mais aussi différents mouvements politiques, sans parler des répercussions potentielles sur le secteur de la tech.

articles.title: All 7 Anthropic founders will each cash out about $250M in IPO | TechCrunch
articles.text:
As Anthropic barrels toward an enormous IPO that could value it at $1.4 trillion, the company has disclosed a tidbit in its new S-1 filing about how many shares each of its seven co-founders plan to sell.
Each will sell 3,378,378 shares. Anthropic has floated an unusually broad initial price range of $70 to $78 a share. At the mid-range of $74, each founder would take in just shy of $250 million.
At the low end, $70, each would have to settle for pocketing just over $236 million cash; at the high end, $78, each would take in just under $264 million.
However, in an IPO as eagerly anticipated as this one, companies can often price shares above the initial range.
The S-1 is already hinting at high demand. Board member Reed Hastings has indicated he wants to buy $300 million worth of shares through his donor-advised fund. Board member Christopher Liddell also wants to buy $3 million worth of shares.
The seven co-founders are CEO Dario Amodei; Daniela Amodei, president and chair of the board; Tom Brown, chief compute officer; Jack Clark, head of public benefit; Jared Kaplan, chief science officer (pictured above); Sam McCandlish, chief architect; and Christopher Olah, interpretability research lead.
After the sale, each of them will own about 3.2% of the total outstanding Class A shares, the S-1 says, or roughly 22% collectively. That’s not their share of the company overall. Class A is just one of Anthropic’s share classes, and other holders, including Amazon and Google, hold non-voting Class N shares, so the founders’ stake in the company’s total equity will be considerably smaller. Even still, they, as a group, remain in control of the company. Each will also receive one share of Class F stock, which carries supervoting rights. Collectively, the founders will control 51.1% of the votes, but no single founder will hold significantly more shares or votes than the others.
As is now industry lore, the seven left OpenAI to start Anthropic in 2021 after disagreements with OpenAI’s leadership over how AI should be built. Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, who held senior research and policy roles at OpenAI, were joined by five fellow OpenAI colleagues in forming a company that has said, very publicly and from the start, that it’s more focused on AI safety than its rivals, including the founders’ former employer.

articles.title: Uber lanzó en su app un servicio para reservar estacionamiento en 15 ciudades de Estados Unidos
articles.text:
Uber lanzó el 9 de noviembre un servicio dentro de su aplicación para buscar, comparar y pagar estacionamiento por adelantado en 15 ciudades de Estados Unidos. El servicio nace de la compra de SpotHero, una aplicación de reservas de estacionamiento, y se dirige primero a quienes manejan su propio auto.
Los usuarios eligen destino, fecha y hora, y ven en un mapa los garajes, playas y servicios con valet, con el precio por adelantado. Al reservar, cargan marca, modelo y patente del vehículo y pagan con el medio guardado en la billetera de Uber. La entrada se hace con un código QR o con lectura automática de la patente.
La cancelación es gratuita hasta la hora de inicio, según Uber. El servicio abre en Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Los Ángeles, Miami, Nashville, Nueva York, Filadelfia, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle y Washington. Bloomberg informó que se sumarán más mercados, sin fecha.
El beneficio para suscriptores tiene condiciones
Los miembros de Uber One, el programa de suscripción de la empresa, reciben el 10% de lo gastado en créditos por cada reserva completada y elegible. Esos créditos se pueden usar después en viajes y pedidos de comida. Uber informó que el programa superaba los 55 millones de miembros al 30 de septiembre.
El blog View from the Wing, especializado en viajes, calculó que la suscripción cuesta USD 9,99 al mes o USD 96 al año. Para recuperar esa cuota anual con los créditos haría falta gastar USD 960 al año en estacionamiento elegible.
Según el blog, el beneficio sirve sobre todo a quien ya es suscriptor. También señaló que el crédito aplica a impuestos y cargos, que llega en general en 24 horas y que no todos los lugares califican.
La red de SpotHero suma más de 13.000 garajes, playas y servicios de valet en 400 ciudades de Estados Unidos y Canadá, según Uber. La propia página de Uber para el servicio, de acuerdo con el mismo blog, listaba 7.000 instalaciones al momento del lanzamiento.
Una reserva no asegura un lugar concreto
View from the Wing advirtió que la reserva no implica que se guarde una plaza específica: SpotHero administra el inventario con los operadores. Si el conductor llega y no puede entrar, Uber lo remite a la opción de ayuda del pase de estacionamiento. Las reglas de entrada, extensión, altura del vehículo y cargos extra dependen de cada local.
Las preguntas frecuentes de Uber indican otras dos limitaciones: los perfiles de empresa no son compatibles y las cuentas de Uber y SpotHero no se pueden vincular. Una reserva hecha en Uber no aparece en la cuenta de SpotHero.
La compra de SpotHero se anunció en febrero, según TechCrunch. Uber también planea usar esos espacios como puntos de espera para vehículos autónomos y así reducir los kilómetros que recorren vacíos. El director ejecutivo Dara Khosrowshahi dijo en la presentación de resultados del tercer trimestre que el trayecto al trabajo es “una de nuestras categorías más grandes”.
Un vocero de Uber dijo, según lo informado por Bloomberg, que la empresa mantendrá SpotHero funcionando como aplicación independiente.

articles.title: Alice Huang reportedly instrumental in securing over $7.5 billion of Nvidia AI GPU imports during three-year relationship with Jensen Huang — helped move 240,000 banned chips into China, mostly H100 and H200
articles.text:
Alice Huang reportedly instrumental in securing over $7.5 billion of Nvidia AI GPU imports during three-year relationship with Jensen Huang — helped move 240,000 banned chips into China, mostly H100 and H200
These complicated business moves helped her network secure thousands of hard-to-get Nvidia GPUs.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is also suspected of being a spy working for the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS). Now, an investigation by The Information has revealed a 'labyrinth' of companies centered around Shanghai Century Litong and connected to Singaporean firm Megaspeed, which has previously been accused of smuggling $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips. The report claims Alice Huang helped move 240,000 banned chips into the country, mostly H100 and H200 systems, and was instrumental in securing AI GPU imports to the tune of $7.5 billion.
Sources in the report link the two companies to Alice Huang via their personal knowledge and corporate registration records, while there have also been reports that some of the Nvidia AI chips Megaspeed bought went to Shanghai Century Litong’s data centers in China. But aside from these corporate ties, there were also numerous reports about Ms. Huang’s personal relationship with the Nvidia chief, and how it gave her the ability to procure chips that were otherwise hard to get elsewhere.
Ms. Huang allegedly boasted about her access to the Nvidia CEO publicly. People familiar with her said that she regularly uploaded photos with Jensen to her WeChat account and even shared other images with customers to establish her credibility. She even claimed that Jensen Huang would often celebrate her birthday with dinner and gifts, while an Nvidia China sales employee said that she was a familiar face at the company’s annual event for local Chinese partners.
When AI shipments hit delays or faced some trouble, Ms. Huang allegedly would step in to get them moving through the supply chain again. One other person who knows her said that she would often cite her close relationship with Nvidia and its suppliers as the reason why she could always get Nvidia AI chips. It’s estimated that $4.6 billion worth of AI chips have been imported through Megaspeed from 2023 to 2025, with another $2 billion routed through Speedmatrix. It was also reported that Shanghai Century Litong bought GPUs from other sources, with the assistance of Alice Huang if the orders faced an issue, with the total value of the GPUs acquired estimated to be around $7.5 billion. The report claims Ms. Huang helped move some 240,000 banned chips into China.
Alice Huang may have appeared in Jensen Huang’s circle much earlier than previously believed. One source told the publication that Kang Wei, Alice Huang’s husband, met Jensen Huang during the 2010s, when Nvidia was primarily a PC gaming GPU manufacturer. According to the report, Kang Wei was a private equity investor focusing on videogame companies back then. In contrast, Ms. Huang reportedly worked for two media companies in China, although some say that there were no records of her doing so. She eventually jumped into banking and finance, working at HSBC and then CITIC Securities, before finally entering the data center industry in 2023 with Megaspeed’s pivot and the founding of Shanghai Century Litong.
Shanghai Century Litong is a data center operator founded in June 2023 by a shareholder that was ultimately under the control of Huang Yu, the sister of Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le. The company then provided compute capacity to AI tech giants in China, including Alibaba, Tencent, and other smaller labs. A few months after its founding, it received coveted Nvidia Preferred Cloud Partner status in October 2023, which is an important milestone as Nvidia requires anyone with this status to have demonstrated sufficient capability in handling and running Nvidia hardware as well as generating revenue at a certain level, although that threshold varies by region and partner type.
In exchange for this, partners get better access to Nvidia’s limited number of chips, which became crucial for Shanghai Century Litong as the China-specific A800 and H800 chips were banned for sale to China around the same period. Although the move immediately banned the sales of these GPUs from Nvidia, it did not affect the chip stocks that were already in the hands of distributors. This meant that Shanghai Century Litong had priority access to the limited supply of these AI GPUs as Nvidia’s preferred partner.

Megaspeed, on the other hand, was reportedly owned by a company called Huang Le Limited and led by Ms. Huang when it pivoted in 2023 and was subsequently sold to Singaporean entity Swiftdata soon after this. Megaspeed then set up a subsidiary called Speedmatrix, which has two offices in Johor, Malaysia, a couple of months after that. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the U.S. agency in charge of monitoring export control compliance, noted that the Nvidia hardware found in Speedmatrix data centers was still in its boxes when they inspected the sites, triggering a deeper investigation into the company. Still, it’s been alleged that Nvidia intervened in the BIS probe, with the company retaining its Nvidia partner status to this day.
Despite her public closeness with the Nvidia chief, she’s rather elusive when it comes to her personal information. Two other people said that she has always been vague about what she does at her companies, and that she’s careful when it comes to signing documents and leaving a paper trail that could easily be followed. Still, the Chinese embassy denies any links to Alice Huang, even as the FBI looks into the situation.

articles.title: Wyndham confirms it exposed hotel customer data after expert finds flaw in app security
articles.text:
Wyndham confirms it exposed hotel customer data after expert finds flaw in app security
Another day, another set of hardcoded credentials discovered
- Wyndham’s Android app exposed customer data and login tokens through hardcoded credentials embedded in the code
- Researchers found access to millions of records, including names, emails, member IDs, and active authentication tokens
- Wyndham fixed the issue after disclosure, but the scope of exposure and any prior access remain unclear
Wyndham Hotels & Resorts, one of the world’s largest hotel chains, has admitted it experienced an embarrassing cybersecurity incident that exposed personally identifiable information and even mobile app login tokens, possibly for millions of people.
The hotel confirmed the news to TechCrunch after an independent researcher tipped off the publication about the security mishap.
Security researcher Robert Wiggins from What Security analyzed Wyndham’s Android app and found a set of hardcoded credentials. Those are credentials that are baked into the app’s code and are usually a leftover artifact from earlier development phases. While building an app, software developers would include admin credentials into the code to work faster and not have to log in every time they want to test a feature or a tool.
These credentials are usually removed in the final audit, just before the app is shipped. However, they are sometimes forgotten, which leaves a revolving double door back access for even the lowliest skilled cybercriminals.
Customer data and login tokens
In this case, the credentials granted Wiggins access to an internal company database containing customer names, email addresses, Wyndham member numbers, and JWTs - customer login tokens that allow users to remain logged into their apps.
These tokens would prove invaluable to malicious actors, since they would allow them to access user instances without knowing their credentials (granted that they are still active and not expired or revoked).
Personally identifiable information, as well as Wyndham files and documents that were also stored in the database, could be used to create highly customized, tailored phishing lures, which could trick victims into installing malware, making fraudulent transactions, or granting attackers access to their employer’s corporate environment.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Wiggins apparently tried reaching out to the hotel but could not find the right channel, so he asked the media for help. When TechCrunch made contact, the company confirmed the security blunder but stressed that the issue had already been resolved.
“Our team has taken steps to address the issue,” a Wyndham spokesperson told the publication. “Our security teams have no evidence of any unauthorized access.”
The issue may be resolved, but plenty of questions remain unanswered. For example, we don’t know how many people had their data exposed this way. Wiggins says the database has “millions of entries”, but he could not determine a more concrete number. Wyndham claims it has 129 million enrolled rewards members.
Wiggins' streak
We also don’t know for how long the database remained exposed this way. When were the credentials hardcoded into the app, and which versions kept them? The company also said there was no evidence of unauthorized access but declined to elaborate. Without a proper audit of server logs, we cannot know for certain if anyone viewed, or downloaded, the information before Wiggins’ discovery.
So far, it doesn’t seem as if Wyndham disclosed the leak publicly, or shared details with its customers whose data was exposed. Usually, incidents like this one need to be reported to appropriate authorities, including data watchdogs and regulators such as the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the European Securities and Markets Authority, or national data protection authorities.
This is the second instance of hardcoded credentials Wiggins found in just as many weeks. In early November, it was disclosed that the American casual dining restaurant chain Applebee’s kept hardcoded credentials in its Android mobile app, exposing customer names, their email addresses (both verified and unverified ones), dates of birth, phone numbers, ZIP codes, veteran status, the number of logins, dates of account creation, and the IP address of the most recent login session, to anyone who knew where to look.
Just as with Wyndham, we don’t know the exact number of people whose data was exposed this way, but it’s safe to say they are in the millions.

articles.title: Anthropic ha descubierto lo que mi madre ya sabía: la IA cuida mejor las cosas cuando cree que son suyas
articles.text:
No es que tuviese demasiadas cosas cuando era pequeño, en mi familia nos apretábamos el cinturón. Por eso cuidaba cada juguete como si fuera un tesoro, porque realmente era tal que así: si rompía algo, me quedaba sin jugar. Esto es algo que siempre me recalcó mi madre: "Cuídalo, que es tuyo". Y es justo lo que Anthropic recomienda decirle a Fable 5.2.
La receta para mejorar el código. Todos los modelos de IA alucinan en mayor o menor medida, lo mejor es no fiarse por completo de cualquier cosa que creen. En el código también se aplica, incluso cuando quien está detrás son grandes modelos como el nuevo Fable 5.2. Y este tiene, además, una manía: si no sabe de quién es el código, añade al que ya existe aunque se repita. Y avisa de los problemas detectados en lugar de arreglarlos.
Según ha explicado Anthropic en su guía para sacarle partido al modelo, Fable 5.2 se comporta de forma distinta según según de quién crea que es el código que está tocando. Un detalle que destacó Simon Willison.
En palabras de la propia Anthropic:
"Cuando el prompt dice que la base de código es del propio modelo, este a menudo fusiona el código repetido y hace correcciones relacionadas sin que se lo pidan".
"Si quieres que el modelo mejore la estructura mientras trabaja, di que el código es suyo".
Anthropic recomienda especificar esta frase a la hora de trabajar con código en Fable 5.2:
Una simple instrucción consigue que Claude mejore el código, todo por hacerse cargo de él como si fuera suyo. Al ponerse como responsable, no se limita a cumplir: ordena y arregla todo lo que encuentra.
La comprobación. Anthropic probó la frase en tareas de programación pequeñas. Con ella, Fable 5.2 fusionó el código repetido en cerca de la mitad de los intentos; sin ella, en menos de uno de cada diez. Las peticiones solían funcionar en ambos casos: la frase en sí no es mágica, pero vale la pena tenerla en cuenta.
No siempre conviene. La propia Anthropic pone límites: recomienda no usar la frase cuando queramos que Claude toque el código lo menos posible. Tiene sentido, porque una IA a los mandos es una IA que puede cambiar cosas que nadie ha pedido.
Mi madre también lo tenía claro: las cosas eran mías, pero no me dejaba invitar a los amigos a jugar con ellas si no había nadie en casa.

articles.title: SUSE points Rancher Prime's AI agents at virtual machines and updates its enterprise Linux - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
SUSE points Rancher Prime’s AI agents at virtual machines and updates its enterprise Linux
Open-source enterprise software company SUSE S.A. today extended the artificial intelligence troubleshooting agents in its SUSE Rancher Prime platform from Kubernetes clusters to virtual machines.
The company released version 16.1 of its SUSE Linux Enterprise Server operating system at the same time. The updates are pitched at enterprises trying to run AI workloads next to existing applications in hybrid environments.
Research sponsored by SUSE found that information technology leaders rank Kubernetes management as their top investment priority, with AI second, and 24% named AI-assisted troubleshooting as one way to make Kubernetes easier to manage.
Thomas Di Giacomo, SUSE’s chief technology and product officer, said companies moving from AI experiments to deployment at scale need infrastructure that can take on the new workloads alongside the applications they already run. He said SUSE’s commitment to open infrastructure lets organizations adopt AI “on their terms, without being locked into a single technology stack or vendor.”
The troubleshooting agents report to Liz, the Rancher Prime assistant SUSE first shipped as a tech preview in November 2025. Virtual machines come within their reach through a new integration with SUSE Virtualization. Peter Smails, SUSE’s general manager of cloud native, told theCUBE in March that customers could also bring agents of their own to Liz. SUSE said nothing the agents propose gets carried out until someone approves it.
New OAuth2 support lets Liz connect to Model Context Protocol servers. SUSE has also introduced an AI-first version of the Rancher command-line interface, and operators can use its server-side dry run to see what a command would change before it takes effect.
Further down the stack, SUSE Rancher Prime Virtual Clusters gains a hosted control plane mode so platform teams can offer Kubernetes as a service on SUSE’s RKE2 distribution. Stateful workloads run up to 10 times faster on the v2 data engine in SUSE Storage, according to the company.
Version 16.1 of SUSE Linux Enterprise Server pulls in deployments that previously needed separate SUSE products. Customers on the immutable SUSE Linux Enterprise Micro or on SUSE Linux Enterprise Real Time can migrate to it, according to the release notes, and keep everything on one support lifecycle.
The release also carries an on-box MCP framework for AI-assisted diagnostics. Support for accelerated infrastructure from Nvidia Corp. is included, as are expanded live patching and preparation for post-quantum cryptography.
The security updates run from the components AI applications are built on through to the workloads in production. SUSE Application Collection now holds more than 1,000 Python libraries built from verified sources, each shipped with a software bill of materials and provenance information that developers can use to assess dependencies.
The upcoming SUSE Security 6.0 release will add SUSE Security Vulnerability Scanner to find and rank flaws in deployed workloads and cluster nodes. Its Runtime Enforcer component will detect anomalous workload behavior and block it.
SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1 is available now, with its MCP framework in tech preview. The AI-first Rancher command-line interface and the hosted control plane mode for Virtual Clusters are in open beta, and the remaining Rancher Prime features will ship on their own release schedules.

Gigabyte Launches the AI TOP AERO Powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark
Gigabyte today announced the launch of AI TOP AERO, a new AI desktop powered by the NVIDIA RTX Spark platform. Positioned as a Personal AI Studio, AI TOP AERO combines an NVIDIA Blackwell architecture GPU, up to 128 GB of unified system memory, and Gigabyte's cooling and compact chassis design. The new desktop expands Gigabyte's AI PC lineup, bringing local AI development, content creation and gaming to personal workspaces.
NVIDIA RTX Spark unites NVIDIA AI, RTX graphics, and unified memory in one slim, powerful Windows PC. Designed to run larger AI models locally--without cloud dependency--and move between creative work, development, and immersive gaming without missing a beat. Connect apps, tools, and workflows into one seamless experience. Private by default. RTX Spark brings NVIDIA's full-stack AI platform, ready for the AI workloads of today and whatever comes next. Delivered on the familiar, trusted Windows platform.Bringing Local AI to Everyday Work
As generative AI expands beyond conversational assistants into AI agents, content generation and workflow automation, users are seeking more options for personal AI computing. Running models, processing data and testing applications on their own devices gives users the flexibility to choose how they work based on data privacy, responsiveness and usage costs. AI TOP AERO addresses these needs with a local computing platform for developers, creators and AI users, bringing AI closer to their everyday tools, personal data and workflows.
An NVIDIA Grace CPU and NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU for Windows AI Computing
AI TOP AERO features the NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X Superchip, integrating a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU with an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU. The platform combines a high-performance, power-efficient CPU with NVIDIA's AI acceleration technologies. Configurations offer up to 128 GB of LPDDR5x unified system memory and up to a 4 TB PCIe Gen 5 SSD, providing computing and storage resources for local models, AI applications and creative assets.
Users can work in a familiar Windows environment while taking advantage of NVIDIA RTX acceleration and compatible AI tools. From model development and content creation to everyday productivity and supported games, AI TOP AERO brings work and entertainment together in a Personal AI Studio.
Gigabyte Cooling Design Supports Sustained AI and Creative Workloads
AI inference, content generation and professional creative applications can keep a system under heavy load for extended periods. Gigabyte integrates its cooling design into AI TOP AERO's compact chassis of approximately one liter, providing thermal headroom to help sustain performance over time and support demanding local AI and professional workloads.
Drawing on Gigabyte's hardware design and system integration experience, AI TOP AERO balances a small desktop footprint with the needs of sustained computing. It fits into personal workspaces, creative studios and offices, with USB Type-C, 10GbE Ethernet and Wi-Fi 7 connectivity for peripherals, data transfers and network access, allowing users to build an AI workspace that suits their needs.
Expanding Local AI Applications with NVIDIA Nemotron and Developer Tools
The NVIDIA RTX Spark platform brings an ecosystem of models, frameworks and accelerated tools to AI TOP AERO. Developers can build, prototype, fine-tune and run the latest open models locally on the NVIDIA CUDA platform. They can use supported NVIDIA Nemotron models and CUDA-accelerated tools to explore local inference, model testing and agentic AI applications. Compatible tools such as LM Studio and Ollama provide additional options for building a local AI environment tailored to individual needs.
From testing model responses and connecting tools to building automated workflows, AI TOP AERO brings computing resources for development and execution onto the personal desktop, keeping long-running agents accessible around the clock, with data and inference staying on the device. With NVIDIA PAIR (Personal AI Router), users can also incorporate AI TOP AERO into a local network inference environment, distributing inference tasks to available devices and extending local AI use across homes and studios.
AI-Assisted Content Creation and DLSS 5 Gaming
For content creation, AI TOP AERO can work with compatible tools such as ComfyUI to build generative AI workflows. NVIDIA Broadcast and RTX Video technologies help enhance audio and video quality and expand options for video processing and content production. From AI-generated assets to post-production, creators can choose the tools that fit their workflows and incorporate AI into everyday production.
AI TOP AERO also supports gaming alongside development and creative work. Its NVIDIA Blackwell architecture GPU and NVIDIA DLSS 5 bring neural rendering to supported games, delivering more detailed lighting and materials. Users can move between AI tasks, content creation and gaming on the same desktop, extending the versatility of their Personal AI Studio.
Building on Gigabyte's existing AI portfolio, AI TOP AERO combines the NVIDIA RTX Spark platform and Gigabyte's hardware integration expertise. The new desktop offers another choice for local AI development, content creation and gaming, further strengthening Gigabyte's personal AI computing lineup.
Gigabyte AI TOP AERO launches on November 10, 2026. Please refer to local Gigabyte announcements for regional product configurations, pricing and availability.
