articles.title: TIM Brasil não está à venda, diz CEO após troca de controle na Itália • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
TIM Brasil não está à venda, diz CEO após troca de controle na Itália
Alberto Griselli afirmou que não há negociações em curso. Estatal Poste Italiane assumiu a Telecom Italia em setembro.
A TIM Brasil não está à venda e pretende manter sua estratégia de expansão no país. A declaração foi feita pelo CEO da operadora no Brasil, Alberto Griselli, nesta terça-feira (10/11), durante a apresentação de resultados financeiros, acompanhada pelo Tecnoblog.
O posicionamento ocorre após Matteo Del Fante, CEO da Poste Italiane, nova controladora da Telecom Italia, afirmar que o Brasil não é prioritário para os planos estratégicos do grupo, embora a operação brasileira tenha relevância financeira.
“Não tem nenhum processo de venda para a empresa”, afirmou Griselli. O executivo reforçou que não há negociações em andamento e que a companhia pretende continuar investindo no país. “Não existe um processo de venda em curso e continuamos com uma estratégia de expansão no mercado brasileiro”, declarou. “Somos uma operação que tem menos valor estratégico, mas que tem mais valor financeiro”.
As especulações sobre uma possível venda ganharam força após a mudança no controle da Telecom Italia. A estatal italiana assumiu o controle indireto da operadora em setembro. Na semana passada, a TIM Brasil já havia informado à B3 que não tinha conhecimento de qualquer processo de venda.
Durante a reunião, Griselli também comentou o desempenho da base de clientes pós-pagos. “Estamos crescendo no pós-pago, mas crescendo menos do que a gente gostaria”, afirmou. Apesar da ressalva, o executivo avaliou positivamente os resultados da companhia: “Nosso resultado é redondo, com avanço concreto em todas as frentes”.
No terceiro trimestre, a TIM registrou receita líquida de serviços de R$ 6,9 bilhões, alta de 5,3% na comparação anual. A geração de caixa operacional somou R$ 5 bilhões nos nove primeiros meses de 2026, crescimento de 11,6% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025.
A operadora também anunciou nesta terça-feira uma parceria com a BYD para conectar cerca de 200 mil veículos com eSIMs no Brasil. Segundo o vice-presidente de B2B da TIM no país, Fábio Costa, os primeiros carros equipados com a novidade devem começar a sair de fábrica em 2027, com uma “rede pública totalmente adaptada” à montadora chinesa.

articles.title: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Oura announced on Tuesday that it’s acquiring AI-native primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million. The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.”
Counsel Health is an AI-powered healthcare platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians. Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June.
Users can connect with Counsel’s medical AI to get personalized medical advice, and chat with a physician when needed, all within the Oura app. Now, the companies plan to expand on their existing partnership to build across preventative care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care.
While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By acquiring Counsel Health, Oura is looking to expand its business and help users access medical care.
“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale in a press release.
Counsel Health raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and GV. PitchBook estimates it had raised a total of $36 million.
Following the acquisition, Oura says Counsel will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of expanding its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura’s membership.
Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as chief clinical AI officer, alongside the company’s 70 employees, Bloomberg reports.
“At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Alagappan said in the press release. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care. From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture, and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.”
The deal is expected to close before the end of 2027.
Oura also announced that its revenue grew 153% year-over-year to $533 million for the quarter ended on September 30. For its fiscal year 2026, Oura generated revenue of approximately $1.75 billion, marking 92% year-over-year growth.
The company reached an $11 billion valuation following a $900 million late-stage funding round in October 2025.

articles.title: GTA 6 réclame jusqu’à 212 Go sur PS5 : ce SSD Corsair 1 To passe à 178,87€ pour le Black Friday Amazon
articles.text:
GTA 6 sort le 19 novembre et réclame jusqu’à 212 Go d’espace libre, de quoi obliger bien des joueurs PS5 à faire le ménage. Pour le Black Friday, Amazon vend le SSD Corsair MP600 Core XT 1 To à 178,87 €, un modèle que la console accepte sur le papier, à condition de lui ajouter un dissipateur.
Le MP600 Core XT est le SSD NVMe PCIe 4.0 à prix serré de Corsair : format M.2 2280, mémoire QLC et, dans cette révision R2, jusqu’à 5 900 Mo/s annoncés en lecture. Amazon affiche la version 1 To à 178,87 €, soit 19 % sous son prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours, 219,99 €.
Le calendrier explique l’intérêt de l’offre. Le préchargement de GTA 6 s’est ouvert le 10 novembre sur PS5, et l’éditeur demande jusqu’à 212 Go d’espace libre selon la console. De quoi intéresser les joueurs qui veulent agrandir leur stockage sans effacer leur ludothèque.
Le SSD Corsair MP600 Core XT 1 To est à 178,87 € chez Amazon pour le Black Friday, contre 219,99 € au plus bas des 30 derniers jours.
Pourquoi choisir le Corsair MP600 Core XT 1 To ?
- Un débit au niveau demandé par Sony : Corsair annonce jusqu’à 5 900 Mo/s en lecture sur cette révision R2, quand Sony recommande au moins 5 500 Mo/s pour un SSD M.2 de PS5.
- 1 To pour absorber GTA 6 : Les 212 Go réclamés par le jeu occupent à peine plus d’un cinquième de la capacité. Le reste accueille vos autres titres.
- Cinq ans de garantie : Corsair couvre le SSD cinq ans, dans la limite de 250 To écrits. Ce plafond modeste correspond tout de même à plus de mille installations d’un jeu de 212 Go.
Dans une PS5 ou dans un PC, ce qu’il faut savoir avant de l’installer
Sur PS5, l’emplacement d’extension accepte les SSD M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 de 250 Go à 8 To, format 2280 compris. Le MP600 Core XT coche ces cases, mais il est livré nu : Sony exige un dissipateur thermique, à acheter en plus, pour un ensemble de 11,25 mm d’épaisseur au maximum. Corsair destine par ailleurs ce modèle aux ordinateurs et ne mentionne pas la PS5 sur sa fiche.
Dans un PC, il se glisse dans n’importe quel port M.2 2280, y compris en PCIe 3.0, au débit de cette interface. Mené en 2023 sur la version 2 To d’origine, notre test du Corsair MP600 Core XT avait relevé 44 °C au maximum sans dissipateur, mais aussi une gestion perfectible du cache lors des très longues écritures. La révision R2 vendue ici n’est pas encore passée sur notre banc de test. Pour copier chaque jour des dizaines de gigaoctets de vidéo, la mémoire QLC n’est pas le bon choix.
Face aux SSD de notre comparatif, un prix dans un marché sous tension
Le MP600 Core XT ne figure pas dans notre comparatif des meilleurs SSD, où le WD Blue SN5000 tient le rôle du meilleur choix. Son argument est ailleurs : le prix, dans une année où la pénurie de mémoire NAND a fait grimper les tarifs. Nous relevions en mai qu’un SSD NVMe 1 To Kingston NV3 était passé de 70 à 160 €. Ce Corsair n’apporte ni cache DRAM ni mémoire TLC, mais il reste sous les 180 € avec des débits de PCIe 4.0.
✅ Les points forts
- Jusqu’à 5 900 Mo/s annoncés en lecture
- Format M.2 2280 accepté par la PS5 et les PC
- Garantie de cinq ans
- Prix en baisse depuis fin octobre
❌ Les limites
- Aucun dissipateur fourni, Sony en exige un sur PS5
- Mémoire QLC sans cache DRAM
- Endurance limitée à 250 To écrits
- Révision R2 pas encore testée par nos soins
Amazon avait déjà descendu ce SSD à 189,99 € fin octobre : le Corsair MP600 Core XT 1 To s’affiche désormais à 178,87 €, à quelques jours de la sortie de GTA 6.
À 178,87 €, le Corsair MP600 Core XT 1 To répond à un besoin précis : gagner un téraoctet avant un jeu qui en réclame plus d’un cinquième à lui seul. La remise affichée mérite une nuance. Amazon la calcule sur 219,99 €, alors que nous avions déjà relayé ce SSD à 189,99 € le 28 octobre : face à ce précédent prix, le gain réel est de 11,12 €.
Pour une PS5, comptez le prix d’un dissipateur en plus, et gardez en tête que Sony ne garantit le fonctionnement d’aucun SSD tiers. Sur PC, l’installation est plus simple et le SSD convient bien à une bibliothèque de jeux. Les créateurs qui écrivent de gros volumes au quotidien regarderont plutôt un modèle TLC avec cache DRAM. Le Black Friday proprement dit tombe le 27 novembre et Amazon n’a pas encore communiqué les dates de son édition : rien ne dit que le prix bougera d’ici là.

articles.title: Louer votre PC à l'IA quand vous n'y jouez pas : Microsoft a de la suite dans les idées
articles.text:
Microsoft a déposé le 30 avril 2025 une demande de brevet publiée le 5 novembre, sous la référence US 2026/0349820 A1. Le texte décrit un système qui découpe l’entraînement de modèles d’IA en micro-tâches, distribuées aux téléphones, aux ordinateurs portables et aux PC de joueurs dont la carte graphique a de la marge. En échange, le propriétaire consentant accumule des crédits à convertir en logiciels, en accès à des modèles d’IA ou en argent, sans qu’aucun barème soit avancé.
Lire aussi : À court de cartes graphiques, Apple réquisitionne les Mac de ses employés
PilotFish, le galop d’essai de 2022
L’idée a déjà tourné en conditions réelles, sur les machines de l’éditeur. En juillet 2022, des chercheurs de Microsoft et de l’université Jiao Tong de Shanghai présentaient PilotFish, un système qui glisse des calculs d’IA dans les temps morts des serveurs de jeu en streaming. En repérant les périodes d’inactivité à l’échelle de la milliseconde, il récupérait jusqu’à 85,1 % du temps de GPU inutilisé sans dégrader l’image pour le joueur. Le logiciel ne lançait un calcul que s’il pouvait se terminer avant le retour de la partie, et l’interrompait dans le cas contraire.
La demande de brevet transpose la mécanique chez les particuliers, avec les garde-fous que le changement d’échelle impose. Le système surveille la température, la mémoire et la consommation, puis réduit ou suspend les calculs quand la machine est occupée ou chauffe. Chaque tâche est taillée selon la puissance de l’appareil, du téléphone d’appoint à la tour de joueur, et selon son historique de disponibilité. Les résultats sont enfin recoupés entre machines, pondérés par la fiabilité passée de chacune. La logique rappelle celle du covoiturage : la place libre est occupée, le trajet du conducteur reste prioritaire.
Rien n’indique qu’un service en découle puisque le texte garde le statut d’une demande en instance d’examen. Ni Windows ni Xbox n’ont annoncé de produit qui pourrait y être associé.
Des crédits contre des kilowattheures
Aucun montant ne figure dans le dossier, et l’électricité, elle, a un prix connu : 0,2001 euro le kilowattheure au tarif réglementé depuis le 1er août. Une carte qui tire 250 watts quatre heures par jour consomme environ 30 kWh par mois, soit 6 euros à couvrir avant le premier centime de gain. L’hypothèse d’usage reste illustrative, la demande ne chiffrant ni cadence ni durée. Le vrai coût se mesurera en consommation supplémentaire, celle que la machine n’aurait jamais tirée sans ces calculs, veille comprise.
Lire aussi : Le patron d’OpenAI juge « terrible » que votre PC garde sa propre RAM et préfèrerait la voir dans ses datacenters
Le scénario vient d’être joué côté Mac, bien qu’Apple n’y soit pas associé. Cet été, louer sa machine à l’IA pendant la nuit faisait miroiter jusqu’à 200 dollars par mois, et un internaute français avait mesuré l’opération de bout en bout, du jeton facturé au watt consommé. Deux mois plus tard, la société à l’origine de l’offre prévenait ses participants que les gains resteraient maigres, sans hausse en vue.

Secretlab debuts monitor light bar add-on to reduce glare and eye strain — ErgoArch has a three-point adjustment arm, costs $179
Light up your monitor
Popular gaming chair and gaming desk manufacturer Secretlab has today unveiled its new ErgoArch monitor lightbar, a new lightbar attachment for owners of its Secretlab monitor arm and a complement to its desk ecosystem. Available now, the new lightbar costs $179.
For owners or prospective buyers of the Secretlab Magnus Monitor Arm (the light bar is an attachment to this accessory), the ErgoArch provides overhead lighting for your desk and monitor, reducing reflections and glare, and smoothing out brightness contrast between your display and workspace. Monitor light bars are generally designed to reduce eye strain while you're working or gaming, while also providing some snazzy ambient lighting; the ErgoArch is no different.
Secretlab says the ErgoArch provides both ultrawide illumination and focused task lighting depending on how you set it up. The lighting itself is smart and can be powered by Nanoleaf, giving you access via your smart home app to 16.8 million colors. There's also a dedicated wireless control puck, and the lighting temperature ranges from 2700K to 6500K.
The light itself is mounted to the monitor arm via a three-point adjustment arm and is compatible with any VESA-mounted monitor, including curved displays. There's also a magnetic webcam mount attachment. Power is provided by USB-C, so you don't need a wall outlet or extension socket to switch it on.
Available globally, the ErgoArch is available to buy from Secretlab now for $179.

articles.title: La Unión Europea prohibirá los falsos contadores de stock y las suscripciones difíciles de cancelar
articles.text:
La Comisión Europea prohibiría los contadores falsos de stock, las casillas ya marcadas para comprar extras y los trámites laberínticos para dar de baja una suscripción, según un borrador de la Ley de Equidad Digital. Las empresas que incumplan arriesgarían multas de hasta 6% de su facturación mundial anual, informó Reuters.
El comisario de Justicia, Michael McGrath, presentará la propuesta el miércoles 11 de noviembre. Después deberá negociarla con los países miembros y con el Parlamento Europeo antes de que se convierta en ley, y ambos podrán modificar el alcance de las prohibiciones y el nivel de las sanciones.
Hasta ahora se conoce el borrador, no el texto oficial. Agence Europe indicó que sería un reglamento, es decir, una norma que se aplica directamente en todos los países de la Unión Europea, y que reemplazaría la directiva de 2005 sobre prácticas comerciales desleales.
La norma alcanzaría a cualquier tienda o servicio en línea, no solo a las grandes plataformas, según Agence Europe. La Comisión recibiría además poder para investigar y sancionar de forma directa.
Diez prácticas quedarían prohibidas sin más trámite
El anexo del borrador, citado por Agence Europe, enumera diez prácticas de diseño engañoso (dark patterns, en inglés). Entre ellas figuran los contadores que simulan cuántas unidades quedan o cuántas personas compraron un producto, las notificaciones falsas, las ventanas emergentes insistentes y las casillas premarcadas. Se prohibirían sin que haya que probar un daño en cada caso.
Las suscripciones también tendrían reglas propias. Cuando un contrato dure seis meses o más, la empresa deberá avisar de la renovación entre un mes y 14 días antes, y ofrecer un botón de baja visible en su sitio o aplicación, según Agence Europe.
Los medios que leyeron el borrador agregan otros cambios. Quienes vendan entradas con precios que varían según la demanda tendrían que informar cuántas quedan en cada categoría y el precio máximo que podría pagar el comprador, según Rapporteur. El borrador no prohíbe esa práctica.
Las promociones de personas influyentes pagadas por una marca deberían llevar una etiqueta como “publicidad” o “colaboración comercial”, según el mismo medio.
Niños, videos automáticos y cuánto se puede multar
El borrador prohíbe la publicidad personalizada dirigida a menores y a consumidores vulnerables, según Reuters. Rapporteur añade que también quedaría vedado cobrar precios personalizados a niños. En los videojuegos, las monedas virtuales vendrían desactivadas por defecto para menores y las cajas de recompensa al azar quedarían prohibidas, según Agence Europe.
Las plataformas cuyas funciones incentiven un uso compulsivo tendrían que permitir apagarlas, una por una o todas juntas. Agence Europe cita como ejemplos, la reproducción automática de contenido y las funciones que premian volver a la aplicación a horas fijas. El texto no exige que vengan apagadas de fábrica.
Las cifras de sanciones aparecen con matices según el medio. Agence Europe y Reuters hablan de multas de hasta 6% de la facturación mundial. Rapporteur precisa que el tope general sería de 4% de los ingresos en los países afectados, y que el 6% se reservaría para infracciones generalizadas en varios países, por medio de otro reglamento de cooperación entre autoridades de consumo.
Un estudio de revisión de la normativa europea, citado por el Servicio de Estudios del Parlamento Europeo, calculó el daño anual a los consumidores por prácticas digitales problemáticas en 7.900 millones de euros, y lo describió como una estimación prudente. En la consulta pública previa, el 69% de los participantes dijo haber tenido dificultades para cancelar un contrato en línea.
Las organizaciones de consumidores y las empresas difieren. La Organización Europea de Consumidores pide que cancelar renovaciones automáticas sea fácil, según el medio Poland Insight. La asociación empresarial DOT Europe reclama coherencia con las leyes vigentes, como la de servicios digitales, y más control sobre las ya existentes.

articles.title: Anker MagGo 3-en-1 : ce socle qui recharge iPhone, Apple Watch et AirPods perd 35 €
articles.text:
Le chargeur à induction 3-en-1 Anker MagGo est à 49,99 € (-41 %)
iPhone, Apple Watch et écouteurs sur un même socle orientable : le chargeur à induction Anker MagGo 3-en-1 passe à 49,99 € chez Amazon, soit 35 € de moins qu'habituellement.
Vendu par AnkerDirect et expédié par Amazon, ce chargeur affiche 49,99 € contre 84,99 € pour le prix conseillé, soit une remise de 41 % dans le cadre des offres pré-Black Friday d'Amazon. C'est aussi 35 € de moins que son plus bas prix des 30 derniers jours (84,99 €).
Trois appareils rechargés sur un seul socle

articles.title: iPhone 18 et 18e : Apple pourrait rendre le choix plus difficile entre ses deux prochains modèles
articles.text:
Les iPhone 18 et 18e pourraient avoir davantage en commun que leur nom. Une nouvelle fuite évoque deux rapprochements qui compliqueraient le choix entre le modèle standard et sa déclinaison plus abordable.
Pas d’iPhone 18 de base cette année. Apple a choisi de modifier son calendrier et de repousser ces modèles grand public à 2027, afin de laisser toute la place à l’iPhone 18 Pro et surtout à son premier smartphone pliant, l'iPhone Duo. Malgré ce report, le développement se poursuit et de nouvelles informations suggèrent qu’Apple pourrait réduire l’écart entre son iPhone 18 et l’iPhone 18e, le modèle d’entrée de gamme qui est lui aussi attendu pour le début de l’année prochaine.
Une même batterie et des écrans de même taille
Selon les informations de Fixed Focus Digital sur le réseau social Weibo, les iPhone 18 et 18e pourraient tous deux recevoir une batterie de 4 430 mAh et un écran de 6,3 pouces, contre 6,1 pouces pour l’iPhone 17e.
Les différences concerneraient le sujet de la photo. L’objectif ultra grand-angle resterait réservé à l’iPhone 18, dont l’appareil photo principal conserverait une définition de 48 mégapixels malgré une réduction de la taille du module évoquée par la fuite. L’iPhone 18e ne posséderait qu’un seul capteur, comme c’est le cas aujourd’hui de l'iPhone 17e, qui vise des utilisateurs souhaitant une caméra à tout faire pour des clichés rapides.
Sur le papier, le modèle le plus abordable récupérerait tout de même deux caractéristiques importantes de son grand frère. Une diagonale identique offrirait notamment une surface d’affichage comparable, même si elle ne dit rien de la fluidité ou de la qualité respective des deux dalles.
Pour la batterie, quelques précautions s’imposent. AppleInsider relève que le schéma à l’origine de ces informations mentionne plusieurs capacités, avec un maximum commun de 4 430 mAh. Nous ne nous avancerons donc pas plus et mieux vaut donc retenir une capacité pouvant atteindre ce chiffre, plutôt qu’une batterie identique garantie pour toutes les versions. Et même à capacité égale, l’autonomie réelle dépendrait de la consommation de chaque appareil.
L’iPhone 18 devra justifier sa différence pour convaincre les utilisateurs
Ce rapprochement entre les deux modèles ne sortirait pas complètement de nulle part. Une précédente fuite attribuait aux deux smartphones la même génération de processeur, l’A20. Comme de tradition chez Apple si l’on regarde l’ancienne gamme iPhone SE, l’iPhone 18e ne rognerait pas sur les performances, et préférerait faire des économies sur le design ou les composants, plutôt que de sacrifier l’expérience utilisateur.
Une autre question reste en suspens : quid de l’encoche ? L'iPhone 17e est le dernier modèle à l’arborer, et un changement de dalle pourrait inciter à Apple à la proposer sur son iPhone le plus abordable, ne serait-ce que pour harmoniser le développement d'iOS.
Il faudra vraisemblablement attendre le printemps 2027 pour répondre à ces questions. Reste que si ces informations se confirment, la comparaison entre les deux prochains iPhone 18 risque de compliquer la tâche des futurs acheteurs ? Privilégier le coût et se passer d’un deuxième capteur photo, ou rajouter 200 € pour profiter d’un produit plus complet ? Les prochains candidats au renouvellement ont encore quelques semaines pour se faire leur avis.

articles.title: The Seestar S30 Plus could be the biggest bargain in astrophotography — compact smart telescope is ideal for beginner stargazers and packs dual 2K sensors, four-element APO optics with ED glass and built-in duo-band filters, but weighs a mere 1.65kg
articles.text:
The Seestar S30 Plus could be the biggest bargain in astrophotography — compact smart telescope is ideal for beginner stargazers and packs dual 2K sensors, four-element APO optics with ED glass and built-in duo-band filters, but weighs a mere 1.65kg
Start your astrophotography journey here
- The Seestar S30 Plus has dual 2K cameras for shooting galaxies, nebulae and the Milky Way
- It's available today, priced at $499 / €499
- It looks like a big upgrade over the S30 and a great first smart telescope
Astrophotographers have never had it so good. Smart telescopes have completely changed the game, making it far easier and cheaper to photograph the night skies — and the new Seestar S30 Plus could be the perfect entry into the hobby.
Technically it slots into Seestar’s ever-expanding lineup between the S30 and S30 Pro models, but it’s effectively a replacement for the no-longer-available base model, offering Pro-level optics at a much lower price.
That price? A mere $499 / €499, compared to $699 for the S30 Pro and $999 for the bigger S50 Pro; I don't have UK pricing, but expect it to be around £450.
And you get a lot for your money: dual 2K (1440 x 2560) cameras with quality optics — one telephoto, one wide-angle — built-in duo-band filters, an included solar filter, tripod and carrying case.
Importantly, it’s also small and light enough to be easily transportable: it weighs just 1.65kg and could easily be slung in a backpack for a hike to a high spot with clear views of the skies.
It’s all controlled by Seestar’s slick and full-featured app, which does most of the heavy lifting for you and which contains a massive database of breathtaking objects to photograph.
Simply select your target and the S30 Plus will position itself and start snapping away, with the resulting image viewable on your phone screen and getting more detailed over time as the software stacks multiple images.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
“Many people are interested in astrophotography but hesitate when they see the equipment and setup traditionally involved,” says Sam Wen, Seestar’s founder.
“With S30 Plus, we wanted to give beginners more room to explore and create without taking away the simplicity that makes Seestar easy to start with. It brings more imaging possibilities into one compact system, so users can spend less time thinking about equipment and more time exploring the night sky.”
Analysis: Beginners start here
I’ve owned and tested several Seestar models, including the original S50 — which reignited my love of astrophotography a decade after I’d all but given up on it because it was too time-consuming.
The S50 was a revelation, enabling me to spend far, far less time fiddling around with arcane software seemingly designed for masochists and far more time taking photos of galaxies and nebulae.
The S30 Pro was even better, with a higher-resolution sensor, wide-angle view and improved build quality in a super-compact and lightweight package. I loved it so much I declared it my favorite smart telescope earlier this year.
So, where does the S30 Plus fit in? Well, it's best thought of as offering the S30 Pro's optics in a cheaper package that represents a big upgrade over the original S30.
For instance, the telephoto camera has a larger 1/1.8-inch sensor and will give you bigger 2K (1440 x 2560) images versus the full HD shots on the older model. As with its more expensive sibling the S30 Pro, it has four-element apochromatic (APO) optics with ED glass — meaning images should be sharper — and comes with a wide-angle camera for grabbing Milky Way shots, a feature that was missing on the original.
There are a few compromises of course. Chief among them are the fact that its dual cameras are 2K rather than 4K as they are in the Pro, and that you can't use the wide-angle camera at the same time as the telephoto one. You also get half the storage: 64GB versus 128GB.
However, the $200 price difference is substantial enough that beginners may well be better going for the S30 Plus and then upgrading to the much bigger S50 Pro when they're ready for the next step. It's certainly a far more exciting prospect than the original S30, which I always thought was a little too basic.
ZWO, which makes the Seestar smart telescopes, has shared some sample images shot on the S30 Plus and I'm impressed. You can check out some of the shots below:
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The images are a mixture of straight-from-camera stacks and some that have been processed using specialist astrophotography software; they may also have been taken in darker skies than those which you have access to — so don't take it as a given that you'll get these results, or at least not without putting in a bit of effort.
But that caveat aside, they look great — there's plenty of detail in the likes of the Rosette and Heart nebula, while it's nice to see that Andromeda fits neatly into the frame without the need to use Mosaic mode.
Speaking of which, it's worth noting that you can't make mosaics with the wide-angle camera, but given that it has a 43.5-degree field of view you don't really need to do that. Mosaic is much more important for the telephoto camera, which has a 3-degree FOV, enabling you to capture larger targets such as the Heart nebula in one shot.
The Seestar S30 Plus is available to buy today and I'll be putting it through its paces for a full test once the skies over southern England finally lift. Look out for my verdict on it soon.

articles.title: Hedra's new Model Factory cranks up the production volume for physical AI model training - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Hedra’s new Model Factory cranks up the production volume for physical AI model training
Autonomous artificial intelligence agents have been a massive hit in the digital realm, and now a startup called Hedra Inc. is hoping to take the next step with physical AI systems that can automate tasks in the real world too.
The company today announced the Hedra Model Factory, a new post-training and inference platform that enables the recursive self-improvement of AI models, or RSI for short, designed specifically to power autonomous robots and other machines.
Hedra says that physical AI requires a very different and more specialized form of intelligence that can enable robots and other real-world hardware systems to perform very specific tasks, such as packing irregular-shaped parcels onto palettes. One of the main challenges of physical AI is that each robot and each task it performs requires a different model.
But training all of those models is not feasible, given the vast amounts of data required to create them. That’s why Hedra wants to use RSI to adapt existing models to new tasks.
RSI is a relatively new technique in AI that describes systems that can autonomously evaluate, train and then improve their own architectures. There has been a lot of research into these systems in frontier AI labs, but until now no one has managed to apply that continuous loop to the physical world.
The challenge is that physical AI models require massive volumes of multimodal data inputs, from sources such as high-resolution video, sensor feeds and 3D simulations. Running RSI against such enormous data environments simply is not practical given the staggering compute costs such an operation would incur.
Hedra says its Model Factory changes that. It’s an autonomous training pipeline offered as a service that’s designed for robotics, manufacturing, biology and defense workloads, pairing Hedra’s in-house research teams with AI agents that orchestrate the training runs, curate the data and iterate autonomously according to the customer’s specifications.
Hedra founder and Chief Executive Michael Lingelbach (pictured) told SiliconANGLE that RSI has already had a major impact on the way frontier models are developed. He believes that the next big frontier is physical AI, where the data primarily comes from video feeds, sensor readings and simulations. “Hedra Model Factory gives robotics, manufacturing, biology and defense teams the infrastructure to post-train, deploy and keep improving their own models,” he promised.
A production line for physical AI
Lingelbach, a former reinforcement learning researcher for visual and physical systems at Stanford University and Nvidia Corp., said what his company has developed is basically an end-to-end production platform for physical AI models. The customer provides the base model, uploads their proprietary simulation and video data, which is then provisioned within a flexible graphics processing unit sandbox environment powered by its proprietary inference engine.
The RSI process then begins, with Hedra’s researchers keeping close tabs on its progress. Lingelbach said they use vision-language models to score data and provide live reinforcement learning feedback in order to continuously optimize the model to perform the task specified by the customer. Once done, customers can then deploy the model on-premises in their own systems, or with one of Hedra’s cloud data center partners.
The models can also be distilled to run on edge systems for lower-latency workloads. Once they’re up and running, they feed data back into the customer’s sandboxed environment, creating an autonomous flywheel that continuously optimizes the model, making it better over time.
Hedra has worked hard to validate the system. For instance, it retrained MiniMax Group Inc.’s open-weight H3 video model to enhance its physical consistency, creating a distilled version that bumped up its score on the Physics-IQ benchmark from 30.3 to 34.9. In another training run, the startup was able to distill the Krea 3 2K image generation model from 30 sampling steps to just 14 while reducing latency from 22 seconds to just 3.6 seconds, a sixfold speed boost that took just one week to achieve.
Lingelbach said Hedra’s ultimate goal is to help create the thousands of bespoke, cost-effective models needed to usher in the physical AI revolution by optimizing training as much as possible. With RSI, sometimes it’s possible to bypass the retraining process altogether. In one example, Hedra demonstrated that it was able to swap out a robot’s gripper with a new one and restore its task success rate to 100% without any additional training, simply by mapping the new hardware’s reach and grasp metrics to the robot’s wrist camera view.
The Hedra Model Factory service is available today, giving enterprises the option to bypass compute-intensive training and quickly develop the specialized autonomous systems needed to bring intelligence into real-world environments.

articles.title: NZXT Launches H7 and H5 Cases in Single-Piece Curved Glass, Plus Kraken Coolers
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 10th 2026
NZXT Launches H7 and H5 Cases in Single-Piece Curved Glass, Plus Kraken Coolers
NZXT, a leading brand in PC gaming components and prebuilt systems, today launched new generations of two case lines and two liquid coolers: the H7 and H7 RGB+, the H5 and H5 RGB+, the Kraken Plus 360 RGB, and the Kraken Core 360 and 420. On the H7 and H5, the front and left side are a single-formed panel of curved tempered glass. There is no corner seam where two flat sheets meet, so nothing interrupts the view of the build. Holding a formed curve through tempering is a tolerance problem, which is why the corner seam is the usual answer. On the H7, a tempered glass top cut to the same radius comes fitted as standard, carrying the glass from front to side to top. NZXT calls that Vista Mode.
Both coolers are Cooled by Asetek, on a copper cold-plate. The Kraken Plus puts a customizable display on the pump cap; the Kraken Core is the version with nothing to manage. "The H7, H5 and Kraken are the heart of our lineup, and they're where most NZXT builds start. This generation refreshes all of them at once: single-piece curved glass across both mid-towers, and an Asetek pump in both new Krakens. We're also adding new case features builders haven't seen from us before, like Vista Mode and the Airflow Scoop," said Johnny Hou, CEO at NZXT.H7 and H7 RGB+ The H7 is the larger of the two mid-towers.
- Vista Mode fitted as standard, on both models: The tempered glass top is cut to the same radius as the front-to-side curve. The glass runs unbroken across three faces, and the build reads as one piece from above.
- A swappable top, with both panels in the box: A steel mesh top panel and its own fan bracket ship alongside the glass. The same chassis converts between a glass showcase and an airflow build without buying a part.
- Made to show off: An angled bracket turns the bottom fans out toward the glass, and vertical GPU mounting, with the kit sold separately, turns the graphics card the same way. A lit NZXT logo (white LED) sits on the side panel.
- A cleaner build from the start: Back-connect motherboard support puts every power connector behind the tray, and a dedicated channel routes AIO tubing out of the sightline.
- Room for the biggest hardware: A graphics card up to 495 mm (with a 30 mm front-right fan) sits on an integrated adjustable anti-sag bracket, beside a CPU cooler up to 188 mm. Up to 10 fan mounts with the mesh top. E-ATX is no longer supported.
- H7 RGB+ ships with its lighting installed: Two F420 RGB Reverse single-frame fans, one F140 RGB fan and a Control Hub Lite arrive installed and wired, ready to tune in NZXT CAM. The H7 ships without fans.
H5 and H5 RGB+The H5 brings the same curved glass to a compact mid-tower.
- One formed panel, front to side: The front and left side are one piece of glass. The H5 vents through a steel mesh top that keeps every top mount; the H5
- RGB+ closes it in Vista Mode glass for a view straight down into the build.
- The Airflow Scoop side intake: The side intake is shaped into the panel. It reads as a line in the form of the case and draws air in across the graphics card. Identical on both models.
- H5 RGB+ ships factory-wired: An F360 RGB Reverse single-frame fan in the bottom, an F120 RGB fan at the rear, and a Control Hub Lite arrive installed and wired. The H5 ships without fans. Both models support vertical GPU mounting, with the kit sold separately.
- Built clean, inside and out: Back-connect motherboard support hides the power connectors behind the tray, and the curved glass, right side and top panels come off by hand. The front I/O carries USB-C, two USB-A ports and a headset jack.
- Room for the build you want: A graphics card up to 420 mm on an adjustable anti-sag bracket and a triple-fan radiator on either model. The H5 RGB+ takes its radiator on the right side with no top mount.
Kraken Plus 360 RGBThe Kraken Plus 360 RGB comes in Black or White.
- Cooled by Asetek: Asetek's new Gen 9 pump works against a copper cold plate, with a suspended impeller that keeps vibration from reaching the case.
- A display that is the pump cap: The 1.8-inch screen fills the cap edge to edge and shows images, GIFs or live system data, set in NZXT CAM. Its orientation is adjustable in software, so it stays upright however the block is mounted.
- Three fans, one frame: The included F360 RGB single-frame fan is one unit—two cables to route rather than three fans to mount, with lighting across the whole frame.
- An aluminium radiator on braided tubing: A 360 mm aluminium radiator on EPDM tubing in a nylon braided sleeve that keeps the lines tidy and bends to a
- tight route.
- Ready in minutes: Thermal paste is pre-applied to the cold plate, and universal mounting covers current Intel and AMD sockets.
Kraken Core 360 and Kraken Core 420
The Kraken Core comes in 360 mm and 420 mm, in Black, with the same cap, pump and cold plate on both.
- Cooled by Asetek: Asetek's new Gen 9 V pump is built to run quiet, with a pump design that keeps vibration from reaching the case.
- Concentric rings under a semi-transparent cap: The cap reveals rings layered inside rather than printing a pattern on the outside, and the magnetic NZXT logo face piece offers 4-way orientation, sitting upright in any mount.
- One fan, one cable: A single-frame static pressure fan tuned for dense radiator fins—three 120 mm fans on the 360, three 140 mm on the 420, on one cable. No hubs and no controllers.
- An aluminium radiator on braided tubing: The nylon sleeve keeps the lines tidy and the tubing bends to a tight route, all in black.
- Straight into any build: Pre-applied thermal paste, a direct connection to the motherboard and broad Intel and AMD socket support.
Also Announced November 10
- F360Q and F420Q Quiet Airflow fans: Single-frame kits that combine three fans in one frame on fluid dynamic bearings, in Black or White.
- C1200 Platinum ATX 3.1 power supply: Certified Platinum by 80 Plus and Cybenetics, fully modular, with a fan that stops under light load.
- Vertical GPU Mounting Kit PCIe 5.0: A 175 mm riser tested for full PCIe 5.0 signal integrity, on a steel anti-sag bracket anchored to the motherboard.
Availability and Pricing
- Availability: Rolling out to retailers globally starting November 10, 2026. Timing varies by region; see nzxt.com/retailers for where to buy.
- Colors: Black and White across the range, except the Kraken Core 360 and 420, which are Black only

articles.title: Google DeepMind usó IA para verificar matemáticamente la seguridad del cifrado de Signal
articles.text:
Investigadores de Google DeepMind usaron inteligencia artificial para demostrar con matemáticas varias garantías clave del protocolo criptográfico de Signal, la tecnología que protege los mensajes de esa aplicación. Según informó Wired, el proyecto duró cuatro semanas y no encontró vulnerabilidades nuevas en las partes analizadas.
El trabajo usó un sistema nuevo de la compañía llamado AlphaProof Code. Los investigadores lo describen como una prueba de concepto, es decir, un ensayo para mostrar que la idea funciona antes de aplicarla a gran escala.
La técnica se llama verificación formal: en lugar de probar un programa con ejemplos y esperar que no falle, se escribe en lenguaje matemático lo que el programa debe cumplir y se demuestra que lo cumple. Para quienes trabajan en seguridad informática, según Wired, es una meta largamente buscada.
Hasta ahora, describir esas propiedades y armar la demostración consumía mucho tiempo de especialistas. Un agente de IA, un asistente que ejecuta tareas por su cuenta, acorta sobre todo la segunda parte, la de construir la prueba.
Qué se comprobó y qué quedó fuera
El análisis no incluyó toda la aplicación móvil de Signal, sino ciertas garantías de su protocolo. Los investigadores también probaron la herramienta con versiones antiguas de Signal que tenían fallas conocidas y ya corregidas: el sistema las detectó y mostró que esas versiones no podían verificarse.
DeepMind publicará la especificación y la demostración que desarrolló, para que otros equipos las usen en trabajos similares. Los investigadores reconocieron que partieron con ventaja, porque la Signal Foundation ya había hecho verificaciones formales sobre porciones más pequeñas del código.
Ese trabajo previo forma parte de un proyecto público llamado Signal Shot, lanzado el 20 de abril de 2026 por la Beneficial AI Foundation, Signal y el grupo Lean FRO, según el sitio del proyecto. Su objetivo es verificar el protocolo y la aplicación completa con el asistente de demostraciones Lean.
El protocolo de Signal también sirve de base al cifrado de WhatsApp y de Google Messages. Por eso, según Wired, el resultado funciona como una validación independiente de la criptografía que protege una enorme cantidad de comunicaciones.
Las voces de DeepMind y de Signal
Ehren Kret, director de tecnología de Signal, afirmó en un comunicado que el enfoque de DeepMind permite una expansión significativa frente a los trabajos anteriores, centrados en partes más pequeñas. Dijo que verificar la implementación da “aún más confianza” en las garantías de privacidad del código, en un contexto de amenazas de seguridad impulsadas por IA.
Swarat Chaudhuri, investigador de DeepMind, fue prudente con el alcance. “Falta mucho para poder escalar esto a todo el software del mundo, y queremos hacerlo”, dijo a Wired. También explicó que el método combina agentes y revisión humana en los momentos clave, y que el equipo no quiere un esquema en el que la IA genere las metas y las pruebas sin control.
Pushmeet Kohli, científico jefe de Google Cloud y vicepresidente de investigación de DeepMind, planteó un posible uso: bancos y otras empresas que dependen de la ausencia de errores podrían decir que pueden probar ciertas propiedades de su software.
La duda que queda abierta es el costo. DeepMind hizo el análisis de Signal sin cargo, como proyecto de investigación, y Google no quiso revelar cuánto costó. La compañía tampoco dijo si planea lanzar un producto o servicio comercial de verificación formal.

articles.title: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery | TechCrunch
articles.text:
David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.
“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”
The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.
The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.
More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.
“A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”
That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.
“An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”
For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies.
“Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines said. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.”
Still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the startup Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation.
“At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world … nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible.
“If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before … and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.”
As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this new world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it.
“As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, said. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.”
“We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who said the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”

articles.title: New framework grades AI jailbreaks across capability gains, scope, and how easy they are to deploy — Frontier Model Forum proposes CVSS-style rating system for new AI models
articles.text:
New framework grades AI jailbreaks across capability gains, scope, and how easy they are to deploy — Frontier Model Forum proposes CVSS-style rating system for new AI models
One ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
In recent months, high-profile headlines about AI models letting loose from their safeguards dominated headlines. Now, the Frontier Model Forum (FMF) has released a new Jailbreak Rating Framework that aims to track how easy it might be for a given AI model to get around safeguards. The framework also estimates the scale of the collateral damage, should an AI model wreak cyber-havoc across the internet.
The project started in 2023 with the support of four founding companies: Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. The published Jailbreak Rating Framework is a rough analog to the well-known CVSS security rating system, but specifically targeted at classifying the type and severity of LLM jailbreaks across various axes and multiple frontier LLM providers.
Many AI companies and evaluation entities already have their own rating systems, but the FMF intends for its scale to be a cross-vendor standard that teams developing patches can rely on.
The FMF's approach is to have a classification method for jailbreaks that can make a model perform cyber-warfare operations beyond what's already out, across both the regular and black market. Version 1.0 of the proposal is a work-in-progress, and the group is taking comments and suggestions on it until December 21, noting that relying on its system in the meantime is inadvisable.
Right now, the framework has four scoring components, split across two main categories: severity, measuring how serious a jailbreak technique is, and likelihood, or how easy it is to find and weaponize it.
A combined final rating adds the scores obtained from the two categories into a final low-to-critical rating. The scientists note that the capability gain is the most important dimension and acts as both a floor and a ceiling for the remaining scores — a jailbreak that doesn't offer results beyond what can already be obtained via other means is meaningless within the purview of the grading system.
The individual ratings pertain to capability gains, capability scope, ease of deployment, and ease of discovery. They're all graded from zero to three, though the FMF stresses that a rating of zero doesn't mean a jailbreak is harmless or ought to be ignored — rather, it means the flaw should be addressed by standard practices like the platform's policies and standard cybersecurity ratings.
An important feature is that the FMF's baseline implicitly changes as models evolve, meaning that a grade of zero for a jailbreak in 2026 likely isn't going to mean the same thing as it would in 2028, or isn't better than alternative tools. A capability-gain rating of zero means that the jailbreak under analysis doesn't offer any improvement beyond what can already be done with existing models or tooling right off the bat.
For example, jailbreaking a model to perform a DDoS on a site isn't all that helpful to an attacker, since there are a number of black-market sites for that — or even other LLMs with fewer safeguards. This doesn't mean the jailbreak isn't handy, only that it's no better than the alternatives. However, the rating can be higher if the attacker can leverage the jailbreak to get a better DDoS than they could otherwise shop for.
On the other end of the capability-gain scale, three means that a jailbroken model can perform cyber-attacks with capabilities similar to those of a model operating without safeguards.
The capability scope measurement is easier to interpret: zero means that the jailbreak only works for one specific action or target and can't be tweaked for other applications, or in other words, is a one-trick pony. A jailbreak gets a rating of three when it can, without specific redesign, make a model perform work across at least two entirely unrelated categories of cyber-warfare — like getting the model to both autonomously discover vulnerabilities or, separately, write malware.
For ease of deployment, the FMF considers the amount of human interaction, or the degree of automation that the jailbreak allows. A zero means that the jailbreak must be steered by humans with a high degree of knowledge, providing additional instructions to be effective, while a three means that, with little effort, it can be used by a novice and results in an automated cyber-warfare task.
Last but by no means least, ease-of-discovery is how hard it is to find the jailbreak. At a zero, the attacker must spend copious amounts of money on inference tokens, need elevated access (like a privileged account given to a white-hat hacker), or specialized infrastructure like a legion of AI servers. A rating of three simply means that anyone can look up the technique and use it.
If all of this sounds familiar, you may be thinking of Anthropic's safeguard-breakage classifiers the company proposed in July 2026, after an incident that led to Claude Fable 5 being temporarily unavailable. Much like the FMF's effort, Anthropic's system would also use a moving baseline and only consider jailbreaks that improve on cyber-warfare capabilities already available.
That document is strikingly similar to FMF's proposal. Anthropic is an FMF founding member, and as such may have had a hand or two in developing the new standard — though we have no confirmation either way.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Chrome : le mode Incognito va lui aussi vous empêcher de visiter un site frauduleux
articles.text:
Google ne rate jamais une occasion de rappeler que son navigateur Chrome vérifie en temps réel la dangerosité des sites visités par ses utilisateurs. Mais ce dispositif n’est pas disponible en navigation privée, ni en mode invité. Les choses devraient prochainement changer.
Selon la documentation de Google, la navigation privée de Chrome ne bénéficie pas toujours des mêmes vérifications Safe Browsing que la navigation classique. Elle se contente d’une liste stockée sur l’appareil.
Pourquoi la liste locale ne suffit pas face à des sites éphémères
Safe Browsing repose sur deux mécanismes. Le premier est une liste d’adresses connues comme dangereuses (hameçonnage, logiciels malveillants), stockée sur l’appareil. Le second est une vérification en temps réel. Dans ce cas, Chrome interroge Google pour savoir si l’adresse visitée figure parmi les menaces recensées à cet instant. Avec la protection standard, réglage par défaut, le navigateur consulte d’abord une liste locale de sites réputés sûrs avant de lancer cette requête, laquelle passe par un serveur de confidentialité chargé de masquer l'adresse IP de l’utilisateur.
En mode Incognito, Chrome peut se replier sur la seule liste locale des sites dangereux. Pour éviter de se faire repérer, de nombreux sites malveillants restent en ligne moins de 10 minutes. Or Google précisait par le passé que cette liste est actualisée toutes les 30 à 60 minutes. Une page d’hameçonnage peut donc apparaître et disparaître entre deux mises à jour. Google avait déjà ajouté à Safe Browsing une vérification en temps réel des adresses visitées, sur ordinateur et sur iPhone, pour réduire cet écart.
Le changement couvrirait la protection standard comme la protection renforcée. Cette dernière ajoute des garde-fous contre les sites, téléchargements et extensions dangereux, mais… au prix d’un partage d’informations plus large avec Google. Alors forcément, en navigation privée, ces vérifications supplémentaires posent une question de confidentialité. De leur côté, les développeurs semblent avoir prévu une parade. Les données de sécurité temporaires générées pendant une session Incognito resteraient en mémoire vive, sans être écrites sur le disque. Aucune information de sécurité propre à la session privée ne doit donc rester stockée sur l’appareil.
Rappelons que le mode Incognito ne rend pas anonyme pour autant. Les sites visités et les administrateurs d’un réseau peuvent observer l’activité, même si Chrome ne la conserve pas dans l’historique. Nous évoquions d’ailleurs un autre chantier sur ce mode, le test d'un blocage du fingerprinting par canvas, une technique de pistage qui exploite les différences de rendu graphique d'un appareil à l’autre. La vérification en temps réel, elle, reste en développement et désactivée par défaut derrière un réglage expérimental de Chrome (un flag). Google n’a communiqué aucune date de disponibilité.
- Navigation rapide
- Écosystème d'extensions très riche
- Synchronisation multi-appareils fluide
Source : DigitalTrends

articles.title: Google tuvo el mejor modelo de IA durante trece días. Anthropic se lo quitó y la respuesta ha tardado 24 horas
articles.text:
La guerra por conseguir el mejor modelo de IA es una pelea constante entre las grandes empresas que mueven el cotarro. Google es un peso pesado del segmento, por más que sus modelos hayan quedado ligeramente por detrás de la competencia. Por eso ha pisado el acelerador: la llegada de Gemini 4 Carbon implica plantarle cara a Anthropic, OpenAI y xAI en los modelos de frontera.
Un trono de trece días. Pese a que Google acaba de anunciar la llegada de Carbon al público general, el modelo lleva casi medio mes al alcance de algunas empresas y analistas de seguridad (a través de su programa Fairwind). Durante esos trece días, Gemini 4 Carbon ha estado en lo más alto de los benchmarks. Al menos hasta que ayer sacó Anthropic su Fable 5.2.
Anthropic incluyó a Gemini 4 Carbon en la comparativa con la que presentó Fable 5.2. Así queda la pelea entre ambos, siempre con los datos de la dueña de Claude.
| Prueba | Gemini 4 Carbon | Claude Fable 5.2 | 
|---|---|---|
| FrontierCode 2.0 (programación agéntica) | 41,1 % | 49,1 % | 
| FrontierSWE v2 | 61,2 % | 69,9 % | 
| AutomationBench (flujos de negocio) | 53,9 % | 51,4 % | 
| Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 | 64,8 % | 74,6 % | 
| OSWorld 2.1 (uso de ordenador) | 81,5 % | 89,3 % | 
| Chartography (lectura de gráficos) | 72,5 % | 73,4 % | 
| Índice de Vals v2.2 | 70,45 % | 71,31 % | 
| Índice de inteligencia de Artificial Analysis | 59 | 65 | 
Google mueve ficha. Tenía el trono con Carbon y Anthropic se lo quitó con Fable 5.2. La ventaja de la dueña de Claude es que puso directamente el nuevo modelo en manos de todos los usuarios de pago, un movimiento que ha permitido probar las novedades con un rango de uso bastante holgado (y con un reinicio de regalo, al menos en las cuentas Pro). Google parece que se ha visto obligada a hacer más o menos lo mismo.
Carbon está ya disponible para suscriptores de la IA de Google a través de distintos caminos:
- API de Gemini en Google AI Studio: nivel de pago.
- Android Studio: nivel de pago de la API.
- Gemini para empresas: por API o en el desplegable de modelos.
- Google Antigravity: suscriptores de Google AI Ultra y empresas.
- CodeMender y AlphaEvolve: agentes especializados, para empresas.
- Aplicación Gemini: solo con Google AI Ultra.
- Modo IA de la Búsqueda: solo con Google AI Ultra.
- Programa para científicos: seis meses gratis en Antigravity, previa solicitud y selección.
- Programa Fairwind: la variante de ciberseguridad, previa solicitud.
Sin acceso aún para la base de usuarios. Quienes no tengan un mínimo de Google AI Ultra, la suscripción más cara a nivel particular, no podrán acceder a Carbon en la app de Gemini. Tampoco a través del buscador de Google y su Modo IA: la empresa lo ha restringido a sus usuarios más premium.
La baza de Google es el precio. Gemini 4 Carbon cuesta 2 dólares por millón de tokens de entrada y 10 de salida hasta el 30 de noviembre; después subirá a 4 y 20. Por su parte, Fable 5.2 se queda en 8 y 40, y eso tras la rebaja con la que llegó. Por lo tanto, el modelo de Google sale por la cuarta parte del precio durante la promoción de salida y por la mitad cuando esta termine.
Quien no pague Google AI Ultra seguirá teniendo acceso a Gemini 4 Argon, que no es precisamente un premio de consolación: Google lo recomienda para la mayoría de tareas. Por su parte, Anthropic hace lo mismo con Opus 5.5. Los dos modelos de altas capacidades son, en el fondo, herramientas de nicho que funcionan muy bien como escaparate.

articles.title: Volkswagen déploie une mise à jour qui accélère la recharge des voitures électriques… mais restreint l'autonomie
articles.text:
C’est une mise à niveau qui tombe à pic pour attaquer l’hiver. Volkswagen va très prochainement déployer la mise à jour logicielle ID. Software 3.9.1 apportant sur ses anciens modèles le préconditionnement de la batterie. De quoi mettre enfin l’accumulateur à température avec une charge rapide, histoire de réduire drastiquement l’attente à la borne. Cet équipement attendu de longue date concernera les véhicules équipés du logiciel 3.x.
Cela touche les ID.4 et ID.5 produits avant octobre 2023, les ID.3 produites jusqu’en 2024 ainsi que les tous premiers ID. Buzz. Le chauffage de la batterie pourra ainsi s’effectuer manuellement via une touche dédiée. Les modèles plus récents équipés des logiciels 4.x et 5.x gardent cependant l’apanage d’une activation automatique via la navigation. En outre, la gestion thermique globale de la batterie a été optimisée pour prolonger sa durée de vie.
85 000 véhicules rappelés : quel est ce risque d’incendie décelé par Volkswagen ?
Il le faudrait bien, car une grande partie de la gamme électrique du groupe fait aujourd’hui l’objet d’un rappel d’ampleur. Les Volkswagen ID.3, ID.4, ID.7 et ID. Buzz, Audi Q4 e-tron ainsi que les Cupra Born produites entre 2022 et 2025 doivent en effet passer à l’atelier afin que leurs composants de batterie soient inspectés. Ce rappel majeur touche près de 85 000 véhicules en circulation dans le monde.
La marque allemande explique que les modèles concernés sont équipés de batteries contenant des pièces qui « pourraient ne pas répondre à nos normes de qualité élevées ». Elles pourraient alors surchauffer si elles sont chargées à plus de 80 % de leur capacité, « ce qui représente un risque d’incendie [pouvant] entraîner des blessures graves, voire mortelles, pour les personnes se trouvant à l’intérieur et à l’extérieur du véhicule ».
Batterie bloquée à 80 % : combien de kilomètres allez-vous réellement perdre ?
80 % de charge maximum, cela reste un bon compromis qui n’impactera aucunement le quotidien car ce niveau de batterie est de toute manière recommandé pour prolonger la durée de vie des cellules. Ce n’est que sur les longues distances que cela pourrait avoir un léger impact. Concrètement, sur une ID.3 en batterie intermédiaire de 58 kWh, cela se traduirait par une perte d’autonomie théorique d’environ 90 km.
Sur une ID.7 équipée du petit pack de 77 kWh, le recul atteint même 130 km. Pas dramatique pour le moins du monde, mais tout de même bon à savoir. Bien sûr, les modèles concernés retrouveront leur pleine autonomie après une inspection physique en atelier débouchant éventuellement sur le remplacement des modules de batterie défectueux. D’autres véhicules pourront être contrôlés et mis à jour à distance. Les propriétaires concernés recevront un courrier.

MSI Introduces MEG X, the Flagship Intelligent QD-OLED Gaming Monitor
MSI introduces the MEG X, a flagship 34-inch QD-OLED gaming monitor combining advanced on-device AI, next-generation display technology, immersive lighting, and a distinctive Infinity Mirror design. The MEG X features a 34-inch (33.98-inch viewable) UWQHD (3440 × 1440) 5th-Gen QD-OLED panel with Penta Tandem technology, an RGB Stripe sub-pixel layout, and DarkArmor Film, delivering a 360 Hz refresh rate and 0.03 ms (GtG) response time. A dedicated AI Processor powers intelligent visual, audio, and gameplay features, while MSI's exclusive SpectrumBar+ adds real-time lighting feedback for greater immersion.
AI at the Core
The built-in AI Processor analyzes on-screen content directly on the monitor, enabling real-time AI features without requiring dedicated PC software.AI Gauge detects horizontal in-game health or energy bars and reflects their status through SpectrumBar+, while AI Vision+ enhances visibility in dark areas and AI Crosshair dynamically adjusts crosshair color for better visibility. AI Super Resolution improves lower-resolution content, while AI Scene analyzes game content and automatically switches to a matching display mode, and AI Audio Scene adjusts the EQ to match the active display mode.
Together, these features bring real-time visual, audio, and in-game enhancements directly to the monitor.
Immersive Feedback with SpectrumBar+
MSI's exclusive SpectrumBar+ integrates lighting feedback directly into the gaming experience.
Glow Sync+ synchronizes lighting colors with on-screen content in real time, while Echo Vision visualizes audio channel distribution through corresponding lighting zones. SpectrumBar+ also supports Mystic Light for synchronized RGB lighting across compatible gaming gear.
Crafted to Stand Apart
Every detail of the MEG X reflects its flagship identity. Selected aluminium elements on the rear housing and stand provide a refined metallic finish while remaining strong and lightweight. The rear Infinity Mirror adds futuristic visual depth, while the MEG nameplate at the top of the stand and MEG logo on the base complete its distinctive design.
5th-Gen QD-OLED with Penta Tandem 
The MEG X features the latest 5th-Gen QD-OLED panel with Penta Tandem technology, using a 5-layer light-emitting structure to improve light efficiency by up to 30%. Its RGB Stripe sub-pixel layout helps minimize color fringing and improve text clarity.
DarkArmor Film delivers 40% deeper blacks and 2.5× better scratch resistance compared with previous QD-OLED panels, while the panel combines a 360 Hz refresh rate, 0.03 ms response time, VESA ClearMR 18000, and VESA DisplayHDR True Black 500 for fast and vivid gaming visuals.
The MEG X also features TrueBright and QuantumView verification, demonstrating its perceived brightness and wide-angle visual consistency.
Smarter OLED Protection and Next-Generation Connectivity
As part of MSI OLED Care 3.0, the AI Care Sensor uses on-device processing to detect user presence and intelligently activate OLED protection functions, helping reduce burn-in risk. Visual data is processed locally on the monitor and is not stored or transmitted.
For connectivity, the MEG X includes DisplayPort 2.1a (UHBR20) with up to 80 Gbps bandwidth, HDMI 2.1, and USB Type-C with up to 98 W Power Delivery.
Backed by MSI's 3-year OLED warranty, including burn-in coverage, the MEG X brings together on-device AI, QD-OLED performance, immersive lighting, and intelligent OLED protection in one flagship gaming monitor.

articles.title: Kora builds AI models and agents into a new Linux OS bound for Qualcomm Snapdragon PCs - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Kora builds AI models and agents into a new Linux OS bound for Qualcomm Snapdragon PCs
Desktop software company Kora Systems Inc. today unveiled Kora, a Linux-based operating system that builds artificial intelligence models and agents into the system itself.
Qualcomm Technologies Inc. has spent close to a year working with the company to bring it to Snapdragon-powered PCs.
The launch goes after what Kora sees as a ceiling on AI in current desktop computers. Most AI software on macOS and Windows runs inside a browser tab or an app sandbox, according to the company, with little view of the computer underneath.
Because both platforms are closed, Kora argues, the integration stops at that point. Linux, by Kora’s account, is the only operating system open enough to be rebuilt around models and agents from the kernel up.
The core of that rebuild is an inference engine Kora calls Cortex. It pools the central processor, graphics processor and neural processing unit in a PC, plus any other machines on the network, and treats them as one computer. Models run locally on the user’s hardware by default, and frontier models get pulled in for heavier jobs.
On screen, the usual layout of folders and apps is gone. What Kora calls neural workspaces take its place, each one arranged around the task a user is working on. The user sets the permissions for any applications and agents sandboxed inside a workspace. Under all of it sits a neural file system, and the company says memory and context stay on the local machine.
Outside developers can build on the same pieces Kora’s own applications use through its software development kit, which opens up primitives such as memory, semantic search and email. Any model, AI service or agent will be able to integrate at the system level, the company said. An agentic service could even run as part of the operating system and take its identity, memory and compute from Kora.
Chief Executive Kirt McMaster called the desktop operating system “the ultimate harness.” About 45 million people account for 80% of spending on AI, he said, and almost all of their work happens on desktops running operating systems built 40 years ago. By 2033 the group will top 150 million people spending more than $400 billion a year, according to Kora’s own estimates. “Nobody has built an operating system for them,” McMaster said.
Kora grew out of Playtron Corp., a company McMaster founded to build a Linux alternative to Windows for gaming PCs. Playtron’s engineers wrote GameOS as a complete Linux operating system and shipped it on gaming devices, and the same team has been building Kora on that foundation since November 2025. GameOS carries on inside the new system as GameFrame, a one-click play mode that turns the desktop into a console for PC games.
With Cyanogen, Android and GameOS behind them, the founders count Kora as their fourth operating system. Chief Business Officer John Lagerling led Android business development at Google LLC, and he said he joined when the platform had 100,000 users and stayed until it had a billion. Openness got it there, in his view, and AI needs the same treatment.
The company believes “50 superpowered engineers can take on Windows,” according to Chief Technology Officer Franck De Girolami. His engineers now work side by side with AI models and agents, he said, to the point that “Kora is built inside Kora.”
The Qualcomm work is laid out in a separate joint release today. The result so far is a complete Linux desktop running on PCs with Snapdragon X2 Elite chips, the two companies said, and Cortex now spreads AI workloads across the whole chip. Qualcomm engineers worked on the project throughout, and the chipmaker is also pushing X2 Elite support into the mainline Linux kernel.
Those machines can run a 26 billion-parameter language model locally, according to the release. Kedar Kondap, Qualcomm’s senior vice president and general manager of compute and gaming, said the X2 Elite was designed to run advanced AI on the device. Kora has also built translation technology that lets selected Windows x86-64 applications run inside the Linux environment, so people switching over can keep using software they rely on.
The first machines to ship will run HUMAIN OS, an enterprise operating system KORA is co-developing with Saudi Arabian AI company HUMAIN. Those PCs are due in 2027, and the companies bill them as the first from hardware makers to pair a Linux-based desktop operating system with Snapdragon X2 Elite. Kora itself follows later in 2027, with pricing to be shared closer to availability.
Kora is a venture capital-backed startup that counts Samsung Next, Square Enix Holdings Co. Ltd., Polychain Capital LP, Van Eck Associates Corp., Circle Internet Group Inc. and Alumni Ventures among its investors. The release did not say how much the company has raised.

articles.title: AI or SI? 'I mean, there’s different names for it,' says Ring's Jamie Siminoff, as the company launches an 'AI Pilot' for its home-surveillance drone
articles.text:
AI or SI? 'I mean, there’s different names for it,' says Ring's Jamie Siminoff, as the company launches an 'AI Pilot' for its home-surveillance drone
Amazon's Jeff Bezos is on board with the switch from 'artificial' to 'super', but the picture is less clear across the company
- Ring just launched AI Pilot
- That should not be read as long-term support for the term 'artificial Intelligence', though
- Company CEO Jamie Siminoff insisted it was not tying "to make any statements"
In its struggle to deliver an effective home-surveillance drone to consumers, Ring struggled with how to balance local intelligence with consistent flying skills. Turned out that the answer was in the cloud, or more specifically, cloud AI.
But in the time it took for Ring to solve that riddle, and launch both the Ring Drone Cam and its AI Pilot, no less a figure than the President of the United States President decided to rename 'artificial intelligence' to 'super intelligence'.
It's been almost two months since Donald Trump stood before the United Nations and announced that the US Government would be renaming AI to SI because, "It sounds much better, and it's much more accurate.... there's nothing artificial about it."
Forget that huge swaths of the tech industry have already hung their company names and branding around 'AI' (you may have heard of a small company called OpenAI, or maybe Apple's Siri AI); Trump sought to make the change official.
What's more remarkable, though, is that tech giants like Google's Sundar Pichai, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, and Nvidia's now-beleaguered CEO Jensen Huang fell into line.
Over at Ring's parent company, Amazon, though, the picture is less clear.
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said he agrees with Trump, telling Fox News last month, "I do like SI because artificial is not a very flattering thing."
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Meanwhile, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy conducted a recent earnings call in which he used "AI" over and over again.
Getting tech execs to choose, though, isn't easy.
During the Ring Drone Cam launch event, I asked Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff about the use of 'AI' in AI Pilot. Would the company be changing the name?
Siminoff smiled like he'd been expecting the question, and replied, "I mean, there’s different names for it. Certainly we’re not trying to make any statements by how we’re using that.”
But in a nod to how quickly the landscape can change under your feet, Siminoff added, "But the AI Pilot was named earlier.” So, there are currently no plans to change it, but also no indication that Ring won't, someday, have an 'SI Pilot' guiding the Ring Drone Cam through your home.
I pressed, and asked if we were safe to keep calling it 'artificial Intelligence.' Simioff would only reiterate, "I think people are using different names for it, and so we’re gonna — uh, but right now it is the AI Pilot”
Super unclear
Siminoff's response is not surprising. After all, the tech industry seems somewhat split on whether to follow Trump's Executive order, which demands that all government agencies "use 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents within the executive branch."
But, outside the halls of the White House, there's little agreement on whether the world should be switching from AI to SI.
As Siminoff points out, "The AI Pilot was named earlier." There was no way for Ring to know that Trump would attempt to rename an entire tech sector while it was trying to figure out how to make a drone light and efficient enough to navigate and surveil your home.
Who knows? The next version of AI Pilot may very well be SI Pilot. On the other hand, it took years for Ring to get this right. By the time the next Ring Drone Cam arrives, Trump will likely be out of office, and we may be done talking about AI vs. SI.
