articles.title: AI security startup Bay launches with $50M to vet agent actions before they run - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI security startup Bay launches with $50M to vet agent actions before they run
Israeli artificial intelligence security startup Bay AI Inc. launched today with $50 million in funding to let enterprises vet each action an AI agent tries to take before it runs.
Bay provides software that tracks the agents working across a company, whether they sit on an employee’s laptop, inside a cloud workload or in a software-as-a-service application. One set of policies covers them all.
First-generation AI security tools mostly filter prompts and responses. Bay argues that misses where the damage happens, since a harmless-looking prompt can still end with an agent deleting a production database.
The founders ran into that kind of failure themselves when one of their own coding agents, working with its normal permissions, tried to expose a cloud environment to the internet to finish a test. They still have the screenshot.
Bay installs through the mobile device management or endpoint detection and response tools a customer already has, and the company says it takes under five minutes. A scanner called Wave inventories the agents, extensions and local models on each machine and leaves nothing running once it finishes.
Each time an agent proposes an action, the AI tool running it hands the request to Bay Enforcer, a static binary, through a native hook. The check happens on the machine itself with the whole session as context, and Bay said a verdict comes back in milliseconds, sometimes as a prompt asking the user to approve the step. Anything judged too risky never runs.
The policy behind those verdicts comes from Bay’s Lighthouse system, which drafts a separate one for each team from the last 30 days of agent activity, so security staff are not writing rules every time someone picks up a new tool. Teams can test a policy against the previous month first and see what it would have stopped. Bay said false positives run under 1%.
Security leaders are often handed an enterprise-wide AI rollout with a year-end deadline, co-founder and Chief Executive Yuval Zacharia said, or find that agents have already spread across the company and “it’s the Wild West.” She wants security to become “the reason AI ships faster, not the reason it stalls.”
Micron Technology Inc., Wix.com Ltd., ClickUp Inc. and Peloton Interactive Inc. are among the dozens of enterprise customers signed in the nine months since Bay was founded. Fortune 100 companies on the platform tripled their use of autonomous agents in just under 30 days, the company said.
Zacharia founded Bay with Chief Product Officer Aner Morag and Vice President of Research and Development Boris Danilovich. The three knew each other from the Israel Defense Forces’ Unit 8200, where Zacharia led a department of about 50 people before becoming the first intelligence officer there to cross into offensive cyber operations. After the military she ran security research and AI at Cyber Hunters Ltd.
Danilovich was an early employee at Preempt Security Inc. and stayed six years at CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. after it bought the startup in 2020. Most of Bay’s research team followed him over. Morag was the first employee at Noname Security.
The $50 million comes from two rounds. Battery Ventures LP led the larger $37 million Series A round, and Micron’s venture arm, Micron Ventures, also participated after the chipmaker started out as a Bay customer. Wiz Inc. Chief Executive Assaf Rappaport put in money personally. The remaining $13 million came from a previously undisclosed seed round co-led by YL Ventures Ltd. and Striker Venture Partners.
Yoav Leitersdorf, managing partner at YL Ventures, said his firm looked at a crowded field of AI endpoint security companies before picking Bay. He believes it can become “as fundamental to enterprise AI adoption as the network firewall was to the internet era.”
Engineering and product hiring will continue in Tel Aviv, where Bay is based, with the sales, marketing and customer teams growing in the U.S. and Europe. Enterprises can buy the platform now.

articles.title: Pangram für Gmail: Dieses neue Tool zeigt dir, wie viele Nachrichten in deinem Posteingang KI-generiert sind
articles.text:
Wer schickt dir KI-generierte E-Mails? Mit diesem neuen Pangram-Detektor findest du es heraus
Das Verfassen und Bearbeiten von Texten ist einer der zentralen Einsatzbereiche von KI-Tools wie Gemini, Claude oder ChatGPT. Inzwischen sind KI-Texte fast überall zu finden – in Speisekarten, Hausarbeiten, Social-Media-Posts und E-Mails. Eine Browser-Erweiterung von Pangram soll jetzt zeigen, wie viele KI-generierte Nachrichten täglich im eigenen Gmail-Postfach landen. Das Tool zur Erkennung von KI-Texten und -Bildern hat schon dabei geholfen, ganze Romane zu entlarven, die zu großen Teilen mithilfe der neuen Technologie erstellt worden sein sollen.
So funktioniert der neue Pangram-Detektor
Die Browser-Erweiterung analysiert eingehende Gmail-Nachrichten mit eigenen Algorithmen, um KI-Text zu erkennen. Für die Nutzung ist ein Pangram-Abonnement erforderlich. In der kostenlosen Version ist sie nicht verfügbar. Nutzer:innen aktivieren die Erweiterung im Posteingang, indem sie die Seite für Gmail-Integrationen aufrufen und auf „Gmail verbinden“ klicken. Alternativ können sie im linken Navigationsbereich des Pangram-Dashboards die Option „Gmail-Integration“ auswählen. Der KI-Detektor versichert, dass der Inhalt der E-Mails nach der Auswertung nicht gespeichert und auch nicht zum Training von KI-Modellen verwenden wird.
Nach der Aktivierung scannt Pangram zunächst die 100 neuesten E-Mails. Danach folgen alle Weiteren, die neu eingehen. Nutzer:innen sehen auf einen Blick, wie viele Nachrichten vermutlich mit KI formuliert wurden, wie viele höchstwahrscheinlich von einem Menschen stammen und wie viele als Mischung aus beidem gelten. Außerdem lässt sich festlegen, dass eingehende KI-Mails direkt ins Archiv oder in den Spam-Ordner wandern. Bestimmte Domains, Absender:innen oder Stichwörter können von dem KI-Scan ausgeschlossen werden. So lässt sich zum Beispiel verhindern, dass private Mails analysiert werden.
David Nield ist als Journalist bei Wired tätig. Er hat das Tool mit seinem eigenen Gmail-Postfach getestet. Von den 108 E-Mails, die Pangram analysierte, kennzeichnete es acht als KI-generiert. 37 stammten demnach von einem Menschen. Der Rest wurden als Mischung identifiziert. Alle Nachrichten von Freund:innen, Verwandten und Kolleg:innen hätten ihmzufolge den „Mensch-Test“ bestanden. Nield schickte sich außerdem selbst ein paar E-Mails von verschiedenen Konten, um die Einstufung zu prüfen. Eine davon verfasste er mit Microsoft Copilot, was der Detektor korrekt eingestuft habe.
Wie KI der Kommunikation schaden kann
Laut einer Analyse von OpenAI ist das Verfassen von E-Mails und anderen Texten mit KI inzwischen weit verbreitet. Der ChatGPT-Anbieter wertete dafür Konversationen von 1,5 Millionen Nutzer:innen aus. Demnach machten das Erstellen und Optimieren von Texten zwischen 2024 und 2025 mehr als 28 Prozent aller Anfragen aus. Aber nicht alle Empfänger:innen sind von KI-Nachrichten begeistert. Laut Leena Rinne von der Edtech-Plattform Skillsoft könnte das dazu führen, dass am Ende nur noch Chatbots miteinander kommunizieren – und wichtige zwischenmenschliche Fähigkeiten verloren gehen.
Ausgangspunkt für Rinnes kritische Einordnung war der Bericht einer Mitarbeiterin. Sie erzählte ihr, ihr Chef habe ihr eine E-Mail geschickt, deren Bedeutung sie nicht ganz verstanden habe. Sie vermutete, dass eine KI die Nachricht verfasst hatte, und bat ihren Chatbot um eine Interpretation. Dieser antwortete und fragte, ob er direkt eine Antwort formulieren solle. Genau auf diese Weise könne ein KI-Teufelskreis beginnen. Rinne nennt dieses Phänomen „Social Offloading“: Dabei delegieren Menschen zwischenmenschliche Fähigkeiten, die Urteilsvermögen, Empathie oder Mut erfordern, an die KI.

articles.title: Carbon emissions are down this year—but that probably won’t last
articles.text:
Evaluating the annual global temperatures each year requires context. There is a fair amount of natural variability from one year to the next, so it’s important to focus on the trend over time. Famously, global warming did not end in 1998, as some claimed a couple of decades ago—we just had a run of La-Niña-dominated years after a very strong El Niño.
Annual greenhouse gas emissions are much less variable, having increased fairly steadily, but many complicating factors can still muddy the picture. Sometimes those factors conspire to throw a year off the trend. It looks like 2026 will be one of those years.
A new analysis led by Corinne Le Quéré at the University of East Anglia estimates that fossil fuel emissions have fallen about 0.4 percent from last year. This probably isn’t a peak that symbolizes heartening progress on climate change, though; the researchers think it’s a short-term dip driven by the war in Iran and its effect on oil prices.
Shifting percentages
This team works on the Global Carbon Project, which compiles stats on fossil fuel use and things like deforestation to track carbon emissions globally and by country. In this case, they looked at the stats and tried to pull out key underlying trends that show us what to expect over the next couple of years.
Last year, fossil fuel emissions increased 1.2 percent, a bit above the 2019–2025 average of 0.8 percent per year. This year’s decline featured a 1.9 percent drop in oil emissions, a smaller 0.3 percent drop in emissions from natural gas use, and a 0.6 percent increase in coal emissions.

articles.title: Loi Résilience : les députés suppriment l’article qui aurait empêché l’État d’imposer des portes dérobées
articles.text:
69 pour, 37 contre et une abstention.
Ce 10 novembre 2026, les députés ont supprimé l’article 16 bis de la loi Résilience.
Ajouté par le Sénat en mars 2025, cet article interdisait à l’État d’imposer aux fournisseurs de services de chiffrement, comme les messageries WhatsApp ou Signal, des dispositifs qui affaiblissent volontairement leur sécurité, par exemple des portes dérobées ou des clés de déchiffrement maîtresses.
Il avait été glissé dans ce projet de loi, qui doit transposer la directive européenne NIS 2 sur la cybersécurité.
Le gouvernement remplace la garantie par une promesse
La suppression a été votée par le RN, les groupes du bloc central, la Droite républicaine, LIOT et une partie des socialistes, tandis que La France insoumise et les écologistes s’y sont opposés.
Pour rappel, l’article 16 bis avait été ajouté en réponse à une mesure adoptée dans une autre loi. Début 2025, le Sénat avait adopté, dans la loi contre le narcotrafic, un article 8 ter qui devait obliger les messageries chiffrées à donner aux enquêteurs l’accès aux échanges des personnes visées.
Les éditeurs de messageries s’y étaient vivement opposés, plusieurs députés avaient exprimé leurs réserves, et l’Assemblée avait fini par retirer la mesure. Les sénateurs avaient alors pris le problème à l’envers et, à l’initiative du sénateur Olivier Cadic, président de la commission spéciale chargée du texte, inscrit dans le projet de loi Résilience une interdiction d’imposer ce type de dispositif.
Le ministère de l’Intérieur et les services de renseignement s’y sont opposés dès le départ. Auditionné par la commission spéciale de l’Assemblée en juillet 2025, Mahamadou Diarra, secrétaire général de la coordination nationale du renseignement et de la lutte contre le terrorisme, avait affirmé que « l’article 16 bis n’a pas sa place dans le projet de loi ».
Le gouvernement s’est finalement rangé à l’avis de l’ancien député Florent Boudié, à qui le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu avait confié en janvier 2026 une mission sur le chiffrement. Remis en septembre, son rapport recommande de renoncer aux portes dérobées, mais aussi de supprimer l’article 16 bis, comme l’a détaillé Le Monde.
En échange, la ministre déléguée au Numérique Anne Le Hénanff s’est engagée à ne pas réintroduire de mesure comparable « d’ici la fin de la session parlementaire », tandis que le ministre de l’Intérieur Laurent Nuñez a parlé d’un engagement valable jusqu’à « la fin de l’actuelle mandature ». Aucune de ces deux promesses n’a de valeur juridique.
Un texte encore loin de s’appliquer
Le sort de la loi Résilience n’est pas réglé pour autant. Les députés poursuivent l’examen du texte cette semaine, avant une probable commission mixte paritaire où ils devront accorder leur version avec celle du Sénat. Il faudra ensuite attendre les décrets d’application, sans lesquels les obligations de NIS 2 ne s’appliqueront pas en France.
Ce retard pèse sur les organisations concernées. Adoptée par l’Union européenne en 2022, la directive NIS 2 impose aux secteurs jugés essentiels, comme l’énergie, la santé ou les administrations, de renforcer leur cybersécurité et de signaler leurs incidents graves aux autorités.
En France, elle doit concerner environ 15 000 entités, contre quelques centaines sous la première directive. Elle devait être transposée avant le 17 octobre 2024, et la Commission européenne a saisi la Cour de justice de l’UE pour ce manquement.

articles.title: Claude Sheets et Whiteboards : comment Anthropic attaque Microsoft Office sur son propre terrain — Frandroid
articles.text:
C’est ironique. Microsoft paie Anthropic pour faire tourner Copilot dans Excel. Microsoft propose donc les modèles Claude dans Copilot pour Word, Excel et PowerPoint, et y a même ajouté Claude Opus 5 le 24 juillet.
Le 9 mars, le géant de Windows se félicitait même, sur son blog, d’avoir « intégré la technologie derrière Claude Cowork dans Microsoft 365 Copilot ». Ce mardi 10 novembre, son fournisseur lance pourtant son propre tableur concurrent. Anthropic décide donc de commercialiser en direct des outils qui marchent ouvertement sur les plates-bandes historiques d’Office.
Anthropic vend d’ailleurs déjà ses propres compléments Claude pour Word, Excel, PowerPoint et Outlook, inclus dès l’offre Pro. Depuis le 6 octobre, l’éditeur propose aussi une extension qui loge Claude dans Google Docs, Sheets et Slides. Avec Sheets et Whiteboards, il ne se contente plus de se greffer sur les suites des autres.
Dévoilée sur le site d’Anthropic et sur le compte X officiel de Claude, cette offensive s’articule autour de deux nouveautés phares. D’un côté, Claude Sheets permet de bâtir un tableur à plusieurs mains avec l’aide de l’IA, gestion des onglets et formules de calcul comprises. De l’autre, Claude Whiteboards prend la forme d’un tableau blanc partagé pensé pour structurer une réunion à la volée avant que l’assistant n’en tire une synthèse propre.
Ces deux briques sont pour l’instant lancées en bêta, une phase de rodage où certaines fonctions restent incomplètes ou perfectibles, et réservées aux forfaits payants à partir de l’offre Pro (20 dollars par mois hors taxes aux États-Unis). Elles viennent épauler Claude Docs et Claude Slides, inaugurés mi-septembre avant d’être élargis en octobre à tous les utilisateurs, offre gratuite comprise.
Claude Sheets et Claude Whiteboards fonctionnent sur le web, dans l’application de bureau et sur mobile. Sur les offres Team, ils sont activés d’office. Sur les offres Enterprise, ils restent désactivés tant qu’un administrateur ne les a pas allumés.
Le second volet de l’annonce s’adresse surtout aux entreprises. Rebaptisé Claude Data, l’ancien module Dashboards, lancé en octobre, sort de bêta. Ses tableaux de bord se branchent sur des outils comme Snowflake ou Salesforce, ces coffres-forts numériques où dorment les données commerciales et financières d’une société. Claude Data y ajoute des récits de données, des vidéos commentées et le partage de chiffres à jour avec des collègues.
Parallèlement, des « connecteurs interactifs » permettent de manipuler des outils tiers signés Adobe ou Atlassian au cœur même de la discussion, sans jamais changer d’onglet. Anthropic annonce enfin Claude Meetings, un agent capable de s’inviter dans les visioconférences pour prendre des notes et mettre à jour lui-même les documents de l’équipe. L’éditeur le promet pour « bientôt », sans donner de date.
Une suite bureautique qui ne dit pas son nom
Là où Microsoft part d’Office pour y greffer une couche d’IA avec Copilot, Anthropic prend le problème exactement à l’envers. Ici, le document naît d’abord dans le fil de discussion avec l’assistant, puis s’exporte en fin de course si nécessaire (au format Word pour Docs, en PowerPoint ou PDF pour Slides).
Office n’y sert plus que de format d’export. Sur le plan tarifaire, l’option Microsoft 365 Copilot Business est facturée 18,20 € HT par mois et par salarié en supplément d’une licence Office existante, tandis que la formule Team de Claude débute à 20 dollars hors taxes par siège (en abonnement annuel), sans rien installer mais sans équivalent à Outlook, Teams ou SharePoint.
Pour défendre son approche, Anthropic met surtout en avant ses propres retours d’expérience. Son service juridique affirme avoir ramené de trois jours à 24 heures la relecture des contenus marketing, grâce à un outil construit avec Claude. Chez le client Advantage Solutions, l’équipe financière dit passer moins de 30 minutes, contre environ 10 heures avant, à préparer les présentations, commentaires et vérifications de chaque cycle de prévisions.
La boutique d’extensions de Claude revendique de son côté plus de 9 000 connecteurs et plugins, en comptant ceux développés par la communauté.
Anthropic ne prétend pas détrôner Excel du jour au lendemain. L’éditeur reconnaît que Claude Sheets se limite pour l’instant aux fonctions de base d’un tableur, et renvoie vers un export .xlsx ou CSV, ou vers son propre module Claude for Excel, quand il en faut davantage. Mais en faisant de la fenêtre de chat le point de départ naturel de chaque dossier, la start-up tente de réduire Office à une simple visionneuse de fichiers finaux. Pour Microsoft, qui finance déjà son rival pour muscler Copilot, la scène a tout du client historique qui regarde son fournisseur inaugurer une boutique concurrente sur le trottoir d’en face.
À Wall Street, l’annonce a fait reculer l’action Microsoft de 3 % ce mardi, selon CNBC.

articles.title: AI made coding faster. It didn’t make software simpler
articles.text:
AI made coding faster. It didn’t make software simpler
Coding is faster, but the winners will be those that create more value from it
For years, the software industry operated under one core assumption: writing code was the primary bottleneck in software development. As a result, companies poured enormous resources into hiring developers, refining development processes, and building tools that could shorten the journey from idea to product.
Then generative AI arrived.
For the first time, the industry gained a technology capable of solving the very problem it had spent decades trying to overcome. The ability to write code – once the industry’s most constrained resource – is now faster, more accessible, and dramatically more efficient.
But if our ability to generate code has increased so dramatically, why aren’t software organizations moving at the same pace?
General Manager of CX Engineering at NiCE.
AI-enabled development offers a more nuanced story. AI coding agents can handle work that previously required additional engineering capacity, from creating the foundations of an application to generating tests and accelerating implementation. A group of two or three people can try out an idea that might once have required a much larger team, more specialized skills, and considerably more time.
But speed is only part of the story. The more important change is that AI expands the ambition of each team.
A 2025 study by researchers at Tilburg University found that while AI coding tools increase output, they also increase the burden on senior developers. After analyzing thousands of open-source projects, the researchers found that experienced developers spent significantly more time reviewing AI-generated code, while their own coding output declined by nearly 20%. In other words, AI accelerates code creation, but it does not eliminate the need for human expertise to govern, validate, and maintain that code over time.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The implications extend well beyond senior developers. They force us to rethink what we actually measure.
More code doesn’t mean more progress
Excess code is only the symptom. The real challenge is keeping it under control. As codebases continue to grow, the question becomes even more pressing: if software can be built faster than ever before, why are organizations still struggling to move at the same pace? Because in enterprise software, writing code is only the beginning.
Every change must go through quality assurance, security reviews, regulatory compliance, and complex integration processes. Those steps cannot be accelerated at the same pace as code generation.
As AI speeds up development, what happens after the code is written becomes even more critical.
Organizations are measured not by how much code they produce, but by their ability to run stable, secure, and maintainable systems over time. That is why the defining challenge of the coming years will not be a shortage of developers, but managing complexity at scale.
AI changes the unit of innovation
AI coding agents are a major reason for this shift. They allow smaller groups to take on work that previously required a larger roster, without narrowing the ambition or depth of what they attempt.
That changes the unit of innovation. Progress is no longer determined only by how many people can be working on an idea.
The implications extend beyond individual developers. As AI changes the role of software engineers, team leaders need to consider not simply how quickly teams can produce code, but how effectively they can define problems, validate results and apply human judgement.
The real question is no longer how much software an organization can produce. It is how much of that software can be operated, maintained, and continuously evolved over time.
What happens after the code is written
The easier it becomes to generate code, the easier it becomes to generate complexity. Organizations can introduce new capabilities at unprecedented speed, but every additional component brings new requirements for testing, security, integration, monitoring, and long-term maintenance. AI shortens the path to writing software. It does not shorten the path to building reliable enterprise systems.
That is the new bottleneck in software development – not the ability to generate more code, but the ability to manage the complexity that code creates.
This is where governance, oversight and maintainability become increasingly important. A prototype is not a finished product, and it should not be treated as one. It still requires validation, product discipline, security, reliability, and a clear understanding of the customer or business need it serves.
The opportunity is to turn AI from a separate initiative into an everyday operating model for innovation, while maintaining the standards organizations expect around security, reliability, governance, and measurable business value.
This also means looking beyond traditional measures of development output. In a world where AI writes a growing share of the code, how many features were delivered, how many tasks were completed, and how quickly projects moved forward tell only part of the story. The ability to run stable, secure and maintainable systems over time matters just as much.
AI has solved one of software’s biggest challenges: generating more code in less time. Now the industry faces a harder question: how do we prevent speed from becoming technical debt?

articles.title: Okra Solar secures $7m debt facility from BII to scale mesh-grids in Nigeria - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian off-grid energy startup Okra Solar has secured a US$7 million debt facility from British International Investment (BII) to accelerate clean energy access.
Founded in 2016, Okra provides mesh-grid technology for off-grid communities, combining solar generation, battery storage and smart controls so that neighbouring homes and businesses can share electricity cost-efficiently. The model delivers more power than typical solar home systems while needing less infrastructure than conventional mini-grids.
Okra currently has more than 13,000 households connected and over 2.3MW of installed capacity. The US$7 million financing from BII, the UK’s development finance institution and impact investor, will allow it to procure equipment for roughly 150,000 new connections, a more than tenfold increase, with the potential to bring electricity to 750,000 people in rural Nigeria for the first time.
The facility tackles a key barrier to scaling distributed renewable energy – access to flexible working capital. By buying inputs upfront and in larger volumes, Okra expects to cut equipment costs and shorten delivery times to Nigeria from four months to about two.
“Every month a project is delayed is another month a community goes without power,” said Afnan Hannan, CEO of Okra Solar. “Until now we would only order components once a transaction had closed, in batches of a few thousand units. With BII’s facility we are procuring long lead time components, batteries, and solar PV equipment upfront and in volume, reducing costs and having stock ready when a developer signs.”
Faster delivery should also help Okra’s developer customers bring projects online sooner and access results-based grant payments earlier. Mesh-grids are eligible under Nigeria’s Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up (DARES) programme, which is run by the Rural Electrification Agency with World Bank support.
“For innovative energy companies such as Okra, access to the right type of finance can be just as important as the technology itself,” said Geoffrey Manley, director and head of infrastructure and climate debt for Africa and South Asia at BII. “We believe this will help demonstrate the commercial viability of mesh-grids and establish the model as an increasingly important part of Africa’s distributed renewable energy market.”

articles.title: Agricultural Autonomy Allows a Farm Robot to Work Alone - EE Times
articles.text:
For corn and soybean farmers in the U.S. Midwest, an autonomous machine could offer something more practical than replacing a worker: the ability to get more done with an already-lean team or spend less time in the field.
Salah Issa, associate professor in the Department of Agricultural and Biological Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign, sees both possibilities. He also pointed out that safety requirements for a large tractor differ from those of a small robot weeding vegetables or carrying produce alongside workers.
Agricultural autonomy encompasses machines with different weights, speeds, tasks, and operating environments. Before a farmer can leave one unsupervised, its manufacturer must establish which conditions allow that and how the machine will respond when those conditions change.
Different applications, different risks
Issa’s research focuses primarily on agricultural safety, with corn and soybean production forming much of his Midwest perspective. In those operations, he expects autonomy to help farmers expand capacity or improve working schedules.
“It’s more of the same operation, either doing it with a better life balance or over more acres to expand operations,” he told EE Times.
Fruit and vegetable production presents different opportunities. Tasks that currently require substantial manual labor can be automated, changing how workers and machines operate together. Issa describes produce-carrying robots that accompany workers and autonomous sprayers operating in orchards. The task and workflow determine where people encounter the equipment.
Across these applications, machines must cope with workers nearby, unexpected bystanders, animals, and changing outdoor conditions. The potential consequences of an encounter vary considerably between a small, slow platform and a large agricultural machine.
Different stopping distances and protective measures are needed for a small robot moving slowly between vegetable rows versus a large tractor. Issa said ISO 18497 provides a broad framework, but more detailed standards are needed for particular machines. The latest version points manufacturers toward additional obstacle-
detection guidance and leaves questions, such as how far from a person a machine should stop, open to be answered by application-specific guidelines.
Issa pointed to the use of a two-cylinder test object as a stand-in for a person when assessing obstacle detection. Other researchers have examined how well that approach translates to encounters with actual people. “They studied machines trained using the cylinders as stand-ins,” he said. “They found that when the machine operates with real humans, the level of accuracy drops.”
For Issa, reliable detection requires accounting for conditions in the field: “Vision systems get dusty. You’re dealing with vibrations, which impact the effectiveness and the longevity of sensors.” He therefore favors combining sensor types rather than depending on one technology.
The choice of safeguards, however, depends on the application. French robotics company Naïo illustrates an approach built around low speed, defined operating boundaries, and mechanical contact detection.
Designing for a defined operating area
Naïo offers two platforms: Oz, a small robot for vegetable growers and other specialist crops, and Ted, a robot that straddles vineyard rows, primarily for mechanical weeding. Matthias Carrière, Naïo’s managing director, is clear about his definition of autonomy. “When we talk about autonomy, we mean work without supervision,” he told EE Times.
Oz illustrates an approach built around a small, slow machine and a defined application. Its customers include vegetable farmers and seed producers, typically on farms of 1–20 hectares. The platform weighs about 150 kg, travels below 2 km/h, and works roughly half a hectare a day. Originally developed for weeding, it also supports sowing, planting, and transporting harvested produce.
Oz uses GPS with real-time kinematic positioning for guidance. A sensitive contact bumper triggers a stop when the machine encounters an obstruction. “A very light bump is enough, and it stops on contact,” Carrière said. He attributes that choice to Naïo’s assessment of the robot’s mass, speed, and intended operating conditions.
Contact-based protection necessarily acts after contact occurs. Its suitability therefore depends on the complete risk assessment, including the machine’s movement and task. Low speed alone does not establish that every possible encounter is harmless.
Naïo’s answer is not to make the perception system more sophisticated. “Our robots don’t use AI,” Carrière said. “We prioritize affordability and straightforward operation.”
The company’s approach extends beyond obstacle protection.
Carrière described a separate boundary-safety loop, with mapping distinct from that used to guide everyday work. “You must always isolate the loops,” he said. Following a route accurately and enforcing an approved operating boundary are separate functions.
Naïo also assesses individual parcels before approving unsupervised operation. Physical barriers can simplify containment; virtual boundaries are used elsewhere. Shared access routes and nearby activity can complicate the assessment.
“You can have all the AI and all the technology in the world,” Carrière said. “If the structure of a farm is not compatible with using a machine, and the farm is not ready to make structural changes, it won’t work.”
Protection can also interrupt useful work. On Ted, Naïo’s vineyard robot, vegetation growing beside a vine can trigger mechanical safeguards. Someone must investigate and clear the obstruction before unattended work resumes.
When people change the conditions
Repeated interruptions create a difficult engineering problem: Protection that gets in the way can encourage users to defeat it.
Issa recalled a demonstration where a manufacturer covered sensors with duct tape so a machine could operate with people nearby. His concern is that farmers, frustrated by frequent nuisance stops, could adopt the same workaround.
A safety mechanism can perform its intended function while prompting behavior that undermines it. Repeated alerts create a related problem: Users become accustomed to warnings and stop noticing them. Asking a person to intervene whenever the machine is uncertain has practical limits if the requests become burdensome.
“We’re now assuming the machines will respond to our interactions,” Issa said. “Then we change the way we interact based on how we assume the machine does.”
Manufacturers must consider how operating modes are communicated and how people may alter their behavior around the machine. The safety assessment also extends to setup, cleaning, maintenance, and other stages where workers remain involved.
Carrière said safety engineering must also anticipate what happens when users try to bypass the safeguards. Naïo prevents its robots from starting if required safety devices have been disabled. Even supervised operation is designed to make circumvention difficult: The operator must interact with the remote control every six minutes, confirming that someone remains near the machine. A farmer who deliberately rigs a way around such safeguards, Carrière said, crosses an important line: The manufacturer has designed for foreseeable misuse, but the user has intentionally defeated the safety system.
But responsibility cuts both ways. If Naïo determines that a robot can operate without anyone watching it, Carrière said the company assumes responsibility for that judgment: “It’s Naïo’s management that signs a document saying that, on this parcel, the robot can operate alone; on that parcel, it cannot—it must be supervised. That is how we assume responsibility.”
The approval relies partly on information supplied by the farmer, including whether an adjoining route is public or private. Users must respect the operating conditions. Carrière describes responsibilities for both parties, with Naïo standing behind its assessment and safety systems rather than assuming every possible liability.
But defining those responsibilities does not eliminate the unknowns that emerge once autonomous machines are operating in the field. Issa argued that learning from near-misses is therefore essential, particularly while deployment remains limited. Waiting for serious accidents would provide feedback too late. Unexpected encounters, confusing behavior, and situations that make users uncomfortable can reveal weaknesses earlier.
That emphasis on practical experience also helps explain Naïo’s priorities. Rather than continually adding technological sophistication, the company is focusing on simpler operation, additional useful tasks, and lower costs. “We’re not going to add innovation for innovation’s sake,” Carrière said. Working alone requires safeguards suited to the application—and evidence that they remain effective when people put the machine to work.

articles.title: Windows 11 : Firefox va s'aligner sur Chrome et Edge et booster le démarrage du navigateur
articles.text:
Mozilla veut que Firefox profite des « accelerated app launches » de Windows 11, déjà utilisés par Edge. Un ticket Bugzilla livre un premier test chiffré, à relativiser.
Fin octobre, nous rapportions que Windows 11 transmettait désormais directement les lancements à Edge. Microsoft entend en faire profiter les autres navigateurs articulés autour de Chromium. Mais il restait une inconnue : quid de Firefox et les développeurs de Mozilla peuvent-ils en faire autant avec Gecko ? Le ticket 2087194 de Bugzilla apporte un début de réponse : David Rubino, product manager de Firefox, explique que Mozilla a déjà réussi à accéder à l’API de Microsoft.
3 ms au lieu de 70 ms, mais sur un seul test
Aujourd’hui, quand Firefox est déjà en cours d’exécution, un clic sur un lien ou un lancement depuis le menu Démarrer ou la barre des tâches crée un nouveau firefox.exe. Ce processus passe la demande au navigateur ouvert, puis se ferme. Avec les lancements accélérés, Windows 11 envoie la demande directement à l’application, sans cet intermédiaire. Cela vaut pour le menu Démarrer, la barre des tâches et les liens que l’application gère par défaut. Edge est le premier navigateur à s’en servir. Microsoft annonce des lancements environ 15 % plus rapides, voire jusqu’à 33 % quand la machine est chargée, sur Windows 11 25H2, 26H1 ou 26H2 avec la mise à jour d’octobre 2026 ou une version plus récente. Microsoft prévoit aussi de porter ce travail vers Chromium et étudie l’ouverture des fichiers PDF.
Pour Firefox, David Rubino a testé un build local. Un lien atteint le navigateur déjà lancé en environ 3 ms, contre 70 ms avant. Les lancements depuis le menu Démarrer arrivent eux aussi directement au bon endroit. Il faut toutefois relativiser : ces valeurs mesurent seulement le temps que met la demande pour atteindre Firefox, sur un seul essai en local. Le navigateur ne s’ouvre donc pas 20 fois plus vite pour autant.
Puisqu’il s’agit d’une « Limited Access Feature », l’éditeur de Redmond verrouille cette API. Les développeurs souhaitant en profiter doivent débloquer un code auprès de l’entreprise. De son côté Mozilla utilise déjà un code lui servant à épingler Firefox à la barre des tâches, et ce dernier ouvre aussi l’accès à cette API.
Reste à savoir comment Mozilla peaufinera ces travaux pour jouer rapidement au coude à coude avec les autres navigateurs du marché.

articles.title: Bancos e inversores frenan los préstamos para centros de datos de IA tras la caída de las acciones tecnológicas
articles.text:
Los bancos y los inversores que financiaron la expansión de la inteligencia artificial empezaron a vender o a rechazar deuda ligada a los centros de datos. El medio Semafor informó que hay carteras de préstamos ofrecidas con fuertes descuentos y que los créditos para comprar chips son los más castigados.
Según Semafor, un inversor consultado dijo que esos financiamientos de chips estaban “getting smoked”, es decir, sufrían golpes fuertes, por el temor a que los préstamos duren más que la vida útil de la tecnología que los respalda.
El viernes, Bloomberg informó de que el banco holandés ING busca vender USD 500 millones en préstamos de centros de datos. Entre ellos hay un tramo de USD 25 millones vinculado a Stargate, el proyecto de OpenAI, SoftBank y Oracle.
La próxima prueba para Wall Street es un acuerdo de USD 40.000 millones para financiar chips de SpaceX, el mayor de su tipo. Goldman Sachs y Apollo ya comenzaron a ofrecerlo a inversores, según Semafor.
Fondos que se retiran del negocio
Algunos actores ya tomaron posición. Michael Arougheti, director ejecutivo de la gestora Ares Management, dijo en una conferencia de resultados que la firma no participará en esos créditos: “No sé cómo evaluar las curvas de caída y depreciación de ese tipo de tecnología”.
Bloomberg había descrito el malestar el 28 de octubre, tras hablar con más de 30 banqueros, gestores de fondos y ejecutivos de capital privado. Todos coincidieron en que conseguir dinero para centros de datos es bastante más difícil que hace unos meses.
Una de las razones son las cláusulas que permiten al cliente retirarse. Un fondo de cobertura dijo a Bloomberg que rechazó una operación porque el contratante podía abandonarla si el proyecto se demoraba más de tres meses.
Esa inquietud creció después de que Oracle emitiera en septiembre un aviso de fuerza mayor para aplazar pagos si se retrasaba un gran centro de datos en Nuevo México, según la misma agencia.
Otras gestoras también pusieron límites. Carlyle Group dejó pasar varias operaciones recientes y KKR evita centros de datos en zonas remotas, por la dificultad de reutilizarlos cuando venzan los contratos de alquiler, según personas consultadas por Bloomberg.
Los intereses suben a dos dígitos
Los números reflejan el cambio. Bloomberg contó al menos 18 financiamientos de centros de datos, en bonos de alto riesgo y préstamos apalancados, con rendimientos de dos dígitos. El préstamo de USD 5.000 millones de la empresa de nube para IA Volta Infrastructure Holdings superó el 11%.
Carolyn Campbell, estratega de Morgan Stanley, dijo en un pódcast que los bonos mejor calificados de centros de datos rendían menos del 5% a comienzos de 2026 y ahora rondan el 7%. Con tasas cercanas al 8%, afirmó, emitirlos resulta mucho más difícil.
Los bancos también tienen problemas para trasladar el riesgo. El responsable de préstamos a tecnología, medios y telecomunicaciones de un gran banco europeo, que pidió no ser identificado, dijo a Bloomberg que su entidad se acerca al límite de lo que puede prestar al sector. Vender esa deuda puede tardar cinco meses.
Citadel Securities advirtió a sus clientes de que incluso las mayores tecnológicas podrían verse arrastradas, porque respaldan con su balance muchos proyectos. La firma aclaró que no prevé una crisis crediticia inminente, y las grandes empresas siguieron reuniendo decenas de miles de millones en nuevos fondos esa semana.
El resultado de la oferta de Goldman Sachs y Apollo para el financiamiento de chips de SpaceX será la siguiente señal sobre cuánto riesgo de IA están dispuestos a asumir los inversores.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 10, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 10, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Tuesday, November 10, 2026.
From Neha Nagar's debut book to tech leaders and startup founders that saw their careers derailed by personal scandals, YourStory brings you this and other latest developments across sectors.
Featured stories
Neha Nagar’s debut book aims to make personal finance accessible
Finance educator and content creator Neha Nagar has launched her debut book, Simple Money Serious Wealth: How to Turn Ordinary Income into Extraordinary Net Worth, to help readers make informed financial decisions and manage their money better.
Published on October 24, the book sold over 3,000 copies within its first 24 hours, according to a post on her Instagram account. Nagar, who has over a decade of experience in finance and seven years in content creation, says she decided to write the book after recognising that while people have access to financial information, many lack a structured approach to managing their money.
Nagar believes financial literacy in India still faces challenges, including the absence of personal finance education in schools, reluctance to discuss money within households, and the overwhelming amount of information available on social media.
Recognised by Hurun India as the country's most-followed female personal finance influencer in 2025, she wants the book to help readers build financial plans, understand investment options and make decisions suited to their needs. Her goal is to help people realise that financial independence is not just about how much they earn, but how confidently they manage their money.
Five tech and startup leaders whose personal controversies affected their careers
From India to Silicon Valley, several prominent technology and startup leaders have faced career setbacks following controversies involving personal relationships or workplace conduct. YourStory looks at five such cases, including former Infosys executive Phaneesh Murthy, who was dismissed as iGate CEO in 2013 following an investigation into his relationship with a subordinate, and The Viral Fever (TVF) founder Arunabh Kumar, who stepped down as CEO in 2017 after sexual harassment allegations surfaced. Kumar denied the allegations and was acquitted by a Mumbai court in 2022.
The list also includes former Intel CEO Brian Krzanich, who resigned in 2018 after the company found that his consensual relationship with an employee violated its non-fraternisation policy; former Google executive Andy Rubin, whose exit from the company came under scrutiny following reports of a sexual misconduct complaint and a $90 million exit package; and former HP CEO Mark Hurd, who resigned in 2010 after an investigation found violations of the company's business conduct standards. The report examines how the circumstances and outcomes differed across these cases.
Other news
IIT Madras, Gauhati University researchers develop new method to identify monsoon onset at local levels
Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras) and Gauhati University have developed a new method to identify when the monsoon arrives at individual locations, distinguishing sustained monsoon rainfall from short-lived local showers.
The climate-network approach tracks how clusters of local rainfall onsets across India connect and evolve into a larger, interconnected monsoon system. The findings were published in the Journal of Climate, a peer-reviewed journal of the American Meteorological Society.
The researchers treated geographical locations as nodes in a climate network, with links representing spatial connections between locations experiencing local rainfall onset. By tracking the growth and movement of these clusters, the study offers an objective method to identify when local rainfall patterns become part of a larger, sustained monsoon system, rather than treating every spell of rain as the monsoon's onset.
The study was co-authored by Yogenraj Patil, Gaurav Chopra, Shruti Tandon and Professor R I Sujith from IIT Madras, and Professor B N Goswami of Gauhati University.
Paras Semiconductors partners with US-based BroadPak
Paras Semiconductors, a subsidiary of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, has entered into a strategic technology partnership with US-based BroadPak Corporation to strengthen India's advanced semiconductor packaging capabilities.
The collaboration will combine Paras Semiconductors' manufacturing ambitions in optoelectronics, photonics and co-packaged optics with BroadPak's expertise in advanced semiconductor packaging, heterogeneous integration and chiplet-based architectures. The partnership aims to establish an advanced heterogeneous integration and 3D packaging facility in India under the Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) model.
The proposed facility will focus on 2.5D and 3D packaging, chiplet integration, hybrid bonding, wafer-level and panel-level fan-out packaging, co-packaged optics, and advanced semiconductor testing and qualification. BroadPak, headquartered in San Jose, California, brings experience in packaging design, manufacturing and system integration, with capabilities spanning architecture, simulation, assembly, testing and production.
IIT Bhubaneswar study identifies silver iodide surface as potential host for stable electron spin
Researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bhubaneswar have identified a specific surface of cubic zinc-blende silver iodide (AgI) as a promising candidate for hosting persistent spin texture (PST), a quantum phenomenon that could have applications in next-generation electronic devices.
The study, led by Dr Manish Kumar Mohanta, Ramanujan Faculty in the Department of Physics at IIT Bhubaneswar, has been published in Physical Review B, a journal of the American Physical Society. Persistent spin texture refers to the stable, unidirectional alignment of electron spins in certain nonmagnetic semiconductors. Since electrons possess an intrinsic property called spin, alongside their electric charge, this phenomenon could enable information to be processed and stored using electron spin.
The researchers note that persistent spin texture can suppress unwanted spin relaxation, allowing spin information to persist longer. This makes materials exhibiting the phenomenon promising candidates for spintronic devices, which use electron spin alongside electrical charge to process and store information.
(The copy will be updated with the latest news through the day)

articles.title: Hackers exploit trusted AWS access to breach multiple cloud environments
articles.text:
A threat actor used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials for a Qubole big data platform's AWS account to access and exfiltrate data from multiple customers' AWS environments.
The campaign ran between October 14 and 26, and affected tens of companies whose AWS environments had IAM roles configured to trust an AWS account associated with Qubole.
Qubole is an enterprise cloud data processing and analytics platform that helps companies manage large datasets and run machine learning workloads. It also offers AWS integration to allow computing resource management.
Companies can grant third-party providers such as Qubole access to their AWS resources by creating cross-account IAM roles. Trust policies determine which external AWS accounts can take these roles, and permissions are set to define the resources and actions allowed.
Researchers at cloud security company Wiz explain that external providers use AWS’s STS AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for accessing customers' resources in the cloud.
Wiz started to investigate the attack after data security and governance company Sentra shared information about suspicious activity observed in some of its customers' environments. The investigation also included cybersecurity company Mandiant.
The researchers found that the attacker had compromised two Qubole IAM users and assumed otherwise unused roles in multiple customers’ AWS accounts that had previously been configured to trust Qubole’s account, granting them access within the role’s permissions.
Wiz says the attacker then surveyed cloud resources, retrieved secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store, and read Lambda environment variables.
They then used the TruffleHog tool to validate discovered AWS keys, Microsoft Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials.
Once they gained deeper access, they downloaded data from all accessible S3 buckets in the AWS environment, following an opportunistic approach rather than carefully targeting specific data.
“The sequence was consistent across environments: assume a role, call ListBuckets to see what the role could reach, call ListObjects and HeadObject to enumerate and inspect the contents, then call GetObject to download them,” Wiz explains.
The report does not specify the exact method used to compromise the Qubole accounts or the number of downstream victims. However, Sentra confirmed dozens of victims and millions of files stolen from one customer alone.
Sentra says the attacker moved quickly and collected secrets at a rate of 100 passwords and keys in seven minutes.
BleepingComputer could not find a public announcement from Qubole about this incident. We have emailed the firm for more information about the attack and await their response.
Potentially impacted administrators are advised to review CloudTrail from October 1 onward for suspicious access from Qubole’s AWS account, investigate subsequent secret and S3 access, rotate exposed credentials, and revoke active role sessions.
It is also recommended to remove unused integrations and restrict remaining roles’ permissions, trusted identities, and permitted source networks.

articles.text:
Ce mardi soir, assez d’abonnés de Bouygues Telecom ont trouvé une connexion pour remplir la page de l’opérateur sur Downdetector, un site qui compile les signalements des utilisateurs. On y comptait plusieurs centaines de signalements en fin de journée, soit le pic des dernières 24 heures, et le site estime que l’opérateur « rencontre des problèmes ». Pour l’instant, on ne sait pas si c’est le mobile, la box ou les deux qui posent problème, ni quelles régions sont touchées. On peut également voir plusieurs signalements sur X de plusieurs clients.
Que faire en attendant
On commence par le classique, qui marche plus souvent qu’on ne le croit : redémarrer son smartphone ou sa box. Ensuite, on regarde le site d’assistance de Bouygues Telecom, qui permet de vérifier s’il y a un incident connu à une adresse précise. Si la box fonctionne mais que le mobile ne capte plus, on peut activer les appels en Wi-Fi pour continuer à téléphoner. Et si la coupure dure, on garde des captures d’écran au cas où il faudrait demander un geste commercial.
À ce niveau-là, on parle d’un incident à surveiller, pas d’une panne générale. Si les chiffres continuent de monter, on mettra cet article à jour. Et si Bouygues Telecom confirme le problème, on le dira aussi.

articles.title: Microsoft despide a varios empleados en Vietnam
articles.text:
Varios trabajadores de Microsoft en Vietnam recibieron una invitación para asistir a una reunión titulada “Actualización importante del negocio” en la que también participaban los responsables de recursos humanos. Así, lo que parecía una reunión de empresa terminó estando relacionado con despidos, según contaron en redes sociales algunos empleados, y la propia Microsoft ha terminado confirmando los recortes.
Según explica el diario vietnamita Tuoi Tre, los despidos afectan principalmente al departamento de investigación y desarrollo (I+D), aunque la tecnológica no ha comunicado cuántas personas han perdido su empleo ni qué puestos concretos han desaparecido.
Microsoft creó su equipo de investigación en Vietnam en 2024
Lo llamativo es que Microsoft había establecido este departamento hace apenas dos años, con equipos de ingeniería en Hanói y Ciudad Ho Chi Minh. Vietnam se convirtió así en el cuarto mercado asiático donde la compañía contaba con una división de este tipo, después de China, Japón y Taiwán. Sus trabajadores participaban en el desarrollo de soluciones de Microsoft 365 para usuarios de todo el mundo.
¿Y qué ha dicho Microsoft sobre estos despidos? En declaraciones a la prensa local, un portavoz explicó que la compañía ajusta continuamente su forma de trabajar y organizar los equipos para adaptarse a sus prioridades. También reconoció que esos cambios pueden implicar decisiones difíciles sobre los puestos de trabajo y aseguró que prestará apoyo a los empleados afectados.
Microsoft lleva operando en Vietnam desde 1996 y, pese a esta reducción de plantilla, insiste en que mantiene su compromiso con el país. Por ahora, la empresa tampoco ha detallado cómo quedará organizado su equipo de investigación y desarrollo tras los despidos.

articles.title: Black Friday : un robot-tondeuse testé à prix réduit
articles.text:
Black Friday – Le robot-tondeuse Anthbot M9 passe à 609 €, une remise pour préparer le printemps
Un prix qui se fait tondre
Le Black Friday s'invite aussi au jardin. L'Anthbot M9, un robot-tondeuse sans fil périphérique que nous avons testé, profite d'une vente flash à 609 € au lieu de 699 €. Une remise valable jusqu'au 30 novembre 2026.
Ce n'est pas parce que la pelouse entre progressivement en hibernation qu'il faut oublier son entretien. Le Black Friday peut justement être l'occasion de s'équiper pour la saison prochaine. L'Anthbot M9, un robot-tondeuse sans fil périphérique destiné aux jardins jusqu'à 1000 m², est actuellement proposé à 609 € au lieu de 699 €, soit une réduction de près de 13 %. Son petit frère, le M5 est proposé à 499 € si votre jardin n'excède pas les 500 m². L'offre prend fin le 30 novembre 2026.
Anthbot M9
Le M9 utilise un système de positionnement RTK pour se déplacer sans câble à enterrer autour du jardin. Une station de référence assure son guidage, tandis qu'une caméra associée à de l'intelligence artificielle se charge de reconnaître les obstacles. Le robot dispose d'une largeur de coupe de 20 cm, d'un réglage de hauteur entre 3 et 7 cm et peut affronter des pentes jusqu'à 45 %.
Un robot qui connaît son terrain
Lors de notre test, l'Anthbot M9 nous avait convaincus par sa précision de navigation et ses déplacements ordonnés. Il sait notamment choisir le sens de tonte le plus adapté à la forme du terrain pour limiter les manœuvres inutiles. Sa reconnaissance des obstacles s'est également montrée efficace, jusqu'à repérer une simple balle de tennis, un exercice qui pose encore problème à certains concurrents.
Nous avions également apprécié sa légèreté et sa façon de négocier les virages sans trop malmener les sols meubles. Quelques réserves subsistent toutefois, notamment l'obligation de placer la station RTK dans un endroit dégagé, un système antivol assez sommaire et une connexion 4G qui devient payante après trois mois.
