articles.title: El asistente de programación de Anthropic dejó contraseñas y claves a la vista de cualquiera en GitHub
articles.text:
Claude Code, el asistente de programación de Anthropic, guardó contraseñas y claves de acceso en archivos de configuración que desarrolladores subieron sin querer a GitHub, la plataforma pública donde se comparte código. La empresa de seguridad Apiiro halló 1.122 archivos con al menos un dato secreto.
Cuando el programa pide permiso para ejecutar un comando y el usuario elige “Sí, y no volver a preguntar”, Claude Code guarda esa orden tal cual en el archivo .claude/settings.local.json, dentro de la carpeta del proyecto. Si el comando incluía una contraseña o una clave, queda registrada en texto plano.
Ese archivo debería quedarse en la computadora del programador. Según la documentación de Anthropic, que cita The Hacker News, la primera vez que lo crea en un proyecto el programa lo agrega a la lista de exclusiones de git, el sistema de control de versiones, del usuario. Esa protección vive en una sola máquina y no viaja con el proyecto.
Si el proyecto se clona en otro equipo, si una carpeta se convierte en proyecto más tarde o si el archivo ya estaba registrado, la exclusión no actúa y el archivo se sube con el resto del código. En 539 de los 1.105 proyectos que Apiiro rastreó, un cambio firmado por Claude como coautor modificó ese archivo.
Más de 100.000 archivos revisados, 1.122 con secretos
Apiiro examinó 104.185 copias públicas del archivo, repartidas en 103.617 proyectos, entre el 1 y el 3 de noviembre, según informó iTnews. Encontró 1.379 secretos distintos en los 1.122 archivos, el 1,1% del total. Más de un tercio abría directamente una base de datos, con 379 contraseñas de ese tipo.
La lista incluye 43 accesos a servidores por SSH, algunos con la clave del administrador, y 23 claves de Amazon Web Services. Los archivos pertenecían a 63 organizaciones, entre ellas una que dejó expuesta la contraseña del propietario de la base de datos de una aplicación de historias clínicas.
Apiiro no probó si las credenciales seguían activas. Una de las organizaciones a las que avisó confirmó que su clave funcionaba. Dos programas populares de detección, gitleaks y TruffleHog, pasaron por alto 215 de los 1.122 archivos, porque muchas contraseñas escritas dentro de comandos no tienen un formato reconocible.
GitGuardian contó 31.088 credenciales desde enero de 2025
GitGuardian, otra firma de seguridad, publicó el 9 de noviembre una medición distinta: no miró lo que sigue expuesto hoy, sino todo lo que se subió a GitHub entre enero de 2025 y el 7 de noviembre. Halló 31.088 credenciales distintas en 23.276 proyectos, y 5.343 funcionaban cuando las detectó.
La firma también encontró 613 secretos en imágenes públicas de Docker Hub, un servicio donde se distribuyen programas ya empaquetados. Un mismo token de Cloudflare, una empresa de servicios web, aparece en 559 versiones de una sola imagen. Borrar el archivo del proyecto no elimina esas copias, advirtió GitGuardian.
Según su análisis, las filtraciones mensuales llegaron a un máximo de 12.535 en abril de 2026 y cayeron a 959 en octubre, una baja de 92%. GitGuardian dijo que no sabe qué cambió y que esa pregunta corresponde a Anthropic.
Anthropic: “Estamos viendo qué podemos hacer”
Boris Cherny, jefe de Claude Code en Anthropic, respondió en el foro Hacker News, según iTnews. “Históricamente Claude Code no ha eliminado secretos (hay muchas buenas herramientas para eso), pero estamos viendo qué podemos hacer para evitarlo”, escribió. Cuando un lector señaló que el modo automático también podía guardar esos comandos, contestó: “Buen punto”.
Cherny sostuvo que, como el programa excluye el archivo al crearlo, las copias expuestas se habían creado a mano y subido a GitHub. GitGuardian lo contradice: en unas 3.000 apariciones que revisó, todos los secretos estaban en una regla con la forma exacta que escribe el aviso de permiso. Usuarios reportaban el problema en GitHub desde agosto de 2025, según iTnews.
Apiiro recomienda cambiar primero toda credencial que el archivo haya contenido y limpiar después, porque el historial del proyecto, las copias y los 211 duplicados públicos que identificó conservan los datos. El equipo de Claude Code dijo que prototipará soluciones, como detección básica de secretos, aunque admitió que quizá no resuelvan el problema.

articles.title: FDA warns GLP-1 drugs may pose risk of rare condition that causes vision loss
articles.text:
The Food and Drug Administration is warning that popular obesity drugs—including Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound, and Mounjaro—may carry a “potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition that can lead to permanent vision loss.
In a drug safety communication Monday, the FDA said it will now require makers of GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs to add a warning about that risk on their drug labels. The specific eye condition it warns of is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or NAION. The condition is caused by restricted blood flow to the optic nerve, which leads to swelling and cell death and ultimately damages the nerve, causing abrupt vision loss that can often be permanent.
It’s unknown how GLP-1 drugs may cause NAION. The condition is rare overall, occurring in somewhere between two and 10 people in 100,000 in the general population, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology. These small numbers have made it more difficult to determine with certainty if there is a connection. Further complicating the potential link is the fact that the risk factors for developing NAION are common among patients taking GLP-1 drugs. The risk factors include diabetes, cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, metabolic syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea.
Mixed data
The first study suggesting a link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION came in 2024 from Harvard University researchers. Their study, published in JAMA Ophthalmology, looked at 710 patients with diabetes and 979 patients with either overweight or obesity. In each group, some of the patients were taking semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy), while others were taking non-GLP-1 antidiabetic or weight loss drugs. The researchers found in both patient groups that those taking GLP-1 drugs after 36 months had higher rates of NAION. Among the diabetes patients, 8.9 percent of patients on semaglutide had the eye condition, while only 1.8 percent of patients in the non-GLP-1 groups developed it. Similarly, among those with overweight/obesity, 6.7 percent of patients on a GLP-1 had NAION compared with 0.8 percent in the non-GLP-1 group.
The study had significant limitations, though. The patients were all from one referral center that treated most of the region’s NAION cases. The overall incidence rates of NAION in the studied patients were much higher than the rates seen in the general population. This suggests there may have been selection bias and that the results are not generalizable. The study also did not look at the severity of diabetes in the patients, which can influence the risk of NAION. Last, the study didn’t offer any hints as to how GLP-1 drugs may contribute to NAION—and researchers remain uncertain of a possible mechanism.

articles.title: Batch Intelligence at Scale: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience
articles.text:
Transcript
Aditya Mulik: My topic today is, Batch Intelligence at Scale, which is, Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience. My name is Aditya Mulik. I work as a senior software engineer at Walmart Global Tech.
The problem I want to walk you through today is one which all retailers are wrestling with right now, which is inventory accuracy. What I want to say is the retail at massive scale, so Walmart has around 4,700 stores within the U.S. They have multiple stores in Canada, Mexico, and so on as well, but the major chunk is in the U.S. itself. There are hundreds of thousands of SKUs. There are varying departments, like varying products, any product that we can imagine of, those are all available at Walmart. The physical space is also quite large and so many items have to be tracked very carefully. The problem that each retailer is dealing with, as I mentioned about inventory accuracy, is where we have to determine what is the right inventory required for a particular occasion. If it's Thanksgiving, we have to make sure that much inventory is available at a particular point in time.
What I want to mention over here is, can we predict what inventory a department needs? I'm particularly looking for a particular department here. Can we predict what inventory a department needs for the next n number of days accurately, automatically, and at scale? Because the scale is quite large, and if you are targeting a particular department, it has to have a particular set of items available. If you are walking towards a shelf and if that shelf doesn't have a particular item available, it's not a good experience. We have to ensure that each item has to be available and in stock.
The Accuracy Imperative
The accuracy imperative. Accuracy isn't a nice-to-have, it's very mission critical, on any particular item. What we worked on was fresh food, or basically the items, you can take an example like rotisserie chicken or fresh beef, these items can expire very quickly. The store manager has to decide very accurately like, what items are there in stock and what items need to be ordered, to make sure that the inventory is very accurate for the next n number of days. The line between a stock shelf and an empty rack is what we are looking over here right now. If there are stockouts or overstock, then it could be a problem. If it's an overstock, obviously the items are going to go to waste. Either it has to be donated or it has to be thrown away. Consider this compounded across millions of square feet of retail. We have 4,700 stores, so you can imagine how critical this could be for a particular store. The next thing I'll say here is, how do we keep inventory accurate at this scale? Our first answer has to be an obvious one, we have to forecast the demand based on the history.
Backward-Looking Machine Learning Model
Now the thing is like, in Walmart, we already have machine learning models which can actually predict the amount of inventory that has to be ordered. We have backward-looking machine learning models which are trained on historical sales data to forecast future demand. We use like a year's or maybe two years of sales data, where we are trying to determine, ok, this much amount of inventory has to be ordered for the next maybe 30 days or maybe next 60 days, and so on. It's reliable for steady, recurring, and seasonal trends. Walmart is very focused on Thanksgiving. We know during Thanksgiving we have to order n number of items. That is very accurate for prediction. It's fully automated and it scales across SKUs and stores. The problem right now is sales forecasting accuracy. The pro over here is like, based on the historical trends, it can get it properly.
What if there are blind unprecedented events. Consider an example where there's a storm coming. Now the machine learning model won't be able to accurately determine if there's a storm, and if we need water or certain other items. Will that be actually available well in advance? That machine learning model might not be able to predict that. These are the things that the store manager has to deal with. They can't just rely on this particular backward trend. The question became, how do we add real-time, real-world context on top of the signals we already trust. The thing is, since we already have the machine learning models and we already know the prediction can be done in a specific way, this was an engineering challenge that came on to us, where we had to determine how should we just not rely on backward trends. Like, this is something that's going to happen, and then this number of stock has to be ordered. What if we can add some real-time context to it?
Agents, Not Monoliths: The Sequential Workflow
That's where we came up with a multi-agent — not monolith — basically a sequential workflow of agents where this agentic flow can actually determine, like get the real-time data along with some forecasting model data as well, and get the exact accurate decision that has to be given to the store manager, where these are the number of items that they need to order. How did we do that? Basically, in the sequential agentic workflow, we added multi-agent orchestration, like one agent after another, where first agent would determine, so in this case, it gathers context from various data sources for a particular department. Consider if it's a department, or like as I said about the fresh food, it's getting all the metadata from various sources like BigQuery and so on. That context is then fed to the agent, which outputs more accurate data. If it's like rotisserie chicken, it has to be ordered for the quantity that needs to be determined.
Then the second agent consumes that data, and then it synthesizes past sales data prepared by the data engineering pipeline. We have another pipeline which is set to get more context. What it does is, there's an amalgamation of two datasets which is collated, and then it is fed to another third agent data. Now this agent is quite important, which analyzes the context and output from the previous agent, and there is a grounding mechanism over here now. Consider, as I said, just a backward ML trend is not going to get us the exact prediction. There might be a weather agent, or there might be some weather API call. There could be a trending event that's happening, a sales event is happening over there. It can gather that context and it can make more accurate predictions, now that it has to order more or either less of the inventory. Then, finally, the fourth agent which produces the final natural language recommendation directive, which is like, increase the stock by this percent, and so on. That's the entire sequential workflow that we created. This was particularly targeted for a specific department.
The Output and the Human-in-the-Loop
Going to the next part, so the output, and this is the human-in-the-loop. What we were trying to do over here was, all this context generation and everything was fine, but our only goal was the store manager has to get a clear directive. The clear directive was not a dashboard, it was just a clear command. Increase apple stock 15% in produce ahead of the weekend. They are having a clear context on what they need to do. It's not just that, they are just going to increase the stock right away. There's a real-time data integration as I mentioned, which is like, MCP lets agents pull live data sources during reasoning. All of that is verified using live tools, MCPs, and so on, which is grounded properly. The critical checkpoint is, the store manager reviews each recommendation, and the store manager can either accept it or override it, because they will manually go and check and verify if there is actually a shortage of apples, if they do want to order it. There was a human in the loop in this entire pattern. This is a feature not a fallback. Human oversight in the final validation layer was catching the local context that the data cannot. That was the additional validation that the store manager was doing.
Production Rollout, and Subsequent Failures
Now this is where the important aspect comes. Then we went to production. The pilot was magic, because we tested it on maybe 10 stores or 15 stores, and then we had a clear output, coherent recommendations, and the stakeholders were quite happy about it. Then we flipped the switch to full-scale nightly runs. This was not like a real-time context where the store manager is communicating with the app, it's just a recommendation that the store manager gets during the start of the day. As Walmart stores open in the early morning, they get this recommendation and then they act upon it. Yes, we did this. We went to full chain, like all 4,700-plus stores that we rolled it out to. Then, what works at the scale of one rarely survives the scale of thousands. Here are the four failures that taught us why. Because we saw that, ok, we went to production, we made it like full chain available.
Initially for a 10-store pilot, recommendations were great, we got good feedback. There were a lot of engineering teams, data science team getting involved, and they had everything analyzed. The main thing was, me and my team's task was to get it to production, and then we started observing a lot of failures. There were four main failures which taught us what exactly happened.
I'm moving on towards the failures now. These are the common failures that we have always seen in the LLM world, and this is how we also tackled it. The very first one was hallucinations and schema violations. Here as you can see, hallucinations and schema violations were like, we had to enforce structured outputs, because the agentic workflow was getting the context, it was getting all the data, the output as well. The output was vague at times, because it was not always validated how it has to be given to the end user. Here you can see like we had to add some schema layer, which is basically to validate outputs via some JSON format of identical validation. I can give a bad example output over here. This was one of the recommendations that went to one of the store managers. As you can see over here, I think you should probably increase some stock for the weekend, maybe around 15% or so, for produce items that sell well.
It's like a coherent recommendation. It doesn't make sense, because it says that you have to increase the stock, but what stock? We don't know. Is it apples? Is it rotisserie chicken? What is it? We don't know. It's just saying that around 15%, and it should be about something that's in the produce section. Now the store manager has to go and verify which is the item that's low on stock. This didn't make sense, and it still gave a pretty high confidence. The thing is it did validate across the schema but it didn't make sense from a good output perspective. What we did is we fixed it with structured output, but also making sure that the item is also validated across a specific SKU, whether it's like which department it belongs to. If it's a produce, the item name has to be there, which is the Honeycrisp Apple right over there, and the SKU.
This confidence level made sure like this is adhering to the department that it has to be. This can be extended as possible. The stock directive, the schema which is given, and this is all validated across a common schema. As I mentioned, here's the same output. Now schema enforced, every field typed and validated: the exact SKU, item, department, and adjustment. No ambiguity left. This was the first failure.
Then, again, now the second failure. This is something that we encountered once we were full chain as well, where it was semantically wrong. What do we mean by that? You're ensuring data integrity with semantic validation. Even though we did have structured output there was a problem. The problem was the data engineering, because the workflow that was created was an overnight job, where we gathered data from various sources. Walmart has so much data for each produce, or each department. Once we pull the data, there were certain things that were getting mapped properly but certain things were not getting mapped accurately. This was a one-off situation maybe out of hundreds of items that we found out there was an issue. I can give an example over here. As you see here, everything is matching to the schema, but as we can see I have highlighted over here.
At Walmart there are multiple departments. The SKUs are unique as well, but the problem is it can map one of the items which has the same item number, but the department is different. The other department might have the same item number. The only varying part is the department over here. If there's a product that's coming as Honeycrisp Apple, but it is coming from auto_parts, so there should be some recommendation for auto_parts which was showing to the end user, but for an auto_part it was showing as a Honeycrisp Apple, which doesn't make sense. This was a failure at the data ingestion layer, where basically, wherever the data was being fetched from, it was not correctly being mapped. We had to also validate if the SKU is correct and also the item name is also coming from the same SKU. This was one of the failures. It was a dangerous kind of failure, perfectly valid JSON, but it maps Honeycrisp Apple to auto_parts because the SKUs collided.
The schema can't catch this, only schema validation can. How did we ensure to fix this? This is the part where we did the grounding mechanism. As you can see, we introduced an MCP tool call over here, basically validate coherence, where if you are getting a stock directive, we have an MCP client which is connecting to the proper data source. From that proper data source, we are looking up the proper catalog that belongs to that item. We made sure that any item that is not relevant to that particular data pipeline, it should not be processed as well. That's where we ensured, ok, this is something that every output coming from an agent has to be validated with some grounding mechanism. This was another failure that we encountered.
Then there was one more. This is the place where it's very common, where outputs were vanished. What do I mean by that? Over here you can see unreliable inference, which is failure disrupts perfect inferences, and then there is resilient inference. What I mean by that is there could be network issues, like network partition can happen as we know. Here you can see we had some logs enabled. Because in the pipeline, the way it was, there are multiple agents doing multiple tasks, and then their task was to just save the output to some persistent storage. What if there is a db_write failure, like here you can see clearly there is a timeout error which is the connection reset that has happened. Because of the connection reset the output has just vanished now. We didn't have a mechanism initially where if the output is vanished, maybe there are like 4700 stores, maybe some of the stores were not even saving the output and the store manager was just opening the app, and seeing like, ok, there's no recommendation today, that means everything is proper.
That was a failure that was observed. How did we fix that as well? This is where the mechanism of the agentic workflow agent comes over here. We had a sequential agent, and we then determined to let's switch it to a loop agent. As you can see, the main thing that I'm highlighting over here is the max iterations. These are the bounded retries that we have added. If there are any sort of failures happening, the agentic workflow will ensure to retry. Right now, you can see there are multiple sub-agents over here, like data gathering agent, synthesis agent, grounding agent. We add an iteration for the entire loop. This might be not that cost efficient, but maybe we can add this max iteration to a particular agent as well where the main work is handled. In this case, I'm showing the entire agent can make sure the workflow is computed properly, so that the output is saved and you can increase the number of iterations as much as you want. Like here, I've just given as an example of five iterations.
Next one, so we were flying blind. Observability is a must. This is a very important thing. Since we had full chain available, the very common thing that we want to ensure is we should have observability in the entire workflow. What do I mean by that? The regular way of doing the engineering is you can have maybe 5xx errors or 4xx errors. Even here it's the same case, like if we saw like there's a schema violation, or if there are retries that didn't happen, or something that went wrong, we were adding structured logging. Structured logging was ensured. Over here you can see, as an example, is how many times the retries happened, like two attempts. Or if there was a schema violation, how much latency it had. All of this was enabled just to make sure that we have clear visibility into what's happening in our entire workflow.
As you can see over here, we had proper logging if the LLM response doesn't match the schema, if there is a tool response that failed, so it was retrying again. We were trying to reach a success rate of 99%, so this is some example that I added, like if there's a 97% error rate, 2.3% of failure rate, and so on. We made sure that observability is also in place.
The Cost Factor
That being said, these were the four main failures. Now I want to get to the very crisp part of what we were building over here. With failures behind us, the next question on the table was cost. This was the biggest question that was running on to us, because we wanted to get this into production. This was a very critical thing that we were trying to get in, but we were leveraging all foundational models, and with a high scale, like 4700 stores, the amount of tokens generated is quite high. How much of this whole solution is going to cost to run, is what was the next question. The thing over here is the PTU problem. When the solution went to production, we had humongous amount of input and output tokens being used. Since it was a foundational model, we decided to secure 400 PTUs for that amount of scale that we need to run.
For 400 PTUs, we were almost being charged around 100k to 120k per month, and the solution was not that, because we are trying to also make sure that the inventory is accurate, also save cost. There should not be wastage happening in a particular department. Running at this position, it doesn't make sense, if these much PTUs are going to be used. PTUs is like reserved capacity, and we have to reserve it for the entire day. Any of these vendors who are providing the PTUs, we have to take it for the entire 24 hours, and it's a monthly or yearly subscription that we have to take in. Now the problem is, this is a batch intelligence application, it's only going to run overnight. It's not going to run the entire day. We are not serving any live traffic. For us, we were being charged 400 PTUs for 24 hours, and PTUs reserve capacity for the entire day.
Our workload was nightly batch run, which was not 24 by 7. We were paying for the round the clock capacity which was being used. This was our most critical problem that we were trying to solve in a particular defined set of time, which didn't make sense because of the cost involved. We started exploring options, what are the options? Because this is a foundational model, the best part about foundational model is they are well trained, they are good for such enterprise scale applications. The next thing that came to us was, what AI model should I choose? Here as you can see, we had cheaper models where we can go with open-source models or any other models, which might introduce some latency, or they could be cheaper compared to the one which we already had, whether it's a GPT-4.1 or Gemini, and so on. Or we can just reduce the PTUs, that was another option. Or we could go with pay-as-you-go. We were debating between quality versus cost, and both were not a good option, because we needed high quality but lower cost. That was the main problem that we had to solve.
How did we do that? The decision that we made was, we went with pay-as-you-go. Now just to go with some background, the problem with PTU versus pay-as-you-go, is pay-as-you-go will come with latency issues, as I've mentioned over here, and there will be rate limiting happening. We did observe a lot of rate limit issues, but now the thing is, as I mentioned in my failures as well, we had added a retry logic. This retry logic enabled us, even if there is a rate limit, if there are any 4xx or 5xx errors, I'm just going to retry again. If I do retry again, the output will be generated again. Now, if it's a pay-as-you-go, it's still a foundational model and it still gives very accurate responses, and there was no reserved capacity as well over here. We were not paying round the clock, we were just using as much compute as we require.
The payoff, so what happened over here is, we were supposed to pay around 100k per month, now we are paying just 10k as the final usage, because even with the retries, the cost is just very low. It's just going to happen in that specific 30 minutes, or maybe the time might increase. We don't mind because the stores are already closed, this is going to be a nightly job. Then, eventually, whatever compute is being taken is going to just happen at night, even if there are retries and everything, the cost will be minimal, output will be still matching the quality that we have set, because there is schema enforcement, and all the data engineering pipelines were fixed. This was our biggest win. As I mentioned, same tokens, same model, just a pricing tier switch from PTU to pay-as-you-go, and for a drastic drop in cost. That was the big win that I wanted to mention over here.
Learnings, When Building at Scale
Every failure and every fix left us with a lesson worth carrying forward. Here's what we learned, building at scale. These are some of the learnings that I'm going to mention once again. Basically, schema enforcement. Since we are retrying, everything is all planned out, but schema enforcement is not just the one thing that happens over here, basic JSON validation. There has to be semantic validation, because data, what is coming from various sources, like in the AI domain, what I've learned very well is context has to be very accurate. With the data pipelines that we have, whatever context we get, if there is even a slight mismatch, it can just return vague output. We have to make sure semantic validation is in place. Data usability, making data easy to understand and use. We need to have some observability as well. Whatever the data that is coming in, we need to see how the pipelines are running.
All those things have to be taken into consideration. Then comes the data integrity. Maintaining accuracy and consistency of data is very important, is what I've learned from this entire perspective. That's one of the key features. Second thing is data engineering limits AI quality. As I mentioned over here, data quality over here is reliable AI results, accurate and trustworthy outcomes, data rectification, fixing upstream data issues, data engineering, ensuring data quality, and flawed data. What do we mean by all of this? The entire context over here, since it was a nightly job that was being run, this had a huge emphasis on the data engineering aspects itself. Because we were getting data from various sources, there was a lot of focus that was added into this perspective, where data coming from various sources has to be verified. The amount of scripts that we created were validated with the business and the data team, with the engineering team.
We ensured that once the data is very accurate, then that context will be fed properly to the agents with a proper particular prompt, and that will generate the exact output that we are looking for. Because it's a multi-agent workflow, we have to ensure that the data that is coming from various sources has to be very accurate. That was our main goal that we learned from this entire workflow. Also, like flawed data, as I mentioned, unreliable input is also like, once the input is not proper, all the agents will react in a weird output, because it might either not match to the schema, or it might just match to the schema also, but just generate vague outputs, and that's how it would return. Building retry logic, this was one of the most important aspects that I went through. We have been very much emphasizing on this.
Retries can be a very bad loop as well, where if you don't plan it properly, it can just keep retrying, and that would just increase a lot of costs. Just because there are tokens involved over here, you have to plan it very accurately. As I mentioned in the initial flow, we used to retry it at the base, like root level, where all the agents are, like where the workflow runs. Ideally, the agentic retry should be in such a pattern where it is actually needed, whether we are getting the context from the proper data source, so that the further agents don't have to hallucinate, or there could be something that can go wrong. Retry over here, implemented from the outset, reduced unexpected failures. There's proactive system enhancement, cost saving and efficiency. It results into better user satisfaction.
The next learning perspective is observability. This is one of the key things from the entire workflow, that everyone is focused on. Traceability is important, structured logging is important, and enhanced system understanding. Because once you have tracing enabled, for us, initially, when we were having this entire workflow running, we were not able to determine, ok, what's going wrong, just because there are no proper traces set up. If you're not able to identify if the LLM is hallucinating, or if the model is just getting rate limited, all that has to be clearly available. There are tools which help us add those visibility, and then having that in place, make sure that your application is very robust, and can survive any failures to make it very resilient. That's a very important aspect that I'll mention over here. The next thing is matching infrastructure to requirements. This is the key thing that we realized, which is the infrastructure should be used for a nightly batch job.
Here, we can see that the real-time infrastructure, like if you have a real-time infrastructure where users are having conversations with the LLM, in that case, you can have an accurate set of PTUs set up, and so on. In cost effective infrastructures, you need to ensure that you don't need to actually have PTUs only allocated. Here, in our case, we were opting either for like pay-as-you-go, or you can even go with open-source models. As long as it's giving you the proper performance, the correct output, that's the ideal approach that you should be going with. The next one is, I've reached the end, which is, tomorrow at 6 a.m., a store manager will confidently adjust the inventory. They don't know about our schema validation, our loop retries, our nightly API optimizations. They don't have to as well. It's just the ultimate metric, which is the resilient engineering. That's what the perspective is.
Summary
Just to recap over here, schema is our table stakes, semantics is the real work. Focus on validation checks that go beyond basic JSON structure. Data engineering limits AI quality, so garbage in results into garbage out as well. Having retry logic is very important. If there are network timeouts, hallucinations, retry can ensure that your output is always accurate. Observability is mandatory. Tracing, logging is very important. Then match infrastructure to the regular requirements. If it's a nightly non-latency sensitive batch job, then you have to ensure that you don't need to actually rely on PTUs, because that would just cost you even more than what's expected. That's the main goal.
Questions and Answers
Participant 1: How did you assess the benefits or effectiveness of the new model compared to your legacy time series forecasting models? You said before you built this agentic flow, you had some forecasting models, the classical ML time series models. How did you assess whether this new agentic model was better?
Aditya Mulik: The thing is, basically, we had like time series forecast model, what we were using in this use case, because we had a lot of sales data. We were looking at the past two years of sales data for the forecasting model. Now that the forecasting model can just output in an accurate pattern for a fixed set of events, if it's a Thanksgiving event, the time series forecasting model will accurately determine what is needed. What if there is a situation where there's a flash sale happening somewhere, or there's a competitor having a flash sale, or consider if there is a certain situation, like a storm is coming. Then now the forecasting model won't be able to determine that. This is where we wanted to introduce agentic workflows. The entire goal was we have to create an output, but we wanted some real-time data mechanism as well. That's where we decided to go with the agentic workflow. That's how we decided to get the output here.
Participant 2: Did you keep the log only in testing, in the trial phase, or what about in production? Do you still keep all the logs in production?
Aditya Mulik: For production, you mentioned?
Participant 2: Did you keep all the logs in production?
Aditya Mulik: How did we determine?
Participant 2: We understand you write down all the logs, you check all the logs, during the testing it will help you to analyze what's wrong. Did you keep all the logs in the production phase?
Aditya Mulik: How did we ensure logging is maintained in production? There are multiple tools that were being used over here. Initially, we opted with cloud vendors themself, where they have their own logging tools and mechanism. We had our own custom logs added to every agentic workflow. Each agent that had custom functions, like as I mentioned in one of the MCP tools, where it was validating across one of the SKUs. In that SKU, we were trying to determine, like we were adding some logs, if there is a failure happening, or if there is any db_writes that's happening or db_reads happening. If there are any failures, we added custom logs, we had our own dashboards. Initially, we went with the cloud vendor dashboards, but we had our own custom dashboards to verify that.
Participant 3: At this conference, we had multiple sessions about evaluating the agents. I think for your case, it's especially interesting to hear, given it's deployed in production on many users, if you do changes to your agent, how do you evaluate it? How do you do regression testing and evaluations?
Aditya Mulik: This is the thing that I didn't include in my presentation as well, because this was our initial workflow where we went with an MVP. Because initially, our process was to come with an MVP, how should we determine the inventory accuracy. The things that we didn't include were evals. We did work upon in an iterative fashion where we had a certain perspective, like if there is a particular department, in this case, as I mentioned about rotisserie chicken, the shelf life is about 24 hours to 48 hours, is what I know about. There should be a certain eval set for particular departments as well. What we did initially was to go with a flow where we are getting real-time data. Once we have that data coming in, then we were able to iteratively add evals and a grounding mechanism, and even governance. Because at times, they were like, we had to make sure there are pricing information and everything that should not be coming in. All that was considered in an evaluation set. That's how we had approached it. That was not one of the perspectives that I did include, because that's something that was iteratively performed.
Participant 4: You mentioned that the store manager needs to act on the recommendation, either agree or override. Is there a possibility that the store manager does not take any action? Does the recommendation become stale because the next nightly run might have different parameters, and that might be a different recommendation.
Aditya Mulik: The thing is, the store managers didn't act upon it right away. The way it was done was initially when we were in the pilot phase, this was all being validated very thoroughly. The store manager has the ability to first go because it's kind of like their day-to-day process, they have their own applications where they're verifying the inventory that's coming in. This was just as a recommendation that was initially being shared to their store manager. They were manually validating it. As this went to full production, and over the iterative process of weeks and weeks, they were able to determine that the predictions were becoming more and more accurate, because that was actually the context that they were getting. The only thing was there was always a human in the loop perspective over here. Because even if the recommendation has come in, they won't just take the action right away, they will verify the inventory and then only they'll take a call. That's how it was done. It's not that they always acted upon it.
Participant 5: You mentioned the cost aspect. How did business decide in the end, is it worthwhile, given the cost to roll it out globally, or is there a tradeoff to take into account?
Aditya Mulik: This was an initial POC that we started off with. The way it was working out was initially recommendations were just based on machine learning models themselves. That's how it was running from a longer time. As this agentic workflow started coming through, and then we did already have something which was planned out to have this rolled out, like to certain pilot stores. The plan was initially to see how this fits in the entire ecosystem, because we didn't want to disturb the existing flow, because as the stores are operating right now, they're well efficient. This is just an additional layer that we added over here, just to make sure like, ok, this is getting more accurate recommendations. Then it went out as a POC, POC to the entire production, like 4700 stores. Then it was foolproof as a concept that got deployed. We iteratively kept adding more and more recommendations. Our initial plan was to do it for a specific department itself. Then that's how we scaled it up.

articles.title: The Download: Pelosi’s successor targets AI and data centers face power woes
articles.text:
The Download: Pelosi’s successor targets AI and data centers face power woes
Plus: The FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
—Grace Huckins
As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.
I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.
“We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it.
The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
—James O’Donnell
As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape.
Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback.
The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Find out why.
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 The FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair
But Trump says he doesn’t think Huang needs to worry. (AP News)
+ Huang hired a PR firm known for handling sex scandals last year. (Wired $)
+ The allegations will likely spur new chip export restrictions. (Reuters $)
+ They also raise questions about Huang’s lobbying on China. (Verge)
+ And threaten the fate of the economy. (WP $)
2 France has accused Iran of hacking its supermarket fridges
Prosecutors are investigating the leaders of an Iranian cyber unit. (NPR)
+ Hackers are shifting to manipulating physical equipment. (Axios)

articles.title: The iPhone 5C is having a Gen Z ‘retro tech’ renaissance, but privacy experts warn against security risks
articles.text:
iPhone 5C searches are up 40,500% as Gen Z boards the retro camera trend — but privacy experts warn it ‘can’t protect personal data in the way more modern iPhones do’
A retro phone with an appealing camera
- Searches for 'buy iPhone 5C' are up 40,500% in the last year
- This is reportedly due to Gen Z looking for retro digital camera alternatives
- However, using an iPhone 5C comes with major security risks if you don't take precautions
While the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo are proving big hits for Apple, you might be surprised to hear that the iPhone 5C is enjoying a resurgence in popularity too.
According to mobile phone recycling comparison site Compare and Recycle, searches for ‘buy iPhone 5C’ — a phone from 2013 — are up 40,500% in the past year. Similarly, searches for ‘iPhone 5C camera’ are up 1,815%, and searches for ‘iPhone 5C’ have risen by 264%.
This is apparently due to Gen Z’s interest in retro cameras and ‘Y2K aesthetic’ photos, which the iPhone 5C, with its 13-year-old 8MP camera, is excellent at capturing.
But buying such an old phone comes with risks. Lee Elliott, chief product officer at Compare and Recycle, notes that “unlike regular digital cameras, the iPhone 5C comes with digital security risks users may not expect. The last iOS version the iPhone 5C can run is iOS 10.3.3, released in 2017. That’s almost a decade without updates or security fixes.”
As such, “the iPhone 5C can’t protect personal data in the way more modern iPhones do, leaving users vulnerable to data leaks, hacking, and other security breaches.”
Use it as a camera, not a smartphone
That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t buy an iPhone 5C if you’re also looking for a retro digital camera alternative, but it does mean you should be aware of the risks and take appropriate precautions.
Lee suggests that ideally you should use the iPhone 5C purely as a digital camera, meaning keeping it offline in airplane mode with no SIM card inserted, and not logging in to your personal Apple ID. You should also therefore transfer photos to your computer using a cable rather than backing them up to iCloud.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
If you absolutely must get online and download apps, then create a disposable Apple ID purely for use on this phone, and avoid logging into any other sensitive accounts, such as email, banking, or social media accounts that include personal information.
Do all that, and you can safely enjoy the retro joys of the iPhone 5C’s camera — along with the universal millennial experience of wishing you’d taken those photos with something better when you look back at them in 10 or 15 years.

He has a love for everything ‘smart’, from watches to lights, and can often be found arguing with AI assistants or drowning in the latest apps. articles.title: Seagate resurrects hybrid storage: Hands-on with the FireCuda Forge – 8 or 20TB external hard drive requires you to bring your own NVMe SSD
articles.text:
Seagate resurrects hybrid storage: Hands-on with the FireCuda Forge – 8 or 20TB external hard drive requires you to bring your own NVMe SSD
Seagate wants you to side-load an SSD in its latest external hard drive.
What's old is new again. Seagate started adding faster flash-based storage to its hard drives in 2010, when solid-state storage was prohibitively expensive. And now that SSDs are stupid-expensive again (thanks, AI hyperscaler demand) the hard drive maker is offering up another hybrid drive, of sorts, with the Firecuda Forge.
Available in 8TB and 20TB capacities, the Forge is an external hard drive that requires that you bring and install your own SSD. That's right, the drive won't work unless you partially disassemble and install your own M.2 2280 SSD, which mounts in the side of the enclosure. 1TB drives with DRAM are recommended. Performance maxes out at PCIe Gen3 drives; newer, faster, and roomier SSDs are supported, but won't improve performance. The Firecuda Forge only has a mounting point for 2280-length drives, and while drives that are less than 1TB are supported, that means less room for frequently used files, so "performance may be reduced."
Interestingly, Seagate sent us a 2TB FireCuda 530R SSD to test with the Forge hard drive, which is both faster (PCIe 4.0) and more spacious than what the company says you should pair with its hard drive. The list of SSD that Seagate has officially qualified to work with the Firecuda Forge is also pretty sparse, including just three other drives: Samsung's 990 Pro, WD/Sandisk SN850X/GX Pro 850X, and the WD/SanDisk SN710/GX7100.
We only received a review sample a few days before launch, and haven't yet had a chance to put the FireCuda Forge through its paces for a full review. But I was impressed that, after I installed the SSD and plugged the drive in, it just showed up in Windows 11 as an 8TB drive. (The company says it also works with macOS 26 and later). There was no software setup involved, and Seagate says you can even remove and upgrade the hard drive to something roomier down the line. Seagate calls the "product architecture" that handles unifying and data handling between the spinning platter drive and the SSD "Alkemi," and says it combines "onboard processing" with the hard drive and the user-supplied SSD to "prioritize active data without requiring users to manually manage separate drives."
Seagate says Alkemi observes workloads and gives priority to currently relevant or often-used data, that it adapts over time to user behavior, and describes it as an "on-device device dynamic caching and workload-aware data-prioritization technology." That sounds pretty similar to the SSD caching used on hybrid drives of the early 2010s, although with up to 1TB of fast SSD storage, you're getting a much bigger fast data pool than those drives of the past, which often made do with 4-16GB.
Interestingly, Seagate says that machine learning is a part of what Alkemi does, but repeatedly points out in its review materials that it is not using generative AI. It's likely the company is worried about customers connecting the many reported instances of LLMs and agents deleting data with this new product. I can understand why Seagate would want to distance its hybrid storage tech from reports of catastrophic data deletion.
What's the FireCuda Forge like to use?
Getting past the somewhat odd-feeling aspect of having to crack open an external drive right out of the box and install another drive into it in order for it to work, the process was pretty painless. You have to remove four screws from the bottom (with a tiny included hex-bit driver) to get the outer shell off the FireCuda Forge. From there, the M.2 drive bay is clearly visible on the side. If you want to remove six more hex screws, you can also pop out the hard drive for future upgrades. But for now, we're just going to install an M.2 SSD.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
SSD installation is pretty much the same as putting one of these drives in any laptop or motherboard. Though you'll need a tool; the drive requires a a tiny screw and Seagate does not include a suitable Phillips head screwdriver. The drive bay is somewhat recessed, and there are two thick thermal pads included in the box that should ensure the drive makes contact with both the inner edge of the bay and the external shroud.
This should provide some heat dissipation, but these surfaces are all's plastic, with only a foil layer on the outer shroud to draw some of the drive's heat away from the SSD itself. This is probably fine for most bursty game and creative workloads. But this design does not feel ideal for workloads that hit the drive consistently for hours on end. During our testing, the edge of the drive where the SSD is installed got noticeably warmer than the rest of the enclosure, but it didn't get hot.
In terms of design, the FireCuda Forge looks very similar to the FireCuda X Vault HDD we looked at earlier this year, complete with some gamer-friendly RGB lighting. The primary physical difference is that you'll need the supplied USB-C cable and external power adapter to use the Forge, while the X Vault only has a USB-C port. Presumably, powering both a 3.5-inch hard drive and an M.2 SSD draws too much power for most (or at least some) USB-C ports. I still would love for drives like this to be able to run off of one single cable, though, which was my favorite feature of the X Vault hard drive.
Preliminary testing
We only received the FireCuda Forge a couple of working days before its announcement. But we were able to run some benchmarks with the Forge drive and a 530R SSD that Seagate provided, and saw some interesting results. The Forge's USB-C connection is USB4, and Seagate's performance claims are up to 2,500 MB/s read and 2,000 MB/s write. That's obviously much faster than a hard drive, but you're also going to be sacrificing the speed of the SSD you're dropping into this drive — especially if it's a PCIe 4.0 SSD.
Trace Testing - PCMark 10 Storage Benchmark
PCMark 10 is a trace-based benchmark that uses a wide-ranging set of real-world traces from popular applications and everyday tasks to measure the performance of storage devices.
On this synthetic test, Seagate's Forge beats recent traditional hard drives (and the slowest external SSD we've tested, Samsung's T5). But Kingston's fast flash drive does better, as does Sandisk's Desk Drive, which nearly doubles the score of the Forge, which isn't surprising given it's a full-fledged external SSD.
Transfer Rates — DiskBench
We use the DiskBench storage benchmarking tool to test file transfer performance with a custom 50GB dataset. We copy 4,617 files (images, videos, and software ISO files) to a folder on the test drive (write). Then, after leaving the system idle for five minutes, we run the same test in reverse, moving the test folder to a different location on our PCIe 4.0 testing drive.
Here , we see the Forge drive easily beating the spinning-platter-only drives and Samsung's T5 Evo on writes, only falling to the SanDisk Desk Drive desktop SSD. But on reads, the Forge leads by the pack.
Synthetic Testing: CrystalDiskMark
CrystalDiskMark (CDM) is a free and easy-to-run storage benchmarking tool that SSD companies commonly use to assign performance specifications to their products. It gives us insight into how each device handles different file sizes. We run this test at its default settings.
Last up (for now), CrystalDiskMark proves the Forge does benefit significantly from its USB4 interface, with its performance on sequential reads and writes jumping well ahead of everything else on our chart — because all other drives here top out at 10 Gbps. There are, of course, faster external SSDs (like Samsung's recent P9). But at 8TB, solid-state options are generally more expensive, and faster external SSDs at 8TB are much more expensive. And of course, 20TB external SSDs aren't really an option, at least in the consumer drive space.
Pricing and final thoughts
The whole reason a product like the Seagate Forge exists is because SSDs are expensive. The problem is, hard drives have faced similar price jumps due to demand. And Seagate says the 8TB Forge will launch at $699 for the 8TB drive, and $899 for the 20TB option. That's a lot of money for a drive you need to also put your own M.2 SSD into for it to function.
We'll also need to do more testing with things like game load times before passing judgment on the FireCuda Forge. But it likely makes much more sense in the 20TB capacity, where no single-drive consumer SSD-based option exists. At 8TB, there are options like SanDisk's Desk drive, which has a slower 10GBps interface, but is a full-fledged SSD, rather than a hard drive with some fast SSD cache. Surprisingly, that Sandisk drive is still on sale for $999. And unless you happen to have an old M.2 SSD lying around to install into the Forge, its price, including the SSD it needs to function, isn't going to be far off traditional solid-state options.
After a rough start with the Mattel Aquarius as a child, Matt built his first PC in the late 1990s and ventured into mild PC modding in the early 2000s. He’s spent the last 15 years covering emerging technology for Smithsonian, Popular Science, and Consumer Reports, while testing components and PCs for Computer Shopper, PCMag and Digital Trends.

articles.title: Which Passing Chips Need More Testing?
articles.text:
Manufacturers are using test data and predictive models to identify marginal chips and determine when additional screening is justified.
Key Takeaways:
A chip passes wafer sort, moves through assembly, and passes final test. Nothing in its results gives anyone a reason to hold it. Yet another chip with nearly identical results could fail in the field because of a weakness neither test exposed, whether that’s a thin timing margin, a slight resistance shift, or a combination of measurements that looks harmless when each is viewed alone.
The challenge for manufacturers is figuring out which of those passing chips deserve another look without retesting everything. Test engineers have always known that a passing result doesn’t guarantee lifetime reliability. What’s changed is how much they can learn about each device. Internal parametric measurements, manufacturing history, and predictive models can now reveal unusual behavior inside a population of passing parts, but spotting a suspicious device is just the beginning.
“The cost of test and the amount of test is exploding, and the ability to test before system-level test is a challenge,” said Kimon Michaels, executive vice president of products and solutions, director, and co-founder of PDF Solutions. “But of course, one of the big challenges is how much of your supply chain is at risk at that point, or the amount of product that you’re throwing away if it fails at that point.”
The longer a marginal device goes undetected, the more value gets invested in it. But testing every device more thoroughly isn’t free. Extra patterns eat tester time, burn-in ties up equipment, a packaged device may need another mechanical insertion, and rejecting every statistical outlier throws away some good silicon. On the other side of the ledger is the part that escapes into a customer’s system.
“Nothing is more expensive than a field failure,” said Michaels. “The challenge is that the advanced technologies, in some respects, are even more sensitive to reliability failures.”
Manufacturing tests can only approximate the conditions a chip will see in operation. Voltage, temperature, timing, and workload are controllable during test, but the interactions inside a fully assembled system are much harder to reproduce.
“Individual dies can pass wafer sort and final test, and then behave differently once the dies, memory devices, interconnects, firmware, and software are all working together,” said Eli Roth, smart manufacturing product manager at Teradyne. “We’re very good at finding hard failures. What’s much harder is finding devices that meet spec but are operating close to a reliability boundary.”
Testing every combination of operating conditions is impractical, and even extensive system-level tests cannot guarantee that every weakness will surface. Manufacturers need a way to identify high-risk devices and decide whether a targeted test can expose the problem before shipment.
Device-level models are exposing hidden outliers
Conventional production testing relies on defined limits, with guard bands for measurement uncertainty and operating variation. Statistical analysis can flag devices near those limits or behaving differently from their neighbors on the same wafer or lot. Nevertheless, a chip can still pass every test while showing an unusual relationship among its measurements.
Device-specific models offer another way to identify those differences. By comparing internal parametric measurements with the behavior expected from a particular device, engineers can detect inconsistencies that population-based statistics might overlook. Process and timing signatures can provide the basis for predicting how a chip should behave, allowing engineers to investigate discrepancies between predicted and measured performance. The pattern of those discrepancies matters. Design-related margin limits tend to show up consistently across a product population, but material problems don’t.
“Material-induced variability behaves differently. It is often localized, asymmetric, or statistically scattered,” said Nir Sever, senior director of business development at proteanTecs. “Only a subset of devices, wafers, or regions on a die may show accelerated drift. The degradation slope may diverge from the population over time.”
Localized or accelerating changes can suggest an emerging physical weakness. The difficulty is determining whether that variation represents a reliability risk worth investigating, and whether another test can reveal anything useful about it. The models making those calls also have a shelf life.
“Data is not static,” said Michaels. “It drifts. It’s physics-based. There are changes to the process, and you have to be cognizant of that in how you retrain, how you monitor, etc.”
Process adjustments, equipment changes, and product revisions can alter the relationships a model learned. That means engineers need to validate the models as carefully as the measurements feeding them, especially when an outlier flag can trigger extra screening or reject a part.
Inspection explains marginal electrical behavior
Some latent defects don’t produce a consistent electrical failure. A weakened interconnect may conduct well enough at room temperature, then become unstable under thermal or mechanical stress. That’s particularly hard to catch in advanced packages. Partial non-wetting, micro-bump voids, delamination, and warpage may not cause an immediate failure.
“Voiding and non-wetting may weaken an interconnect without causing an immediate open,” said Chris Rand, principal technical engineer at Nordson Test & Inspection. “Variation in bump height, solder volume, or interconnect geometry can shift resistance or create continuity that changes under load, temperature, or handling.”
X-ray or acoustic inspection can provide physical evidence of a suspected interconnect problem, while electrical measurements help establish whether an observed irregularity affects device behavior. Neither technique necessarily provides a complete diagnosis on its own. Correlating the results can narrow the possible failure mechanisms and help engineers select a stress condition more likely to expose the weakness.
Comparing measurements across test insertions offers another clue. A chip may pass at every stage while its electrical characteristics slowly shift, a trend that individual pass/fail decisions would miss.
“An unexplained drift is not a healthy sign,” said Greg Prewitt, director of Exensio Solutions at PDF Solutions. “If a device just changes, and you don’t think it’s a problem with the test setup, it requires more scrutiny.”
Flagging that device and carrying the flag to later insertions lets manufacturers focus extra screening on parts with suspicious histories. But engineers first have to rule out differences in temperature, calibration, contact resistance, or instrument configuration. Otherwise, they risk chasing a healthy device while missing a problem in the measurement path.
Failure mechanisms determine which test comes next
Once the evidence points to a credible failure mechanism, the question becomes which additional test has a reasonable chance of exposing it. The options aren’t interchangeable. Suspicious timing may call for characterization at a different voltage or temperature. An interconnect concern may need electrical or thermal stress, while a reliability-risk signature may justify burn-in. Repeating the original test under the same conditions adds little if that test was never sensitive to the defect in the first place.
Burn-in is a particularly tough call. Elevated temperature and voltage can accelerate certain failure mechanisms, but the process consumes equipment time, power, and capacity, and the stress itself can affect reliability. That makes blanket burn-in hard to justify when only a small fraction of passing devices are at risk.
“People are burning in large fractions of their inventory, or nearly all of it, which is expensive and can cause damage by itself,” said Michaels. “But a fairly broad model can learn the insights as to what multi-dimensional part of your process-based plus your test state predicts, and what the sweet spot is where you can skip it and focus your resources on the more marginal parts where you have concern.”
Predictive burn-in uses manufacturing history and test data to identify devices most likely to benefit from stress screening. Adaptive test takes a related approach, using wafer-level and die-level results to determine how a device should be tested after assembly. Information gathered at one insertion can influence the limits and patterns used at the next, provided the manufacturer can preserve device identity and connect the results across operations.
”We have established a kind of cloud infrastructure that is fetching data from the different test insertions and reusing the data collected at earlier test insertions to optimize the die matching inside advanced packaging, the test conditions, and consequently the yield for the following test insertions,” said Fabio Pizza, test technology director at Advantest. “You can have a kind of adaptive test to make sure that when you test the device after assembly, you are using the right limits and even the right pattern.”
Changing limits or patterns within an existing insertion generally imposes less overhead than routing a packaged device through another operation, which adds handling, equipment demands, and time. The economics become more complicated as additional value is invested in each device. An extra test may be inexpensive compared with scrapping an assembled multi-die package, but every added operation competes for finite manufacturing capacity.
“When you look at the economics, test costs are dwarfed by scrap costs once you start packaging these devices together,” said Teradyne’s Roth.
The challenge is deciding where that additional screening produces enough value to justify its cost. Connecting wafer, assembly, and final-test results can help engineers identify suspicious devices before more manufacturing value is added, while avoiding test operations that contribute little useful information. A few seconds of targeted screening may prevent an expensive downstream failure, but an extra insertion that rarely finds anything can reduce throughput without improving outgoing quality.
Retesting is creating its own uncertainty
Retesting has an obvious appeal. If engineers don’t trust a result, another measurement seems like cheap insurance. But production test involves physical interfaces, and those interfaces aren’t passive. Packaged devices are pressed into sockets with substantial force to make contact across hundreds or thousands of terminals. Contacts wear, surfaces get contaminated, and small seating variations change resistance, so a second insertion may not reproduce the conditions of the first, even when the test program is identical.
“Every time you put that part into the socket, there’s risk involved,” said Jack Lewis, chief technologist at Modus Test. “So retest is a problem. You don’t want to be retesting. Test times are long.”
Repeated insertions consume capacity and expose the package to more handling. If the underlying issue is contact-related, a second test may produce a different result without explaining which measurement better reflects the device. A pass after an earlier fail is especially ambiguous. The device may have been healthy all along, with the original failure caused by poor contact, or it may carry an intermittent defect that simply didn’t show up the second time. Changing the bin without keeping the history throws away the information needed to tell those cases apart.
Comparing results across probe pins, boards, and testers can help establish whether a failure belongs to the device or the measurement system. That requires more than routine calibration, particularly when a tester resource or load-board component begins drifting toward its operating limits.
“Customers also want to do some dedicated measurements to monitor if there is any parameter of the complete test cell that is deviating, if there is any resource in the tester, load board, probe card or thermal control system that is going closer to the limit and potentially creating some marginalities when testing such devices,” said Advantest’s Pizza.
Monitoring tester and load-board performance helps engineers distinguish changes in the measurement environment from changes in the silicon. That history becomes particularly valuable when deciding whether a previously passing device needs more screening, because another insertion may reproduce the symptom without identifying its cause. In that case, other evidence has already raised the possibility of latent risk, so the added insertion should have a real chance of revealing the suspected defect, particularly when the part is expensive or a field failure would be severe. A method that catches more marginal devices but sharply increases false rejects, handling damage, or tester occupancy may not be worth it.
Decision latency is limiting what screening can catch
Even a good screening model fails operationally if its answer arrives too late. Some production test operations are completed in fractions of a second, and an analysis completed after the lot has moved on may help future process improvements without changing the disposition of the parts that generated the data.
Historically, test systems have been optimized to maintain throughput, sometimes at the expense of immediate data availability. Roth described an IDM customer whose test infrastructure deliberately deferred building its test data files until the tester had idle time. That approach kept production moving, but it also limited opportunities to respond to problems as they emerged.
“In extreme cases, STDF files aren’t built until the end of a lot,” said Roth. “So if something goes wrong on an early wafer, we’re not collecting or presenting that data in time for anyone to act on it. Historically, that’s been the trade-off in the push for throughput.”
Getting information sooner is only part of the problem. Data must be tied to the correct device, available in usable form, and delivered while the test program or manufacturing system can still respond. Enabling an extra measurement within the current test sequence may be relatively straightforward. Routing a device to another operation, placing it on hold, or evaluating it against data from elsewhere in the flow is more complicated.
The rules governing those actions need attention, too. If a model starts flagging a growing share of passing devices, engineers have to determine whether the process changed, the devices became more marginal, or the model drifted. Automatically ramping up screening in response could consume test capacity without improving quality. The reverse risk applies when a model learns that a particular test rarely finds defects and recommends running it less often.
Establishing a reliable baseline becomes especially difficult with new chip designs. Complex devices generate enormous amounts of measurement data, but engineers may have little historical information against which to judge an unusual result. Without a dependable reference, even a sophisticated model can struggle to distinguish a meaningful anomaly from normal variation.
“Being able to accurately, empirically assess the data and find out what’s anomalous and what’s not is by no means an easy task,” said Brent Bullock, test technology director at Advantest. “Engineers may not have reliable historical data for comparison, particularly when testing a new chip design or moving to a different architecture.”
A screening model needs to establish what constitutes normal behavior for the device and operating conditions being evaluated. That baseline must remain valid as manufacturing processes, product revisions, and test conditions change. Otherwise, engineers risk increasing test coverage in response to harmless variation or reducing coverage when a genuine weakness is developing.
Engineers also need to know why a device was selected, what evidence triggered the decision, what the extra test found, and whether the result supported the original risk assessment. Without that feedback loop, manufacturers accumulate screening rules that are expensive to maintain and hard to justify. With it, they can judge screening by actual outcomes rather than by the apparent sophistication of the model.
Conclusion
The decision to release a marginal device comes down to what manufacturers can establish about it and how much uncertainty they’re willing to accept. Flagging a component as at risk isn’t the same as predicting failure. A risk score may justify further characterization, a different stress condition, or closer monitoring of a population, but it doesn’t automatically justify scrapping the part. Some failure mechanisms also remain hard to reproduce under practical production conditions, so even a well-chosen test may reduce uncertainty without eliminating it.
The calculation also varies by market. A supplier of high-volume consumer devices may accept a different balance of test cost and residual risk than one serving automotive, industrial, or other high-reliability applications. Even within a product family, the right response depends on how severe the suspected failure mechanism is and how well the available screening methods can expose it.
As more data becomes available about each device, the hard question is shifting from whether a manufacturer can take another measurement to whether that measurement is likely to change the outcome. Manufacturers have spent decades getting better at determining whether a chip passes. Now they also have to decide which passing chips deserve another look, and when the evidence is strong enough to leave them alone. The better they get at that, the less extra testing they may need.

Employing more stress testing at the wafer level improves quality while reducing burn-in time and cost. So why isn’t it happening?

articles.title: Binance warns of iOS flaw that could leak crypto wallet secrets
articles.text:
Binance is warning about a vulnerability in Apple’s iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 that could allow third-party apps to read private files stored by other apps, including cryptocurrency seed phrases, secret keys, and login credentials.
The crypto exchange clarifies that the issue is at the iOS level and does not impact only the Binance app.
“A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem,” Binance says.
At this time, no cryptocurrency losses have been confirmed, but Binance urges users to install the update immediately as a precaution.
The company recommends that users delete any unnecessary and untrusted apps and apply the latest versions for iOS and other apps.
Where compromise is suspected, Binance advises users to transfer funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.
Public exploit available
“worse_query” is a publicly disclosed iOS sandbox escape technique that allows an application to cross security boundaries and access the storage of other applications.
Yesterday, a proof-of-concept exploit has been published that uses a tool called WQ Files to perform attacks relying on the technique. Specifically, WQ Files uses “worse_query” to browse, export, edit, and delete other apps’ data without requiring a jailbreak.
An attacker could
The tool must be installed on an iPhone for the attack to work, but an attacker could distribute it through untrusted sources as a sideloaded app, bypassing Apple's App Store.
WQ Files has been confirmed to work on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2, the same versions that Binance warned about.
Apple on November 9 released iOS security updates (iOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3, and 18.7.12) that address nine flaws. One of the fixed vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-113963, could allow an app to access sensitive user data.
It is unclear if this is the same security issue Binance is warning of, though.
The CVE-2026-113963 problem was reported by László Várady flaw, who found that the access occurred through App Intents, not App Group containers.
BleepingComputer has contacted Apple for clarifications and a request for comment, and we will add an update once we receive more details.
