articles.title: Why storytelling can be a startup's strongest competitive moat
articles.text:
Why storytelling can be a startup's strongest competitive moat
At TechSparks 2026, Shweta Rajpal Kohli, President and CEO of Startup Policy Forum, explained why founders need to tell authentic, distinctive stories and how storytelling can help build trust and differentiate a business.
Technology, capital, and talent can help startups build and scale their businesses. But as competitors gain access to similar resources, founders also need to explain what makes their companies different.
At TechSparks 2026, Shweta Rajpal Kohli, President and CEO of Startup Policy Forum, spoke about the role of storytelling in building a business.
Leading a masterclass titled ‘Startups and Storytelling: Making Narrative Your Moat’, Kohli said founders often treat storytelling as something to consider after developing their products. However, before achieving product-market fit, their story is often what they are selling.
“Every startup is a story no one believes in yet,” she said.
The ‘why’ behind the business
Kohli began by asking the audience why storytelling matters. Participants spoke about building trust, creating personal connections, and differentiating a business.
She then used her own career to demonstrate what founders often leave out of their stories.
After summarizing nearly 28 years of work in a few minutes, she asked the audience what was missing. It was the reason behind her decision to establish Startup Policy Forum.
While she had explained how founders approached her to work with them, she had not mentioned the gap she had identified: India lacked an institution to represent the startup ecosystem’s policy concerns to the government.
Kohli said a mission alone does not make a startup distinctive because competitors may have similar goals.
Founders must also explain why them—what makes them suited to building the business—and why now—what makes the timing relevant.
Their passion and the community supporting their work also help make the story harder to replicate, she said.
Why details matter
Kohli said people tend to remember stories more easily than statistics. Instead of simply presenting market-size figures, founders should explain how their products could change someone's life.
She encouraged them to use techniques learned in school English classes, including anecdotes, sensory details, drama and emotion.
Drawing on her own experiences, Kohli described how Startup Policy Forum's logo came about.
An early backer had dismissed her initial designs as “tacky”. The eventual idea came to her while watching her son play with a Rubik's Cube.
She also recalled how a chance meeting with a member at an airport became a social media post that gained traction. On another occasion, a session she attended at an awards evening reminded her of how the forum got its name and prompted a LinkedIn post.
Her point was that founders need not wait for major milestones to find stories worth sharing.
She advised them to document the early stages of their businesses, from the first garage office and notebooks to whiteboards and the arrival of their first employee.
For founders who struggle to write, Kohli suggested talking through their experiences with a friend, recording the conversation using an AI voice tool and turning the transcript into a post.
“You'll realize that you've actually said it well,” she said.
Using AI without losing authenticity
Kohli said AI has made storytelling easier, but it has also made it harder to stand out.
Generic stories can now be produced in seconds, and readers can often recognize content that does not reflect a founder's own experience.
She encouraged founders to use AI to improve their language, but not to generate facts or experiences.
“You can write stories; you can't cook them,” she said.
Referring to her own experience with the Rubik's Cube, Kohli said AI could help present the incident more clearly, but should not add details that never happened.
She also stressed the importance of consistency. Founders may speak to investors, customers, the media, and government representatives, but the underlying story should remain the same. Changing it to suit different audiences can affect credibility.
Knowing when to tell the story
The masterclass also addressed how often founders should communicate and when their public presence could become a distraction.
Kohli said storytelling should accompany meaningful business developments, such as a new feature, product launch, or milestone.
However, founders must balance the time spent communicating with the time needed to build their businesses.
She also cautioned that a founder’s public presence could become a liability if not managed carefully.
While formats and audiences may change, Kohli said the facts behind a founder’s story must remain consistent.
Storytelling can help startups attract attention, build trust, and connect with their audiences. But those stories need to be based on real experiences rather than manufactured narratives.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: Installez vite iOS 27.2.1 : Apple colmate des failles dans iMessage et le Bluetooth de votre iPhone
articles.text:
Ce lundi 9 novembre, Apple a déployé iOS 27.2.1 sur tous les iPhone compatibles. La mise à jour arrive deux semaines seulement après iOS 27.2, qui avait colmaté plus de 160 failles de sécurité. Cette mise à jour ne contient pas la moindre nouveauté. Comme souvent avec les versions mineures d’iOS, Apple se contente de corriger des bugs et de combler des brèches, sans déployer d’améliorations. Dans la foulée, Apple a aussi déployé iPadOS 27.2.1 sur les iPad compatibles, ainsi qu’iOS 26.7.3 et iOS 18.7.12 sur les smartphones qui ne sont pas passés à iOS 27.
À lire aussi : Panique sur l’iPhone – Apple met en garde contre une opération d’espionnage dans 99 pays, dont la France
Deux failles dans iMessage
Au total, iOS 27.2.1 corrige neuf vulnérabilités. On trouve surtout deux failles dans iMessage. Comme l’explique Apple dans son bulletin de sécurité, la première faille permet à un attaquant distant de « rejoindre une conversation de groupe iMessage et de recevoir ses messages » sans en avoir l’autorisation. En d’autres termes, un pirate peut s’inviter dans une discussion sans y avoir été convié par ses participants. Une fois dans le groupe, il peut lire tout ce que disent les utilisateurs.
Une seconde brèche a été décelée dans iMessage. Cette deuxième défaillance permet à un utilisateur ajouté à un groupe iMessage d’accéder à tous les messages envoyés avant son arrivée… ce qui peut évidemment engendrer des conversations déplaisantes. Les deux failles ont été découvertes par un chercheur anonyme.
À lire aussi : Failles de sécurité iOS – Apple change de stratégie pour contrer les pirates et protéger votre iPhone
Une série de failles Bluetooth
Apple a aussi colmaté plusieurs failles liées au Bluetooth. La vulnérabilité la plus sérieuse permet à un appareil Bluetooth de s’appairer à l’iPhone sans la moindre intervention de son propriétaire. C’est la porte ouverte à toutes les dérives, et à la propagation de logiciels malveillants. Le géant américain a aussi décelé une autre brèche, qui permet à un pirate situé à portée du Bluetooth de contourner les limites d’essai du code d’appairage. En clair, un pirate peut multiplier les tentatives de connexion jusqu’à tomber sur le bon code. Le même type de faille a été corrigé dans le protocole AirPlay, le service qui fait communiquer des appareils Apple entre eux.
Pour exploiter ces failles, l’attaquant doit impérativement se trouver à portée Bluetooth de sa cible. Dans le cas de l’AirPlay, il doit simplement se trouver sur le même réseau Wi-Fi. Enfin, Apple corrige aussi une faille de corruption de mémoire dans le Bluetooth, une brèche qui peut permettre à une application d’accéder à des données sensibles, et un bug dans brotli, une bibliothèque de compression de données.
Bonne nouvelle, rien n’indique que les failles ont été exploitées par des pirates dans le cadre de cyberattaques. Néanmoins, il faut s’attendre à ce que des pirates se servent des informations publiées par Apple pour mettre au point des tactiques d’exploitation. C’est pourquoi on vous recommande d’installer sans tarder la mise à jour sur votre iPhone. Pour installer iOS 27.2.1, rendez-vous dans Réglages, puis dans Général et enfin dans Mise à jour logicielle.

articles.title: SpaceXSI quietly flips Grok API text watermarking to off by default
articles.text:
SpaceXSI quietly flips Grok API text watermarking to off by default
The thorny issue of watermarking AI-generated text took an interesting turn this past week, with SpaceXSI seemingly U-turning on plans to automatically watermark text generated by its Grok AI models.
As per its updated output watermarking documentation, Elon Musk’s AI company — which recently rebranded from SpaceXAI — says the feature is now off by default, with developers able to enable it for individual models through their team’s administration settings.
News of the watermarking feature itself started to emerge in late October, though there was no formal public announcement. The earlier version of the documentation, captured for posterity by the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine on both November 1 and November 6, was quite different to the existing one, noting that watermarking would be on by default starting from November 7. The pending change was spotted by some X users on October 31.
SpaceXSI has now reversed course, however, making watermarking an opt-in feature for developers using Grok through its API. One online documentation archiving service, Spybara, indicates that the change happened some time between Monday night (November 9) and Tuesday morning (November 10), suggesting that the documentation continued to describe watermarking as enabled by default for nearly three days after its scheduled November 7 rollout.
“SpaceXSI has now reversed course, however, making watermarking an opt-in feature for developers using Grok through its API.”
The company has given no public explanation for the change, and it’s unclear whether the original default-on policy ever fully came into effect.
Meeting the watermarking obligations
To rewind just a little, text watermarking is a technique for embedding an invisible, machine-readable signal into AI-generated text. The process subtly influences which words or tokens a model chooses when generating a response, and over a sufficiently long passage of text, those choices create a statistical pattern that can be detected later, helping to establish whether it originated from an AI model.
Detection typically requires access to specialised tools, with the major model labs restricting access to their watermark detectors to approved applicants.
The technology has become increasingly relevant in Europe, where the EU AI Act introduced transparency obligations for providers of AI systems that generate synthetic content. Under Article 50(2), providers must ensure that AI-generated text, images, audio and video are marked in a machine-readable format, with the relevant provisions taking effect on August 2, 2026. A subsequent amendment introduced a limited grace period until December 2 for systems already on the market before August 2, meaning that the clock is ticking for AI companies yet to meet the requirements.
It’s worth noting that the various AI companies have taken different approaches to their text watermarking obligations. In August, Anthropic became one of the first major AI labs to announce text watermarking, applying the feature globally across supported Claude models and products, including its API. The decision proved somewhat controversial, particularly among developers concerned about how watermarking might affect generated code, and the fact that Anthropic provided no mechanism for opting out.
Meanwhile, OpenAI followed suit in October, introducing its own text watermarking system called textGrain. However, it took a different approach, making the feature optional for API developers while introducing automatic watermarking for eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the EU.
Google, for its part, has been deploying its own SynthID watermarking technology across various products and services over the past couple of years, including its Gemini API. The technology supports text alongside images, audio and video, with the text watermark embedded into the model’s output as it generates responses. In July, the company confirmed it was signing the EU’s Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content.
Notably, SpaceXSI’s updated documentation also confirms that it’s using SynthID Text for its own watermarking feature.
A change of heart
SpaceXSI was the only major AI lab that hadn’t signed the EU’s Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content, with at least one report at the time suggesting it would steer clear of watermarking Grok’s text.
However, the emergence of SpaceXSI’s documentation in late October was the first clear indication that it was preparing to join the fray. And the original text was quite explicit about the company’s rationale. “SpaceXSI watermarks text model output to comply with the EU AI Act,” the document noted.
“Watermarking can help enable compliance with the EU AI Act.”
That statement has since been replaced by more cautious language. “Watermarking can help enable compliance with the EU AI Act,” it now reads.
That shift is notable, insofar as the original wording reflected a policy in which SpaceXSI took it upon itself to automatically watermark Grok’s output, ostensibly to comply with the EU AI Act. Now, the company appears to be passing the responsibility for enabling watermarking to developers, while being more circumspect about whether the technology is sufficient to satisfy the bloc’s legal requirements.
There are some practical consequences to all this, too. The feature is controlled at team level, meaning an administrator can enable or disable watermarking for individual Grok models, with the setting applying to every API key belonging to that team. There is no option to switch watermarking on or off for individual requests, meaning developers serving customers in different regions can’t apply different watermarking policies to the same model within a single team. They would need to maintain separate team configurations to do so.
The company’s revised documentation establishes that watermarking is available across seven Grok models, including Grok 4.7 and 4.6, but disabled by default. What remains unclear is why SpaceXSI abandoned its previously stated plans to make the feature automatic.
The New Stack has reached out to SpaceXSI for comment, and will update when, or if, we hear back.

articles.title: Simeone (56 años), entrenador y con 180 pisos en propiedad en Madrid: “Si me preguntasen dónde voy a vivir cuando deje de entrenar, lógicamente respondería en la Argentina”
articles.text:
Diego Pablo Simeone (Buenos Aires, 1970) lleva tiempo desarrollando un negocio inmobiliario en Madrid junto a su mujer Carla Pereyra. Los dos tienen en su haber una cartera de unos 180 pisos (según la propia Pereyra). Además de pisos, tienen edificios y residencias de estudiantes. “Si me preguntasen dónde voy a vivir cuando deje de entrenar, lógicamente respondería en la Argentina”.
Han pasado de comprar pisos para alquilar a entrar en proyectos de construcción. Tienen su propia agencia de comercialización. Se hace bajo la marca MyLocation.
El patrimonio y los alquileres
Una de las sociedades en las que organizan sus inversiones es Carpersim. Es un nombre que mezcla las primeras sílabas de Carla y Pereyra con el apellido de Simeone. En el ejercicio 2024, el total de activos de la sociedad estaba cerca de 40 millones de euros (según Cote Villar). Esto es el total de activos de la empresa, no es el dinero que tiene en mano o su fortuna personal.
La propia Pereyra es “el gran motor del negocio inmobiliario de Simeone” (según la periodista Cote Villar). “Han abierto una agencia desde donde se pueden alquilar estos pisos y apartamentos”.
Pereyra es la que está detrás del proyecto, ya que tiene un conocimiento del sector por su entorno familiar. Su abuelo era arquitecto y en su entorno ya trabajaban en este ámbito .
Han ido creciendo y llegó un momento en que entraron en edificios y residencias de estudiantes. Han creado su propio aparato de gestión y comercialización. Forma parte del negocio de alquiler de viviendas del que también hemos hablado en Genbeta.
Una casa reformada en Madrid
Su vivienda familiar en Madrid tiene unos 1.900 metros cuadrados de superficie construida. Está en una parcela de unos 3.000 metros cuadrados. Dispone de jardín, piscina y gimnasio. Tras la compra hicieron una reforma integral para adecuarla a sus necesidades familiares.
Entre otras cosas, destacan los grandes ventanales que dan paso al jardín. De esta manera se relacionan las distintas estancias. Los colores son claros. Las líneas son simples. Se utilizan materiales naturales. En el salón destacan algunos muebles de gran tamaño. Por ejemplo, un sofá blanco de líneas redondeadas que va acompañado de unos sillones y unas mesitas auxiliares.
En una de las paredes destaca un revestimiento de madera. Incluye la chimenea. También hay una obra abstracta que introduce colores rojos, rosas y negros. En la mesa de centro hay algunos libros de arte, arquitectura, fotografía y diseño. También hay velas y objetos decorativos. Y un tablero de ajedrez.

articles.title: Le Goncourt britannique récompense un roman de SF qui résonne avec la polémique sur l'IA en France
articles.text:
S’il y a bien une chose que l’on doit à Thélyson Orélien, c’est d’avoir placé l’intelligence artificielle au cœur du débat littéraire et d’avoir sensibilisé un public qui ne mesurait pas forcément tout ce qu’elle était capable de faire. Après la polémique provoquée en France par son roman C’était ça ou mourir, le sujet revient sur le devant de la scène outre-Manche. Cette fois, c’est un roman qui explore les conséquences de l’intelligence artificielle qui est récompensé, et non une œuvre qui s’en sert pour être écrite.
Ce lundi 9 novembre, l’écrivain britannique M. John Harrison a remporté le Booker Prize, souvent comparé à notre prix Goncourt, avec The End of Everything. Ce roman de science-fiction postapocalyptique met en scène d’étranges entités capables d’imiter le langage et les comportements humains. Un univers qui fait directement écho à certaines interrogations actuelles sur l’intelligence artificielle.
Le Booker Prize avait déjà mis en avant des romans qui empruntent à la science-fiction, comme Never Let Me Go de Kazuo Ishiguro, finaliste en 2005. Mais M. John Harrison est, selon Gaby Wood, directrice générale de la Booker Prize Foundation, le premier lauréat « issu du vrai monde de la SF ». À 81 ans, l’auteur, dont The End of Everything est le treizième roman, devient également le plus vieux lauréat de l’histoire du prix.
Paru en anglais le 18 juin 2026 chez Serpent’s Tail, The End of Everything n’a pas encore été traduit en français.
Un roman de science-fiction qui interroge notre rapport à l’IA
L’intrigue se situe dans un futur proche, dans une Angleterre frappée par une catastrophe mystérieuse. Phillip Tennent gagne sa vie sur le littoral en ramassant les objets rejetés par la Manche. Les mers sont peuplées de nouvelles créatures et l’Europe semble avoir disparu. Phillip vient de repêcher un objet qu’il ne peut pas garder et qu’il doit emporter vers l’intérieur des terres. Un étrange artefact qui ne cesse de se transformer et d’imiter les êtres humains.
Le parallèle avec les IA génératives est assez évident. Ces technologies savent aujourd’hui reproduire notre manière de parler, d’écrire et de créer. Comme les origines et les intentions de ces « visiteurs » restent floues, de nombreux critiques lisent le roman comme une allégorie de l’IA, note CNN. À l’heure où l’IA brouille la frontière entre l’humain et la machine, le choix du jury tombe à point nommé.
Dans un entretien publié par le Booker Prize ce 9 novembre, l’auteur explique que la crise financière de 2008 lui a d’abord donné l’idée du livre. Il dit s’être inspiré de l’actualité pour imaginer une société dans laquelle nos repères et nos explications habituelles ne suffisent plus à comprendre ce qui arrive.
Mary Beard, l’historienne britannique qui présidait le jury, a décrit le roman comme « la politique du présent vue à travers le prisme du futur ». Selon elle, l’ouvrage « met le lecteur sens dessus dessous, lui arrache un sourire en coin et – chose surprenante compte tenu du sujet – laisse une pointe d’optimisme ».
Cette victoire est aussi symbolique pour le genre. Créé en 1969, le Booker Prize aura attendu 57 ans avant de récompenser un écrivain issu directement du milieu de la science-fiction.

articles.title: Moins de dix jours avant la sortie de GTA VI, ce SSD NVMe de 1 To, idéal pour la PS5, chute sous les 125 € pendant le Black Friday chinois — Frandroid
articles.text:
Avez-vous assez de place dans votre PS5 pour stocker le prochain GTA VI ? Si ce n’est pas le cas, on vous conseille vivement de vous équiper d’un second SSD NVMe, à l’image du Netac NV7000-t. Alors que les tarifs des SSD ne cessent de grimper depuis plus d’un an, la version 1 To profite, elle, d’une promotion qui fait passer son prix sous la barre des 130 euros pendant le Black Friday chinois. Oui, c’est devenu rare.
Les points forts du Netac NV7000-t
- Un espace de 1 To
- Une vitesse de lecture allant jusqu’à 7 300 Mo/s
- Une plaque fine pour dissiper la chaleur
Initialement proposé à 140,39 euros, le SSD Netac NV7000-t de 1 To est aujourd’hui disponible en promotion à 122,40 euros sur AliExpress grâce au code promo FRD1124. Les frais d’import sont inclus.
Un SSD qui peut se glisser dans une PS5…
Le Netac NV7000-t est un SSD NVMe PCIe Gen 4 qui remplit, côté interface et débits, les critères de compatibilité de Sony concernant les SSD destinés à sa PS5. Le constructeur japonais recommande notamment une vitesse de lecture séquentielle d’au moins 5 500 Mo/s. Avec sa vitesse de lecture pouvant atteindre 7 300 Mo/s et sa vitesse d’écriture capable de grimper jusqu’à 6 600 Mo/s, le NV7000-t coche tout à fait cette case. Vous pourrez donc y installer et y lancer vos jeux PS5, comme le prochain GTA VI.
En revanche, notez que le Netac NV7000-t n’est pas équipé d’un véritable dissipateur thermique, destiné à limiter les risques de surchauffe, et donc les éventuelles baisses de performance. Sony exige pourtant une solution de refroidissement efficace, comme un dissipateur, pour tout SSD installé dans sa console. Le NV7000-t est bien livré avec une fine plaque métallique pour aider à dissiper la chaleur. Sur PS5, ajouter un dissipateur compatible avec la console reste toutefois la solution la plus sûre. Avant d’installer le SSD dans votre PS5, vous pourrez vous référer à cet article, qui vous expliquera pas à pas comment procéder.
… ou dans un PC
Avec 1 To de stockage supplémentaire, soit 1 000 Go, vous pourrez installer davantage de jeux sur votre PS5, sans devoir en désinstaller constamment pour libérer de l’espace. Quand on sait que la console de Sony ne dispose, dans sa version originelle, que de 667 Go de stockage interne réel (825 Go de base), cet espace en plus n’est vraiment pas de trop.
Mais la PS5 n’est pas la seule machine à pouvoir accueillir ce disque interne. Il peut en effet prendre place dans un PC trop lent pour le ranimer et lui offrir plus de réactivité, notamment s’il embarque encore un disque dur mécanique. Pratique pour le montage vidéo ou la conception 3D, par exemple. Vérifiez toutefois que la carte mère dispose d’un port M.2 NVMe, ce qui n’est pas toujours le cas sur un vieux PC (et en PCIe 3.0, les débits plafonneront autour de 3 500 Mo/s). Enfin, notez que le Netac NV7000-t de 1 To affiche une endurance de 640 TBW. On peut donc écrire jusqu’à 640 To de données sur ce SSD avant d’arriver au bout de son endurance théorique. Il devrait ainsi largement tenir plusieurs années, même en cas d’utilisation quotidienne intensive. Netac le garantit d’ailleurs 5 ans.

articles.title: Molly, le fork soi-disant durci de Signal, est vulnérable et n'a pas été mis à jour depuis juillet
articles.text:
Molly, la version « durcie » de Signal pour Android, n’a pas reçu de mise à jour depuis le 31 juillet. Pendant ce temps, Signal a corrigé plusieurs failles, dont un bug d’appel qui laissait le micro ouvert après le raccrochage.
Un message publié sur la communauté « You Should Know » de PieFed tire la sonnette d’alarme. Son auteur conseille de revenir à Signal et de supprimer Molly en attendant une reprise des mises à jour.
Pendant que Signal colmate les brèches, Molly reste à quai
Molly est un « fork » de Signal maintenu à part et auquel ses développeurs ajoutent des protections. L’application est proposée sur GrapheneOS, via la boutique Accrescent. Sa dernière version, la v8.19.2-4, date du 31 juillet. Elle réglait une fuite DNS apparue dans la version précédente quand un proxy SOCKS5 était configuré. Les requêtes qui servent à retrouver l’adresse d’un serveur sortaient du proxy et pouvaient révéler les serveurs contactés. Rien n’a été publié depuis, soit plus de trois mois.
Le souci d’un fork, c’est qu’il ne reçoit pas les correctifs automatiquement. Chaque patch de Signal doit être repris, intégré puis diffusé par l’équipe de Molly. Il y a notamment eu cette faille majeure rendue publique le mois dernier et corrigée dans Signal 8.27. Celle-ci serait toujours présente dans Molly. Mais ce n’est qu’un exemple.
La vulnérabilité en question touchait RingRTC, la bibliothèque qui gère les appels de Signal (CVE-2026-113380, notée 9,3 sur 10 en gravité). Chaque action d’un appel passe par une file d’attente, y compris le raccrochage. Un appelant malveillant pouvait saturer cette file et bloquer la demande. Dans ce cas, l’écran affichait un appel terminé, mais le micro continuait d’émettre. Avouons que ça serait un comble pour un smartphone sous GrapheneOS…
L’équipe développant Molly reste pour l’heure muette. Dans les rapports de problèmes sur le dépôt GitHub, les contributeurs s’interrogent depuis quelque temps déjà sur l’absence de correctifs.

articles.title: How pricing fractures and network gaps protect M-PESA’s market dominance
articles.text:
Kenya’s state-owned Postbank has opened its network of more than 600 branches and agent outlets to customers from other banks through PesaLink, the country’s interbank payments network.
The deal means customers of participating banks can walk into a Postbank outlet, deposit cash, and have it credited directly to an account held elsewhere, without opening a Postbank account.
Until now, banks largely had to negotiate individual agreements to access another institution’s agent network. Gituku Kirika, chief executive of Integrated Payment Services Limited (IPSL), the company behind PesaLink, said banks and SACCOs now have an opportunity to “open their existing agent networks to other institutions, allowing customers to access cash services through agents beyond those operated by their own financial institution.”
Postbank’s addition takes PesaLink’s network to 80 financial institutions, including commercial banks, microfinance firms and savings and credit co-operatives (SACCOs). The network added 12 members over the past year, bringing all 38 licenced commercial banks in Kenya onto the same payments system. It now processes an average of KES 4 billion ($30.8 million) daily, up 24% from a year earlier, and KES 110 billion ($846.5 million) monthly, up 41%. According to PesaLink, about 98% of transactions are successful.
The Kenya Bankers Association incorporated Integrated Payment Services Limited (IPSL) in 2015 under the National Payment System Act. Banks had a problem; Safaricom’s M-PESA had grown from a service for sending money between people into the payment system that much of Kenya’s economy ran on. Banks were watching customers move money through a network they did not own.
IPSL was meant to provide an alternative. Its job was to build a shared, round-the-clock system that let customers move money directly between bank accounts, without relying on telecom operators or waiting for traditional clearing processes. The goal was to make bank transfers cheaper and reduce reliance on cash while giving banks a bigger role in Kenya’s digital payments market.
Can the goal ever be achieved?
PesaLink competed with a service Kenyans already used to pay for almost everything. M-PESA had spent years building a network of more than 260,000 agents, while shops, supermarkets, small traders, and utility companies had made it a routine way to collect payments. Customers could send money, withdraw cash and pay bills from the same wallet. Banks had no comparable reach beyond their branches and ATM networks.
Banks also made life difficult for their own platforms. For years, some charged hefty fees for transfers between bank accounts and mobile wallets, while PesaLink remained buried in mobile banking apps. Customers had little reason to seek out a service they barely knew existed, especially when M-PESA was already on their phones. Banks also couldn’t sell PesaLink as a shared consumer brand with the same recognition as M-PESA.
PesaLink’s future also depends on a project being developed by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK). The regulator is working on a national Fast Payment System (FPS), which could provide banks, mobile money operators and other financial institutions with a common network for moving money. The project could expand PesaLink’s role, but it could also create a rival.
If the CBK builds a separate system, banks could find themselves competing with infrastructure they had hoped to control.
So far, PesaLink has made more headway with businesses than with ordinary consumers. Companies use it to pay suppliers, process payroll and send money in bulk. Getting someone to use it for a KES 500 ($4) shopping bill or to send money home is a different matter. M-PESA already handles those transactions, and banks will need a good reason to change.
Pricing fractures among partner banks
One of PesaLink’s biggest problems has been its price. For years, banks set their own transfer charges, with some fees reaching KES 250 ($1.92) for larger transactions, which made it difficult to sell PesaLink as a cheaper alternative to mobile money.
A group of 19 banks and microfinance institutions, including KCB, Absa, Diamond Trust Bank, and Stanbic, have since adopted the discounted pricing model. Transfers below KES 1,000 ($7.69) are free, while those between KES 1,001 ($7.70) and KES 999,999 ($7,692.30) incur a flat fee of KES 20 ($0.15).
Not everyone has signed up. Equity Bank, Co-operative Bank, Standard Chartered and NCBA still set their own transfer fees, which can be much higher than the flat KES 20 ($0.15) charge. Smaller transfers can cost up to KES 35 ($0.27), while customers moving larger sums may pay up to KES 250 ($1.92). As a result, the cost of sending money depends on which bank you use, even though the money moves through the same network.
M-PESA also uses tiered pricing, with small transfers costing little or nothing and larger ones attracting higher fees. Transfers below KES 100 ($0.77) are free. Sending a few hundred shillings costs up to KES 13 ($0.10), while larger transfers cost up to KES 108 ($0.83). This is the maximum charge, even when sending the service’s full transaction limit of KES 250,000 ($1,923.08).
Airtel Money takes a different approach to transfers within its own network, which remain free. Sending money to other mobile wallets attracts tiered charges like M-PESA’s, ranging from KES 7 ($0.05) to KES 13 ($0.10) for transfers below KES 1,000 ($7.69), and KES 100 ($0.77) to KES 108 ($0.83) for larger amounts, up to its KES 250,000 ($1,923.08) transaction limit.
The mobile money contest: PesaLink vs M-PESA and Airtel
On price, PesaLink has a clear advantage when customers move larger sums. Sending KES 200,000 ($1,538.46) through M-PESA costs KES 108 ($0.83). A customer using a bank on the discounted PesaLink tariff pays KES 20 ($0.15). PesaLink also allows transfers of up to KES 999,999 ($7,692.30) in one transaction, compared with KES 250,000 ($1,923.08) on M-PESA and Airtel Money. Both mobile money services have a daily transaction limit of KES 500,000 ($3,846.15).
Price is only part of the decision, though, considering mobile money has the advantage of being ready to spend. Airtel Money makes transfers within its network free, while M-PESA charges according to the amount sent. Both services also let customers send and receive money without worrying about which bank holds the account or which payment network processes the transaction.
PesaLink has a less convenient last mile because funds received through the service are deposited into a bank account. Spending it may require a debit card, an ATM withdrawal, or another transfer to a mobile wallet. Money received on M-PESA or Airtel Money is already in a wallet that customers can use to pay a kiosk, buy airtime, or settle household bills.
Postbank and the other partner banks give PesaLink wider reach, but it does not solve the banks’ bigger problem. Customers need a reason to use bank accounts for everyday payments, not just a cheaper way to move money between them. Until banks fix their pricing and make PesaLink easier to use, M-PESA will remain the first stop for most Kenyans paying for goods and services.

articles.title: Claude Code's "don't ask again" button is leaking passwords and API keys to public GitHub repos
articles.text:
Facepalm: A feature in Claude Code meant to save developers a few clicks is exposing database passwords, API tokens and private keys in public GitHub repositories. When a developer tells Anthropic's coding agent to stop asking for permission to run a shell command, the agent saves the exact command, along with any credentials inside it, to a settings file in the project folder. Researchers at security firm Apiiro found that file in more than 100,000 public repositories, and about 1,100 of them contained secrets.
Claude Code asks for approval before it runs shell commands on a developer's machine. One of the options is "Yes, and don't ask again." Choosing it creates an allow rule in a file called .claude/settings.local.json. Sometimes the rule is a general pattern, but often it's the full command, stored word for word. If that command included a password, a token or a root login, the credential now sits in plain text in a JSON file inside the project directory.
Anthropic's documentation says Claude Code adds an entry for this file to the developer's global Git ignore configuration. That normally keeps Git from tracking it. But a global ignore list lives in the developer's own Git configuration, not in the repository. If the repository is cloned to a different machine, or if a folder that already holds the file is turned into a repository later, that protection may not be in place. Apiiro also reports that Claude Code often commits changes to the settings file on its own, without the user taking any action.
The exposed secrets Apiiro found came from 63 organizations. They included API tokens, database passwords, private keys and root logins. Deleting the file from a repository does not fully solve the problem. If someone forked the project before the cleanup, the credentials remain in that fork.
Developers usually rely on secret scanners to catch this kind of mistake, but scanners didn't catch everything here. Of the roughly 1,100 exposed secrets, 215 were not flagged by either gitleaks or TruffleHog, two widely used open-source scanners. That is close to one in five.
The problem had already been reported. A bug filed in Anthropic's Claude Code GitHub repository in August 2025 described it. Later reports said the settings file was sometimes not added to .gitignore at all, and that Claude Code could write sensitive commands to a different file that had no protection from Git. All of those reports were closed automatically after 60 days without activity, with no fix.
Boris Cherny of the Claude Code team discussed the findings in a Hacker News thread over the weekend. He said the team is "looking into what we can do to prevent this." He also said these settings files should almost never be checked into source control, and that the cases appeared when "the files were manually created and checked in."
Cherny pointed users to Claude Code's auto mode, which uses classifiers to handle "routine permission prompts" instead of relying on what he called "manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists." Another commenter replied that auto mode can still save sensitive commands to the settings files. Cherny called it a "good catch" and said the team is "thinking through what we can do to improve this."
He also advised developers to use secret scanners, and said the team is considering building secret scanning into Claude Code itself. Apiiro's results suggest that would be a partial fix at best, since the two leading open-source tools missed 215 of the exposed credentials.
The underlying design issue is that the permission system stores raw command strings. For an agent that writes and runs shell commands on its own, those strings will often contain credentials. Any fix that leaves those strings unchanged on disk still depends on ignore rules working correctly on every machine and in every repository setup.
Claude Code is not the only AI agent to leak user data recently. Last month, Meta suspended the sharing feature in its Muse agent after security researchers found that the URLs for shared conversations could be easily guessed.

articles.title: Polestar has a new look with its Formula 2030 concept
articles.text:
Perhaps only a small percentage of Ars readers will care about the Polestar 2030 concept, debuted today by the electric automaker. Spun out of Volvo—once upon a time, Polestar was a racing team—the brand has leveraged the resources of parent-automaker Geely to create electric vehicles that marry a modern minimalist style with rewarding driving dynamics. But you now can’t buy any Polestars in the US, since Geely is Chinese, and banning Chinese-owned car brands enjoys remarkable bipartisan support in Congress.
The Formula 2030 is about the same length as a Polestar 2 but with a very low roofline. If anything, the two-box shape reminds me of the Saab Aero-X, one of the final concepts from the then-terminal Swedish automaker. (In many ways, Polestar has adopted Saab’s mantle.)
Polestar says the concept fits into its own segment somewhere between the next Polestar 2 and the Polestar 7—it numbers its cars chronologically (mostly), not based on size—although it’s not saying if the hatchback design will go into series production. Successfully packaging rear-seat passengers and a lithium-ion battery pack is something a concept needn’t worry about, after all. Rather, it’s a styling exercise, or more than one.

articles.title: LLM Reliability Layers Under Test: Accuracy, Yield, and the Limits of Verification
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Reliability layers sorted answers by trustworthiness but corrected almost none; yield, right answers over all records, exposes what accuracy hides.
- Deterministic code can prove an answer wrong, never right: it catches nonexistent codes and spans missing from the post, but plausible answers still need a model or a person.
- Recognition beats generation: recalling SNOMED codes from memory, the model invented 13 to 18 percent that don’t exist; picking from a menu, it scored ten times higher.
- Determinism held: four of five model families reproduced their output exactly at temperature zero; the fifth agreed on 70 percent of mentions across three runs.
- Detection sets a hard ceiling: no layer recovers a mention the extractor missed, so the largest gains came from matching the corpus’s annotation conventions, not domain-adapted models.
The theory: More layers should mean more accuracy
Clinical notes, incident reports, support tickets, and forum posts are prose, and a language model can read them. What it produces is not dependable. Ours was right about one answer in three on the task below and reported full confidence on two-thirds of its answers; wherever a wrong answer costs something, that is unusable.
We tested six layers, checks wrapped around the model, that each evaluate the model's output and flag what is wrong so that it can be put right: check each answer against something deterministic, send provable failures back to the model [1], sample it several times and vote [2], have a second model judge it [3], withhold what cannot be corroborated, and send the rest to a person. The theory we set out to test is that these layers are additive: each one catches errors the layers below it missed, so accuracy rises with every layer added. That assumption is what justifies stacking them at all. We ran all six on the same records, each priced, with the free check entered as a competitor. The theory did not hold. The layers sorted the answers by how far to trust them and corrected almost none.
Testing it needs a graded task, so we chose an annotated corpus: CADEC, the CSIRO Adverse Drug Event Corpus [4], 1,250 forum posts about two drugs, every adverse reaction marked as a span, the writer's exact words such as "rectal bleed", and given a SNOMED CT code. A gold answer for every mention lets us score each layer's verdicts instead of trusting them — and that assumes gold is the only right answer, which is not always true. Running one development document through the pipeline, the span "extremely sick" is gold-coded 213257006 |Generally unwell|; the model answered 39104002 |Illness| — an equally active, equally general reading that shares no wording with the span or with gold's own name. Naming either is a real answer; only one is scored correct. We did not build a CADEC system or tune for it: the aim was to evaluate open-weight models and measure how much each layer raises their accuracy, and CADEC is the instrument.
A supervised system does far better. CONORM [5], fine-tuned on 875 of CADEC's 1,250 files, reaches an end-to-end F1 of 0.72 under lenient span matching. Our zero-shot extractor, everything it returns, reaches 0.47 to 0.50 under the same matching on our development split, 0.39 to 0.43 span-exact. We are not competing with it: it needs those 875 annotated files, and still cannot say which of its answers to trust. Our held-out split was spent once: 60 documents, one run; every other number is development-side and says so. Two things would move the absolute numbers: the judge is small, and CADEC, public since 2015, is almost certainly in its training data. The comparisons between layers should hold.
The system under test: the model reads, the vocabulary knows
The model is never asked for a code, and everything above it depends on that choice.
Figure 1: The pipeline, left to right, on one illustrative post (CADEC is non-transferable). Teal: a model call; grey: deterministic code. Each card shows what that step produces for the example; code appears for the first time in the last one. Image: the authors.
The model quotes each reaction; a retriever with no language model in it searches 227,554 keyword-to-code rows — every description in the SNOMED CT Australian edition of 31 July 2026 — embedding each quote with granite-embedding:30m, 384 dimensions, run locally, and showing the model a menu of the 20 nearest concepts to pick from. Codes are written as 271782001 |Drowsy|, SNOMED's bar notation, throughout.
We chose this shape by measuring the alternatives on 40 development documents, three cold runs each: recall the code from memory, name the concept and look it up, or pick from the menu.
Figure 2: F1 of the extractor alone under three ways of getting the code, one dot per cold run, with tokens per run and unparseable replies beneath. Image: the authors.
Recalling the code is not weak but broken: eight to twelve times worse than naming the concept. It answered null on up to 38 percent of records, and of the codes it committed to, 13 to 18 percent exist in no SNOMED release.
F1 is span-exact throughout: a wrong boundary is both a false positive and a false negative.
That is the extractor the six layers sit on. Before measuring what a layer adds, we had to know how much its output moves between runs of the same inputs.
The noise floor: three runs of the same system
Three identical runs of the unchanged extractor differed by four points of F1, at temperature zero.
We ran the extraction step three times, cold, on the same 40 documents. Two runs were byte-identical. The third diverged and finished with 98 correct mentions against the pair's 87. Grouped by mention, the runs give 233 mentions:
| across the three runs | mentions | 
| all three agree on span and code | 164 (70%) | 
| same span, different code | 22 | 
| same code, different span | 1 | 
| span and code both differ | 10 | 
| found by only two runs | 15 | 
| found by only one run | 21 | 
Where all three found the same span, they agreed on the code 84 percent of the time, so what moves between runs is mostly the reading, not the coding. We did not ask why those 22 were coded differently, and we should have.
The variation is a property of this model: four other families run three times each, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b-instruct, qwen3:8b, and granite4:micro-h, returned byte-identical output every time. Our extractor, gpt-oss:20b, is the only mixture-of-experts model of the five and the only one that varied. Why, we could not settle: the diverging request, sent alone eight times, returns one reply; it moves only inside a full run. We kept it for its 6.5 extra points of F1 over llama3.1:8b.
From then on, every change was measured on three runs and reported as the range across them.
What each layer bought, and what it charged
The two free layers did their jobs: the vocabulary check sorted the answers, and refusal withheld the doubtful ones, and neither changed an answer. Of the three paid layers, self-correction almost never fired, voting did not help, and the judge worked, but nothing read its verdict.
Development split, three runs of 40 documents; figures below are ranges across the runs:
- Vocabulary check, 0 tokens. Did its job. It changes no answer; It gives each answer one of three verdicts. REJECT: the code does not exist, or the span is not in the post. 2714004, claimed as |Pale skin|, is in no SNOMED release. ACCEPT: the span's words match one of the vocabulary's own names. "chronic pain" matches |Chronic pain|. BAND: the span's words match none of the vocabulary's names, so the check has no evidence either way. "bit drowsy" against |Drowsy| happens to be right; "truck hit" against |Injury due to motor vehicle accident| is a fabricated finding — the check cannot tell the two apart.
- Self-correction, about 1,500 tokens. Barely exercised. It fires only on REJECT, restating the failure to the model as a fact ("code 999999 does not exist"). It fired two or three times per run and corrected nothing: unmeasured, not refuted.
- Voting, 411,000–432,000 tokens. Did not help. Three samples of the extractor, the majority wins. It changed about 27 codes a run, as many right-to-wrong as wrong-to-right: net −1 to +1, destroying 2 to 5 right answers. The voter is the answerer, so a vote carries no information that the answer lacked.
- Second-model judge, 84,000–88,000 tokens. Work once shown the menu; nothing read its verdict. A second, smaller model, 3.2B parameters against the extractor's 20B, is asked whether each answer is right. Shown only the span and a nine-digit code, it barely told right from wrong. Shown the menu the extractor chose from, it separates 3.4 to 4.2×, more sharply than the free check, and can say the right answer is not on this menu. No later layer reads its verdict.
- Refusal, 0 tokens. A guard, and it held. It passes answers that meet a chosen verdict and holds the rest for a person. On ACCEPT, our measured setting, 21 to 23 percent of records pass at 0.74 to 0.82 accuracy. A confidence threshold was tried and retired: the extractor's confidence is 1.0 on two-thirds of answers, right or wrong.
- A person. Not measured. What refusal holds back goes to a reviewer, whose decisions are corrections that a later model can be trained on.
Then we removed the three paid layers and replayed refusal: what it passed differed by one record on the first run and by none on the other two.
Voting and the judge's verdicts are good for diagnosis, not repair: a split vote marks an answer the model cannot reproduce, and a judge answering not on this menu marks a failed menu, not a failed pick. We did not use them that way, and should have.
Layers withhold; they don't add
One dial, not a staircase.
Every verdict carries information. None makes the system produce more right answers, and they do not stack.
Figure 3: The first run's 230 records under each shipping rule. Dark green: right code on the exact span; light green: exact span, wrong code; light teal: right code, boundary off; grey: neither; amber: to a person. Dotted lines: the most the extractor found. Image: the authors.
Figure 3 reads each verdict as a shipping rule over the same 230 records. Three things hold.
First, any verdict raises the accuracy of what passes, because withholding is a layer's only lever. No rule ships more than the 88 right answers the extractor found, so every gain in accuracy is paid for in right answers held back. Accuracy alone flatters any withholding layer. Yield, right answers as a share of all records, cannot be flattered, so we report both.
Second, the price differs by verdict. ACCEPT is the most precise rule and the most expensive: moving to it removes 128 errors at the cost of 49 right answers and 177 records for a person, because the check can endorse only 32 percent of mentions whose wording matches the vocabulary. The menu-shown judge's verdict is informed rather than lexical, and it is the one rule whose F1 beats shipping everything, 0.420 against 0.397.
Third, the verdicts nest rather than add. Nearly everything the free check endorses, the judge endorses too, so a second verdict mostly confirms the first and can only remove records, never recover one the first held back; that is why removing the paid layers changed one record. Where every verdict agrees, the answers are almost all right; where only a vote does, almost all wrong. Each verdict is a different trade between errors, lost answers, and reviews; we recommend none.
The held-out split, run once, tells the same story. Before any check, one answer in three was right. Of those, the vocabulary check marked ACCEPT, five in six were right; of the rest, one in five. The check changed no answer; it only sorted them.
Where the model loses
The domain knowledge was never missing. The model loses at reading, and nothing above it can see what it did not read.
Figure 4: Where the development split's 226 annotated mentions go through the shipped extractor, gpt-oss:20b, first run. Each bar is what the stage above kept; the dotted steps are what each stage lost. Teal: a model call; grey: deterministic code. Image: the authors.
Once a mention is found, the pipeline is reliable: the right concept reaches the menu for 93 percent of found spans and the model picks it 81 percent of the time. The loss is at finding. Nearly half the annotated mentions are never quoted as the annotators marked them, and none of the reasons are medical: single words go untouched where the annotator marked them, boundaries stretch — an extra adjective swept into a span the annotator left bare — and figures of speech are read literally, an idiom for exasperation coded as a nocturnal behaviour. Two domain-adapted models did not help: BioMistral-7B could not reliably return a parseable reply, and SapBERT as the retriever's encoder improved the menu and worsened the answer. A worked example and a denied-reactions rule did.
No layer can add a mention. Every layer above the extractor checks, re-asks, votes on, judges, or withholds an answer the extractor already gave; none can find a mention it missed. So the most any stack can ever get right is what the extractor found in the first place: on the held-out split, just over half the annotated mentions, a detection F1 of 0.521. The one way past that ceiling is a second reader: a different model family shown the post and the first model's spans, asked what was missed. We did not build it. Its additions would be proposals, needing the same measurement as the extractor's.
Does it hold beyond CADEC?
Four of the five lessons were held on other data. What changed is where the model loses, and where the free check can be trusted.
Seven further corpora [6–10], five model families; for each lesson, does the data agree?
- Layers sort; they do not fix. I agree. On PsyTAR, the paid layers changed nothing in any run.
- Start with the free check. Holds where the vocabulary's names are evidence and reverses where they are not. Clinical vocabularies behave as SNOMED did — the endorsed lane is right 76 to 100 percent of the time across five model families. Gazetteers do not: a place name matches the vocabulary and is still the wrong place, and the same lane is right 7 to 26 percent. On financial tag names, it never fires.
- Ask the model to read, never to remember. Not re-tested; every corpus used the menu.
- Make repeat runs a validation step. I agree. Every other family repeated itself exactly; our extractor's one instability elsewhere was refusing a document on one run of three.
- Study the data before adding layers. Agreed, with a change: where the model loses is not the same everywhere. On CADEC, it loses at reading; on the financial corpus, it reads well and coded badly, and its worst error was a habit, picking the menu's first line, not a gap in domain knowledge.
Two more findings met the same test:
- Self-correction barely fires. Sharpened. On PsyTAR, the check wrongly rejects some right codes in the answer key, so self-correction had work; it fired zero times, because the check never rejects what the model actually writes.
- A fact recorded once will be wrong silently. Repeated. Seventeen matrix cells ran with the wrong prompt or the wrong model, caught only because each run also saved the configuration it received.
The judge, the nesting of verdicts, and the diagnostic use of split votes were measured on CADEC only.
Defects between the layers, and inside the metric
Every layer passed its own tests. The two defects that mattered sat between the layers and inside the metric.
The first was the unread verdicts. The second was the metric: voting overwrote codes without re-running the vocabulary check, so records shipped marked verified for a code they no longer held. Fixing that moved the held-out F1 from 0.204 to 0.204, because precision and recall cannot tell an unwarranted answer from a wrong one. We built six layers to decide which answers to trust, then scored them with a metric that cannot see the difference.
Both defects share a shape: a load-bearing fact recorded once, so nothing could disagree with it. Three checks built from that lesson, gatecheck, crosscheck and stagecheck, are reached from the repository below; stagecheck is a standalone package with no dependencies.
Six practices that transfer
What transfers is not the layers but six practices, each earned above.
- Read the data before you add a layer. Our two largest gains were a worked example in the corpus's conventions and a rule for denied reactions; no layer and no domain model were supplied either.
- Never ask the model for an identifier. Have it quote and pick; let a lookup produce the code. Asked to recall codes, it invented them 13 to 18 percent of the time and scored ten times worse.
- Anchor confidence in something that does not resample: a vocabulary, a schema, a compiler. Test it on the answer key, where every rejection is false by construction, and on your own vocabulary, where it may reverse.
- Measure your floor before any improvement. Three runs minimum, reported as a range, and decide in advance what difference you will accept.
- Treat disagreement as a to-do list. A split vote, a judge's not on this menu, a mention coded differently on a repeat run: each marks where the task is underspecified. Read them offline; do not pay for them online.
- Find the reader of every field a layer writes, and check your metric can see the defect you prevent. A forty-line search found three verdicts nothing read; yield beside accuracy shows what a withholding layer hides.
We set out believing that stacking reliability layers buys reliability. Measured end to end, they sorted the answers by how far to trust them and fixed almost none: worth a great deal, and not what we bought them for. The model reads. Almost everything else belongs to code, and one choice to you.
Code, ledger, decision records, and every figure's source. CADEC is non-transferable; we ship document IDs, never text.
References
- Madaan et al., Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback, 2023.
- Wang et al., Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models, 2022.
- Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, 2023.
- Karimi, Metke-Jimenez, Kemp and Wang, Cadec: A corpus of adverse drug event annotations, Journal of Biomedical Informatics 55, 2015.
- Yazdani, Rouhizadeh, Bornet, and Teodoro, Context-Aware Entity Normalization for Adverse Drug Event Detection (CONORM), medRxiv 2023.
- Gritta, Pilehvar and Collier, A Pragmatic Guide to Geoparsing Evaluation, Language Resources and Evaluation, 2020. — GeoWebNews, LGL and TR-News all ship here.
- Loukas et al., FiNER: Financial Numeric Entity Recognition for XBRL Tagging, ACL 2022.

articles.title: How TCS built an agentic test orchestrator with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How TCS built an agentic test orchestrator with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This post was co-written with Varun Valsan from Tata Consultancy Services (TCS).
Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) runs large-scale testing for Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) clients, where the slowest part of a release is rarely writing application code. The larger constraint is the chain of work that follows: interpreting requirements, designing scenarios, writing and maintaining automation, preparing execution environments, investigating failures, and assembling evidence for review.
BFSI clients need to increase testing throughput while preserving the controls expected in financial services. The objective wasn’t to replace quality engineers. It was to remove repetitive translation and execution work so that engineers could spend more time on risk analysis, exploratory testing, and release decisions. These industry needs generated four specific requirements for TCS. First, every test must be grounded in project-specific context rather than generic prompts. Second, it had to cover both API and browser-based UI testing to match how BFSI applications are built. Third, security is paramount, so every tenant’s data and knowledge store must be isolated. Finally, it must provide a repeatable path from requirement ingestion to test evidence and reporting, so the gains hold across teams and releases. In this post, we show how TCS built an agentic test orchestrator that turns requirements into executable, governed tests, and what it changed for its BFSI testing teams.
Why conventional automation and systems weren’t enough
TCS already uses traditional test automation for its clients, and it does improve execution speed. But it leaves the slow work untouched: teams must still create the scenarios, convert them into scripts, maintain locators and dependencies, and diagnose failures. When a linked user story changes, scripts generated for an earlier story can quickly become stale. A single generative AI prompt also doesn’t provide the control needed for a multi-stage engineering workflow.
TCS therefore designed the Agentic Test Orchestrator to decompose testing into specialized tasks. Each task has its own agent, tools, validation rules, and context. A deterministic supervisor routes work, while an execution workflow controls retries, error classification, persistence, and reporting.
To run these agents, TCS chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Three capabilities drove the decision. First, Amazon Bedrock offers a choice of models, so each agent uses the model that fits its task, such as scenario design or code generation, and TCS can adopt newer models as they become available. Second, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scales with demand, so testers across many tenants can run generation and execution sessions at the same time without TCS provisioning or tuning agent servers. Third, the runtime runs each session in its own isolated microVM, which gives TCS session-level separation for its multi-tenant platform without having to build that layer itself. Together, these capabilities let TCS focus its engineering effort on testing logic rather than agent infrastructure, which shortened the time to bring the platform to its BFSI clients.
Solution overview
The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the platform across five stages, with a per-tenant security layer underneath. Inputs from Jira, business requirement documents (BRDs), and GitLab enter a tenant web application that runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) behind Amazon CloudFront, with sign-in through Amazon Cognito. TCS uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to host the platform’s specialized agents, built with the Strands Agents SDK. These agents generate the tests, refine them with the tester, and manage their execution. Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) runs the generated tests. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon DynamoDB store the results, and Amazon CloudWatch captures the logs. Throughout, AWS WAF, Amazon Cognito, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), and AWS Secrets Manager enforce per-tenant security and isolation.
The TCS Agentic Test Orchestrator is a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) solution built on AWS. A tester provides requirements through Jira stories, business requirement documents (BRDs), Swagger specifications, uploaded documents, GitLab source folders, or captured UI flows. From those inputs the platform then generates test scenarios, Gherkin feature files, and executable Java or Python tests. It runs those tests on Amazon ECS, stores artifacts and results, and shows progress and reports in a per-tenant web application. The sections that follow describe how each part of the platform meets one of the four requirements TCS set.
1. Separate the control plane from each tenant application plane
TCS required strict isolation of each tenant’s identity, data, and keys, so the platform uses pooled compute with siloed data and identity. A shared control plane provides the Amazon EKS cluster, container registry, administrative portal, tenant registry, onboarding automation, Amazon CloudFront distributions, and AWS WAF protection. Each tenant application plane receives its own Kubernetes namespace, Amazon Cognito user pool, AWS KMS key, Amazon S3 bucket, Amazon DynamoDB tables, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. This separation gives each BFSI tenant the data and key boundaries that financial-services controls demand.
Tenant onboarding is event driven. The administrative API writes a pending tenant record, emits an event through Amazon EventBridge, and starts an AWS CodeBuild project that deploys the tenant infrastructure with AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). This pattern makes tenant provisioning repeatable while retaining tenant-specific identity and data boundaries that TCS needed.
2. Ground every agent in project context
TCS’s first requirement was that generation reflect each project’s domain rather than a generic prompt, so grounding is built into the platform. The platform stores uploaded requirements and generated artifacts in Amazon S3 and session metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Project documents and synchronized source files are indexed in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases using vector embeddings. Before material reaches an agent, retrieval is filtered by tenant, project, and session context, so one client’s context doesn’t inform another’s tests.
This context layer supports the many ways a BFSI team expresses requirements: Jira stories and linked story chains, BRDs, Swagger definitions, reference code, locator documents, setup modules, test data, and GitLab source folders. For UI automation, a separate capture service uses Puppeteer to convert a URL and a natural-language goal into a UI flow document and an XPath locator document.
3. Use specialized agents instead of one large prompt
Because a single prompt can’t give a regulated workflow the control it needs, the platform divides the work among specialized agents that run as containerized services in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime using the Strands Agents SDK. A generation runtime routes requests to dedicated scenario, Gherkin, code-generation, and validation tools. Additional runtimes support conversational refinement, BRD-to-story conversion, incremental generation across linked Jira stories, and test execution. Each agent owns a stage of the lifecycle. Here’s a brief overview of each specialized agent:
Generation agent: Creates structured scenarios, converts them to Gherkin, generates Java or Python automation, and validates generated code.
Chat agent: Classifies a request as an information query or an update request, then answers or revises the active artifact.
Dynamic task agent: Retrieves BRD context and produces a structured user story with requirements and acceptance criteria.
Incremental agent: Extends scenarios, Gherkin, or code across a linked Jira story chain instead of starting from scratch.
Execution agent: Fetches artifacts, chooses an execution environment, runs tests, classifies failures, applies controlled fixes, and saves final results.
4. Route API and UI tests to the right execution environment
TCS needed to cover both API and browser-based UI testing, which place different demands on infrastructure, so the execution agent detects the test type from the generated code and routes it accordingly. API tests are routed to Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate. Selenium UI tests are routed to an Amazon ECS cluster backed by Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), where the executor can run Chrome with a virtual display.
For UI runs, the executor can capture the virtual display with FFmpeg and publish an HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) stream to Amazon S3 for delivery through Amazon CloudFront. Test logs are sent to Amazon CloudWatch, and generated Cucumber reports are stored in Amazon S3 with time-limited access.
5. Control the execution and correction loop
To keep automated correction safe enough for a BFSI pipeline, the execution agent defines its fetch, execute, fix, and save steps as a LangGraph workflow. LangGraph’s explicit state graph gives TCS a fixed step order and a bounded retry loop, while AgentCore runtime hosts, scales, and isolates the agent that runs it. The fetch node retrieves the test project and generated assets, sanitizes files, and detects the framework. The execute node launches the selected ECS task, monitors status, retrieves logs, and parses results.
When a failure is classified as a code error and the retry policy allows it, a fixing agent receives a constrained error context and proposes a targeted correction. Safety checks reject empty files, unexpected new files, or extreme changes in file size. Environment errors, such as connectivity or authentication failures, are not sent to the code fixer. The save node persists the final code, status, attempts, logs, parsed results, and report location.
6. Security and operational controls
Because the solution serves regulated BFSI tenants, it applies controls at the identity, network, data, and application layers. For identity, separate Amazon Cognito user pools serve platform administrators and each tenant, with backend JSON Web Token (JWT) validation and role-based authorization. For data, each tenant has its own AWS KMS keys and encrypted Amazon S3 storage, DynamoDB access is tenant-scoped, and AWS Secrets Manager holds Jira and GitLab credentials. At the workload level on Amazon EKS, Kubernetes namespaces, NetworkPolicy, and ResourceQuota separate tenants, and containers run as non-root with dropped Linux capabilities. At the network edge, AWS WAF managed rules and request-rate controls protect the platform. Traffic is delivered over HTTPS through Amazon CloudFront and the Application Load Balancer, and responses carry restrictive security headers. Across all of these, OpenTelemetry traces capture agent activity while Amazon CloudWatch logs and Container Insights provide application and execution observability.
Outcomes
TCS runs the Agentic Test Orchestrator in production for its BFSI clients. To quantify the effort savings, TCS measured the solution against its existing process on a representative BFSI workload of about 100 test scenarios. In the manual process, each scenario takes roughly two hours of engineer effort to design, script, and execute, or about 200 hours for the full set. With the Agentic Test Orchestrator, the average effort was approximately 14 minutes per scenario, bringing the same workload to about 24 hours. This represents an 88 percent reduction in effort in this comparison. (These figures come from a controlled internal benchmark that TCS ran across approximately 100 scenarios. Actual results vary by workload, application complexity, and team.)
For TCS, the effort number matters less than the operating model behind it. Requirement ingestion, generation, execution, correction, and reporting now form one traceable workflow instead of a chain of disconnected handoffs. Quality engineers review and govern AI-produced artifacts rather than hand-building them, which returns their time to the risk analysis, exploratory testing, and release decisions that the manual process crowded out. That is the outcome TCS set out to reach.
Conclusion
The problem TCS set out to solve was not simply slow test execution. It was the fragmented, manual path from business requirements to trustworthy test evidence. This is the part of a BFSI release that consumes engineering time without adding assurance. In this post, we showed how TCS built the Agentic Test Orchestrator on AWS to close that gap by combining contextual retrieval, specialized agents, workload-aware execution, isolated per-tenant services, and observable infrastructure.
The result is a reusable pattern for applying generative AI to software quality engineering without reducing testing to a single prompt. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts and scales the agents, Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supply the AI capabilities and project context, Amazon EKS hosts the per-tenant application layer, Amazon ECS provides fit-for-purpose execution, and AWS security, storage, integration, and observability services support the full lifecycle. For TCS’s BFSI teams, the payoff is a faster, more consistent testing process that returns engineers’ time to risk, quality, and release decisions.
To learn more and deploy the solution in your own environment, visit the TCS Agentic Test Orchestrator in AWS Marketplace. If you would like help applying this pattern to your own testing workflows, contact the AWS team. Have questions or a similar use case? Share them in the comments.

articles.title: Evolving metal extraction processes
articles.text:
Sponsored
Evolving metal extraction processes
Rethinking how metals are extracted could unlock lower-emission production, make better use of mineral resources, and strengthen critical-material supply chains.
Provided byOutokumpu
The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible.
Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize.
Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?
EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted:
“We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.”
A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem
As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on.
Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience.
That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions.
Beyond optimization
For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways.
The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential.
Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness.
Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology
Source: Outokumpu
Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT.
“The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste.
Innovation happens at the boundaries
EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies.
Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work.
“Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production.
Building a technology platform
A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications.
Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point.
“The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains.
That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing.
The future of materials companies
The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise.
Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible.
The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives.
The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030. Beyond producing low-CO2, chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum.
The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today?
The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on.
Read more about this topic and hear more from Caspar Stinn and Antoine Allanore.
This content was produced by Outokumpu. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.
