articles.title: ¿A qué hora se estrena 'El Señor de los Anillos: Los Anillos de Poder' temporada 3?
articles.text:
Llega por fin la temporada 3 de Los Anillos de Poder, la serie de El Señor de los Anillos que nos relata el ascenso al poder del Señor Oscuro Sauron. En esta nueva entrega, que tiene lugar 5 años después de la anterior, la Tierra Media está en guerra. Los ejércitos de Sauron han avanzado por todo el continente, conquistando cuanto encuentran a su paso. Solo unos pocos bastiones aislados se interponen entre el Señor Oscuro y la victoria total: Khazad-dûm, donde los enanos permanecen ahora recluidos en las profundidades de sus salones bajo la montaña, y los reinos élficos de Lindon y Rivendel, protegidos por sus Tres Anillos.
Mientras tanto, en las profundidades de Mordor, en su recién erigida torre de Barad-dûr, el Señor Oscuro trabaja sin descanso, obsesionado con forjar un poder capaz de doblegar a los últimos enemigos que aún se le resisten: «Un Anillo para gobernarlos a todos…». Ahora, todos los pueblos libres de la Tierra Media —enanos, elfos, hombres y magos— deberán encontrar la forma de unirse en una carrera contrarreloj para impedir que Sauron alcance su objetivo: someter toda forma de vida bajo su dominio absoluto.
Acerca de dónde podrá verse, a diferencia de otros títulos, aquí no depende para nada del territorio. En Estados Unidos, España, Latinoamérica y en el resto del mundo, Los Anillos de Poder temporada 3 estará disponible en Amazon Prime Video. La plataforma alberga los derechos exclusivos de toda la serie, por lo que contará de nuevo con su tercera entrega en el catálogo.
Hora de estreno de Los Anillos de Poder temporada 3
En cuanto a la hora de estreno de Los Anillos de Poder temporada 3, en Estados Unidos se emitirá el miércoles 11 de noviembre a las 12:00 am P.T. En España y Latinoamérica, llegará a Amazon Prime Video en la conversión horaria de cada país:
- España: 9:00 h.
- México, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica: 2:00 h.
- Perú, Colombia, Panamá, Ecuador: 3:00 h.
- Chile, Venezuela, Bolivia, República Dominicana, Puerto Rico: 4:00 h.
- Paraguay, Argentina, Brasil, Uruguay: 5:00 h.
Prueba Amazon Prime Video totalmente gratis durante 30 días y disfruta del catálogo completo de la plataforma sin límites. Solo con darte de alta tendrás acceso instantáneo a las mejores películas y series, además de envíos gratis en Amazon y otras ventajas.
A partir de ese momento, los fans podrán disfrutar de los 4 primeros capítulos de la temporada 3 de Los Anillos de Poder. A partir de ahí, la serie llevará una estrategia de estreno semanal muy particular. Dos nuevos episodios verán la luz durante los próximos dos miércoles. Así se llegará al octavo y último capítulo, que se estrenará el 28 de noviembre, manteniendo la serie en activo durante apenas tres semanas.

articles.title: Dominion Dynamics aims to go public in three to five years, CEO says | BetaKit
articles.text:
Dominion Dynamics, a Canadian defence tech company that hopes to compete with major players like Lockheed Martin, wants to be listed on public markets within five years.
The news: Dominion Dynamics CEO Eliot Pence outlined the plan in an online policy briefing hosted by the National Angel Capital Organization (NACO) on Tuesday. The event featured a conversation between Pence and Summit Lithium Technologies CEO Amanda Hall. Moderated by NACO CEO Claudio Rojas, it was part of a discussion on how the 2026 federal budget will affect entrepreneurs.
From the source: For Dominion to be successful, Pence said Canadians need to buy into the idea of building a “big defence company.”
“Canadians need to feel as though they are invested in the success of Dominion, hence the desire to list the company,” Pence said. “We have a plan to list in three years; we want to move as fast as we possibly can to that end, but I think listing the company in three to five years time is where we want to be.”
The context: Pence teased his timeline for taking the company public in an appearance on Paul Wells’ podcast last week, saying he wants Dominion Dynamics to be the best and biggest defence company in North America.
Since launching in June 2025, Dominion has been featured in BetaKit Most Ambitious and raised multiple record-setting funding rounds, including a $139-million Series A round earlier this year. The company is explicitly trying to become a Canadian competitor to big-name US defence contractors; it has taken on contracts to build an “autonomous wingman” to fly alongside crewed air fighters, as well as to build Ukrainian uncrewed ground vehicles.
Final thought: While Dominion has so far sustained itself on private capital, other companies looking to take advantage of Canada’s defence spending boom have taken to the public markets sooner. So far this year, Vancouver-based Juno Industries has listed on the TSX Venture Exchange and the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, while Montréal-based NorthStar and Brampton-based MDA Space have listed on the New York Stock Exchange.
Feature image courtesy The BetaKit Podcast.

articles.title: All net-connected vehicles from two major automakers allowed hackers to remotely unlock doors and start the engine — now-patched hard-coded credentials and bypassed MFA security showcase a lack of 101-level best practices
articles.text:
All net-connected vehicles from two major automakers allowed hackers to remotely unlock doors and start the engine — now-patched hard-coded credentials and bypassed MFA security showcase a lack of 101-level best practices
Backend infrastructure failures included hardcoded, user-visible administrator credentials.
Before proceeding further, we'd like to advise our dear reader to sit down and perhaps grab a helmet, for this post will elicit quite a few face-palms and forehead-slaps. Two security researchers joined forces and, during early 2026, managed to hack the vehicle connectivity backend infrastructure of two automakers, managing to remotely open the doors on any of their net-connected cars and start their engines across multiple world regions.
The vulnerabilities were quickly fixed, and they pertained to a handful of belief-begging security issues with multiple server APIs that their respective mobile applications use. Furthermore, although remotely opening the cars and starting them were the most concerning bits, the vulnerabilities also exposed the vehicles' location, mileage, fuel, range, door states, and the customers' personal information.
The white-hat hacking duo isn't disclosing the name of the impacted automakers, but they managed to get access to Automaker #1's U.S. vehicles, while vehicles from Automaker #2 were susceptible to unplanned lock disengagement in Australia, the U.S., and Canada. As far as we can tell by visual inspection alone, the second firm may be Toyota, as the hack demonstration video appears to depict a RAV4 SUV.
Both affected automakers use ForgeRock's authentication and authorization services, though with the one small exception, the vulnerabilities found by Shubham Shah and Sam Curry pertained to poor implementations and security practices. One of their writeups goes over the ForgeRock-related affairs in detail for both companies, while Shah's article discusses the specifics on automaker #2 and their Australian connected-car infrastructure.
Shah first decompiled the company's Android application and found network calls to a telematics subdomain, quickly finding an "admintool" location containing a "TEST HARNESS" page with a login prompt. If you haven't been keeping track by now, the first problem is that this endpoint is reachable from the internet at large. But what really piqued Shah's interest was problem #2: a bundle of JavaScript code that should have been stripped of any unnecessary cruft actually contained the code for the backend's entire functionality, providing a map for further shenanigans.
This alone was enough to grant Shah the ability to pull up customer information with API keys that were hard-coded into said JavaScript. After some careful chaining of requests and connecting a license plate to a VIN with publicly available info, he connected that to a customer and found their email. At this point, the team noticed that the automaker was using ForgeRock's authentication mechanisms, and spent "a couple weeks" finding how they were used.
And this is also where they assess that the easiest path to victory is managing to mint an access token for any user, a task made way easier by the "cursed" JavaScript bundle they found at an endpoint containing hard-coded administrator credentials. These were likely meant for the staging environment, but the duo estimated, correctly, that they could be leveraged nevertheless.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
At this point, they ran into the WAF in front of the service. A Web Application Firewall is similar to a network firewall, but instead of working with IPs and ports, it considers endpoints (URLs) and the requirements to access them. The researchers hypothesize that although it's a good and standard practice, the WAF was put in place because of how bad things were underneath.
And they were right. The app decompilation had revealed a "pinService", and Shah found that it was accessible through the WAF. From thereon, they found "getUser", and correctly guessed that they could retrieve users' information with their email, phone, and ID. Remember those admin credentials? They came in handy, revealing the users' password hashes, but as these were SHA-512, cracking them was unfeasible.
At this point, they let GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra loose to brute-force path names, and found an unprotected one that ultimately let them overwrite any user's password, partially enabling taking over their accounts. However, there was still MFA to contend with.
As it turns out, even that too was misconfigured, as the Australian environment would let users skip MFA entirely. With some judicious token shuffling across endpoints and the mobile app, they eventually could mint access tokens, letting them fully impersonate any user account... and unlock their cars. Then, it was as simple as sending out an API request for the "door-unlock" command, and sure enough, the test car promptly opened.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: IA do Google analisa código do Signal em busca de falhas de segurança
articles.text:
O Google utilizou inteligência artificial (IA) para analisar e verificar propriedades de segurança do Signal, um dos aplicativos de mensagens mais conhecidos por seus recursos de privacidade. O trabalho foi conduzido pelo Google DeepMind, divisão de pesquisa em IA da empresa, e empregou demonstrações matemáticas para examinar partes do código do mensageiro.
A análise utilizou o AlphaProof Code, sistema desenvolvido para trabalhar com demonstrações formais. Durante aproximadamente quatro semanas, a ferramenta examinou o código do Signal e ajudou os pesquisadores a verificar se determinadas propriedades de segurança eram matematicamente válidas.
A iniciativa representa aplicação da IA que vai além da geração de textos, imagens e programas: a tecnologia também pode ajudar a identificar falhas e conferir formalmente se sistemas computacionais seguem regras estabelecidas.
Como a IA verificou a segurança do Signal?
- O trabalho utilizou a linguagem de programação Lean, empregada na construção de provas matemáticas formais. Nesse ambiente, uma propriedade de segurança pode ser descrita matematicamente e submetida a um verificador capaz de conferir se a demonstração está correta;
- Diferentemente de uma análise convencional, que procura possíveis vulnerabilidades por meio de testes e inspeções, a verificação formal permite demonstrar que determinadas propriedades são satisfeitas sob condições e premissas específicas;
- Durante o trabalho, os pesquisadores também utilizaram versões do código com vulnerabilidades antigas inseridas propositalmente. A ideia era avaliar se o sistema conseguia identificar problemas conhecidos e verificar as propriedades de segurança estabelecidas;
- O processo durou cerca de quatro semanas e envolveu a análise de componentes do aplicativo.
Leia mais:
- Google lança chips de IA para proteger dados e ampliar memória
- Google é processado por conversas sobre suicídio entre IA e garota de 13 anos
- Google, Meta e TikTok processam Califórnia para barrar lei de proteção a menores
O que a descoberta significa para a segurança digital?
A verificação formal pode ajudar desenvolvedores a encontrar problemas que passariam despercebidos em revisões tradicionais. Também permite aumentar a confiança em componentes importantes de softwares utilizados para proteger informações pessoais.
No caso do Signal, o trabalho é especialmente relevante porque o aplicativo tem a privacidade como um de seus principais pilares. O mensageiro utiliza criptografia de ponta a ponta para proteger as conversas, impedindo que terceiros tenham acesso ao conteúdo das mensagens durante a transmissão.
Ainda assim, é importante entender o alcance da pesquisa: verificar matematicamente determinadas propriedades do código não significa comprovar que todo o aplicativo está livre de vulnerabilidades.
Problemas em outros componentes, falhas de implementação ou ataques aos próprios dispositivos dos usuários continuam sendo possibilidades.
A iniciativa do Google mostra como sistemas de IA podem contribuir para tornar softwares mais seguros, auxiliando especialistas na análise de códigos complexos e na construção de provas matemáticas que sustentem suas garantias de segurança.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Statt Endlager: Forscher der TU Dresden wollen Atommüll recyceln
articles.text:
27.000 Kubikmeter Atommüll: Wie Forscher der TU Dresden das Problem lösen wollen
Rund 27.000 Kubikmeter Atommüll sind in Deutschland durch den jahrzehntelangen Betrieb von Atomkraftwerken angefallen. Die Bundesgesellschaft für Endlagerung (BGE) ist auf der Suche nach einem sogenannten Endlager. Nach eigenen Angaben verfolgt die Gesellschaft das Ziel, einen Standort zu ermitteln, der den Abfall für eine Million Jahre sicher einschließt – eine knifflige Aufgabe. Kürzlich wurde die Suche eingegrenzt und die infrage kommenden Gebiete für ein solches Endlager deutlich reduziert. Die Technische Universität Dresden arbeitet jetzt an einem Projekt, das die Endlagersuche überflüssig machen könnte.
Was die Forschenden der TU Dresden vor haben
Die TU Dresden plant den Bau des Experimentalrecyclingreaktors „DEMO“ in einem Forschungsprojekt unter Einsatz eines sogenannten Flüssigsalzreaktors. Dieser verwertet die hochradioaktiven Stoffe aus dem Leichtwasserreaktorbetrieb energetisch und stofflich.
Mit dem Einsatz von „DEMO“ wollen die Forschenden einen entscheidenden Machbarkeitsnachweis erbringen. Dabei sollen vorhandene abgebrannte Kernbrennstäbe und verglaste Materialien ohne die bisher nötige Aufbereitung direkt in emissionsarme Energie transformiert und zu größtenteils kurzlebigen Spaltprodukten umgewandelt werden. Durch dieses Verfahren würden lediglich Spaltprodukte als Reststoffe zurückbleiben und die Endlagerung der nuklearen Abfälle gemäß StandAG entfallen. Das Gesetz regelt das mehrstufige Verfahren für die Suche nach einem Endlager für langlebige, wärmeentwickelnde radioaktive Abfälle.
Ökonomisches und gesellschaftliches Potenzial des Reaktors
Die Forschenden erhoffen sich durch ihren Reaktor erhebliche Einsparungen von rund 50 Milliarden Euro. Ihre Schätzung beruht auf der Annahme, dass ein Atommüll-Endlager nicht mehr nötig sei. Zudem erschließe die Technologie Energie-Ressourcen, die dem 300-fachen jährlichen Stromverbrauch Deutschlands entsprechen. Konkrete Angaben zur methodischen Grundlage ihrer Schätzungen enthält die Pressemitteilung zum Projekt allerdings nicht.
Ob das Konzept tatsächlich funktioniert und auf politische Akzeptanz stößt, muss sich in weiteren Entwicklungsschritten unter Beweis stellen. In frühestens fünf Jahren ist mit ersten Erkenntnissen zu rechnen, heißt es in der Pressemitteilung. In dieser Zeit will das Forschungsteam der TU Dresden den Experimentalreaktor bauen. An Reaktoren, die aufgebrauchte Brennstäbe oder in Atomreaktoren entstehende Transurane nutzen können, wird seit Jahrzehnten geforscht. Die Idee der TU Dresden ist also nicht neu, muss sich allerdings noch in der Praxis bewähren.

articles.title: New WhatsApp head wants to make the app easier to use, give its AI more chops | TechCrunch
articles.text:
WhatsApp has grown into one of the most popular messaging apps in the world, used by over 3 billion people. But with that growth, the app has also become complex, packing in features like communities, channels, stories and business features, and a lot of people find it hard to navigate.
Kunal Shah, who took over leadership of the app’s development from Will Cathcart earlier this year, now wants to make the app and actions within it simpler to use. In a new note shared on Tuesday, Shah said the company wants to make voice notes, groups, stickers, and video “simpler and more expressive.”
WhatsApp has long also tried to develop an ecosystem that lets users explore products and make purchases, and Shah’s note indicates more of that is coming, hinting at partnerships with payment companies and telecom providers to enable bill payment, loans, and eSIM purchases.
Shah also said the company wants to use AI to surface important information to users.
“It should quickly find what you need, get things done, and make sure you never miss a booking or an appointment. The best technology saves you time, so you can get back to the connections that matter,” he wrote.
WhatsApp currently offers an AI assistant that can summarize messages and create drafts. It’s not clear if the company will use its Muse agent to collate information and send reminders to people.
Here is Shah’s full note:
My Thoughts 5 Months In*
I think of WhatsApp like a shared language, spoken by 3bn+ people. Sometimes we use words, and sometimes it’s a voice note to a parent, a sticker that ends an argument, or a “home safely” at 2am. Language is at the heart of everything we as people do. We write letters, tell stories, send hard messages and make plans for the future. A WhatsApp chat is often where we start.
Like any language, the people who use it shape it. They don’t wait for permission. They find new things to say, and new ways to say them. Often, our users show us what should come next based on how they’re using the app and communicating in the world.
I’ve spent the last few months listening and understanding what our users need and want from us and, and what I heard is simple: Help people stay close to those who matter to them, and get more done on WhatsApp.
So that’s what we’ll build.
First, we want to make connections richer. Sometimes hearing someone’s voice, sending a joke, agreeing on a plan or knowing they’re safe is the whole point. People send over 10 billion voice messages and over 4 billion stickers on WhatsApp every day. As the way people communicate evolves, we will evolve these experiences with them. We’ll make voice notes, groups, stickers and video simpler and more expressive, because how people feel close keeps changing.
Second, we want anything you do to be as simple as sending a message. Too many things start in a chat and end with many more steps somewhere else: paying a bill, borrowing money, staying connected when you travel. Each handoff to another task costs time. We’re working with financial services and telecom partners so that finishing something feels as easy as starting it.
Third, we want to make sure AI makes it all more efficient. It should quietly find what you need, get things done and make sure you never miss a booking or an appointment. The best technology saves you time, so you can get back to the connections that matter.
None of this matters without trust. Trust takes years to earn and a moment to lose, and I don’t take it lightly. Whatever we build, WhatsApp must remain simple, reliable and private. These principles we’ve had for years aren’t changing. Your personal messages and calls stay end-to-end encrypted. That isn’t changing, and neither is our quality bar.
What happens inside WhatsApp only matters for what it makes possible outside it: more time together, stronger communities, and fewer barriers between people and the lives they want to live.
Onwards.

articles.title: 'We want data centers in Norway, but we can’t have all types of data centers': Norwegian government halts new grid connections as it looks to limit AI facility construction until late 2027
articles.text:
'We want data centers in Norway, but we can’t have all types of data centers': Norwegian government halts new grid connections as it looks to limit AI facility construction until late 2027
Norway says no more new data centers for the time being
- Norway has temporarily halted new data centers from connecting to its power grid
- Restrictions could continue until late 2027 until regulations catch up
- Norwegian government also reveals plans for new licensing system for data center operators
Norway has temporarily halted the building of new data centers in the country as it looks to limit the fast roll-out of new AI facilities.
System operator Statnett and the Norwegian government confirmed the move will look to halt the rapid expansion of power-intensive data centers across the country until regulations are in place.
The Norwegian government also revealed plans to introduce a new licensing system to regulate the expansion of large-scale cloud operators, instead favoring facilities which serve vital areas such as defense, police and emergency services, health services and other critical infrastructure such as the mobile network and the financial system.
"Control the growth"
“We want data centers in Norway, but we can’t have all types of data centers,” Digitalization Minister Torgeir Micaelsen said.
“We must therefore control the growth and ensure that Norway gets the data centers we actually need — those that provide the greatest societal benefit.”
The announcement will pause any new data center developments - but any projects already approved for a grid connection, or those already connected, will be unaffected.
Norway has become a popular location for new data centers, and Statnett said it expects the restrictions to be in place until at least August 2027, as fluctuating data center loads could destabilize grid operations across the country.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Statnett said it believes around 800MW of data centers are currently connected in the Norway, with an additional 4.2GW is reserved, and 9.1GW is in the capacity queue.
However around 18GW is currently being requested for connection - over a third of the country's peak power demand.
Norway has already imposed a temporary ban on the establishment of new data centers used to mine cryptocurrencies, and is already the site of existing and planned data centers from big players such as Microsoft, Nscale, TikTok (through Green Mountain), and CoreWeave.
The news comes at a critical time for data center developers, with opposition to new facilities spreading across the world.
More than 100 organizations across 15 European countries recently came together to campaign against ongoing AI data center developments, calling for an immediate moratorium on new large-scale campuses.

articles.title: The PlayStation Plus PC app is shutting down next month
articles.text:
Sony is retiring the PlayStation Plus app for PC on December 10th. Sony says it will notify users directly about the shutdown. The app allowed PlayStation Plus Premium subscribers to stream certain games on PC, but according to Sony, there aren’t many people using that perk:
The PlayStation Plus PC app is shutting down next month
Sony said less than 0.4 percent of PlayStation Plus Premium members were using the PC app.
“With a very small number of eligible PlayStation Plus Premium members (less than 0.4%) using the PlayStation Plus app on PC, making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use. As a result, the PlayStation Plus cloud streaming app on PC will no longer be available.”
PlayStation Plus Premium subscribers can still stream games on a console or on the PlayStation Portal. Sony’s decision to take the PC app offline follows reports earlier this year saying Sony is pulling back from PC and no longer plans to release PC ports of PlayStation exclusives.

articles.text:
In 2026, the global electronic components supply chain continues to navigate choppy waters.
For buyers and engineers across Europe and the US, the real headache is never simply “can I get the part?” It is four problems hitting at once: unstable lead times, volatile pricing, counterfeit and refurbished parts flooding the market, and critical part numbers that can go out of stock without warning. When a single chip’s lead time stretches from 8 weeks to 20, a production line grinds to a halt. When a batch of parts of unknown origin slips into a BOM, the cost isn’t just money — it’s delivery credibility and customer trust.
Over the past three years, the industry has been through a full downcycle. Demand contracted, inventory piled up, and prices fell. Many buyers thought they could finally breathe easy. But the reality is the opposite: the colder the market, the more traps appear in the supply chain. Mainstream part numbers are readily available with short lead times — but the moment you hit an allocation-constrained, end-of-life, or hard-to-find part, lead times can jump from weeks to months overnight. Meanwhile, unscrupulous dealers, driven by high margins, continue to supply substandard products — and the tougher the market, the more willing some are to cut corners. Prices swing, quotes are hard to hold, and buyers are squeezed between suppliers and internal cost targets. And when a critical part goes out of stock, the entire line stops — followed by breach-of-contract penalties and reputational damage.
Put simply: the cost of poor-quality components isn’t just money — it’s time. That’s the lesson Chang Ming has drawn from twelve years in the supply chain.
The Parts European and American Buyers Need Most This Year — And How We Deliver Them
In a volatile market, what truly separates one distributor from another isn’t whether they can supply standard chips — it’s whether they can get you the parts nobody else can. Chang Ming has stable sourcing and rapid response capabilities in several categories that keep European and American buyers up at night.
Scarce part numbers from ADI and TI.

NVIDIA allocation, with lead times under three months.

DDR5 and DDR4 support from Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix.
Memory has been one of the most volatile categories this year. Chang Ming integrates DDR5 and DDR4 supply from the three major manufacturers — Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix — to help you stabilize costs amid memory price hikes and shortages.
These three areas are where Chang Ming can help European and American buyers most urgently this year.
What a Reliable Distributor Can Do for You
Chang Ming International Technology Co., Ltd. was founded in 2013 and is a global hybrid distributor of electronic components — combining authorized distribution with independent distribution resources to deliver comprehensive supply chain solutions. Our advantage brand coverage includes TI, ADI, Infineon, NXP, ST, Microchip, Xilinx, Intel, Renesas, Toshiba, Broadcom, Marvell, Qorvo, NDK, Hamamatsu, and 24 other mainstream brands.
On service, Chang Ming provides six categories of support covering the full procurement cycle: authorized brand selection and design-in assistance to shorten your development cycle and reduce trial-and-error costs; one-stop BOM kitting with kit-completion rates up to 90%; multi-category, low-volume supply with virtually no minimum order quantity or value, ideal for R&D and pilot runs; supply of allocation-constrained, end-of-life, and hard-to-find parts, sourced across Europe, North America, and Asia with over 3,000 qualified global suppliers and on-hand inventory ready to ship; consignment and clearance of surplus inventory to help you quickly unlock tied-up capital; and value-added services such as Kitting and NET Terms to turn dead stock into working capital.
At the end of the day, the six things buyers care about most — avoiding production line shutdowns, avoiding reputational damage, avoiding breach-of-contract penalties, reducing procurement costs, improving cash flow, and accessing better value-added services — are all things Chang Ming delivers.
Why Trust Us: Quality Is the Baseline at Chang Ming
What European and American buyers fear most isn’t price — it’s counterfeit parts. That’s why Chang Ming has built quality into a traceable process, not a slogan.
From the moment goods arrive, Chang Ming runs a nine-step quality inspection process: outer packaging inspection, documentation verification, original label validation, visual inspection, dimensional measurement, non-destructive X-ray inspection, chip decapsulation, chemical testing, and issuance of an internal inspection report. Every step is photographed, documented, and uploaded to our system — fully traceable. Chip decapsulation is performed by a third party, and chemical testing is specifically designed to detect refurbished chips — striking directly at the industry’s most painful problem.
For third-party testing, Chang Ming partners with CNAS, White Horse (founded in 2004, compliant with IPC/JEDEC standards), and CECC, offering ten inspection services, including appearance inspection, X-ray fluoroscopy, decapsulation, cross-sectioning, solderability testing, reliability testing, and failure analysis. In addition, Chang Ming holds ISO9001, ISO14001, ISO13485, and ISO45001 certifications, along with Dun & Bradstreet enterprise certification. Our 365-day warranty reflects our confidence in quality control — and that confidence rests on the most rigorous supplier screening, testing methods, and inspection workflows.
In Closing
Whether it’s a tiny capacitor or an FPGA with millions of logic gates, the failure of any single component on a board brings both time and economic losses to the manufacturer.
What Chang Ming wants to do is simple: let European and American buyers sleep soundly, even when the market won’t sit still. We value every bit of trust our customers place in us, and we’re ready to be the most stable link in your global supply chain.

articles.title: AI's Efficiency Challenge For The Semiconductor Industry
articles.text:
AI is reshaping the tools, data, and collaboration models used to design, manufacture, and test silicon.
This post is based on John Kibarian’s keynote given at the PDF Solutions CONNECT event on October 15, 2026. The recording and slides of this presentation can be found here.
AI is the most consequential shift the semiconductor industry has faced, not because it is driving an upcycle, but because it is changing how the industry works.
The industry has seen big transformations before. Mobile and the internet reshaped what semiconductor companies sold, but they did not change how fabs, fabless companies and their supply chains operated. AI does both. It drives unprecedented demand for silicon, and is simultaneously reshaping the tools, data and collaboration models used to design, manufacture and test silicon.
We began reimagining our portfolio around an AI-first premise roughly four years ago, when ChatGPT first appeared. Today, the result is a next-generation platform that spans three long-standing areas of our work. The first two are accelerating yield ramps for new technologies and applying the latest IT technology to manufacturing data. The final area is connecting manufacturing operations across the supply chain, a thread strengthened by the 2025 acquisition of secureWISE.
Efficiency is today’s watchword. Efficiency is what matters. A manufacturing executive told suppliers recently that he could not get more tools than had already been promised. His only path to meeting demand was getting more out of the tools he had, a sentiment now heard across the industry, and shapes three challenges AI poses for semiconductor manufacturing:
Growth numbers are no longer in question, as the semiconductor industry reached a trillion dollars earlier than projected. Looking forward, McKinsey & Company’s base case has device revenue rising from $975 billion in 2025 to about $2.3 trillion in 2030. That’s an 83.5% increase in volume, with 58% of that growth coming from data centers and servers, the one vertical compounding at 29% a year.
Translated into physical capacity, the figures are striking. Installed AI data center capacity of 45–60 GW in 2026 is projected to reach 100–160 GW by 2030. At 150,000–200,000 wafers per gigawatt, half being HBM, that implies 9.6–17.5 million additional wafers and 16–29 new fabs of 50,000 wafer starts per month. This estimate could be conservative, as no company yet builds 50,000-wafer fabs at the leading edge. A modern leading-edge logic fab runs closer to 20,000 wafer starts, so the real fab count could double.
With AI revenue projected at $3.9 trillion in 2030 and margins at roughly $30 million per megawatt, the temptation is to treat this as a capital problem. Nation states look at the numbers and conclude they can write the check. Anyone who has run a fab knows better. Building capacity is only part of the answer. The harder problem is getting more compute out of every data center.
That pressure is already reshaping the landscape, and efficiency is coming from new designs. For years, most of our new customers came from Asia, where fabs and fabless companies were being started. Today, foundation model companies and hyperscalers are designing their own silicon with energy efficiency as the headline metric. Workloads are also being tuned for efficiency. Training keeps a chip saturated at its design point, while a GPU doing inference can spend over 90% of its power on memory updates and idle time.
Using that measure, the industry still has about a factor of a million of headroom, according to Richard Feynman’s lectures from the 1980s on the fundamental limits of computing.
Fabless companies previously could not justify manufacturing software because they were not manufacturers. They are now. What happens after a wafer leaves the front-end fab is where much of the industry’s action now sits.
A few examples illustrate the rapid change. Energy-efficient, bespoke designs carry operational consequences that land squarely on manufacturing and test with smaller production volumes across more products. Custom designs are proliferating rather than a few high-volume parts.
The breadth of new product introduction (NPI) testing carries through into production for accelerated yield ramps with wider datasets and test programs running to millions of test items.
And new technologies such as co-packaged optics and similar integrations mean more than electrons are moving through the production line, requiring new process controls.
PDF Solutions’ portfolio answers these pressures. Characterization Vehicle and DirectScan address co-optimization of design and manufacturing at sub-7nm nodes using more design information to know where and how to look, including e-beam technology designed to find buried systematic defects in 3D structures. Exensio Aurora, Exensio Test Operations and Exensio Scalable Analytics handle rapid analysis of wide test data and deploy rules and AI workflows at the edge. A Python-first, natively parallel compute engine moves analysis from the client to a scalable back end, delivering 20–40x the performance of the same hardware spend through more efficient use of cores. Sapience and Exensio Process Control extend advanced process control, application integration and supply chain orchestration.
According to an interview in The New York Times, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang noted, “Only in the last six months, after 15 years of trying, has AI become useful.” It’s been useful somewhat longer, but the framing raises the right question for semiconductor manufacturing. What does useful mean?
For the semiconductor manufacturing industry, it means combining common-knowledge industry data with company-specific data; efficiently using all available manufacturing data; efficiently managing the compute cost of AI for ongoing analysis; and deploying agents at the manufacturing edge across applications and the supply chain.
Each is harder than it looks.
Large language models already know a great deal about semiconductors. Ask one about wafer maps, parametric test, bins, lots, SPC charts, etch-rate drift or failure mechanisms, and it reasons competently. It selects methods, generates code, interprets results and summarizes unstructured data. Give a general-purpose LLM a yield loss in lots and ask what analysis to run and it will produce a decent first pass, roughly what a junior engineer would propose.
The problem is what comes next. A less experienced engineer runs the analysis, sees a signal they cannot explain, dismisses it as noise and reports that there is nothing in the data. A senior engineer looks at the same chart and sees what is going on because they carry context the model does not. What LLMs miss is company-specific data and IP, the historical baseline, product and process specifics such as recipes, design rules, test flows and bin definitions, large volumes of statistical computation, and validation.
Using available data is its own challenge. Our tools worked through many yield crashes, and the post-mortem almost always finds the data was already there. An engineer cannot know which are relevant until there’s an event. Getting efficient at working with wide datasets is what enables a reaction before the crash.
The most important factor in applying AI to semiconductor manufacturing is accessing and processing complex private company data.
The scale is formidable. Leading fabless and giga-scale foundries hold petabytes of data per site across more than 20 data domains, each with 100 or more file formats. A new 3D-IC can carry 2–10 million test parameters at NPI. Mixed-signal companies that consider their test programs modest, perhaps 10,000 parameters, still accumulate around 200 TB of analytics data. All of them have more products than employees, let alone product and test engineers. At one foundry, the task is analyzing 2–3 trillion sort parameters across roughly 2,000 distinct products every week, with 100,000-plus features per unit.
That’s why PDF Solutions built Exensio Aurora using 30 years of semiconductor manufacturing knowledge for AI context. We have petabytes of manufacturing data managed on isolated customer cloud sites, more than 1,000 test chips taped out for process characterization in the past 15 years, over 660,000 analytics templates and best practices built by customers across those sites. We also have an extensive semiconductor ontology for collecting and aligning data that is never commingled across sites, and neither are the agents that run on it.
Tokens have become the single largest and fastest-growing IT expense. One developer ran out of tokens at 2 p.m. The work left in the day would take five hours by hand. Once the cap was lifted, it took five minutes with tokens, illustrating the value and cost of LLM compute.
Manufacturing has a problem with the cost. Manufacturing analysis is repetitive by design, but running an LLM on every analysis is also expensive in a way that does not improve with scale. Consider the goal of repeatedly analyzing a 100,000-row, 10-column data sample:
| Approach | Tokens | Energy | 
| LLM runs every analysis directly against the data | 30K per analysis | 30 Wh per analysis | 
| LLM creates the analytical workflow once | 20K, once | 20 Wh, once | 
| Stored workflow runs on each new data sample | — | 0.02 Wh per run | 
The repeated run costs of the LLM-created workflow are roughly a thousandth of the energy of a complete LLM approach. For repeatable analytical tasks, LLMs do not provide economies of scale, and the cost of using them for every analysis can be prohibitive.
The conclusion we reached in building Exensio Aurora is that LLMs need a language, and that language is Python expressed as workflows. The approach has four elements:
This architecture also air-gaps customer data from the LLM. Customers can experiment with different models, including ones that do not run on premise, without their data leaving the premises. Captured knowledge can be revisited, which is how hallucinations are prevented. The net result is predictability, repeatability and cost efficiency. An engineer cannot keep track of 10 million parameters. An algorithm can.
Material moves around a great deal. In the world of hybrid packages, all manufacturing is a complex supply chain execution problem. Wafer fabrication, die preparation, wafer bonding, die stacking, TSV and interconnect, advanced packaging, and test and metrology are distinct stages done in a different facility by a different company in a different country.
This is why PDF Solutions acquired secureWISE, the largest secure network connecting fabs and their equipment vendors, deployed in 3nm fabs in and moving exabytes of data between equipment suppliers and factories. Several equipment vendors’ own AI solutions are built on it by collecting data across their installed fleet, drive learning, and push improved algorithms back to the tools.
secureWISE’s differentiation is control. Traffic is double-encrypted and contents of the packets are not shared. The factory team decides what data leaves, when it leaves, what data and algorithms come back in, what virus scanning is applied to anything entering the facility, and keeps a full audit trail of all of it.
The semiconductor industry is an industry of collaboration that’s becoming agentic, raising the bar for how tightly, and how securely the industry is interconnected.
secureWISE was created to let humans collaborate. In practice, most traffic on the network, and most of the revenue associated with it is data moving out and software or algorithms moving back. It is more driven by agents and AI than by people. That balance will keep shifting.
The efficiency pressure will not go away. Data centers need more compute per megawatt. Manufacturers need more insight per token and per core. Supply chains need to move data and algorithms increasingly between agents as securely as they once moved people.
Our architecture ties together energy efficiency, data and compute efficiency, and supply chain efficiency on one platform. In new-product development, manufacturing, and at supply chain partners such as OSATs, the same stack repeats. Exensio Aurora and enterprise applications run on Sapience with apps and agents on top. In the fab and at the OSAT, Cimetrix connects equipment, including eProbe, to manufacturing systems and enterprise data warehouses. secureWISE provides secure edge deployment and control across all of it, enabling data, rules, workflows and agents to move between sites under the control of the people who own the data.

articles.title: Amazon wants SA small businesses to sell more online
articles.text:
Amazon, a global marketplace and logistics company, is looking to attract more South African small businesses to its marketplace as it targets a bigger share of the country’s growing e-commerce market
The Small Business Digital Adoption Report, a new study of 1,400 South African small and medium-sized businesses by World Wide Worx, an independent technology market research firm commissioned by Amazon, found that 86% of respondents generate sales online. Yet only 32% of businesses selling online use major marketplaces, while logistics, delivery and returns remain significant obstacles to growth.
The findings, released on Tuesday, show that South African small businesses have moved beyond getting online. Their bigger challenge is managing the costs, deliveries and customer expectations that come with growth. Amazon is positioning its marketplace and logistics network as a way to help them scale locally and reach international markets.
“We expected to find a market that was still wrestling with the basics of getting online. Instead, we found a market that has moved past that stage and is confronting an entirely different set of challenges,” Arthur Goldstuck, chief executive (CEO) of World Wide Worx, said at the launch on Tuesday.
The research found that 62% of active online sellers identify logistics and delivery as a major challenge, while 46% struggle with returns management. By comparison, only 5% cited connectivity and 12% cited payment systems
Nearly two-thirds of the surveyed businesses have been selling online for at least six years, while 76% have a physical store presence, pointing to a hybrid retail market where digital channels increasingly complement traditional operations.
“The question is no longer whether they can sell online, but how do we get them the right partnerships, networks and tools to help them scale to the next level,” said Suzelle Abe, Amazon South Africa’s head of marketplace.
Abe said marketplaces could help businesses consolidate their online operations while accessing a broader customer base and infrastructure that would otherwise be difficult to build independently.
Through Fulfilment by Amazon (FBA), sellers can send inventory to Amazon’s fulfilment network, where the company handles storage, picking, packing, shipping, customer service and returns. The proposition is designed to free business owners from operational tasks so they can concentrate on their products and customers.
But outsourcing those activities comes at a cost, a particularly important consideration for small businesses already struggling with recurring digital expenses. The report found that 48% of respondents were concerned about ongoing subscription and administration fees, while 41% cited digital transaction fees.
Robert Koen, Amazon’s managing director for sub-Saharan Africa, told TechCabal in a separate interview on Tuesday that businesses should compare the full cost of operating their own e-commerce infrastructure with the fees a marketplace charges.
“Building your own website, buying the books, hiring your own team and having someone manage all those activities are significant costs. Sometimes those costs aren’t factored into the equation,” he said.
Koen said Amazon was currently offering referral fees of around 5%, alongside fulfilment fee promotions to encourage South African businesses to join its marketplace. The rate should not be confused with the total cost of selling, however, as fulfilment and other charges also affect sellers’ margins.
“If you put the two profit-and-loss statements side by side, even after accounting for the fees, it can be a no-brainer for sellers,” he said.
Beyond domestic sales, Amazon sees an opportunity to turn its South African marketplace into a stepping stone for local businesses seeking international customers.
“Once they understand how the South African marketplace works, listing products in the United States, United Kingdom, Brazil, Egypt or other markets is almost identical,” he said.
Amazon operates marketplaces in 23 countries, giving eligible sellers the potential to reach customers beyond South Africa. Koen said this could create additional export income and contribute to economic growth, although international expansion also requires businesses to navigate market-specific regulations, logistics and costs.
The company hopes its fulfilment network, nearly 5,000 pickup points and artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tools, can help businesses manage those demands, building on more than $2.5 billion it has invested in South Africa over the past decade, Koen said.

articles.title: Nvidia and Jensen Huang face class-action lawsuit after affair with alleged Chinese spy wipes $190 billion off company
articles.text:
Sounding off: In what's turning out to be the most costly mistake ever, Nvidia and its CEO are now facing a class-action lawsuit from shareholders after Jensen Huang admitted he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang has confirmed that he was romantically involved with the woman, an admission that has already wiped around $190 billion off Nvidia's market cap.
Huang admitted to the extramarital affair over the weekend following reports that he was targeted by a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen. US intelligence services claim she was acting as a honeypot, tasked with gathering information about American AI chips and influencing the Nvidia chief to push for China to get the company's most advanced processors.
In a letter to employees, Huang apologized to his wife, family, and colleagues, taking responsibility for his actions and promising to cooperate with an investigation.
Rosen Law Firm has now filed a class-action complaint against Nvidia and its CEO in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. It's been brought by individual investor Mark Kistenmacher and "on behalf of all persons similarly situated," covering those who purchased Nvidia stock between October 9 of last year and November 8 of this year.
The suit alleges that Nvidia and Huang deceived investors by making false and misleading statements regarding the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang.
A former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed International, Alice Huang was reportedly monitored by US intelligence agencies after they concluded she had collaborated with Chinese intelligence. US authorities have also been investigating allegations that Megaspeed routed Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China through intermediaries.
 – Pix🔎 (@PixBuilds) November 9, 2026
Soon after The New York Times reported on Huang's contact with Alice Huang late last month, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement that "the interactions Jensen had with Ms. Huang were not unusual or unexpected," adding that "meeting with customers is part of a CEO's job, and Jensen speaks with executives from thousands of customer companies every year."
The suit claims that Rizzo's statement was a deliberate falsehood intended to conceal the personal nature of the pair's relationship. It also cites Jensen Huang's comments in a Bloomberg interview, in which he said Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed were "normal and not unusual."
The plaintiffs argue that the relationship raised national security questions about Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed and that revealing it would have harmed the company's reputation and business prospects. They allege that concealing it led investors to buy shares at artificially inflated prices, only to suffer losses when Huang acknowledged the relationship and the stock dropped.
Other law firms are investigating the matter, so Nvidia could soon be spending some of the billions it's earning from the AI boom on legal fees.
Nvidia shares fell almost 5% following Huang's admission, wiping around $190 billion off its value in a single day. In the past month, its stock price has gone from $228 to $176, a drop of almost 23%.
Jensen's actions could have a bigger impact than lawsuits. With Nvidia's share price dropping and the company facing the prospect of losing its influential leader, some warn this could have set off a chain of events that ultimately pops the AI bubble. Unsurprisingly, the internet is having a field day.

articles.title: New CNCF report: 75% of cloud-native developers ship code with AI. Jonathan Bryce explains why.
articles.text:
New CNCF report: 75% of cloud-native developers ship code with AI. Jonathan Bryce explains why.
Today’s developers are AI-pilled. Cloud native developers even more so. That’s the key takeaway from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation’s (CNCF) latest report on cloud-native developers, released on Tuesday during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City.
The data is clear: As of the third quarter, there were 21.2 million cloud-native developers, or 41% of the total developer population.
And while half of non-cloud-native developers use AI to help code, a full three-quarters of their cloud-native peers use AI to ship code today. (Just under two-thirds of all developers using AI to write code use the technology as a central, or core, part of their workflow, according to the dataset.)
Why are cloud native developers so comfortable using AI? According to the CNCF’s executive director Jonathan Bryce, “they’re looking for an edge, they’re looking for an opportunity to work on the latest things and really push the envelope in their career and in their technology use.”
Ahead of the report’s release, Bryce sat down with The New Stack to chat all things CNCF and developer trends. And we left the conversation with good news: Alongside a growing developer pool — “more folks are making their way into development roles,” in part-time and full-time fashion, Bryce told TNS — the collection of production-ready tools for the cloud-native developer is rapidly expanding.
“More folks are making their way into development roles”
Like many open-source software foundations, the CNCF has a tiered approach to adopting, maturing, and releasing new tools. First, there’s the ‘sandbox,’ where projects “develop the kind of rigorous processes that make an open source project trustworthy and predictable and something that you might integrate into a real system,” according to Bryce.
Next is the incubation stage, followed by graduation. Of some 250 projects under the CNCF, only a handful reach full graduation.
See also: The CNCF is graduating projects faster than ever. AI agents are helping with the due diligence.
But their ranks may swell in the coming years. New in the sandbox at CNCF? KubeRay, Agent Substrate, OpenShell, OpenRL, and others. New to incubation? Meshery, K8GB, and others. And KubeVirt, Karmada, and KubeFlow are graduating.
Lost amidst the sea of project names? Better do your research. “[W]herever you are in the industry, whatever type of organization you are right now, you need to understand open source technologies because that’s going to give your company leverage options,” Bryce argues.
And as we saw from the data we started today with, the number of developers hungry to put the new to work is only getting larger.
Our chat covers the Q3 2026 State of Cloud Native Development report, new and graduating projects, the Kubernetes AI Conformance program, and more. Sit back, hit play, and let’s have some fun!

articles.title: Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake
If you need an observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock workloads, you’re not alone. When you’re running thousands of model invocations a day across multiple accounts, after a request is sent you might be wondering, what happened? You can see the aggregate bill, but you can’t see what happened inside each call.
You might start to ask questions: what prompt was sent, what the model returned, how many tokens it used, which model handled it, and whether the response was any good! If you’re a platform or machine learning (ML) engineer looking after a fleet of Amazon Bedrock workloads across teams, that’s a real problem. You can’t debug a spike, you can’t spot wasteful prompts, and you can’t tell one team’s usage from another’s.
We built something to help: a centralized observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock invocations. In this post, I cover what native data you have and how we designed the lake. I also show how to use it to see your prompts and derive the per-invocation cost. The AWS CloudFormation templates, AWS Lambda code, and SQL queries are all in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository. This post walks through the architecture and deployment steps. The repo has everything you need to deploy it.
What Amazon Bedrock visibility do you have today?
Amazon Bedrock offers model invocation logging, and it’s genuinely powerful. You turn on invocation logs in the settings in each AWS account you are using Bedrock. It delivers a full record of requests and responses to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch.
The data exists, but it’s locked inside individual accounts. What you really want is a single, fast, queryable view of every invocation across your whole organization. That’s what the data lake gives you.
What is the Amazon Bedrock observability data lake?
A centralized Amazon Bedrock invocation log data lake pulls raw model invocation logs from your linked accounts into Amazon CloudWatch. Subscription log filters then forward those records to your central account. The central account processes the data through Amazon Data Firehose, and exposes them through Amazon Athena as one clean table you can query across your organization.
Everything is deployed as Infrastructure as Code using two AWS CloudFormation templates, so you can roll it out repeatably across every account in your organization. This can be found in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository.
What does each Amazon Bedrock invocation log capture?
After we run this solution, you will have a combined set of data across the linked account you deploy to so you can query with Athena. What you get per invocation after the logs are flattened into the processed table:
- The prompt the user or application sent.
- The model response that came back.
- Input and output token counts, so you can measure the true weight of each call.
- The model used, so you can understand utilization of models across teams.
- The stop reason (for example, max_tokens), which tells you when a response was cut off.
- The account and timestamp, so you can attribute and time-slice everything.
- The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, so you can see who sent the prompt.
After every invocation is captured like this, you go from “We used X tokens on Amazon Bedrock” to “Here is exactly what each model calls contained, and how efficient it was.” That’s the visibility platform and ML teams have been missing.
How is the Amazon Bedrock data lake designed?
The data lake moves each invocation through five stages, from the moment Amazon Bedrock writes a log to the point you can query it in Athena.
1. Amazon Bedrock writes an invocation log
Every time an application calls an Amazon Bedrock model, Amazon Bedrock can record what happened: which model, which account, which IAM identity made the call, how many input and output tokens were used, and the prompt and response text. You turn this on once per account with a single API call, pointing Amazon Bedrock at a CloudWatch log group and giving it a role that can write there.
2. CloudWatch forwards the logs to a central account
Each source account gets a subscription filter on its Amazon Bedrock log group. Think of it as a permanent forwarding rule that says “send every new event to this address.” The address is an Amazon CloudWatch Logs destination living in your central account. Source accounts don’t get permissions on the central pipeline. They hand events to the destination, and the central account’s own role takes it from there.
3. A small Lambda tidies each record
CloudWatch doesn’t hand over clean JSON. It bundles events into batches and wraps them compressed and encoded, so what arrives looks like gibberish until you unwrap it. A small Lambda function does three jobs:
- Unwraps the batch back into individual log records.
- Throws out the noise. CloudWatch sends occasional housekeeping messages and plain-English notices like “Permissions are correctly set for Amazon Bedrock logs.” These aren’t invocation data, and letting them through breaks the next stage.
- Flattens one awkward field. The caller’s identity arrives nested one level down. The Lambda lifts it to the top so it’s straightforward to query later.
4. Amazon Data Firehose converts to Parquet and writes to S3
Amazon Data Firehose buffers the records and writes them to an Amazon S3 bucket, converting from JSON to Parquet on the way through. Firehose also files each object under a date path (year=2026/month=08/day=27/).
5. Use Athena to query the data and connect it to cost data
An AWS Glue table tells Athena how to read those files, so you can query the lake with ordinary SQL. You can see which users are using the most tokens, which models are commonly selected, and what people are prompting. If you want, you can also connect this to the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) to get the spend of user prompts by day.
What do you need before you start?
A few things need to be in place before you deploy:
- AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with credentials for each account.
- CloudFormation CAPABILITY_IAM and CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM permissions.
- At least one linked account (the account running your Amazon Bedrock workloads) and one central account to receive the replicated logs (these can be the same account).
- Python 3 with Boto3 (pip install boto3), for the end-to-end test script.
- Cloned repo with all the resources in it.
How do you deploy it?
The order matters here. The central account stack has to exist before the linked account stacks can reference it.
Stage 1: Deploy the central data lake stack
Deploy the central CloudFormation stack first, into the account that will own the pipeline. Note two values from the stack outputs before moving on: the CloudWatch Logs destination ARN (which every source account needs) and the AWS Quick Sight role ARN (needed later if you deploy the dashboard).
Stage 2: Deploy the logging stack in each source account
Deploy the linked account CloudFormation. Repeat this for every account running Amazon Bedrock workloads. The source stack is small and takes a single input: the destination ARN from Stage 1.
Stage 3: Turn on Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging
Deploying the stack doesn’t start the logging. Amazon Bedrock logging is an account-level setting, not a CloudFormation resource. Activate it once per source account, pointing Amazon Bedrock at the log group and the logging role from Stage 2. Turn on CloudWatch delivery only.
Stage 4: Verify data is arriving
Run a test invocation in a source account, wait for Amazon Data Firehose to flush its buffer (roughly a minute, sometimes longer), then confirm Parquet objects have appeared under the data lake’s data/ prefix. Finally, check your S3 bucket to see data.
Stage 5: Create the Athena view and query the data
The central stack saves the view definition as a named Athena query but doesn’t run it. Execute that saved query once to create the flattened view. Run queries in the dedicated Athena workgroup, against either the raw table or the flattened view. The view is straightforward: token counts, cache tokens, stop reason, and prompt/response previews are already flat columns.
How can you see costs of your Amazon Bedrock tokens?
When you want a dollar figure against all of this, join the processed table to your CUR 2.0 data. The join key is the IAM ARN. You can use the following example queries in the Bedrock Data Lake SQL file.
That one join turns the observability lake into cost attribution too: which prompts cost the most, cost per team or account by day, and what your least efficient invocations are actually costing you. It’s a great addition, but the data lake earns its keep well before you get there.
What is tokenomics and why does this data lake matter for it?
Tokenomics, the practice of managing the economics of artificial intelligence (AI) token consumption, was announced as a formal FinOps domain at the 2026 FinOps Foundation conference. It’s built on the same See, Save, Run, and Plan pillars as Cloud Financial Management, but applied to tokens instead of infrastructure. The challenge is that you can’t optimize what you can’t measure. Most organizations today lack the granular data needed to answer basic tokenomics questions: which teams are consuming the most tokens, and which prompts are wasteful. With per-invocation token and cost visibility, teams can match each workload to the model that fits it. That’s exactly what this data lake gives you. With per-invocation visibility into prompts, responses, token counts, models, and IAM identities, you have the foundation to start running a tokenomics practice rather than only tracking an Amazon Bedrock bill.
Create an Amazon Bedrock invocation log dashboard
If you want to visualize your token consumption, we have an AWS Quick Sight dashboard. This shows you the data from the table over time so you can share it with stakeholders in your organization. Using AWS Quick Sight, you can customize the dashboard and add organization metadata such as team information to make it your own. To deploy this, use the cid-cmd deploy CLI command. Full step-by-step deployment instructions are in the repository README, including AWS Quick Sight role configuration and datasource setup.
What can you now do with Amazon Bedrock invocation logs?
With every invocation in one fast, queryable table, you can finally answer questions that used to be a pain:
- Debug and audit invocations – Pull the exact prompt and response for specific calls, in an account, without digging through raw log files.
- Measure token efficiency – Compare input_tokens against output_tokens and model choice across teams to find where you’re burning tokens for no reason.
- Spot prompt engineering opportunities – Find requests where the response was cut off (stop_reason = max_tokens), which is a good sign the prompt or config needs work.
- Review model families – The data shows which model serves each pattern so teams can confirm each model matches its workload.
- Govern usage across teams – Each invocation is tied to an account so you know who’s running what.
Data governance
Because this solution centralizes full prompts and completions from every team into a single Amazon S3 bucket, security and governance are built into the architecture from the start. The bucket is protected by server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), so data is encrypted at rest by default. Access to the bucket and to Amazon Athena query results is controlled through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies. You can scope permissions to the teams and roles that need them. Prompts might contain personally identifiable information (PII), depending on how your users interact with Amazon Bedrock. We recommend reviewing your IAM policies and Amazon S3 bucket policies to confirm that only authorized principals can reach the data.
Clean up
If you wish to delete the resources made, empty the buckets of objects then delete the CloudFormation templates. Be mindful to empty the S3 buckets before deleting and delete the Athena Workgroup by hand.
Summary
You now have a way to turn the raw invocation logs from Amazon Bedrock into a single, fast, org-wide observability layer. Instead of a closed system, you get a clear view of every prompt, response, token count, and model choice across your accounts. When you want it, you also get a direct line to the cost of each one.
As with any system project, don’t try to boil the ocean. Start with one or two linked accounts, get comfortable querying the invocations table, then expand across the org. Your Amazon Bedrock usage is only going to grow, so the sooner you build this visibility, the more straightforward every future debugging, efficiency, and cost conversation gets.
If you have any questions, or want to share how you’re building observability into your own workloads, visit the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository.

articles.title: ¿Qué pasará con las próximas películas y series del 'Universo DC' de James Gunn? Así queda el futuro de la saga tras su salida
articles.text:
Contra todo pronóstico, la fusión de Paramount Skydance y Warner Bros. les ha costado el puesto de presidentes de DC Studios a James Gunn y Peter Safran. Ambos asumieron el trabajo hace 4 años con la firme intención de diseñar un nuevo universo cinematográfico y hacerle justicia a los personajes de la compañía. Pero ahora, con su salida del cargo, la incertidumbre es máxima.
Como parte de su proceso de reestructuración, Paramount informó a finales de la semana pasada a Gunn y Safran de que su trabajo en DC había llegado a su fin. Al menos en lo que a la dirección de la compañía se refiere. Y es que ambos seguirán vinculados (por el momento) a la compañía en el apartado creativo. Porque ya tenemos algunas pistas de lo que sucederá en el futuro del Universo DC.
Por lo pronto, se ha anunciado que Jeremy Latcham, un veterano de Marvel, será el sustituto de James Gunn y Peter Safran como nuevo CEO de DC Studios. Ni la compañía ni él mismo se han pronunciado al respecto de sus planes para los próximos años, pero sí se han dejado caer ciertos detalles muy reveladores.
Así queda el Universo DC tras la salida de James Gunn
De cara a las próximas películas y series del Universo DC hay tres certezas muy concretas. La primera es que se sabe que Superman: Man of Tomorrow, secuela de la película de 2025, sí llegará a los cines en verano de 2027. James Gunn vuelve a ser el director y guionista, y ya se encuentra en el proceso de postproducción tras completar su rodaje. Por tanto, volveremos a ver a David Corenswet como el Hombre de Acero.
Se rumorea también que esta secuela de Superman presentará a la nueva Wonder Woman, presumiblemente interpretada por la actriz Adria Arjona (Andor), favorita de los fans para el papel. Este proyecto, por tanto, está totalmente a salvo dentro del Universo DC de James Gunn y Peter Safran.
La segunda certeza es que la serie The People v. Gorilla Grodd también se estrenará en streaming el año que viene. El curioso proyecto se rodó a lo largo de este año y servirá como una suerte de spin-off de Superman, con Jimmy Olsen y otros reporteros del Daily Planet en un papel central.
La tercera y última certeza sobre el futuro del Universo DC es que The Batman 2, la ansiada secuela protagonizada por Robert Pattinson, también se estrenará en cines en 2028. El proyecto se encuentra en las fases finales de su rodaje. Su director, Matt Reeves, ha tenido que dar un paso a un lado para esta última parte del título por asuntos personales, con Steven Soderbergh tomando las riendas. Pero la segunda entrega del Caballero Oscuro de Pattinson tampoco corre peligro de ser cancelada.
Así eran los planes de James Gunn en el Universo DC
A partir de ahí, todos los demás proyectos del Universo DC de James Gunn y Peter Safran quedan totalmente en el aire. De hecho, según informa PuckNews, la idea de Paramount Skydance sería cancelarlo prácticamente todo y buscar un nuevo camino a seguir. Veremos sin con los mismos personajes y actores ya presentados o si se reinicia de cero todo una vez más.
Según revela The Hollywood Reporter, James Gunn estaba escribiendo ya una tercera película de Superman que completaría su trilogía. Esto daría paso, además, a una película de La Liga de la Justicia. Y es que con Superman, Supergirl, el Linterna Verde John Stewart y Wonder Woman en escena, todo apuntaba hacia un gran crossover más pronto que tarde. Más aún si finalmente salía adelante The Brave and the Bold, la película que presentaría al nuevo Batman y que lleva años de retrasos.
Ahora, sin embargo, todo este escenario para el futuro del Universo DC parece bastante improbable. Jeremy Latcham tiene la sartén por el mango. En su mano está darle continuidad a algunas de estas ideas u optar por paralizarlo todo y empezar de nuevo, poniendo el punto y final a la saga antes de tiempo.

articles.title: Government of Canada signs international declaration on AI safety and security | BetaKit
articles.text:
Canada’s federal government has co-signed a new AI standards pledge with a handful of other countries and major AI developers.
The news: The Government of Canada revealed on Monday that it has backed a fresh international declaration on AI that is geared towards establishing “the necessary foundations for safe adoption.” Leaders from five other countries (Bahrain, Finland, France, Norway, and the Netherlands) and 10 AI companies (including Anthropic, Mistral, OpenAI, and Canadian champion Cohere) have also agreed to the “Paris call for AI safety and security.”
The firms have committed to permitting some independent testing of their models, providing early warnings, and shutting down their systems when things go awry “to prevent cascading systemic risks and to formulate collective responses to emerging threats.”
From the source: “Frontier models transcend national borders in their development, deployment and impact, and their opportunities and risks are therefore inherently global,” the joint statement reads. “We all have a role in protecting our societies while enabling research, innovation and the wider use of AI … No actor, be it a state, a company, or an international organization, can solely manage all these risks.”
The context: Political and industry leaders have become increasingly concerned about the risks associated with AI as rogue agents have attempted, sometimes successfully, to hack other businesses and governments. A decade ago, large language models (LLMs) struggled to string together a sentence; in recent months, AI systems have executed a decade’s worth of progress in mathematics and shown their capacity to complete sophisticated real-world plans over time.
The declaration’s signatories have agreed to disclose frontier model capabilities, limitations, and risks, develop and adhere to common technical standards, and closely monitor and report on these systems to minimize potential harm. Canadian AI leaders like Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio have been calling for measures like this to be implemented.
Final thought: The United States and Chinese governments, as well as other leading AI firms like Google and Meta, have not signed the declaration, which remains open to new endorsements. It is not yet clear how these commitments will be enforced, or the extent to which they will be effective without broader buy-in, especially from the two nations leading the global AI race.

articles.title: Exploited Outlook Zero-Day Among 1,094 Flaws Patched by Microsoft
articles.text:
Microsoft’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates fix 1,094 vulnerabilities across its products, including an Outlook bug that the company says has been exploited.
The zero-day, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, has been classified as a spoofing flaw and stems from Outlook not alerting users before a potentially dangerous action takes place.
Microsoft has assigned it a severity rating of ‘moderate’ and a CVSS score of 6.5. The company’s advisory provides no information about the observed attacks.
For an attack to work, the victim needs to be tricked into opening a malicious file, according to Microsoft.
“An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook. Opening the file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user,” the tech giant said.
The flaw cannot be triggered through the Preview Pane, Microsoft said. It also clarified, “This vulnerability discloses a user’s NTLMv2 hash to the attacker who could use this to authenticate as the user.”
The vulnerability was not publicly disclosed before the fix became available. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Office LTSC 2021, and Office LTSC 2024.
Microsoft’s advisory credits a researcher using the moniker ‘nono’ and Benoît Sevens with the discovery. The acknowledgment for Sevens mentions the use of Anthropic’s Claude AI model.
Windows accounts for 726 of the flaws patched this month, followed by Office with 174. Microsoft also resolved 59 vulnerabilities in SQL Server, 53 in developer tools, 27 in SharePoint Server, 20 in Azure, and nine in Exchange Server.
In addition, the company republished 165 CVEs from third parties, noting that Chrome vulnerabilities are not listed.
Microsoft’s release summary lists critical-severity updates for Windows 10, Windows 11, Windows Server 2016 through 2025, Office, Exchange Server Subscription Edition, Edge, and the Malware Protection Engine. Azure OpenAI and Azure Managed Grafana are also on the list.
The November release is smaller than October’s, when Microsoft patched a record 1,413 vulnerabilities. With the latest round of patches, Microsoft has fixed more than 5,000 vulnerabilities this year.
This month’s updates are also the final ones for the Enterprise and Education editions of Windows 11 version 23H2. Devices running these editions will not receive any further monthly security updates.
Adobe’s latest Patch Tuesday updates fix roughly 110 vulnerabilities across nine products.
