articles.title: Guerra no Irã ajuda a reduzir emissões de carbono, mas há um problema
articles.text:
As emissões globais de dióxido de carbono (CO₂) provenientes da queima de combustíveis fósseis devem cair 0,4% em 2026. À primeira vista, a previsão representa avanço no combate às mudanças climáticas. No entanto, parte importante dessa redução está relacionada a fator preocupante: os impactos da guerra envolvendo o Irã sobre o mercado internacional de petróleo.
A estimativa faz parte de novo levantamento do Global Carbon Project, divulgado nesta terça-feira (10). O estudo aponta mudança em relação à tendência observada entre 2019 e 2025, período em que as emissões globais de CO₂ provenientes de combustíveis fósseis cresceram, em média, 0,8% ao ano.
A expansão da energia solar e eólica contribui para a redução, mas não explica todo o resultado. A alta dos preços do petróleo, provocada pelas consequências do conflito no Oriente Médio, também tem levado empresas e consumidores a diminuir o consumo do combustível.
Guerra no Irã influencia queda nas emissões
- Desde fevereiro de 2026, o conflito envolvendo o Irã tem provocado interrupções no transporte marítimo pelo Estreito de Ormuz, passagem estratégica entre o Golfo Pérsico e o Golfo de Omã. A rota concentra aproximadamente um quinto do petróleo comercializado mundialmente;
- A redução na oferta internacional contribuiu para elevar os preços do combustível. Como consequência, consumidores e empresas passaram a queimar menos petróleo, influenciando diretamente as projeções de emissões para este ano;
- Segundo o levantamento, os Estados Unidos, responsáveis por aproximadamente 13% das emissões globais, devem registrar redução de 1,3%. Na China, maior emissora de CO₂ do planeta, a queda projetada é de 0,9%;
- O avanço das fontes renováveis também aparece nos resultados. O estudo identificou 59 países, incluindo África do Sul, Tailândia, Colômbia e México, que registraram emissões menores em 2025 do que em 2019, mesmo com crescimento econômico;
- Apesar disso, os pesquisadores alertam que uma redução pontual não significa que o mundo tenha atingido o pico de emissões.
Emissões globais ainda podem aumentar por causa do desmatamento
O Global Carbon Budget estima que a queima de combustíveis fósseis produzirá 38,2 bilhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono em 2026.
Mesmo com a perspectiva de redução, a demanda mundial por energia continua crescendo. Fontes renováveis e veículos elétricos atendem a quase dois terços desse aumento, mas ainda não avançam em velocidade suficiente para garantir diminuição contínua das emissões no longo prazo.
Outro problema está na mudança do uso da terra. As emissões associadas a atividades como o desmatamento devem acrescentar aproximadamente 500 milhões de toneladas em comparação com o ano passado.
Com isso, a concentração de CO₂ na atmosfera deve alcançar 427,7 partes por milhão (ppm) em 2026, nível 54% superior ao registrado antes da Revolução Industrial.
Leia mais:
- Ciclones tropicais estão emitindo menos carbono e podem se tornar esponjas de CO₂ até 2035
- Microsoft: emissões de carbono cresceram 25% em 2025, diz relatório
- NASA aprimora satélites e revela registro mais preciso de CO₂ na atmosfera
Queda temporária não significa vitória contra as mudanças climáticas
Ao IFLScience, Glen Peters, professor e pesquisador do Centro de Pesquisa Internacional sobre o Clima CICERO, disse que uma redução nas emissões em apenas um ano não representa um pico definitivo se não for resultado de mudanças estruturais.
O pesquisador destaca que a expansão de painéis solares, turbinas eólicas, baterias e veículos elétricos já ajuda a reduzir as emissões em diversos países. Entretanto, essas transformações ainda não são suficientes para garantir queda global duradoura.
James Renwick, professor de geografia física da Universidade Victoria de Wellington (Nova Zelândia), também avalia que a redução prevista está fortemente relacionada à guerra no Irã. Segundo ele, quando as mudanças no uso da terra são consideradas, as emissões globais totais devem aumentar em 2026.
O cenário lembra outras quedas temporárias registradas ao longo da história, como durante a pandemia de Covid-19, a crise financeira de 2009 e a crise energética da década de 1970.
Em todos esses casos, a diminuição esteve associada a acontecimentos extraordinários, e não necessariamente a uma transformação permanente dos sistemas de energia.
O estudo foi publicado na revista científica Nature Climate Change.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Adobe brings AI agents and new creative tools to Photoshop, Premiere, and Firefly | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Adobe is pouring more AI into its products, including Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, and InDesign, in a major product feature announcement at its MAX event in Miami. The company is also expanding AI capabilities in its creative tool, Firefly, and releasing a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that lets other chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini use Adobe features.
Adobe’s Firefly app is moving into Figma’s territory with a new prototyping tool in private beta called Builder, which lets users create designs to show off ideas. There is also a new tool to create on-brand graphs, along with an image-editing tool that lets you change part of an image without changing other objects.
A new AI-powered video tool in Firefly will allow users to assemble a video from clips and other elements like images and sound effects. The company is making its agent proactive and always on so that it can get more context about work and be present for any action. Adobe is also making it easier for people to take quick action, like removing the background or generating a thumbnail for a video.
The company has already added a ton of AI features across its apps like Photoshop, Express, Premiere, and Illustrator. At the MAX event, Adobe is continuing the trend. Photoshop is getting a new relighting feature and sliders for prompt-based generative styles; Premiere will have a new color grading system for professionals and an object removal feature for video; and Lightroom has a way to correct blinking eyes and a blemish removal tool.
Adobe already offers a lot of third-party models from companies like Google, Runway, ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs, OpenAI, Kling, and ByteDance. One of its newer acquisitions, Topaz Labs, is releasing two image models, called Wonder 4 for upscaling and denoising, and ImageHDR, to turn standard images into HDR.
The company already has ChatGPT and Claude integrations to let users access some of its product functions. Now, Adobe is releasing a local MCP to expose more features of its Creative Cloud apps to users.
Adobe vice president Deepa Subramaniam told TechCrunch that the company is still figuring out what capabilities to expose and will rely on user feedback.
“We are still figuring out where and when and how to draw the line. What we’re putting out there is a number of endpoints and capabilities across Illustrator, Photoshop, After Effects, and Premiere. We’re just going to see how people use it, what they’re trying to do, and keep showing more. We don’t have any need or desire to sort of limit what the MCP endpoint can expose. What we really want to do is to support that creative workflow, how you choose to do it,” said Subramaniam.
Last month, Adobe rival Figma co-founder Dylan Field said at an event in India that MCP is not a perfect standard and benefits frontier labs more.

articles.title: Starlink Mini 2 adds a swappable battery
articles.text:
SpaceX announced a new version of its all-in-one satellite internet terminal that integrates a dish, Wi-Fi router, and now a battery into a single device about the size of a laptop. According to some users on X who shared screenshots of invitations to order Starlink Mini 2, the dish is priced at $999, which includes a full year of Roam Unlimited service that SpaceX values at $2,100.
Starlink Mini 2 adds a swappable battery
The all-in-one satellite dish can now operate for over four hours without an external power source.
The Starlink Mini 2 will run for up to 4.5 hours on a full charge, SpaceX claims, but that can be expanded by hot-swapping in additional batteries that will be sold separately, or by connecting the dish to a 60W power source over USB-C.
Despite the addition of an integrated battery, the Starlink Mini 2 dish is thinner than the original Mini. SpaceX has managed to slim it down to 23.1mm thick, while the previous version of the Mini was 38.5mm. The Starlink Mini 2 is slightly heavier at around 3.5 pounds as a result of the added battery weight, but carries forward an IP67 dust- and waterproof rating so it’s still safe to use outdoors.
Preorders are now open “by invitation for select US customers,” according to the Starlink website, but “coming soon” to more customers and countries.

articles.title: Google Gemini can now transform your handwritten notes into professional-looking PDFs — and it's one of those AI features that could actually make your life easier and that I'll use all the time
articles.text:
I tried Gemini's new feature that turns handwritten notes into polished PDFs — and it's made me rethink how useful AI can be for everyday tasks
From scribbled notes to a neatly formatted document
My handwriting has never been particularly well suited to the digital age. It's perfectly readable to me, at least most of the time, but turning a page of hurried notes into something I'd actually want to share usually involves typing everything out again. Google's latest Gemini upgrade promises to eliminate much of that work, offering to create and edit documents, PDFs, spreadsheets, and more directly inside Gemini.
You can generate a file from a prompt and refine it without repeatedly downloading new versions. Any Gemini user can try it out. Just upload a file to Gemini and ask Gemini to transform it into a document.
You can preview it directly in the conversation, expand it to make manual edits, or highlight a particular section and ask the AI to change it. That means a minor correction no longer has to become a lengthy conversation with multiple regenerations of entire documents.
Sandwich history
For my experiment, I started by taking handwritten notes during a short presentation about the history of sandwiches. The page covered the ancient origins of putting food on bread, the famous story of the fourth Earl of Sandwich, and the role of industrialization in making sandwiches a familiar convenience. It also included the introduction of sliced bread in 1928, a development that presumably made life easier for everyone except people who preferred cutting their own.
The notes were recognizable as the product of someone trying to write faster than the speaker was talking. I photographed the page and uploaded the image to Gemini, asking it to turn the notes into a neat, readable PDF.
Most importantly, the content largely survived the transformation. Gemini retained the story of John Montagu supposedly ordering meat between bread during a card game in 1762, along with the explanation that sandwiches became popular because they were inexpensive and convenient. It also preserved the important distinction that the gambling story is probably exaggerated, rather than presenting the legend as unquestionable historical fact.
It's easy to see the applications for students, who could photograph handwritten lecture notes and produce a study guide, or a meeting attendee who could turn a page of hurried observations into a document others will understand. You'd still need to check that Gemini has interpreted everything correctly, but it removes much of the tedious retyping that would ordinarily follow.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Revamping the doc
The PDF came out alright, but I wanted to see how the editing performed. I asked Gemini to move the line about medieval stale bread to its own section and add some more detail to go with it, but asked Gemini to otherwise keep it the same.
It did pretty well except for deciding to add visible citation markers that didn't actually cite anything. The document was based on my own notes, but Gemini seemed to think it needed more documentation. That could be fixed in a follow-up, but it was a flaw nonetheless.
The second version also simplified some of the original wording. The explanation of industrialization became shorter, while the detail about sliced bread was reduced to a brief mention of 1928. None of those changes ruined the document, but they showed how asking AI to improve something can sometimes cause you to lose details you wanted to keep.
For ordinary users, that ability to keep refining a file within the same conversation is arguably more valuable than generating an impressive first draft. The feature won't eliminate the need to proofread, especially when Gemini interprets handwriting or adds information beyond the original material. It can misunderstand a phrase or introduce unsupported details, and a polished layout can make those mistakes easier to overlook. But combining document creation and editing makes the process feel much more complete. Neat and efficient, much like the dream of the Earl himself.

articles.title: Orbiting ESA satellite plays Doom after receiving voice commands from amateur radio operators on Earth — 27 MB AI speech model executes the game on the seventh attempt
articles.text:
Orbiting ESA satellite plays Doom after receiving voice commands from amateur radio operators on Earth — 27 MB AI speech model executes the game on the seventh attempt
An Oslo rooftop, about 80 watts, and a hand-aimed antenna were enough to reach orbit.
An Oslo radio amateur group, working with Tanagra Space, got a European Space Agency satellite to recognize and launch the 1993 game Doom after catching the word in a voice command sent over the 23 cm band. It took seven attempts, shared with a group in Poland, and the command finally got through on the last two, on the same day in late July. The satellite “understood its assignment,” with the help of a matcher after the 27 MB onboard speech model transcribed the audio, returning a postcard with details of the launch.
The satellite, named OPS-SAT PRETTY and flying under the ESA’s OPS-SAT Space Lab program for outside experiments, ran the game in an experiment punningly called PRETTY DOOMed. Doom ran on a different satellite, the OPS-SAT-1, in 2023, but this time is different, as the game was launched with a voice command.
The radio club sending the command in question is LA4O, of the Norwegian Radio Relay League, hams transmitting as part of the experiment. The club’s signal went over 1296 MHz narrowband FM at about 80 W, indicated, using an Icom IC-9700 radio and a Wimo helix antenna at 15.1 dBi, directed by hand. As for the voice, Run 6, the morning pass, used a looped synthesized voice from a keyer, with three of six captures detecting the command. Run 7, the evening pass, used a live operator at a microphone, with one of five usable captures detecting it.
The live operator’s command was “LIMA ALFA FOUR OSCAR, PRETTY PLAY DOOM DOOM DOOM, PRETTY PLAY DOOM DOOM DOOM.” The call sign is for legal identification.
On board the satellite, the voice is transcribed by a 27 MB quantized English speech-recognition model, picked because it could fit the satellite’s limited computer. The voice was handled by software-defined radio (SDR), which was able to narrow in on the voice and demodulate the source for the speech model. Tuning and demodulating a signal is usually handled by fixed circuits, but using software has the advantage of being mutable with an uploaded update. The voice used this time “was only the test signal,” project lead Georges Labrèche said, and the same setup could handle other things with a new model.
The live-voice transcript caught “AND FAR BRIEFLY PLAYING DOOM STEAM DOOM PRECIPATED” with two exact DOOM matches, although one DOOM is enough. Morning detections passed only on fuzzy tolerance with transcripts such as “PLAY DOON.” The achievement is less on the understood side and more about differentiating a voice and a specific command out of the noise in orbit.
This can be an iffy business, which is one reason it took seven runs, and being able to update proved useful. The spacecraft heard LA4O, but the output was mostly static, because about 170 kHz reached the FM discriminator for a signal of about ±5 kHz. Offline analysis brought a fix: find the peak within ±100 kHz, shift to baseband, low-pass, and decimate before demodulation. It’s effectively like tuning a car radio to a specific station.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Tanagra then reproduced the fix and was able to remove a redundant audio filter. Delivery of the fix took about a week, although the Oslo group’s effort took 59 days and about 7,200 NOK (about $770), pizza included.
Tanagra proposes repeat runs that keep the original data and send it back down to Earth, so the researchers can test the live-voice result properly. Better detection may be possible with larger speech models, too, which the team could test on the ground first. Labrèche says the team has demonstrated “a satellite that can listen to any type of radio signal.” Hopefully, the setup can one day detect “mayday” calls and even radio bursts from space.

articles.title: Google Cloud Spend Caps Reach General Availability with API and Monthly Resets
articles.text:
Google Cloud has made spend caps generally available on Cloud Billing Budgets, letting customers pause new usage of a service in a project once a monthly budget is reached, without deleting resources. The GA release adds an API, estimated live costs that trigger caps within minutes for AI services, and automatic monthly resets, but enforcement remains limited to Gemini API, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions.
A spend cap is a budget with enforcement attached: according to the documentation, when estimated spend on the capped service reaches the target amount, new requests to that service in that project are blocked, in-flight requests run to completion and are charged, persistent resources keep running, and nothing is deleted. Usage covered by committed-use discounts is paused along with pay-as-you-go usage, while Provisioned Throughput for AI models is never halted. Billing administrators and project owners receive alerts at 50, 80, and 100 percent of the cap.
The company changed three things between the July public preview and the GA release:
- Caps can now be created, lifted, and deleted through the existing Cloud Billing Budgets API, which the company suggests wiring into project provisioning, so a new sandbox gets a cap on creation.
- Enforcement for AI services now runs on estimated live costs shown in Cost Reports rather than on settled billing data, which can lag by hours.
- A triggered cap resets automatically at the start of the next month; in preview, the block stayed in place until someone lifted it in the console, an option that remains.
(Source: Google blog post)
The limits are as specific as the features: a cap covers one project and one service for a calendar month, so folders, organizations, labels and multi-service budgets are out of scope, as are reseller accounts and subscription charges such as Gemini Enterprise seats. The estimate that drives enforcement is calculated at list price and excludes credits and discounts. Enforcement is also not instant: the documentation states that "any cost overages are billed as normal" and advises setting the cap "slightly below your absolute limit." Compute Engine, Cloud Storage, and networking are not among the eligible services, which means the cap addresses a runaway model or agent loop and not a forgotten GPU instance.
The narrower scope drew criticism when the preview expanded in October. On a Hacker News thread, one commenter who had asked Google for the capability a year earlier to control AI spend called the result "very crude, not granular like the rich IAM system," noting the four-product, month-only design. Another observed that Cloud Run had been added that morning, so the service list was still growing.
Developer Simon Willison argued in October that pay-by-usage services should default to hard caps, because coding and personal agents make it far easier to spin up code that calls paid APIs, and that "most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill." He cited Google's caps alongside a project-level spend limit in AWS's new account experience, which pauses the whole project and stops its resources when reached, preserving data for 90 days, and which AWS is rolling out to a limited number of customers. Azure's spending limit remains confined to free accounts and credit-based subscriptions; Microsoft states it isn't available for subscriptions with commitment plans or with pay-as-you-go pricing.
Spend caps pair with early anomalies, a daily baseline model that flags directional cost variances per service and names the top SKUs behind a spike, which Google positions as the detection half of the same control loop. Both are configured from the Budgets and Alerts page in the Billing console or through the Budgets API.

articles.title: Neha Nagar wants to help people take control of their financial future through her debut book
articles.text:
Neha Nagar wants to help people take control of their financial future through her debut book
'Simple Money Serious Wealth', which sold over 3,000 copies on launch day, is another feather in the cap of this popular finance educator and content creator.
Finance educator and content creator Neha Nagar recently launched her debut book Simple Money Serious Wealth: How to Turn Ordinary Income into Extraordinary Net Worth.
Neha, who has been in the finance field for over a decade and in content creation for about seven years, decided to don the role of an author when she realised that, while people in India know more about money today than earlier, they aren’t necessarily good at managing it.
“Almost everyone has watched a video on SIPs, insurance or tax-saving. They have information, but they don't have a structure. People start investing with excitement, but when markets fall or an unexpected expense comes up, they stop. Often, it's because they never had a plan behind that investment,” Neha tells YourStory.
While a social media platform helps disseminate information, it has its structural limitations. A book, on the other hand, gives the author the space to explain an entire concept elaborately.
“We wanted to help people build their own financial plan, choose products that actually suit their lives, and understand how to structure their money better. For me, social media can introduce people to money. But this book is about teaching them how to manage it,” says the New Delhi-based author.
Her debut book Simple Money Serious Wealth was published on October 24. It sold over 3,000 copies in the first 24 hours, according to a post on the author's Instagram account.
“At a bookstore in the city, we saw people in the 60–70 years age group picking up the book. Some were buying it for themselves, while others wanted it for their children and grandchildren. We also saw students, young professionals, working women, and parents,” she says.
Educating a nation of billions
While embarking upon the book project, Neha thought that having explained finance through videos for seven years, writing a book would be a piece of cake. But she soon realised that was not the case.
“A book has to work even when the author isn’t around. In my videos, if someone doesn't understand something, they can leave a comment and I can respond. But when someone is reading a book alone, every step has to be clear,” says Neha, who was recognised by Hurun India as India's most-followed female personal finance influencer in 2025.
The creator-turned-author believes India is still far away from reaching financial literacy. There are many reasons for this, she says.
One, our education system never teaches students how to manage salary, calculate insurance requirements, save taxes, or plan for retirement.
The second reason is that money isn’t discussed openly in many Indian households. “So, one goes from never being made aware of finance to suddenly stumbling upon an information overload on social media. That transition makes it very hard for people to identify needful information from noise,” she elaborates.
The ultimate reason is fear, says Neha. Many Indians still associate the stock market with gambling. Due to this notion, they do not make attempts to understand different investment options, and a lot of money remains in savings accounts without a clear purpose.
“My goal with Simple Money Serious Wealth is to help people understand their own money, make informed decisions, and take control of their financial future. Because financial independence isn’t just about how much you earn; it’s about how confidently you can manage what you earn,” she says.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: Facebook, Instagram, Threads : Meta déploie la vérification d’âge par IA dans le monde entier
articles.text:
Depuis plusieurs années, face aux nombreuses critiques dont elle a été la cible, Meta a mis en place plusieurs mesures de sécurité pour protéger les plus jeunes utilisateurs de ses plates-formes. Pour s’assurer que les moins de 13 ans, qui ne sont officiellement pas autorisés à utiliser ses services, Meta a mis en place il y a quelques mois un nouveau système de vérification d’âge par reconnaissance faciale.
Déployée à l’origine uniquement aux États-Unis et en Europe pour Facebook et Instagram, la vérification d’âge par l’IA est sur le point d’être déployée à l’échelle mondiale sur les différents réseaux sociaux de l’entreprise, Threads inclus.
Avec cette initiative, Meta espère protéger ses utilisateurs les plus jeunes ayant contourné les restrictions de ses services en indiquant une fausse date de naissance.
Les plus jeunes automatiquement basculés sur des « comptes ados »
Concrètement, le système mis en place par Meta doit permettre d’identifier les mineurs qui ont renseigné une fausse date de naissance pour prouver faussement leur majorité et donc accéder à un compte sans restriction. Pour estimer l’âge des utilisateurs, l’IA de Meta (et de son partenaire ConnectSafety) n’utilise pas la reconnaissance faciale pour identifier directement les utilisateurs, mais simplement pour effectuer une analyse visuelle visant à estimer l’âge.
Le système s’appuie par ailleurs sur le contenu des profils, les biographies, publications, commentaires et légendes publiées par les utilisateurs pour identifier leur âge, notamment en repérant d’éventuelles mentions d’anniversaire.
Dans le cas où l’IA de Meta qu’un utilisateur entre 13 et 17 ans utilise un compte adulte sans restriction, celui-ci sera basculé automatiquement sur un compte ado. Ces comptes disposent de limitations strictes, notamment sur qui peut les contacter. Meta applique par ailleurs un filtrage plus strict sur les comptes ados pour bloquer les contenues inadaptés ou appliquer une limite de temps d’écran. Pour les profils détectés comme provenant d’utilisateurs de moins de 13 ans, le compte sera tout simplement désactivé.
Meta souhaite une limite appliquée dès les app stores
Dans les pays où l’accès aux réseaux sociaux est limité pour les plus jeunes, comme c’est le cas en Australie où ils sont interdits aux moins de 16 ans, Meta s’appuie sur le signale de tranche d’âge fourni par iOS sur les iPhone ayant été configurés avec un contrôle parental. Pour Meta, un système de vérification d’âge centralisé au niveau des app stores serait plus efficace et préserverait mieux la vie privée des utilisateurs par rapport à un système de vérification isolé mis en place individuellement sur chaque application.

articles.title: Vous vous garez, le robot fait le reste : BYD réinvente la recharge électrique avec cette borne autonome
articles.text:
BYD dévoile un bras robotisé qui branche lui-même votre voiture électrique à une borne de recharge
BYD vient de dévoiler un bras robotisé capable de brancher automatiquement une voiture électrique à une borne de recharge envoyant jusqu’à 1000 kW.
Tout comme pour faire le plein, recharger une voiture électrique nécessite habituellement de sortir du véhicule pour le raccorder à une borne. BYD a donc décidé d’éliminer cette contrainte en optant pour un bras robotisé, présenté en grande pompe lors d’un récent événement médiatique organisé aux Émirats arabes unis. Bonus pour la route : cette technologie est couplée à la puissance de recharge ultrarapide du constructeur, atteignant les 1000 kW.
Bras robotisé de BYD : l'automatisation totale de la recharge
Pour réussir à brancher son câble à une voiture électrique, ce bras articulé s’appuie sur des caméras de reconnaissance visuelle, chargées de localiser la prise, ainsi que sur des capteurs à retour de force qui mesurent la pression exercée.
Une fois le véhicule immobile, le dispositif ouvre la trappe, insère le connecteur, puis le retire et referme le tout en fin de session. À noter que ce système prend déjà en charge plusieurs standards de prises internationaux. Le constructeur chinois va même plus loin avec une fonction de stationnement et de recharge en un clic. Le conducteur peut descendre de son véhicule et le laisser rejoindre seul l’emplacement avant que l’automate ne prenne le relais.
Côté performances, l’installation a atteint une puissance de 1000 kW lors de la démonstration sur un Yangwang U8, le modèle haut de gamme de BYD (alors que son successeur a récemment fait le show). La station combine des panneaux photovoltaïques et batteries de stockage stationnaires pour délivrer de très fortes puissances ponctuelles, tout en pouvant fonctionner indépendamment du réseau électrique dans des zones isolées.
Stations Flash Charging : un déploiement massif prévu d'ici 2027
En attendant, BYD prévoit d'installer en Chine 20 000 stations Flash Charging allant jusqu’à 1500 kW, et 100 en Europe d’ici la fin 2026, avec pour objectif d’atteindre 3000 unités européennes fin 2027. Quant à la version équipée d’un bras robotisé, aucune date de sortie n’a pour le moment été communiquée. Il s’agit donc avant tout d’une vitrine technologique, prouvant que la marque s'inscrit dans la tendance actuelle de la robotique.

articles.title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
articles.text:
A Ukrainian soldier holds a tangle of fiber optic cable from the Russian FPV (First-Person View) drone that struck her vehicle on July 19, 2026 in Kramatorsk, Ukraine.
Credit:
Scott Peterson/Getty Images
A Ukrainian soldier holds a tangle of fiber optic cable from the Russian FPV (First-Person View) drone that struck her vehicle on July 19, 2026 in Kramatorsk, Ukraine.
Credit:
Scott Peterson/Getty Images
Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting.
Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones.
Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider.
Ukraine and Russia have been producing an estimated 50,000 fiber-optic drones per month in recent years. That’s a lot of optical fiber that has effectively become a one-time battlefield consumable.
But China’s economic and security ties with Russia have enabled Russia to import significantly larger amounts of fiber-optic cable than Ukraine—at least according to China’s official customs data. For example, Russia imported 328,000 miles of fiber-optic cable from China in August 2025 alone, compared to Ukraine getting just 72 miles of cable from Chinese companies, according to The Washington Post.
To get a better sense of how drone warfare has increased demand for optical fiber technology, Russia alone bought more than 37 million miles (60 million kilometers) of fiber-optic cable in 2025, according to The Insider and Russian business publication Vedomosti. That means Russia’s purchases amounted to more than 10 percent of all fiber produced worldwide last year, when it had previously never accounted for more than 1 percent of global demand.
The global AI boom and ongoing data center buildout have also strained optical fiber supply, with an expected worldwide shortfall of 111 million miles (180 million kilometers) in 2026, according to the market research firm TrendForce. That has further increased the cost of optical fiber purchased by Russia and Ukraine, including the bend-insensitive fiber that is especially coveted for fiber-optic drones.
One Ukrainian drone manufacturer navigating these supply-chain challenges is BlueBird Tech, which produces fiber-optic drones along with other military drones, a ground robot, drone detection systems, and electronic warfare systems. Ars reached out to BlueBird Tech to learn more.
The following Q&A represents written responses from Oleksiy, a BlueBird Tech R&D representative, after an initial conversation with Ars. The responses have been lightly edited for clarity. Oleksiy is only being identified by first name for security reasons.
The Zhakh series of FPV quadcopter drones made by the Ukrainian company BlueBird Tech can unspool fiber-optic cable to maintain communications with human operators.
Credit:
BlueBird Tech
The Zhakh series of FPV quadcopter drones made by the Ukrainian company BlueBird Tech can unspool fiber-optic cable to maintain communications with human operators.
Credit:
BlueBird Tech
Ars Technica: How has the use of fiber-optic drones by Ukraine and Russia evolved, and where does the technology stand today?
Oleksiy: Fiber-optic drones are a specific type of drone used for particular operations. One of their main characteristics is that they do not produce the same radio-frequency (RF) emissions as conventional RF-controlled FPV drones. That means conventional RF detectors cannot detect them in the same way, and electronic warfare systems cannot disrupt their control link in the same way either.
At the same time, fiber-optic drones have their own operational limitations. A pilot who is experienced with a conventional RF-controlled FPV drone cannot necessarily switch immediately to a fiber-optic drone. It requires specific skills, and fiber-optic drones have different flight characteristics.
So there are significant advantages, particularly when operating in an electronic warfare environment, but there are also limitations in terms of operation, pilot training, and cost.
Because of the high density of electronic intelligence and electronic warfare systems on the battlefield, using conventional radio-controlled FPV drones has become increasingly difficult.
Fiber-optic technology provides a way to operate in these conditions, although it also comes with certain limitations.
So today, both sides are using fiber-optic drones on the battlefield, but radio-controlled drones still make up the larger share overall.
Ars Technica: What are the main disadvantages or limitations of fiber-optic drones?
Oleksiy: One of the biggest limitations today is cost. If we compare fiber-optic prices in 2025 and 2026, we have seen increases of roughly six to 10 times. The most difficult period in terms of prices and shortages was around March. Since then, the situation has stabilized to some extent.
But the underlying issue remains that the material primarily comes from China. That means Ukrainian manufacturers depend on Chinese supply, logistics, availability, and pricing.
There is also broader global demand for fiber-optic material. FPV drones are only one application. Data centers around the world consume large amounts of fiber, and the growth of AI infrastructure is also contributing to demand.
So Ukrainian drone manufacturers are operating within a much larger global market for fiber optic, and that affects both availability and price.
Ars Technica: How are Ukrainian manufacturers adapting to these supply-chain and quality challenges?
Oleksiy: One important change is that many manufacturers are moving the spooling process in-house. Instead of buying a finished fiber-optic spool for an FPV drone, they can buy the fiber in much larger spools and produce the smaller drone spools themselves.
This does not remove the dependence on China for the material itself, but it gives manufacturers more control over the finished product.
Quality is a major reason for doing this. We have seen problems and defects in finished spools supplied from China. By doing the spooling themselves, manufacturers can introduce their own quality-control procedures and achieve a more consistent result.
It can also make the finished spool somewhat cheaper than buying a finished product in China and transporting it to Ukraine.
But quality is the most important factor. If a fiber-optic spool has a defect, you can lose the drone, lose the mission, and lose the target.
Fiber optic is also not the only component in this supply chain. Media converters are another component manufacturers need to source, and China is important for that supply as well.
Ars Technica: So Ukrainian companies are buying large quantities of fiber and producing the FPV spools domestically?
Oleksiy: Yes. A manufacturer can buy a large spool of fiber-optic material and then use that material to produce smaller spools designed for FPV drones.
That also allows the manufacturer to perform its own quality checks during production rather than relying entirely on the quality of a finished imported spool.
Ars Technica: Has this become the standard approach across the Ukrainian industry?
Oleksiy: It depends on the manufacturer and on the size of the company. Larger companies may have the resources to do the spooling themselves. That requires spooling equipment, people who understand the process, testing capabilities, and quality control.
Smaller manufacturers may not have those resources. In those cases, they may buy finished spools from larger Ukrainian manufacturers or from suppliers abroad, including China.
So there is no single model across the industry. It largely depends on the scale and capabilities of each manufacturer.
Ars Technica: Can Ukraine source fiber-optic material from countries other than China?
Oleksiy: You can buy fiber-optic material through suppliers in other countries, but in practice China remains the main source in this market.
There can be intermediaries in other countries, and prices can differ depending on the country and the purchasing route.
But in the end, China remains the main source of the fiber-optic material we are talking about.
Ars Technica: Have Ukrainian companies experienced actual shortages or situations where suppliers were unable or unwilling to fill orders?
Oleksiy: Yes, there have been situations like that. It depends on many factors, including how the material is purchased, which supplier is involved, and the logistics.
There have also been cases where Chinese manufacturers have told Ukrainian buyers that they did not have material available for them because they were from Ukraine.
Russia also has more direct logistics with China, so from a practical supply-chain perspective it has an easier route for sourcing this material.
Ars Technica: Are there other important supply-chain challenges beyond availability and price?
Oleksiy: Yes. Logistics is another important factor. Once the material reaches Ukraine, it still has to pass through customs and then be transported to manufacturers.
Air raid alerts can interrupt this process. Customs operations and other parts of the logistics chain may stop during alerts, which adds time before the material reaches the manufacturer. So companies have to take these delays into account when planning production.
There are also security considerations. I cannot discuss specific cases involving attacks on fiber-optic production because of security restrictions. But manufacturers are potential targets for the enemy, so security measures are extremely important for developers, suppliers, and manufacturers.
Ars Technica: Is the physical transportation route from China to Ukraine also a challenge?
Oleksiy: Yes. The route from China to Ukraine is much longer, and that creates challenges in terms of both time and logistics costs.
So the problem is not only obtaining the material itself. Manufacturers also have to account for the time and expense required to transport it over a long distance.
Ars Technica: How do these price, logistics, and supply-chain challenges affect how a drone manufacturer approaches fiber-optic systems?
Oleksiy: Planning becomes extremely important. You need to plan production and logistics together. If you understand your manufacturing requirements in advance, you can plan your logistics and your next orders accordingly.
Having more of the manufacturing process under your own control is also important.
Quality is another major factor. If the fiber has fewer defects, you can produce more usable FPV spools from one large spool of material. If there are many defects, you ultimately produce fewer usable spools from the same amount of fiber.
So production planning, logistics planning, in-house manufacturing capabilities, material quality, and the skills of the people doing the work are all closely connected.
Ars Technica: Does producing fiber-optic spools require specially trained personnel?
Oleksiy: Yes. We do not have universities that specifically train people to manufacture these FPV fiber-optic spools. So it comes down to training, training, and more training.
When people first learn the process, they naturally make mistakes and create defects. They need practical experience to improve.
Training itself also consumes fiber-optic material because people have to practice the actual manufacturing process.
So developing skilled personnel is another part of scaling production. The goal is to develop the skills required to manufacture consistently high-quality spools with as few defects as possible.
Ars Technica: What makes manufacturing a fiber-optic spool technically difficult?
Oleksiy: You need to understand a lot about the fiber itself, about the spooling process, and about what happens when the fiber unwinds from the spool during operation.
Fiber-optic cable is fragile and can be damaged or broken relatively easily. If something goes wrong during manufacturing or while the fiber is unwinding, you can damage the fiber and lose the connection.
That is why practical experience is so important. You need to practice the manufacturing process, and that can require many kilometers of fiber just for training.
The equipment used for spooling also matters. If you use low-quality equipment or the equipment is not configured properly, you can introduce more defects into the finished spool.
So both the equipment and the people operating it affect the quality of the final product.
Ars Technica: How automated is the spooling process?
Oleksiy: It depends on the type of equipment. Some systems require more manual involvement, while others are more automated.
But even with automated equipment, skilled personnel are still required. Someone has to configure the equipment correctly and understand how the process works. The way the system is set up also affects the quality of the finished product.
So automation does not remove the need for expertise.
Ars Technica: How do manufacturers test the quality of finished fiber-optic spools?
Oleksiy: There are different levels of testing. Every finished spool should be checked to make sure the optical link itself is working properly.
But if you want to ensure consistent production quality, that is not enough. You also need to take a portion of the finished spools from a production batch, install them on actual FPV drones, and fly them under real conditions.
That allows you to test not only the optical connection itself, but also whether the finished spool performs properly during an actual flight.
So every spool should undergo link testing, while some of the finished spools from each production batch should also be tested in real flights. That combination is important if you want to maintain consistent quality in production.
Jeremy Hsu is a reporter exploring a wide range of topics across deep tech and AI. He has previously written for New Scientist, Scientific American, IEEE Spectrum, Wired, Undark Magazine and MIT Tech Review, among many other publications, about topics such as deepfakes, data centers, drones, battery tech, robotics, and GPS jamming. He also has a Master of Arts in Journalism from NYU, and a bachelor's degree from University of Pennsylvania in History and Sociology of Science, with a minor in English.

articles.title: Qué pasó con el experimento de Bukele de convertir a El Salvador en el "país del bitcoin"
articles.text:
En 2021, Nayib Bukele anunció que El Salvador se convertiría en el primer país del mundo en adoptar el bitcoin como moneda de curso legal, una decisión con la que pretendía atraer inversiones, facilitar el envío de dinero desde el extranjero y acercar los servicios financieros a la población. Cinco años después, el panorama es bastante diferente: el dólar vuelve a ser la única moneda de curso legal, utilizar bitcoin es voluntario y la ciudad futurista que iba a construirse junto a un volcán sigue sin existir.
Según recoge BBC Mundo, el Gobierno destinó 150 millones de dólares a un fondo para poner en marcha el proyecto y ofreció 30 dólares a cada ciudadano que descargara Chivo Wallet, su billetera digital. También invirtió otros 50 millones en cajeros y otros gastos, pero la iniciativa nunca terminó de convencer a buena parte de los salvadoreños. De hecho, una encuesta publicada en enero de 2025 reveló que el 91,8% de los consultados no había utilizado bitcoin durante el año anterior.
El Salvador sigue teniendo bitcoin, pero ya no es el proyecto que prometió Bukele
La situación cambió especialmente a finales de 2024, cuando el Gobierno alcanzó un acuerdo de financiación de 1.400 millones de dólares con el Fondo Monetario Internacional (FMI). Una de las condiciones era reducir los riesgos relacionados con la criptomoneda y, apenas un mes después, El Salvador reformó su legislación para eliminar la obligación de aceptarla como medio de pago.
Tampoco se han cumplido otras grandes promesas, como la construcción de Bitcoin City (una ciudad que utilizaría energía volcánica para alimentar la minería de criptomonedas) o la emisión de los llamados bonos volcán. Y aunque el bitcoin iba a facilitar las remesas de los salvadoreños que viven fuera del país, entre enero y abril de 2026 las transferencias mediante billeteras de criptomonedas apenas representaron el 0,7% del dinero recibido desde el extranjero.
Eso sí, el Gobierno no ha renunciado completamente al bitcoin. Según los datos recogidos por BBC Mundo, El Salvador acumulaba cerca de 7.800 bitcoins en octubre de 2026, mientras que la mayoría de Chivo Wallet pasó a manos privadas. El FMI también ha confirmado que no se prevén nuevas adquisiciones más allá de las donaciones documentadas.
El experimento tampoco ha dejado las mismas sensaciones entre sus protagonistas. Mientras algunos economistas consideran que no consiguió los beneficios prometidos, sus defensores destacan que El Salvador fue el primer país en llevar a la práctica una idea que hasta entonces parecía impensable. Lo que sí reconoció el propio Bukele, en una entrevista con Time en 2024, es que la adopción del bitcoin no había alcanzado sus expectativas.

articles.title: Ransomware recovery is now a client retention metric
articles.text:
The ransomware attack is over. Your team has restored the client’s data, brought systems back online and put business operations back on track. From a technical standpoint, the recovery was a success.
But the client still has questions. Why did updates go quiet for two days? What drove the recovery costs up? And where did the 31 hours of emergency labor on the invoice come from?
Recovering from ransomware is only part of the job. Clients also need to know what happened, what recovery involved and what it cost them. When communication falls short or unexpected charges appear, even a technically successful recovery can leave clients questioning the value of their MSP relationship.
The disruption may be behind them, but their doubts can carry into the next renewal conversation.
The trend: Slow, fragmented recovery erodes trust and renewals
Ransomware recovery can take days, even when teams have backups and a response plan in place. According to industry reports, only 16% of affected organizations fully recovered within a day. Over half (55%) recovered within a week. For businesses that depend on their systems to serve customers and generate revenue, every additional day of disruption carries a cost.
The stakes extend to the MSP, too. Kaseya’s 2026 Cybersecurity Outlook report found that 12% of MSPs lost clients following security incidents, with ransomware, account takeover and business email compromise among the main reasons.
When recovery involves delays, fragmented efforts or gaps in communication, clients struggle to understand what is happening and when they can expect normal operations to resume. They may also question unexpected costs or wonder whether their provider has the situation under control.
Clients expect cyberattacks to happen, but they also expect their MSP to respond quickly, coordinate recovery and keep them informed. When those expectations go unmet, a technically successful recovery may still leave clients questioning whether they should renew their contracts.
A successful recovery depends on both the technical response and the client experience. MSPs that set expectations early, communicate consistently and explain costs before they become surprises have a stronger chance of preserving client trust long after the systems come back online.
Resolve Incidents Faster and Keep the Clients You Recover For
Slow, disconnected recovery puts renewals at risk, even when the restore itself goes well.
Download the AI Playbook to see how MSPs use AI to cut resolution times and keep clients confident when it matters most.
Download the Playbook
Where your recovery process breaks down
Most MSPs have skilled people. The trouble starts when those people work across disconnected tools in the middle of a crisis.
Tool sprawl slows everyone down
Backup, monitoring, ticketing and billing live in separate consoles. Your techs spend incident hours piecing together context instead of restoring systems.
Handoffs break
An alert fires in one tool, a ticket opens in another and a restore job runs in a third. Nothing links them, so no one can say what the attack touched or what’s still down.
Billing falls through the cracks
Emergency labor, restore time and after-hours work often go untracked. Someone reconstructs those hours from memory days later. You either lose margin or send an invoice the client doesn’t recognize, and you do it at the worst possible time.
Client updates depend on who’s free
Without a single ticket trail, communication comes down to whoever has a spare minute. Some clients get a call every few hours. Others hear nothing until the work is done.
Each of these problems looks small by itself. Together, they turn a recoverable incident into a trust problem.
5 signs your recovery process is costing you client trust
- Clients chase you for updates. They have to ask what’s happening instead of hearing from your team.
- Your team scrambles across tools. Technicians waste valuable recovery time piecing together information from disconnected systems.
- No one owns the full picture. Handoffs leave gaps in who knows what’s restored, what’s still down and what needs attention.
- Recovery bills come as a surprise. Emergency labor and after-hours work appear on invoices without clear explanations.
- Recovery ends without clear answers. Clients are left unsure what happened, what it cost or what you’ll do to prevent a repeat.
What good recovery looks like for an MSP
Strong recovery runs on one timeline and one source of truth. Everyone on your team sees the same facts, so your client hears the same story no matter who calls. Updates go out on a schedule you set, before the client asks.
When the incident closes, the invoice matches the work, because your team logged the work as it happened.
Track three numbers to see how you’re doing:
- Time to first client update: How long after detection does the client hear from you?
- Time to restore: How long until their critical systems run again?
- Time to invoice: How fast can you send an accurate bill after closing the incident?
If any of these takes too long, you have a process gap that clients will notice. Closing those gaps takes more than working harder during an incident. It takes tools that share data from the start.
The fix: Unifying RMM, PSA and BCDR with Kaseya Trifecta
The 2026 Kaseya Cybersecurity Report found that two factors supported faster incident recovery: well-trained internal IT or security teams (35%) and integrated security and IT management tools (18%).
Kaseya Trifecta puts RMM, PSA and BCDR in one connected platform. The idea is simple. When your monitoring, ticketing and recovery tools share a workflow, your team stops stitching context together and starts fixing the problem.
Here’s how it maps to the breakdowns above:
- Fragmented context: RMM, PSA and BCDR run on one workflow and one data set, so your techs see the full picture in one place.
- Slow handoffs: Recovery events tie directly to tickets and endpoints. You know what’s affected and what’s restored without chasing updates.
- Billing blind spots: Time and labor land in the ticket as the work happens, then flow to billing. Your invoice reflects what your team did.
- Inconsistent updates: One auditable incident record gives every team member the same facts. Your client gets consistent communication, whoever is on shift.
This matches what the report found. Teams that recover quickly pair skilled people with tools that connect. Trifecta gives your people that connection.
Keep the client, not just the data
Surviving the attack is the baseline. Your clients expect it. What they remember is whether recovery felt organized, transparent and fair.
Faster resolution gives you the foundation for all of that. It shortens downtime, makes your updates credible and keeps your invoices accurate. Those benefits help protect renewals long after the incident closes.

articles.title: Oviedo se ha convertido en una ratonera para encontrar a un hombre que ha matado a un policía con una mochila bomba
articles.text:
Lo que partía como un conflicto vecinal ha terminado como una de las mayores desgracias de la región. La Policía Nacional llegó al portal de Rafael Urrusti número 2, en el barrio de Villafría (Oviedo) por un aviso de disparos y se encontró con una mochila entreabierta cuya luz parpadeaba. Pocas horas antes, en ese edificio donde buena parte son viviendas sociales, alguien había disparado contra una joven de 17 años. Hacia las nueve, la mochila estalló.
Claves. El presunto autor es un hombre de 64 años, calvo y con gafas según la descripción difundida para localizarlo. El Español publica sus iniciales, M. F., y El Correo Gallego lo identifica como Manuel F. A., conocido como “El Ruso”, con varios antecedentes penales. Continúa en paradero desconocido, si bien algunos medios anunciaban erróneamente su detención.
Quien sí ha sido puesta a disposición policial es su pareja. El tiroteo contra una joven de 17 años se produjo entre las 7:00 y las 7:30, y la mochila estalló hacia las 9:00. En dicha explosión ha fallecido el subinspector Juan José, de Guías Caninos; un agente del TEDAX está en estado crítico tras perder una pierna. Hemos podido confirmar que la joven está fuera de peligro. Según fuentes policiales, el origen es un conflicto vecinal, y por ahora se descarta el móvil terrorista.
Del tiroteo a la explosión. Como indicábamos, el aviso llegó pasadas las siete de la mañana. EFE sitúa el tiroteo hacia las 7:30. Al llegar, los agentes vieron en el rellano una mochila entreabierta con una luz parpadeante y pidieron la intervención de los TEDAX y de los guías caninos. Vehículos Zeta del Grupo de Atención al Ciudadano de la Policía Nacional se personaron en el lugar.
Según EFE, los especialistas decidieron sacarla a la calle para evitar peligro a los vecinos, y explotó mientras la manipulaban. Entretanto y según El Mundo, los agentes subieron a la vivienda y vieron a la chica que había recibido varios impactos de bala. Su padre intentaba llevarla al hospital. Pidieron ayuda sanitaria.
Las víctimas. El fallecido es Juan José, alias Jota, subinspector de la Unidad Especial de Guías Caninos. La Policía Nacional expresó en redes su consternación por la muerte de su compañero. El agente del TEDAX-NRBQ sufrió la amputación de una pierna y está hospitalizado en el HUCA, en estado crítico. Tal y como ha publicado Policía Nacional en sus redes, también ha fallecido Deny, el pastor alemán de 3 años que trabajaba con la unidad canina.
Presunto autor. La Policía identificó pronto a un hombre de 64 años, calvo y con gafas, y desplegó un dispositivo de búsqueda que bloqueó los accesos a la ciudad. Según EFE, tiene múltiples antecedentes por delincuencia común, y fuentes policiales consideran que ese perfil descartaría una motivación terrorista. En su primera versión, El Mundo hablaba de un solo antecedente por hurto y de que podría ir armado con un arma corta y otra larga, por lo que los investigadores consideraban la huida “de alto riesgo”.
La mujer, Tatiana B. T, está siendo interrogada en el marco de la investigación, que mantiene como uno de sus principales objetivos localizar al sospechoso, que continúa fugado. La principal hipótesis es que fue él quien dejó tirada la mochila al huir. Se presupone que iba a usar el explosivo, elaborado con aluminio y amoníaco, “como venganza”.
Tras la explosión, la Policía Nacional activó en Oviedo lo que elDiario.es describe como una operación "jaula", es decir, el cierre de todos los accesos a la ciudad para cerrarle el paso al sospechoso. En la búsqueda participaron las distintas brigadas operativas de la Jefatura Superior de Policía de Asturias, y se avisó a los taxistas de la ciudad para que informaran si habían llevado durante la mañana a este tipo calvo y vestido con un albornoz de cuadros.
Ahora mismo se ha cancelado la agenda pública en Oviedo, así como la precampaña electoral en Asturias. Se han declarado dos días de luto. Entretanto, la investigación sigue abierta. Actualizaremos según dispongamos de más información.

articles.title: Orange espère que vous utiliserez sa nouvelle « super-app » même si vous n’êtes pas chez Orange
articles.text:
Dans quelques années, la super-app « Orange France » deviendra-t-elle une application couteau suisse utilisée par un grand nombre de Français, abonnés ou non à Orange, pour gérer plusieurs aspects de leur vie numérique ? Orange est ambitieux : l’opérateur vise des millions d’utilisateurs d’ici 2030.
Le 9 novembre, Orange avait vendu la mêche publiant une mise à jour majeure de l’application Orange et Moi sur l’App Store. La marque a officialisé le 10 novembre sa nouvelle stratégie : Orange France, qui remplace l’ancienne application, est une « super-app » qui réunit tous ses services, des mini-applications partenaires et un agrégateur d’intelligence artificielle au même endroit. Deux applications sont lancées en même temps : Orange France et Sosh, qui remplacent Orange et moi et MySosh. Un choix étonnant à l’heure de la fusion des services, mais Orange ne souhaite toujours pas réunir ses deux marques.
Orange dévoile une super-app et va, à terme, débrancher ses autres applications
Le rêve d’Orange est très ambitieux : l’opérateur veut faire de son application un réflexe pour les Français, sur le modèle des super-apps chinoises comme WeChat. Orange a déjà testé cette stratégie en Afrique, l’opérateur pense que ses abonnés français sont susceptibles de trouver un intérêt dans une app qui regroupe tous leurs services. L’application Orange réunit au même endroit :
- L’espace client avec l’accès aux contrats, aux factures, à la consommation et aux équipements.
- La boîte mail Orange, qui est utilisée par des millions de Français.
- La TV d’Orange pour regarder la télé sur mobile, un service que beaucoup d’abonnés n’utiliseraient pas par méconnaissance.
- L’application Orange Cybersecure, avec les bloqueurs d’appels et de SMS ainsi qu’un outil pour détecter le phishing.
- La Maison protégée d’Orange, pour les détenteurs de l’option.
- Un onglet News qui présente l’actualité dans un format proche des réseaux sociaux.
- Un accès au magasin Orange pour acheter des produits high-tech, neufs ou reconditionnés.
- Des services partenaires accessibles sans téléchargement : AlloCiné Mini, Deezer Hits, Playzer Originals, Quizz de Génie et ViaMichelin sont les premiers alliés d’Orange.
Preuve de l’inspiration WeChat, ces mini-applications reposent sur la technologie de Tencent, le géant chinois derrière WeChat. Le principe rappelle les App Clips d’Apple ou les Instant Apps d’Android, mais l’intégration se fait directement dans l’app Orange. L’opérateur ne veut pas créer son propre magasin d’applications : c’est lui qui choisira ses partenaires. Orange indique à Numerama qu’il ne compte pas surcharger son application : le but est d’offrir des services essentiels et demandés par ses abonnés. Il prévoit une grosse mise à jour par mois et compte s’appuyer sur les retours des utilisateurs (et nous avons demandé : une version adaptée à l’iPhone Duo est en développement).
À terme, Orange indique à Numerama que ses autres applications (Mail Orange, TV d’Orange, Orange Téléphone…) seront débranchées au profit d’Orange France. Mais l’opérateur prendra le temps : tous les services ne sont pas encore identiques entre la super-app et les apps dédiées. Orange indique aussi qu’il ne veut pas brusquer les utilisateurs, les applications indépendantes seront encore mises à jour pendant plusieurs mois. On note également que l’app Orange fonctionne sans abonnement Orange : il suffit de créer un compte gratuit. L’opérateur espère que des non-abonnés l’essayeront.
Orange IAs : Orange a-t-il vraiment ses chances dans l’intelligence artificielle ?
Pour attirer des utilisateurs dans sa nouvelle application, Orange mise beaucoup sur l’IA. L’opérateur intègre trois services différents :
- L’assistant de la barre de recherche basé sur le modèle GPT-5.6 d’OpenAI. Il comprend le contexte d’une question sur son offre, ses équipements ou ses factures et oriente vers la bonne page. Il s’agit davantage d’une aide à la navigation que d’un vrai chatbot.
- L’assistant cyber, gratuit pour tous. On lui envoie la capture d’un SMS, d’un QR code, d’un numéro ou d’un lien suspect, et il indique s’il s’agit d’une arnaque.
- Orange IAs : un agrégateur qui donne accès aux modèles d’Anthropic, Google, OpenAI et Mistral et permet de comparer leurs réponses. C’est le premier essai majeur d’Orange en intelligence artificielle, avec une version gratuite et une version payante.
Orange IAs existe en deux versions. Orange IAs Découverte est gratuit pour tous, clients ou non, à condition de créer un compte Orange. Orange IAs Plus coûte 10 euros par mois sans engagement, sans offre d’essai, et reste réservé aux clients Orange et Sosh. Le service donne accès à des modèles plus puissants, à des quotas plus élevés, à une meilleure génération d’images, à l’analyse de documents jusqu’à 20 Mo. Orange vise notamment les débutants avec un accompagnement téléphonique par des spécialistes, par exemple pour apprendre à écrire un prompt.
| Modèle | Orange IAs Découverte (gratuit) | Orange IAs Plus (10 € par mois) | 
|---|---|---|
| Claude Haiku 4.5 | Oui | Oui | 
| Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite | Oui | Oui | 
| GPT-6 Luna | Oui | Oui | 
| Mistral Large 4 | Oui | Oui | 
| Claude Sonnet 5.5 | Non | Oui | 
| Claude Opus 5.5 | Non | Oui | 
| GPT-6.1 Sol | Non | Oui | 
| Gemini 3.5 Flash | Non | Oui | 
Selon l’opérateur, beaucoup de gens ne savent pas choisir entre ChatGPT et Claude. Son service Orange IAs permet de changer d’IA en cours de route, avec un transfert du contexte. Mais il n’y a pas de mémoire globale : Orange IAs n’apprend pas à connaître son utilisateur (on peut juste lui fournir une description commune à toutes les conversations). Orange mise aussi sur des options étonnantes comme un mode éco pour utiliser une IA qui pollue moins (en se basant sur les calculs des grands groupes américains) ou un système qui détecte automatiquement la meilleure IA pour une question.
Orange IAs ne vise pas les utilisateurs quotidiens de ChatGPT, mais ceux qui n’ont jamais touché à l’IA. Orange veut remplacer les recherches sur le web et voit Orange IAs comme un moyen d’attirer du monde dans l’application. À terme, un widget pour accéder plus vite à l’IA est à l’étude. L’opérateur réfléchit aussi à l’hébergement de modèles open source sur ses propres serveurs pour ne pas dépendre des géants américains et de Mistral.
Orange a-t-il vraiment des chances en IA ? Orange a une grosse carte à jouer : le site orange.fr. En septembre 2026, le site a attiré 24,5 millions de visiteurs uniques en France, dont 8,7 millions chaque jour en moyenne, selon Médiamétrie. Si la barre de recherche du portail renvoie vers Orange IAs dans le futur, l’opérateur pourrait grignoter des recherches à Google. Pour l’instant, on doute que son application soit utilisé par les gens qui ont déjà installé ChatGPT ou Claude.
Orange France peut-elle s’imposer comme la super-app de référence en France ? Orange a encore beaucoup de travail pour y parvenir, à commencer par trouver des idées intéressantes pour faire venir les clients des autres opérateurs. L’intégration des systèmes anti-spam, avant réservés à Orange Téléphone, est une première étape pour y parvenir.

articles.title: GoMoWorld : notre avis sur l'eSIM de voyage de Xavier Niel en 2026 — Frandroid
articles.text:
GoMoWorld propose les meilleures offres eSIM de voyage sur le plan du rapport qualité/prix.
Dans la « mafia des eSIM », GoMoWorld provient de l’opérateur irlandais eir, détenu à plus de 70 % par NJJ Boru, une structure contrôlée par Xavier Niel et Iliad. C’est un fournisseur d’eSIM pour voyager qui couvre plus de 200 destinations.
L’application vous permet d’acheter vos forfaits à l’avance et de programmer la date et l’heure d’activation de l’eSIM, pour qu’elle démarre une fois arrivé à destination. Elle a besoin d’une connexion internet pour fonctionner.
Sur Trustpilot, GoMoWorld récolte la note de 3,9 étoiles pour 2000 avis, ce qui est positif. Elle offre notamment en plus de ses plans de datas un service de VPN intégré pour éviter les restrictions géographiques avec la promesse d’une connexion haut débit.
Pour ce test, nous avons utilisé l’eSIM GoMoWorld sur un Samsung Galaxy S24 FE, avec deux forfaits : l’un de 15 Go pour la France et l’autre de 4 Go pour le Royaume-Uni. Les deux plans ont été payés de notre poche.
Qui est GoMoWorld ?
GoMoWorld est un service d’eSIM internationale lancé en février 2023 par l’opérateur irlandais eir. Il couvre aujourd’hui plus de 200 destinations, contre 160 pays à son lancement, et propose aussi des offres groupées par région.
GoMoWorld fonctionne comme un « light MVNO » : la marque s’appuie sur l’infrastructure technique et le cœur de réseau d’eir. Pour ses options de data à l’étranger, elle profite des accords d’itinérance déjà négociés par l’opérateur pour acheter de la data en très gros volumes et à bas prix.
GoMoWorld ne fournit que des données mobiles, sans numéro, ni appels ni SMS. Votre carte SIM habituelle reste active en parallèle : vous restez joignable sur votre numéro pendant le voyage.
Comment installer et activer une eSIM GoMoWorld ?
L’installation de l’eSIM GoMoWorld débute par l’achat d’un premier forfait sur le site officiel. Il faut d’abord choisir le forfait que vous souhaitez acheter. Au moment du paiement, l’opérateur vous demande une adresse e-mail, qui sert à confirmer l’achat et sera liée à votre compte.
Une fois la transaction validée, un mail vous est donc envoyé. Celui-ci vous invite à télécharger l’application GoMoWorld, disponible sur iOS et Android. Il faut ensuite saisir la même adresse e-mail dans l’application pour y voir apparaître le forfait acheté.
Lors de notre premier achat, l’application n’a pourtant pas reconnu notre compte. Il ne nous a donc pas été possible de racheter un plan depuis l’application. Il a fallu réinstaller l’application pour que tout rentre dans l’ordre.
Une fois le plan reconnu, l’installation de l’eSIM est on ne peut plus classique, avec un QR code à scanner. GoMoWorld recommande de ne jamais supprimer l’eSIM de votre téléphone : la même eSIM sert ensuite pour tous vos forfaits, quelle que soit la destination. Vous devrez donc désactiver cette dernière une fois votre plan entier consommé.
Le parcours client est globalement facile à réaliser et somme toute assez classique. Rien à reprocher à GoMoWorld, si ce n’est peut-être le petit bug qui nous a forcés à réinstaller l’application.
Application
L’apport d’une application compagnon est quasiment indispensable sur le marché des eSIM de voyage. En effet, le logiciel est idéal pour vous accompagner dans vos usages. L’application GoMoWorld est disponible à la fois sur iOS et Android. La condition de l’installation est que votre appareil soit compatible eSIM pour en profiter.
Sur la page d’accueil, on retrouve d’abord les plans qui sont actifs et un onglet des plans expirés vous permet de consulter votre historique. Les plans actifs vous donnent la quantité de données utilisées ainsi que le nombre de jours restants. Vous avez aussi les destinations populaires ainsi que la documentation importante.
L’onglet Promo vous donne un code de parrainage, une fois votre adresse e-mail confirmée. Vous pouvez le partager avec vos proches pour obtenir des réductions. En revanche, il faut pour cela accepter les communications marketing de GoMoWorld. Ce choix peut être modifié ensuite, mais c’est une manipulation de plus.
L’onglet Destinations permet d’acheter directement dans l’application un nouveau forfait selon votre lieu de voyage. Vous avez ensuite une FAQ assez complète pour répondre à chacune de vos interrogations. Enfin, la gestion du compte et le service client sont aussi disponibles dans le dernier onglet.
Dans la gestion de votre compte, il est par exemple possible de choisir la langue de l’application (neuf au choix, dont le français) ainsi que la devise de paiement (neuf également, dont l’euro, le dollar et la livre sterling).
Réseau et performances
Comme indiqué plus haut, nous avons utilisé l’eSIM GoMoWorld en France et en Angleterre. Mais GoMoWorld revendique de son côté jusqu’à 200 destinations disponibles sur son catalogue. Là encore rien de révolutionnaire, l’entreprise loue un accès au réseau des opérateurs locaux dans chaque pays.
Sur le territoire français, notre eSIM a donc oscillé entre Orange, Bouygues Telecom, SFR et Free, toujours en 5G. Au Royaume-Uni, nous avons pu profiter des réseaux d’EE, d’O2, de Vodafone UK et de Three UK, en 5G ou en 4G+ selon les endroits. Nous n’avons jamais eu à déplorer une zone blanche ou une absence totale de connexion si ce n’est dans le métro londonien.
Sur notre séjour de deux semaines en Angleterre, le réseau est resté stable. Tous les forfaits GoMoWorld incluent par ailleurs le partage de connexion.
Cerise sur le gâteau, les offres intègrent aussi un VPN européen sans toutefois donner plus de précision à son propos. C’est salutaire, mais l’on aurait aimé encore un peu plus de transparence.
Dans mon domicile, l’écart de performances entre mon propre forfait mobile B&YOU 130 Go 5G et l’eSIM GoMoWorld est assez significatif. Le résultat reste malgré tout surprenant avec un écart de score de presque 10 000 points sur nPerf.
Notre retour d’expérience en Angleterre
Sur nos benchmarks réalisés en Angleterre aussi l’eSIM GoMoWorld a eu de bons résultats. Bien entendu, c’est à l’extérieur au beau milieu de la capitale britannique que nous avons eu les meilleurs résultats. En intérieur, les débits baissent (23 Mb/s en réception, contre 120 Mb/s dehors), mais cela reste largement suffisant. À Winchcombe, dans la campagne des Cotswolds, les résultats sont bons aussi (30 Mb/s en réception), même si notre eSIM récupère principalement de la 4G+.
Petite fausse note dans l’expérience malgré tout, il aura fallu patienter un peu pour activer le plan GoMoWorld. Comme vous le savez, en Eurostar il y a un petit trajet directement en Angleterre. Or pour activer notre plan, il aura fallu attendre d’être à St Pancras pour tout mettre en place.
| Localisation | Réception (Mb/s) | Envoi (Mb/s) | Latence (ms) | Score (nPoints) | Navigation | Vidéo | Connexion | Opérateur / Réseau | 
| Winchcombe | 30,03 | 13,81 | 74 | 46 540 | 65,48 % | 53,29 % | 5G / 4G+ (LTE-A) | GoMoWorld / EE T-Mobile | 
| Londres Extérieur | 120,63 | 33,27 | 63 | 95 767 | 82,58 % | 89,64 % | 4G+ (LTE-A) | GoMoWorld / EE T-Mobile | 
| Londres Intérieur | 23,46 | 10,72 | 60 | 60 655 | 76,72 % | 88,04 % | 5G / 4G+ (LTE-A) | GoMoWorld / EE T-Mobile | 
Notre retour d’expérience en Chine
Notre collègue François a aussi utilisé un forfait GoMoWorld lors d’un voyage professionnel en Chine. Comme pour nous au Royaume-Uni, il a dû patienter un peu après son arrivée pour que le forfait s’active.
L’expérience de François avec son eSIM de voyage a été bonne sans être transcendante. À titre de comparaison, le forfait spécial voyage de chez Sosh a de meilleures performances sur le territoire chinois.
| Forfait | Réception (Mb/s) | Envoi (Mb/s) | Latence (ms) | Score (nPoints) | Navigation | Vidéo | Connexion | Opérateur / Réseau | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GoMoWorld plan Chine | 38,92 | 5,29 | 515 | 30 957 | 12,38 % | 86,51 % | 4G (LTE) | GoMoWorld / China Mobile | 
| GoMoWorld plan Chine | 31,51 | 6,77 | 480 | 43 127 | 57,33 % | 88,77 % | 4G (LTE) | GoMoWorld / China Mobile | 
| Forfait voyage Sosh | 78,28 | 19,96 | 238 | 59 491 | 52,67 % | 82,99 % | 4G (LTE) | Orange F / – | 
Service client
Pour le service client, il faut aussi passer par l’application mobile. Bien entendu, il y a toute la documentation à disposition pour répondre aux problématiques fréquentes.
Sinon, un chatbot est disponible dans la rubrique Réglages vers Nous contacter. Lorsque nous avons eu des soucis pour installer notre eSIM, pas encore validée dans l’application, nous avons contacté le service client. Il nous a répondu dans la demi-heure pour nous aider à régler le problème.
GoMoWorld promet par ailleurs un service client disponible 24 heures sur 24, 7 jours sur 7. Une bonne chose pour les voyageurs à l’étranger qui peuvent ainsi avoir une réponse assez rapidement en cas de désagrément. En revanche, si votre problème est un peu plus complexe et nécessite une intervention humaine, le délai peut être un peu plus long.
L’autre bon point, c’est que votre historique de conversation reste ouvert de nombreux jours après. Vous gardez ainsi une trace des échanges, utile en cas de litige. Une option permet aussi d’envoyer directement un e-mail.
Combien coûte une eSIM GoMoWorld ?
GoMoWorld classe ses offres en deux catégories. Vous avez le choix entre les destinations au cas par cas, ou bien des offres par zones.
Les offres par zones couvrent les îles anglo-normandes, l’Europe, les Antilles françaises, les Antilles néerlandaises, l’Amérique latine, l’Amérique du Nord et l’Asie du Sud-Est.
Les offres de 7 jours, avec une quantité de données réduite, démarrent à 3,99 euros. Les autres forfaits courent jusqu’à 30 jours, avec plus ou moins de données selon vos besoins. GoMoWorld propose aussi un essai gratuit allant jusqu’à 1 Go, sur certaines destinations et uniquement depuis l’application.
Au Royaume-Uni, par exemple, GoMoWorld affiche 4 Go valables sept jours à 3,99 euros, 15 Go sur quinze jours à 10,99 euros et 50 Go sur trente jours à 19,99 euros. Le forfait de 50 Go revient ainsi à 40 centimes le gigaoctet, contre environ un euro le Go pour le petit forfait de 4 Go : plus le volume grimpe, plus GoMoWorld devient intéressant.
Si vous êtes à la recherche de gros volumes de data pour un prix pas trop élevé, GoMoWorld est sans nul doute l’un des meilleurs rapports qualité/prix du marché. En face, Roamance met en avant des offres certes un peu plus variées mais parfois moins intéressantes. Airalo est aussi un peu plus cher tandis qu’Ubigi reste l’un des plus intéressants pour l’étendue de son catalogue.
