articles.title: Effect 4.0 Ships: Dependency-Free Rewrite with 5x Smaller Bundles and Long-Term Support
articles.text:
Effect, the TypeScript framework for building production-grade applications with typed errors, structured concurrency and dependency injection, has released Effect 4.0. Published on 30 September 2026, it is the first stable version of a line that spent eight months in beta and six weeks in release candidate.
Effect 4.0 is a from-scratch rewrite of the fiber runtime, aimed at smaller bundles, lower memory use and higher throughput. The team's own figures put a minimal program using Effect, Stream and Schema at 7.1 kB against 35.6 kB in 3.x, a 5x reduction. The heap used by 50,000 fibers drops from 157.5 MB to 21.8 MB, an 86% cut, and concurrent task throughput moves from 0.71 million to 4.57 million tasks per second, roughly 6.4x. The numbers are medians of nine fresh-process runs on identical source, and as noted by stork.ai, have not been independently reproduced.
Alongside the rewrite, the ecosystem has been consolidated. Core modules from @effect/platform, @effect/rpc and @effect/cluster now live inside the main effect package, every @effect/* package shares a single version, and the core ships with zero runtime dependencies after the final removal of pg (replaced by a native PgProtocol client) and MessagePack.
With 4.0, the team has introduced a long-term support policy. Effect 4.x receives bug fixes until September 2029, or one year after 5.0 ships, whichever is later. Security fixes run until September 2029 or two years after 5.0, again whichever is later.
Stork.ai points out that the 43.9 million weekly downloads cited at launch covers the whole ecosystem across beta and RC tags, while stable Effect 4.0 itself recorded "approximately 150,000 downloads on its first day".
On HackerNews, one commenter has been using the beta for some time and has had a very positive experience:
I’ve been using the beta on three separate projects for quite a while now and it has been totally pain-free. I mostly use the v3x core library (which has expanded to contain other libraries in v4) and Schema so I can’t speak to much outside of those, but I trust they’ve done a great job all around.
I don’t see it mentioned here, but 4 also comes with a much simpler API in some modules. Schema is much better. It’s an exceptional update. I followed many of the video logs on YouTube and was impressed by the team. This is one of my favourite software projects, period. This rebuild is incredibly well done, and I hope a lot of people are willing to try it out and adopt it, especially with the LTS.
The team's own Effect 4.0: The First Week post, published alongside patch releases 4.0.1 and 4.0.2 on 8 October, admitted that several modules intended to ship as unstable went out without a @stability tag, implicitly promising they were stable. The missing tags were added, and every exported API now declares its stability explicitly. The same window moved HTTP, SQL, RPC and AI spans to the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions.
Effect 4.1 followed on 20 October 2026 with new effect/crypto modules covering randomness, hashing and signing, a Glob module backed by FileSystem.glob on Node, Bun and Deno, a streaming Csv module in effect/encoding, and support for RFC 9457 Problem Details in HttpApi.
For teams on 3.x, the v3 to v4 migration guide is the starting point, with the team suggesting coding agents can handle most of the mechanical work. Effect sits in similar territory to ZIO in the Scala world, alongside TypeScript libraries such as Effection 4.0 that target structured concurrency with a deliberately smaller surface.
Effect is an open-source TypeScript framework maintained by Effectful Technologies, providing typed error handling, structured concurrency, dependency injection and observability primitives for both frontend and backend applications.

articles.title: Review: Apple's M6 MacBook Pro is good, but it's missing all the exciting stuff
articles.text:
I’ve written more than once about the weird positioning of Apple’s entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro, which has always occupied an uncomfortable perch between the MacBook Air and the higher-end MacBook Pros. The best versions of this laptop, like last year’s M5 refresh, come with the same basic design and external features of the higher-end MacBook Pros, just with a more modest processor and a lower ceiling for specs like RAM and storage.
The lesser versions stick with older designs or other compromises, reserving Apple’s most updated designs and screen technologies for the more expensive high-end models. Recall the 13-inch M1 and M2 MacBook Pros, which stuck with Apple’s 2016-era MacBook Pro designs for everything, up to and including the now-abandoned Touch Bar. (If you’re someone at Apple maintaining Touch Bar support into the 2030s for the sake of these two laptop models, I’d like to hear from you. Not for a story! I’d just like to know how you are.)
This year’s entry-level MacBook Pro mostly falls into that latter category. It does get an Apple M6 chip, and the M6 is great—rumors suggest the M6 won’t get Pro, Max, or Ultra configurations, so there are some fringe benefits here that you can’t get in the top-tier MacBook Pros. But it uses the same MacBook Pro design Apple has been using since 2021. There’s no touchscreen, no OLED panel, no Dynamic Island, no half-pound weight reduction, no glowing Apple logo on the lid.
In other words, it has very little of what makes the “PROLED XDR” MacBook Pros interesting, despite starting at an objectively very high starting price of $1,999. This is $700 more than the basic M1 MacBook Pro from 2020 and $400 more than the starting price of the M5 MacBook Pro from a year ago (though that model also got a mandatory 1TB storage upgrade and a $400 price hike when Apple raised most of its prices back in June).
That doesn’t mean there’s no constituency for the base-model MacBook Pro, which remains the cheapest way to get a 120 Hz ProMotion display or the anti-glare nano-texture display finish from one of Apple’s laptops. I just wish paying this kind of money was enough to get you Apple’s best technology.

There’s nothing new here compared to the M5 MacBook Pro, but just in case it’s been a few years, let’s run down the basics and go over what makes this laptop different from the MacBook Air.
Though it’s now a few years old, this iteration of the MacBook Pro design still looks and feels good, particularly with a nano-texture display installed. The laptop looks and feels (and is) thicker and heavier than either the 13- or 15-inch MacBook Air, but it also comes with more ports. In addition to the MagSafe port, a pair of Thunderbolt 4 ports, and a headphone jack on the laptop’s left side, you also get a dedicated HDMI port, another Thunderbolt 4 port, and an SD card reader on the right side.
For those who use USB-C chargers, it’s nice to be able to plug the laptop in to charge it from either side. For everyone else, it’s just nice to have more ports and need fewer dongles.
The MacBook Pro keyboard and trackpad are broadly pretty comparable to the Air’s, though if pressed, I’d say the Pro’s feels ever-so-slightly crisper and firmer to type on.

At 14.2 inches, the MacBook Pro’s screen sits between the 13.6- and 15.3-inch MacBook Air, though in practice it feels closer to the 13. And while it’s not OLED, it still comes with some notable upgrades to the Air’s regular old 60 Hz IPS laptop screens. These include a mini LED display panel with local dimming support that helps to improve contrast and lower black levels, a higher resolution than either MacBook Air display, a maximum SDR brightness of 1,000 nits and HDR brightness of up to 1,600 nits, the $150 nano-texture matte display upgrade, and, of course, the 120 Hz ProMotion refresh rate.
This is no longer a cutting-edge screen within Apple’s lineup, but it’s still very nice. It’s the biggest selling point for the basic MacBook Pro—aside from the M6, though the Air will presumably get that chip eventually, as it usually does. More on that in a bit.
But now that Apple is using OLED touchscreens in its flagship laptops, we’ll hopefully see all these models benefit from the gradual technology trickle-down that we generally see in Apple products. Just as the older iPhone eventually inherited OLED panels and ProMotion support from the iPhone Pro, I hope that in the next generation or two, we see OLED/touch come to this baseline MacBook Pro and ProMotion and/or nano-texture displays come to the MacBook Air. At least, I’d like to see those things if Apple can add them without a big price hike.
Performance and power: M6 redux
Apple’s M6 debuted in the new Mac mini a couple of months back, and it performs about the same in the M6 MacBook Pro (and in the M6 iMac) as it did there.
As a recap, the M6 is a fairly major refresh for Apple’s lowest-end chip. Both the M4 and the M5 used a mix of four high-performance CPU cores and six high-efficiency CPU cores (up from four of each in the M1/M2/M3 generations), and a maximum of 10 GPU cores (M2 and M3 also had 10, M1 maxed out at 8). And all Apple Silicon chips up until the M6 shipped with a 16-core Neural Engine NPU.

The M6 gets more CPU cores: two top-performance super cores, four performance cores, and six high-efficiency cores, for a total of 12. The GPU core count also increases to 12. And the Neural Engine is doubled, for a total of 32 NPU cores. RAM will still be the biggest limitation for the kinds of models that run well on an M6, but tasks that do engage the NPU should feel faster.
The RAM configurations on offer haven’t changed: 16GB is still the base, with 24GB and 32GB upgrade options. For the 16GB config, memory bandwidth is locked at 153 GB/s, the same as in the M5, but the 24GB and 32GB versions get a bump to 170 GB/s.
That brings us to our benchmark charts. The MacBook Pro review unit Apple sent ships with 16GB of RAM, down from the 24GB of RAM in the M6 Mac mini. That means the system is working with 90 percent of the memory bandwidth the Mac mini has; in practice, you mostly see this manifest as slightly lower graphics/gaming benchmarks, but they’re usually not enough to move the topline more than a couple of percentage points.
The chip is still a solid upgrade from the M5. Compared to last year’s M5 MacBook Pro, this year’s 16GB version offers around 7 percent and 15 percent better single- and multi-core CPU performance and between 20 and 30 percent better GPU performance, depending on the test.
As usual, Apple’s year-over-year performance upgrades add up when you’re jumping multiple generations at once. Compared to the M3 MacBook Pro, the M6 version offers around 30 percent better single-core CPU performance and between 40 and 60 percent faster multi-core CPU and graphics performance. So if you’re still using an M1 or M2 MacBook Air or Pro, you’re in for a sizable upgrade you should notice in day-to-day use. Compared to an M4 or M5, it will feel faster, but likely not staggeringly so.
As with the Mac mini, the basic MacBook Pro getting an M6-generation chip while the rest of the lineup sticks with the M5 means there are some specific ways in which this cheaper Mac is faster than the more expensive versions. While the M5 Pro’s higher core count definitely swamps the M6 for multi-threaded CPU work, the M6 still delivers Apple’s best single-core CPU performance, as well as the larger Neural Engine.
If and when the MacBook Air gets an M6, the MacBook Pro should still be the faster system, especially for sustained workloads. The MacBook Pro and Mac mini include active cooling fans, while the MacBook Air is fanless—the Airs have historically performed a little worse because they throttle their performance more quickly to keep temperatures in check.
Finally, a word on power usage. When I reviewed the M6 Mac mini, Apple’s built-in powermetrics tool wasn’t working with the M6 yet—it would run, but wouldn’t give any actual numbers. That’s been fixed since then, and the good news is that the power usage numbers are very boring. Under load, the M6 is faster than the M5 while consuming the same amount of power, which means it’s more power-efficient.
Pro-ish
Apple’s M6 MacBook Pro.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
Apple’s M6 MacBook Pro.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
It’s an exciting year for the MacBook Pro! Just not for this MacBook Pro.
That’s to be expected, I suppose, since this MacBook Pro tier didn’t get the 2021-era design updates until the M3 version was released in 2023. I would not be surprised if we were left waiting at least two years for an OLED touchscreen to trickle down to this laptop.
After all, the OLED MacBook Pros haven’t even fully replaced the non-OLED versions of the M5 Pro and M5 Max laptops. I’d expect the next-gen versions of those laptops to bring the OLED touchscreens down to those price points and eliminate the non-OLED versions, and then for the basic MacBook Pro to get the new screens sometime after that. But that’s assuming some kind of normal-ish technology progression, and the times are still anything but normal, mostly thanks to the ongoing RAM and storage shortages.
The long and short of it is that this isn’t a bad laptop, but it is an awkwardly positioned one. This is always true, but this year more than usual. This laptop’s target buyer is “someone who is OK with MacBook Air-ish performance, but with more ports and the best-possible screen,” and the M6 version no longer gets Apple’s best-possible screen. Especially if you don’t need the now-mandatory 1TB storage allotment, it’s hard to look at the 13- or 15-inch MacBook Air, then look at this, and determine that you’re getting $500 to $700 worth of upgrades.
The good
Excellent screen, keyboard, and trackpad
M6 is more than fast enough for most consumer and many professional workloads, memory-hungry local AI models notwithstanding
Having more ports than the MacBook Air is genuinely handy, especially if you plan to use this docked at a desk
The bad
Comes with 1TB of base storage whether you need it or not, which helps boost the starting price to $1,999, $400 more than last year’s M5 model launch price
Thicker and heavier than the redesigned OLED model
Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue.

articles.title: GTA 6 : une très mauvaise nouvelle technique se confirme
articles.text:
La douche est même glacée pour GTA 6. Le jeu tournera exclusivement à 30 images par seconde, même sur les machines les plus puissantes.
Rockstar a ouvert ce mardi 10 novembre le préchargement de GTA 6, neuf jours avant sa sortie, prévue le jeudi 19 novembre sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S. Si l’annonce de la disponibilité des fichiers en pré-téléchargement (pour les précommandes numériques comme pour les versions physiques à code) va rassurer ceux qui veulent être prêts le jour J, la section consacrée aux performances techniques fait déjà grincer des dents au sein de la communauté.
La mauvaise nouvelle est officielle pour GTA 6
C’était la grande crainte des férus de technique, elle est aujourd’hui gravée dans le marbre : il n’y aura pas de mode Performance à 60 FPS au lancement. Rockstar le confirme sans détour, GTA 6 a été intégralement conçu pour cibler une fréquence d’affichage fixée à 30 images par seconde sur l’ensemble des consoles de cette génération.
Pour justifier cette contrainte technique majeure, le studio met en avant l’ambition démesurée de sa nouvelle création. Selon le communiqué, Rockstar a choisi de pousser la PlayStation 5 et les Xbox Series dans leurs ultimes retranchements afin d’offrir l’État de Leonida le plus vaste, le plus riche et le plus crédible possible. La priorité absolue a été donnée à la densité de la population, à la richesse des environnements et à la fidélité visuelle globale, mais aussi le ray tracing. Quitte à faire l’impasse sur le confort des 60 FPS.
La PS5 Pro limitée elle aussi, malgré le PSSR et le Ray-Tracing
Ceux qui espéraient que la PS5 Pro vienne sauver la mise en débloquant un taux de rafraîchissement supérieur seront déçus. La console haut de gamme de Sony devra elle aussi se contenter d’un gameplay en 30 images par seconde.
Rockstar précise néanmoins que la PS5 Pro bénéficiera d’une qualité d’image supérieure grâce au PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) et à des ombres en ray-tracing exclusives. Sur l’ensemble de la gamme PS5, le titre tirera également parti du retour haptique de la Manette DualSense, de l’audio spatial Tempest 3D et de temps de chargement optimisés.

articles.title: AliExpress ya tiene sus ofertas para el 11/11: presta atención porque algunas son imprescindibles en caso de emergencia
articles.text:
Hace poco más de un año, España entera sufría un apagón general. Durante varias horas no hubo suministro eléctrico. Y es ahí donde uno se da cuenta de lo que es realmente necesario. El ejemplo más claro fue el de las linternas. Muy pocas personas tienen linternas en casa y es algo que debería cambiar. Ahora en AliExpress, y aprovechando las ofertas del 11/11, puedes encontrar todo tipo de linternas con descuentos increíbles.
Pero no sólo eso porque AliExpress ha rebajado todos sus productos durante el periodo de ofertas del 11/11 donde, aunque se celebra a final de mes, ya podemos ir viendo ofertas muy buenas en una amplia selección de productos.
Además, AliExpress celebra el primer aniversario del lanzamiento de Marcas+, ofreciendo productos de tecnología de marcas reconocidas a precios muy ajustados. Life, Sofirn, Wurkkos, 70Mai, Netac, chuwi, frankberg, elitewheels y oukitel tienen ahora un descuento añadido al precio habitualmente bajo que suelen tener. Pero hay muchas más.
Por otro lado, también acaban de lanzar Elite, un programa de fidelización para usuarios donde obtienen recompensas por comprar, con ventajas exclusivas y sin necesidad de pagar una cuota. Además, los miembros del programa Elite tienen un 5% de descuento adicional en millones de productos seleccionados, incluidos los de los canales Choice, Local+ y Marcas+.
Las mejores linternas para tener en casa o para exteriores
Estas linternas son de dos marcas propias de AliExpress, Sofirn, Wurkkos, que se han especializado en todo tipo de alumbrado, tanto para casa como para el exterior. Aquí te dejamos algunas recomendaciones interesantes de linternas.
La primera es la linterna de Bolsillo Sofirn, perfecta para llevar encima todo el día. Por ejemplo si vamos al garaje, no hay suficiente luz y necesitamos buscar algo. Al tener formato llavero, podemos llevarlo en cualquier lugar. Tiene un precio inferior a los 20 euros y te sorprenderá mucho toda la luz que emite.
El segundo producto es Sofirn HS21, una linterna en forma de faro para colocarlo en la cabeza y tener las manos libres. De los productos más cómodos y útiles que hay. Se carga con un cable USB-C y tiene una visibilidad a más de 200 metros. Cuesta menos de 40 euros.
La tercera linterna es la EDC Wurkkos TS28, pequeña pero potentísima. Más de 3.000 lúmenes y con una visibilidad de más de 500 metros. Te sorprenderá todo lo que hace en un tamaño tan pequeño. También se recarga con un cable USB C, es resistente al agua y sirve como herramienta para romper cristales si es necesario. Tiene un precio inferior a los 40 euros.
Por último está la linterna EDC Wurkkos HD02 MINI, también compacta pero mucho más resistente. Sólo pesa 112 gramos (con la batería incluida) y la clave está en su material, aluminio aeroespacial, con resistencia al agua y resistente a caídas de hasta metro y medio. Si el modelo anterior era perfecto para un entorno doméstico, este es el ideal para exteriores. Tiene un precio que ronda los 40 euros.
Los mejores controladores gaming en AliExpress
Da rienda suelta a tu pasión gaming con estos mandos de GameSir. Para que puedas adaptarlo a tu presupuesto, te dejamos tres modelos que parten de los 23 euros. Tienes para empezar el modelo básico, compatible con Nintendo Switch, iPhone, Android, PC o Steam que se queda en 23,99 euros. El segundo modelo es similar, pero ya añade disparadores en la parte trasera. Perfecto para jugadores que necesitan más controles, por ejemplo en shooters. Tiene un precio de 44 euros.
El tercer modelo es el más profesional de todos. Se trata del GameSir G7 Pro y ya te adelanto que con este mando tienes una ventaja con respecto al resto de jugadores. Es compatible con todos los modelos de Xbox, tiene sensores especiales en los triggers y joysticks para que la precisión sea extrema en esa partida clave. Te sorprenderán otros aspectos como la batería de larga duración y la posibilidad de personalizar todos los botones. Tiene un precio de 85 euros pero compensa mucho, sobre todo para jugadores extremos.
Estas han sido sólo algunas de las ofertas que AliExpress ha preparado para su 11/11, pero hay muchísimas más.

articles.title: Software Transparency Is Changing: Allan Friedman on SBOM, AI BOMs and What Comes Next
articles.text:
Modern software is built on layers of dependencies, open source components, third party libraries and increasingly, artificial intelligence models and external data sources. For security teams, understanding exactly what is running inside an application has become less of a compliance exercise and more of an operational necessity.
That is the foundation behind the Software Bill of Materials, or SBOM.
In a recent episode of the SecurityWeek Podcast, host Brian “SchleiF” Schleifer sat down with cybersecurity policy expert Allan Friedman for a wide-ranging discussion about the origins of SBOM, how organizations should actually use the data, the emergence of AI BOMs, vulnerability management, VEX, and where software transparency may be heading next.
Friedman, who helped drive early government and industry work around SBOM, offered perhaps the simplest explanation for why the concept matters.
“Software isn’t written, it’s assembled,” Friedman said. “What’s it assembled out of? More software.”
In practical terms, an SBOM provides a structured representation of the components and dependencies that allow software to function. But Friedman emphasized throughout the conversation that producing an SBOM is not the end goal. The real value comes from what organizations, and their suppliers can do with the information.
SBOM Is About Response, Not Just Inventory
Much of the early SBOM conversation focused on whether vendors could generate the documents and whether customers should require them.
The more important question today may be: What happens after you receive one?
Friedman argues that one of the first indicators of software supply chain maturity is simply knowing that a supplier can generate an accurate SBOM.
That capability becomes critical when organizations face the next Log4j style vulnerability, compromise of a major software package, malicious update, or other widespread supply chain event.
A supplier that understands the components within its products can determine its exposure far more quickly than one forced to reconstruct dependencies during an incident. For customers, the same visibility can dramatically shorten response time.
Instead of spending days or weeks contacting vendors and attempting to determine which systems contain a vulnerable component, security teams can analyze their software inventory and dependencies directly.
The objective, however, should ultimately be deeper integration.
Friedman said SBOM information needs to become another source of enterprise security data, feeding vulnerability management, asset management, procurement and continuous risk management processes rather than existing as a static document stored somewhere for future reference.
That distinction matters because attackers are not limited to vulnerabilities associated with the name of the software vendor.
A smaller vendor’s application may contain an outdated framework, library or open source component with a known weakness. Without component level visibility, an organization may never associate that vulnerability with the commercial product deployed in its environment.
Not Every Vulnerability Creates the Same Risk
More visibility can also create another problem: more alerts.
Finding that a vulnerable component exists inside an application does not necessarily mean the vulnerability is exploitable within that specific implementation.
Friedman highlighted the Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange, or VEX, as an important companion to SBOM. VEX provides a machine processable method for communicating whether a vulnerability actually affects a product.
An application, for example, may contain a vulnerable version of a software library but never use the functionality associated with the vulnerability. VEX can provide the context needed to distinguish between the presence of a vulnerable component and an exploitable condition.
That becomes increasingly important as organizations face what Friedman jokingly described as the “vulnerpocalypse”: an environment in which security teams have far more vulnerability information than they have resources to investigate manually.
The combination of SBOM and VEX creates the possibility of better prioritization rather than simply more data.
AI Makes the Transparency Problem More Complicated
The next evolution is already underway.
As organizations embed machine learning, generative AI and autonomous agents into applications, traditional software inventories may no longer capture everything security teams need to understand.
Friedman described the emergence of the AI BOM as inevitable.
At its core, AI is still software, meaning traditional software components remain relevant. But AI systems introduce additional elements that may need to be documented, including the model itself, the data supporting the model, external data sources and the surrounding infrastructure or “harnesses” used to operate the system.
That creates new questions.
- Where did the model originate?
- What data was used to support it?
- What external data is being introduced at runtime?
- Who owns the model?
- What happens when an agent dynamically creates a tool, executes an action and then disappears?
The last question becomes particularly challenging as AI systems become more dynamic and agentic.
Friedman suggested that the answer may increasingly involve a convergence between traditional BOM concepts, logging, information architecture and third party risk management.
The goal is not necessarily to force every piece of information into an AI BOM. Instead, organizations need enough transparency and supporting evidence to reconstruct what happened, understand dependencies, enforce controls and conduct forensic analysis when necessary.
Transparency Should Favor the Defender
Resistance to SBOM adoption has often centered on concerns about intellectual property and the possibility that providing detailed information about software components could benefit attackers.
Friedman challenged that argument.
Modern reverse engineering capabilities already allow determined attackers to analyze software and identify many of its underlying components. Automated attack frameworks and ransomware operations also frequently do not require an SBOM because they simply test systems against known exploits.
Defenders face a different problem. They need to know where vulnerable components exist across potentially thousands of systems.
“You know who does need visibility into what’s in a piece of software? Blue Team,” Friedman said.
SBOM standards can also support redaction where legitimate proprietary concerns exist, allowing suppliers to disclose the existence of a dependency without necessarily revealing every detail associated with it.
The larger issue, Friedman argued, is determining what information actually needs protection and balancing that concern against the operational value software transparency provides defenders.
From SBOM to an “Omnibomb”
SBOM may ultimately be only one layer of a much larger transparency ecosystem.
AI bills of materials are emerging alongside cryptographic bills of materials designed to identify cryptographic dependencies as organizations prepare for crypto agility and post quantum computing.
Hardware bills of materials can provide similar visibility into physical components such as semiconductors.
Friedman suggested that those different transparency mechanisms could eventually converge into what he jokingly called an “omnibomb.”
Before that happens, however, there is significant work left to do.
Even today’s SBOM ecosystem continues to struggle with interoperability. Two quality SBOM tools analyzing the same software may not necessarily produce identical dependency graphs, making harmonization, minimum requirements and common expectations critical.
Friedman pointed to continuing work among governments, cybersecurity agencies, industry and the open source community to define those expectations and create an ecosystem in which SBOM information can move between suppliers, customers and security tools in a meaningful way.
The ultimate destination is not another compliance document, it is continuous software transparency.
Organizations should be able to understand what their systems depend on, correlate that information with emerging threats and vulnerabilities, determine where actual exposure exists and make risk decisions quickly enough to matter.
Or, as Friedman repeatedly emphasized during the conversation, SBOM is not supposed to solve every cybersecurity problem. It is data. What organizations do with that data is where the security value begins.
Watch or listen to the full SecurityWeek Podcast conversation with Allan Friedman for a deeper discussion on SBOM, AI BOMs, VEX, software supply chain security, continuous monitoring and the future of software transparency.

articles.title: Why an ex-Cohere leader doesn’t want you to call his new law firm “AI-native” | BetaKit
articles.text:
Former Cohere and Blue J leaders have founded a Toronto- and New York City-based law firm to challenge the industry’s costly pay-by-the-hour pricing model.
The news: Blackletter has raised $6 million USD ($8.5 million CAD) in seed funding to hire more lawyers and engineers, the startup announced on Tuesday.
The company was founded by ex-Cohere product and engineering leaders Jonathan Rosenbluth and David Stewart, alongside former Blue J COO Avi Brudner, to build a law firm on top of its proprietary AI legaltech platform. The firm uses an outcome-based, fixed-fee pricing model, claiming it can provide quality legal work faster and cheaper than traditional firms.
From the source: Rosenbluth told BetaKit in a phone call that Blackletter is building tools for its lawyers to work optimally, rather than building tools for other lawyers who are “disincentivized” to use them to their fullest. However, he rejects the notion that Blackletter is an “AI-native law firm.”
“We’re hiring great lawyers; to say that we’re an AI-native law firm feels like it connotes cheap and fast,” Rosenbluth said. “Nobody would describe a law firm that uses Microsoft Word as a Microsoft-native law firm.”
The context: The round was led by New York City-based venture capital firm Lerer Hippeau, with participation from Seven Stars, Maple VC, Garage Capital, and Ripple Ventures. Cohere co-founders Aidan Gomez, Ivan Zhang, and Nick Frosst, as well as TwelveLabs CEO Jae Lee and Adaption CEO Sara Hooker, also participated.
Since emerging from stealth this past June, Rosenbluth said Blackletter has courted 75 clients for its corporate, commercial, financing, merger and acquisition, and employment law services. Some of its clients include TwelveLabs, Fanatics, and Toronto-based Ada, which recently agreed to a $600-million CAD merger deal with US-based Dialpad, though Rosenbluth didn’t comment on whether Blackletter helped with the transaction.
Final thought: Rosenbluth said that Blackletter came together because it was “abundantly clear” to him while he was working at Cohere that AI should be improving legal services, but that he wasn’t feeling that improvement as a client. By building Blackletter on both sides of the border, Rosenbluth said the team thinks the company will ultimately make top-tier legal services more abundant and pressure the rest of the sector to innovate.

articles.title: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anthropic intends to push ahead with its IPO despite shakier markets and the broader pullback from AI investing.
The Claude-maker said in an updated IPO filing on Tuesday that it would be offering a total of 825 million Class A shares at an estimated price range of $70 to $78 per share. The sale is expected to raise anywhere from $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion.
The company could end up being worth a hefty $1.404 trillion if its shares list at the top of the price range, on a fully diluted basis. That would represent a significant jump up from the $965 billion valuation Anthropic reached in a May fundraise, but it’s still lower than the $2 trillion the company was reportedly targeting a couple months ago.
Separately, Anthropic said it had struck a deal to privately sell $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC. Google and Nvidia are investing $10 billion apiece.
All up, Anthropic estimates net proceeds to reach somewhere between $84.6 billion and $93.7 billion (the latter if the IPO underwriters exercise their option to buy additional shares).
Underwriters, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, will have the option to buy up to 123.75 million more shares from Anthropic at the IPO price.
As a public benefit corporation, the founders hold a Class F share with 50.1% of the voting power. The Long-Term Benefit Trust will also elect a board majority, so Class A buyers will have limited influence.
Anthropic intends to start trading on the Nasdaq close to November 19, per reporting from CNBC, under the ticker symbol “ANT.” The company expects up to 20% of the offering to be allocated to retail investors.
Anthropic also gave out a few new details in the updated filing. The company said its run-rate revenue reached $81 billion by the end of October, about $10 billion more than at the end of September.
Also, the filing now lists how many shares the company’s co-founders expect to sell in the IPO: CEO Dario Amodei, president and chairperson Daniela Amodei, chief compute officer Tom Brown, Anthropic Institute head Jack Clark, chief science officer Jared Kaplan, chief architect Sam McCandlish, and interpretability research lead Christopher Olah are all selling nearly 3.4 million shares each. At the $74 midpoint of the IPO price range, that would land them about $250 million each.
The updated filing also has a small but important change that hints at the company’s stance toward the Trump administration: The company at many points uses “super intelligence” and “SI” interchangeably with “artificial intelligence” and “AI,” citing Trump’s executive order from September that directed government departments and agencies to use that new terminology to refer to AI.
The company’s third-quarter revenue came in at $17 billion, and nine-month revenue was $33.2 billion. The company reported a nine-month net loss of $104 billion, with compute and infrastructure commitments hitting $900.9 billion. It has nearly $132 billion in cash and short-term investments.
OpenAI, Anthropic’s biggest rival, was reportedly valued at $1.25 trillion last week after it raised $11 billion, nearly half the $20 billion it had first tried to raise.
Note: This story has been updated with additional details and color from the updated IPO filing.

articles.title: Law firm files class-action lawsuit against Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang confirms affair with alleged Chinese spy — more to come as multiple other law firms investigate securities fraud following stock drop
articles.text:
Law firm files class-action lawsuit against Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang confirms affair with alleged Chinese spy — more to come as multiple other law firms investigate securities fraud following stock drop
Everybody wants a piece of Jensen these days.
The baying of the hounds can be heard at a distance. Yesterday, Nvidia's Jensen Huang confirmed that it was indeed true that he had a romantic affair with Alice Huang (not related to the family), who U.S. intelligence services claim is a Chinese honeypot tasked with facilitating smuggling of the firm's advanced GPUs into China. Now, a class-action lawsuit and investigations have started flying from almost everywhere.
This development is not unexpected, as basic securities law allows shareholders to sue their investees if they misrepresent facts or otherwise perform actions that cause a drop in stock prices. They may have a point, as Nvidia's shares dipped significantly when the confirmation of Jensen's infidelity and the ramifications thereof hit the press everywhere.
The legal proceedings are bound to be numerous, but as of right now, the first class-action lawsuit was filed by the Rosen Law Firm. The suit claims that Nvidia and Jensen Huang failed to disclose or misled investors regarding Jensen's affair with Alice, lied about it when asked, raised national security concerns, and caused a subsequent loss of Nvidia's reputation. You can check out the case docket at PacerMonitor here.
While legal analysis is beyond the scope of this news, Nvidia did downplay Jensen's relationship with Alice, saying that "Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year."
Other legal firms have launched their own investigations into the recent development, with essentially the same justification: Schall, Brown & Schwartz attributes a 5.5% pre-market-trading drop to Nvidia, as does Levi & Korsinsky. The office of Frank R. Cruz mentions an 8.8% figure related to intra-day exchanging, and is interested in shareholders with $50,000 in losses. The percentage-drop figure is 5.88% premarket for Bronstein, Gewritz & Grossman.
Every investigation and suit mentioned here requires no upfront fees from complainants, as with most class-action lawsuits. The underlying condition is often that the law firms involved get a cut of whichever damages or settlements may appear at the end of the lawsuit. Some of them, like the one by Levi & Korsinsky, even aim to relieve investors who've already sold their Nvidia shares and sold them at a loss, with no minimum amount required.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: 'It was super important to Casey Hudson to have something musically memorable for that' — Original Mass Effect composer calls Mass Effect 2's Suicide Mission 'one of the 10 best endings for a video game ever'
articles.text:
Original Mass Effect composer says working on Mass Effect 2's Suicide Mission was one of his 'favorite' memories working at BioWare — 'Probably one of the 10 best endings for a video game ever'
Jack Wall says Mass Effect 2 was a "technically challenging score" due to the branching paths
- Original Mass Effect 1 and 2 composer Jack Wall shares his favorite memories from working on the games at BioWare
- Wall says director Casey Hudson was "so passionate about the story," and they worked together on Mass Effect 2's Suicide Mission
- He considers it "one of the 10 best endings for a video game ever"
Mass Effect 1 and Mass Effect 2 composer Jack Wall has shared his favorite memories from working at BioWare and on the series, and revealed which he considers one of the "best" of all time.
In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, where the original Mass Effect composer also discussed the closure of BioWare, Wall said he last worked at BioWare in 2010 on Mass Effect 2, but has fond memories of beginning his work there alongside the team
"My absolute favorite memory of working with BioWare was flying up to Edmonton to kick off both ME1 and ME2," Wall said. "I really liked the people there. They were so kind to me. [Game director] Casey [Hudson] was always so passionate about the story."
The composer went on to discuss specific missions he recalled making music for, revealing that Mass Effect 2's infamous final quest, Suicide Mission, was one of the first things he and Casey Hudson worked on together.
"Probably to date one of the 10 best endings for a video game ever," Wall said. "It was super important to him to have something musically memorable for that, and so we went back and forth until we got something we could both be proud of."
The editing process for Suicide Mission was much more complicated than any other mission, he explained, and so it ended up being a bigger and more challenging task because of the number of endings associated with the quest.
"Then MUCH later, cutting the ending together (in the very last hours before shipping), that ending, as it branched off this way or that way depending on how you played the game, was very satisfying," Wall added.

articles.title: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker is now available
articles.text:
After years of third-party Android trackers from companies like Samsung, Motorola, and Pebblebee, Google’s Pixel Tag is now available for purchase. First announced in August, the Pixel Tag is designed to work with Google’s tracking network and app that was renamed the Find Hub last year. The Pixel Tag is priced similar to Apple’s AirTag 2. A single tracker costs $29.99 while a four-pack is discounted to $99.99.
Google’s Pixel Tag tracker is now available
The Pixel Tag launches today for $30 each or discounted to $100 for a four-pack.
At 0.4 ounces, the Pixel Tag is slightly lighter than the AirTag 2 and while its oblong design is longer than Apple’s tracker, Google’s is a bit thinner. It doesn’t include a hole to attach it to keys, luggage, or other items you want to track, but you can pair it with accessories that make it easy to tether to objects. Unlike Apple’s AirTags, the Pixel Tag has a button that can be pressed to trigger a sound should your phone get misplaced instead of the tracker.
The Pixel Tag is slightly thinner than Apple’s AirTag but has an oblong shape.
Google says the Pixel Tag will run for over a year on a single CR2032 coin battery, and it has an IP67 rating so it’s dustproof and can survive a shallow dunking. The tracker also features ultra wideband (UWB) support and Channel Sounding through Bluetooth 6.0. Android phones with a UWB chip can display the exact distance and direction to the Pixel Tag in the Find Hub app once you’re close to it, while Bluetooth Channel Sounding is limited to just distance.
The Pixel Tag is compatible with smartphones running Android 9 or later, but you’ll need devices that specifically include a UWB chip or support Bluetooth 6.0 to take advantage of Find Hub’s precise locating features.

articles.title: „Niemand will diese Arbeit machen“: Roboter übernimmt das Putzen deiner Wohnung – was dabei schief geht
articles.text:
Ich habe einen humanoiden Roboter meine Wohnung putzen lassen – was dabei schief ging
Ich gehöre nicht zu den Menschen, die eine Reinigungskraft beschäftigen. Ich bin zu geizig, und irgendwie macht es mir auch Spaß, einen Podcast anzumachen und mich mit einem Wunder-Reinigungsschwamm an meiner Badewanne auszutoben. Aber als ich auf X einen Beitrag über einen neuen Reinigungsdienst mit humanoiden Robotern in San Francisco sah, habe ich mich sofort auf die Warteliste setzen lassen. Ich wollte, dass sich meine Wohnung wie bei der 1960er-Jahre-Cartoonserie „Die Jetsons“ anfühlt, und sei es auch nur für eine Stunde.
Außerdem war ich aus journalistischem Interesse motiviert. Um ein authentisches Erlebnis zu gewährleisten, habe ich Tau Robotics, dem Startup hinter dem X-Beitrag, nicht gesagt, dass ich Journalistin bin – obwohl ich meinen richtigen Namen angegeben habe, sodass es möglich ist, dass jemand mich ausfindig gemacht hat.
Für 30 US-Dollar kommt ein humanoider Roboter in meine Wohnung zum Putzen
Das langfristige Ziel von Tau ist es, autonome Reinigungsroboter Wirklichkeit werden zu lassen. Das vorweg: Ganz so weit sind sie noch nicht. Derzeit werden die Roboter von Menschen ferngesteuert, die über Kameras, die an den Köpfen und Handgelenken der Roboter angebracht sind, beobachten, was vor sich geht. Während die Roboter reinigen, sammeln sie Daten, die Tau nutzen wird, um ihre unabhängigeren Nachfolgemodelle zu trainieren. Jede erfolgreich abgewischte Arbeitsplatte und jedes erfolgreich gefaltete T-Shirt helfen den Modellen, die die Roboter steuern, beim nächsten Durchgang besser zu werden.

articles.title: New-Generation GD32H7 High-Performance MCUs EE Times
articles.text:
Munich, Germany – November 10, 2026 — GigaDevice, a leading semiconductor company specializing in Flash memory, 32-bit microcontrollers (MCUs), sensors, and analog products, officially launches its new-generation GD32H7 MCU portfolio built on a unified chip architecture. Developed from a homologous silicon die with tailored IP configuration, peripheral optimization and scenario-specific tuning, the comprehensive product lineup precisely covers three core industrial application scenarios: industrial HMI human-machine interaction, general industrial automation, and robotic servo joint control. It delivers industrial manufacturers with a high-performance, fully integrated MCU solution featuring unified architecture, clear product classification and exceptional development reusability.
GigaDevice New-Generation GD32H7 High-Performance MCU Portfolio
Universal Core Hardware Features – Building a Unified High-Performance Foundation for Industrial Applications
All MCUs in the GD32H7 family are powered by the high-performance Arm® Cortex®-M7 core, offering dual frequency options of 600 MHz(GD32H77x series) and 750 MHz(GD32H78x series) with a maximum CoreMark® score of 3,736, delivering outstanding computing power and operational efficiency. Equipped with 640 KB CPU-synchronous Tightly Coupled Memory (TCM), the devices support zero-wait instruction and data execution, significantly enhancing operational stability and response speed for complex algorithms, high-frequency tasks and real-time control workloads.
The entire portfolio adopts unified storage specifications, including 2 MB high-speed executable Flash, 8 MB large-capacity storage Flash and 1.2 MB high-speed SRAM. Dual OSPI high-speed interfaces support a 200 MHz clock frequency and double data rate (DTR) mode, enabling flexible expansion of external memory devices to meet the demands of high-definition graphic caching, high-speed data logging and complex program execution. Integrated with a dedicated hardware math acceleration engine that supports trigonometric calculation, FFT and FIR filtering, the series greatly improves processing efficiency for motor control, signal analysis and algorithm computation.
Universal security and functional safety capabilities are implemented across the full product lineup. The GD32H7 family has obtained IEC 61508 SC3 (SIL 2/SIL 3) functional safety certification from TÜV Rheinland, supported MIPI by a complete functional safety development suite including safety manuals, FMEDA reports and dedicated self-test libraries. Integrated hardware security modules feature AES encryption, SHA-256 hash verification, a True Random Number Generator (TRNG) and unique chip UID. Supporting secure boot, authenticated firmware upgrade and anti-rollback mechanisms, the series is designed to help customers address the cybersecurity requirements of the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and mainstream industrial safety compliance standards.
The GD32H7 series integrates extensive industrial-grade peripherals, including multiple U(S)ART, I²C, SPI and I²S interfaces, two 10/100 Mbps Ethernet ports and 3 CAN-FD high-speed buses. Complemented by multi-channel high-precision ADC/DAC, comparators and high-speed digital filters, as well as USB HS/FS and SDIO interfaces, the portfolio fully supports high-speed industrial communication, precise analog acquisition and complex system interconnection. Covering a wide operating voltage range of 1.71 V to 3.6 V and offering multiple configurable low-power modes, the devices balance high-performance operation and power efficiency for diverse industrial operating conditions.
Differentiated Product Positioning for Targeted Industrial Scenarios
GD32H7xR Series (GD32H77R) – Dedicated MCU for Robotic Joint Servo Control
Custom-designed for collaborative robots, humanoid robots and high-precision servo equipment, the GD32H7xR series is optimized for space-constrained, high-reliability and high real-time joint control applications, serving as the core controller for robotic joint modules, miniature servo drives and high-precision CNC devices.
Featuring extreme integration and miniaturization, the single-die MCU integrates an EtherCAT® slave controller and two 100 Mbps Ethernet PHYs, eliminating the need for external PHY components. It achieves a transmission latency below 50 ns and supports the FSoE safety protocol, ensuring high-speed real-time communication and reliable equipment operation. Compatible with mainstream industrial position feedback protocols, the series delivers precise closed-loop control of motor position and speed. Packaged in a compact 9mm×9mm BGA169 form factor, the chip drastically reduces PCB footprint for joint drive boards, perfectly adapting to the limited installation space of robot joints. Optimized for dynamic power consumption and thermal performance, it ensures stable long-term operation in high-temperature and harsh industrial environments.
GD32H7xD Series (GD32H78D/77D) – High-End Dedicated MCU for Industrial HMI Applications
Deeply optimized for industrial human-machine interaction, the GD32H7xD series enhances multimedia and graphic processing capabilities based on the unified hardware foundation, serving as a dedicated solution for industrial touch panels, embedded display terminals, industrial control consoles, portable medical interactive devices and high-end smart home HMI systems.
The series features a native 2-Lane MIPI DSI display interface that directly drives mainstream high-definition screens with full-resolution support ranging from QCIF to XVGA. A dedicated Image Processing Accelerator (IPA) enables smooth, high-quality graphic rendering. Fully compatible with mainstream GUI frameworks including LVGL, emWin, Embedded Wizard and ThreadX GUIX, the solution lowers development barriers for high-resolution interface design. Equipped with 4 SAI channels, 4 I²S channels and S/PDIF high-fidelity audio interfaces, it supports multi-microphone array processing and audio decoding to deliver immersive audio-visual interaction. Offered in 750 MHz (GD32H78D) and 600 MHz (GD32H77D) variants, the series enables flexible performance scaling to support diverse mid-to-high-end industrial HMI scenarios.
GD32H7xE/7×9 Series (GD32H78E/77E, GD32H789/779) – General-Purpose & Real-Time Motion Control MCU for Industrial Automation
Tailored for core industrial automation applications, this product lineup includes two specialized variants for high-precision real-time motion control and high-performance general-purpose industrial control, covering industrial main control units, variable-frequency drives, digital power supplies, industrial gateways and multi-axis linkage control systems.
The GD32H7xE series specializes in high-precision real-time motion control, integrating a hardware-based EtherCAT® slave controller with a DC synchronization accuracy up to 62.5 μs, delivering industry-leading real-time performance for high-speed multi-axis synchronization and servo control. Native support for major industrial encoder protocols including EnDat, BiSS-C, Tamagawa and HIPERFACE DSL, together with an integrated resolver-to-digital conversion module, removes the need for external signal conditioning circuits, enabling direct interfacing with servo motors and precision sensors to simplify hardware design and reduce BOM cost.
The GD32H7x9 series serves as a high-performance general-purpose industrial MCU. It retains the family’s universal high-computing power and full-range safety features while enhancing high-precision analog processing capabilities. Equipped with a 14-bit high-resolution ADC and HPDF high-speed digital filter, it is ideal for high-precision data acquisition, variable-frequency speed regulation, digital power control and process automation. Rich high-speed bus and expansion interfaces support efficient equipment networking, data interaction and system expansion, making it the optimal standardized main control solution for general industrial automation devices.
Compared with discrete industrial chip solutions, the GD32H7 portfolio delivers unique advantages through unified hardware foundation, scenario-specific differentiation and full ecological reusability. Based on a consistent hardware platform, software ecosystem, development toolchain and safety certification system, customers can complete multi-node device development efficiently. This effectively resolves common industrial challenges including cumbersome cross-platform adaptation, fragmented supply chains, high certification costs and slow product iteration, fully aligning with the standardization, modularization and integration trends of modern industrial equipment R&D.
GigaDevice delivers comprehensive technical support covering evaluation boards, firmware examples, FOC motor reference projects, joint drive development kits, GUI development kits and complete functional safety documentation. Customers can apply for samples and technical materials through local sales representative. Full sample availability is targeted for January 2027, while mass production is scheduled for April 2027 to enable large-scale deployment for global industrial customers.
About GigaDevice
GigaDevice Semiconductor Inc. is a leading global fabless supplier. Founded in April 2005, the company has continuously expanded its international footprint and established its global headquarters in Singapore in 2025. Today, GigaDevice operates branch offices across numerous countries and regions, providing localized support right to customers. Committed to building a complete ecosystem with major product lines – Flash memory, MCU, sensor and analog – as the core driving force, GigaDevice can provide a wide range of solutions and services in the fields of industrial, automotive, computing, consumer electronics, IoT, mobile, networking and communications. GigaDevice has received the ISO26262:2018 automotive functional safety ASIL D certification, IEC 61508 functional safety product certification, as well as ISO9001, ISO14001, ISO45001, and Duns certifications. In a constant quest to expand its technology offering to customers, GigaDevice has also formed strategic alliances with leading foundries, assembly, and test plants to streamline supply chain management. articles.title: Binance quitte la France et facturera les comptes non vidés dès le 29 novembre : voici comment partir
articles.text:
Début novembre, les clients français de Binance ont reçu un mail qui met fin à plusieurs mois d’incertitude. La plateforme y annonce que leurs comptes seront clôturés à compter du 31 décembre 2026 et leur demande de récupérer d’ici là l’ensemble de leurs cryptomonnaies.
En réalité, Binance France fonctionnait déjà au ralenti depuis le 1er juillet. Depuis cette date, toute société qui propose des services crypto dans l’Union européenne doit disposer de l’agrément MiCA, que l’entreprise n’a pas décroché à temps.
La plateforme n’acceptait donc plus de nouveaux clients, et les utilisateurs existants pouvaient seulement vendre ou retirer leurs avoirs. Désormais, ils sont appelés à ne plus laisser leurs fonds dormir sur leur compte.
Des frais qui pénalisent surtout les petits comptes
Le mail envoyé aux clients précise que ceux qui détiendront encore des cryptos sur leur compte le 29 novembre devront payer des frais mensuels.
Ils s’élèveront à 0,025 % du solde, mais ne pourront pas descendre sous 10 USDC, un stablecoin dont la valeur suit celle du dollar.
Avec un portefeuille de 1 000 dollars par exemple, le pourcentage ne représenterait que 25 centimes, mais Binance prélèvera bien 10 USDC. Un compte qui contient moins de 10 USDC sera entièrement vidé.
Deux prélèvements sont prévus avant la fermeture, le premier début décembre et le second après le 24 décembre. Après le 31 décembre, la plateforme considérera le compte comme inactif, ce qui « peut entraîner la conversion, le transfert ou tout autre traitement de vos crypto-actifs », prévient-elle dans son message.
Comment retirer ses cryptos de la plateforme Binance
Pour vider votre compte, la première étape consiste à choisir où envoyer vos fonds. Vous pouvez les transférer vers une plateforme agréée MiCA, dont le statut se vérifie dans le registre de l’ESMA ou sur la liste blanche de l’AMF, ou vers un portefeuille physique. Dans ce cas, conservez soigneusement sa phrase de récupération, la suite de mots qui permet de retrouver l’accès à vos fonds en cas de perte ou de panne de l’appareil.
Copiez ensuite l’adresse de dépôt fournie par la plateforme ou le portefeuille de destination. Dans l’application Binance, allez dans Actifs, puis Vue d’ensemble, Envoyer et Retirer l’actif, avant de sélectionner la crypto.
Comme le précise l’aide en ligne de Binance, le réseau choisi doit être le même que celui de l’adresse de dépôt, et il ne faut pas opter pour le réseau le moins cher s’il n’est pas compatible avec la destination.
Certains actifs comme le XRP demandent aussi un mémo ou un tag. Lors d’un premier envoi vers une nouvelle adresse, envoyez d’abord un petit montant pour vérifier que tout arrive bien. Pour récupérer des euros, revendez vos cryptos contre de l’EUR, puis demandez un virement vers un compte bancaire à votre nom. Pour rappel, cette revente est imposable si elle dégage une plus-value.
Supprimer son compte une fois vidé
Une fois le compte vidé, il reste à le clôturer. Binance prévient que la suppression est irréversible et que vous ne pourrez plus consulter ensuite l’historique de vos transactions. Pensez donc à l’exporter d’abord au format CSV, car vous en aurez besoin pour votre déclaration fiscale.
Dans l’application, ouvrez le Centre de compte, puis allez dans Sécurité, Gérer le compte et Supprimer le compte. Sur le site, la même option se trouve dans Compte, Sécurité, rubrique Gestion du compte.

articles.title: iPhone Duo : Apple aurait trouvé pourquoi certains écrans se fissurent
articles.text:
L’affaire du « crackgate » de l’iPhone Duo a fait pas mal de bruit. Pour rappel, certains propriétaires ont constaté que l’écran interne de leur téléphone se brisait après seulement quelques utilisations. De son côté, iFixit avait pointé du doigt « un énorme problème d’écran » lors de son analyse approfondie de l’appareil.
Quant au youtubeur Zack, son verdict a été sans appel : « l’iPhone Duo n’a pas réussi mon test de résistance ». Le constat était à chaque fois similaire : une ligne lumineuse apparaissait sous la pliure de l’écran interne, avant de s’étendre horizontalement vers la droite. Et si Apple a réagi en affirmant que le problème affectait « un petit nombre d’iPhone Duo », le défaut semble désormais avoir été identifié, mais aussi en grande partie corrigé.
Un problème de matériaux chez l’un des fournisseurs
Selon l’informateur chinois Kang, le problème d’écran affectant un certain nombre d’iPhone Duo « a été en grande partie résolu ». Il précise sur le réseau social chinois Weibo : « Il s’agissait d’un problème de matériaux chez l’un des deux fournisseurs, et non d’un défaut de conception ». Le défaut proviendrait donc d’un problème au niveau de la chaîne d’approvisionnement.
Seule une partie des iPhone Duo fabriqués serait ainsi concernée, comme l’a donc indiqué Apple. Il faut en revanche voir ce que l’entreprise à la pomme qualifie de « petit nombre » d’iPhone Duo concernés. À l’échelle d’Apple, ce « petit nombre » peut représenter plusieurs milliers d’appareils. Toujours selon l’informateur Kang, Apple serait même en mesure de localiser les iPhone Duo défectueux à partir de leur numéro de série.
Le défaut semble avoir été identifié, mais les échanges s’annoncent compliqués
Apple s’est pour l’instant contenté de reconnaître le problème, tout en invitant les personnes concernées à échanger leur appareil défectueux en magasin. Seulement voilà, les stocks d’iPhone Duo sont actuellement très limités. Certaines commandes ont même glissé jusqu’en janvier 2027. Il ne suffit donc pas de se rendre en magasin pour pouvoir bénéficier aussitôt d’un nouvel appareil.
Aussi, Apple n’a pour l’instant pas annoncé la mise à disposition d’un outil permettant de vérifier si un iPhone Duo est défectueux. Nous pouvons imaginer par exemple une plateforme sur laquelle il serait possible d’indiquer le numéro de série de l’appareil afin de vérifier s’il est préférable de l’échanger ou non. Espérons que cela soit le cas prochainement.

articles.title: Hackers now exploit critical Barracuda ESG flaws to gain root access
articles.text:
Cybersecurity company Barracuda Networks warned that attackers have begun exploiting two recently patched Email Security Gateway (ESG) vulnerabilities that let them run commands with root privileges.
Barracuda released security updates to address the two flaws (tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560) one week ago.
The first stems from an Email Security Gateway (ESG) authentication weakness that can be exploited to modify an appliance's global configuration, while the second lets unauthenticated attackers inject OS commands that execute with root privileges.
Barracuda also said that successful attacks require access to the administrative user interface (Admin UI) of targeted devices and advised customers to restrict access to trusted internal networks and use appropriate network access controls to limit exposure.
"Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product. If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device," the company explained.
On Monday evening, Barracuda updated the initial advisory to warn admins that the two flaws are being exploited in attacks targeting a limited number of customers.
"Barracuda immediately initiated a comprehensive remediation process and released security patches for affected products. We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations," it warned.
"If a patch has not been automatically applied, customers should manually apply the appropriate patch as soon as possible. If customers have turned off automatic patching, Barracuda recommends setting devices to automatically receive patches."
The table embedded below lists all affected devices and available security patches.
| Affected Product | CVE-2026-116606 | CVE-2026-111560 | Patch | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Email Security Gateway (ESG) | Yes | Yes | BNSF-40425 (9.4.017+), BNSF-40430 (<9.4.017) | 
| Load Balancer ADC | No | Yes | BNADC-16586 | 
| Message Archiver (BMA) | No | Yes | BNMA-32468 | 
| WAF Control Center (WCC) | No | Yes | BNWF-60060 | 
| Web Application Firewall (WAF) | No | Yes | BNADC-16586 | 
| Web Security Gateway (WSG) | No | Yes | BNYF-24789 | 
Three years ago, Barracuda patched another Email Security Gateway flaw (CVE-2023-7102) that the UNC4841 hacking group exploited in zero-day attacks to execute arbitrary code. The same year, UNC4841 abused another zero-day (CVE-2023-2868) to target Barracuda ESG appliances as part of a series of cyber-espionage attacks.
The company later revealed that the flaw had been exploited as a zero-day for at least seven months, since at least October 2022, to drop previously unknown SeaSpy and Saltwater malware and steal data from compromised devices.
According to cybersecurity firm Mandiant, almost a third of systems breached in the 2023 campaign belonged to government agencies, most of them hacked between October and December 2022.
Barracuda was founded in 2003 and now has more than 200,000 customers worldwide, including small- to medium-sized businesses (SMBs), large enterprises, and managed service providers (MSPs).
