articles.title: 👨🏿🚀TechCabal Daily – ‘Too much Access’ - TechCabal
articles.text:
Good morning. ☀️️
The biggest news in global tech is not about artificial intelligence (sorry, Anthropic, your IPO plans are exciting), but a very human affair. And, as it turns out, a possible intelligence operation. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an affair after reports linked him to a former chip distributor executive whom US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence. NVIDIA’s board is now investigating whether Huang was targeted in a foreign espionage operation.
The $4.28 trillion NVIDIA makes the chips powering much of the global AI boom, and the US has spent years restricting China’s access to its most advanced technology. The company said it has no reason to believe its secrets were compromised, but the affair has raised questions about the security of one of the world’s most valuable companies.
Let’s get into today’s dispatch.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Banking
Access Holdings may sell a foreign subsidiary in rethink of its African expansion strategy
Building a banking empire across Africa sounds good until some branches start costing more than they bring in. Access Holdings, the parent company of Access Bank and one of Nigeria’s largest banking groups, has found itself at that point. After years of expanding into new markets through acquisitions and new subsidiaries, it’s considering selling at least one overseas.
What happened? Access Holdings chairman Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede disclosed that the group is considering exiting at least one foreign market after identifying an underperforming subsidiary. Speaking to Bloomberg on the sidelines of the African Financial Industry Summit (AFIS) in Luanda, Angola, he said the group would be prepared to sell businesses that fail to meet their cost of capital or strategic objectives.
Explain like I’m new here: Under Section 19(8)(c) of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020, Nigerian banks cannot invest more than 10% of their shareholders’ funds in foreign banking subsidiaries. The provision is intended to prevent banks from committing too much capital to overseas operations at the expense of their financial strength at home.
Access was making moves: Access has spent years growing beyond Nigeria through acquisitions and new banking subsidiaries. It now operates across 16 African markets, including Tanzania, Kenya, Angola and Sierra Leone. In May, the bank’s exposure stood at 19.4%, almost twice the regulatory limit.
Access is considering either recalling excess capital from subsidiaries, selling minority stakes, or restructuring businesses. It has completed one capital repatriation exercise involving six subsidiaries and is engaging regulators in five countries to facilitate further capital returns. The group has not disclosed which five countries are involved.
Who could be leaving? Access has not named the subsidiary it is considering selling. However, the group’s international operations have not all performed equally. Its South African operation has recorded persistent losses, while its Kenyan business reported a loss in H1 2026. Mozambique, which previously struggled after an acquisition, returned to profitability in 2025.
In 2014, the tier-1 bank sold its loss-making Ivory Coast subsidiary after an earlier CBN directive restricted Nigerian banks from using parent-bank capital to support foreign operations. In July, it sold a 7.44% stake in its Ghanaian subsidiary. The current exercise could follow a similar route.

Banking
Kenya’s banks have two bosses arguing over their capital
Kenya’s banks have been given two different timelines to raise capital, and the regulatorsare now trying to agree on which one counts. The Treasury (the Finance Ministry) wants to give lenders until 2032 to reach KES 10 billion ($46 million) in core capital, but the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) wants them to do it by 2029.
What’s happening? John Mbadi, Kenya’s Treasury Cabinet Secretary, and CBK Governor Kamau Thugge are in talks to settle the disagreement, which became public after Mbadi announced an extension in his 2026 Budget speech, in June.
Mbadi’s proposal would scrap the CBK’s annual capital targets and give banks three extra years. The regulator wasn’t having it. It told lenders to stick to the original schedule and ordered banks with less than KES 5 billion ($38 million) in core capital to explain how they would meet the December 2026 target.
Under the CBK’s plan, banks must hold $38 million by December 2026, KES 6 billion ($46 million) in 2027, KES 8 billion ($62 million) in 2028, and KES 10 billion ($77 million) in 2029.
Why it matters: Smaller banks have warned that meeting the higher capital requirements could force them to cut lending to businesses and households, putting them at odds with the government’s push to increase private-sector credit.
As of June 2026, 14 banks had less than the KES 5 billion ($46 million) required by December. Seven had already missed the previous year’s KES 3 billion ($23 million) target. For these lenders, the extra three years Mbadi is proposing could make a big difference.
The bigger question: The CBK wants banks with larger capital buffers, but parliament wants to avoid a process that drives smaller lenders out of the market or limits access to credit. Both have a point. But until Mbadi and Thugge agree on a timeline, banks are left planning for two different deadlines.
Telecoms
MTN and Cell C disagree over network deal
In South Africa, MTN helps keep Cell C’s customers connected. Cell C helps banks and retailers become mobile operators without building their own networks. Now MTN wants more of that business for itself.
What’s happening? In a trading update published on Monday, MTN, Africa’s largest telecom operator, said it failed to agree with Cell C, the South African mobile network operator, on certain terms of their longstanding commercial relationship. MTN didn’t disclose what the disagreements were, but said both companies would work to resolve them under their existing agreement. Cell C confirmed that the deal runs until 2032 and that existing terms remain unchanged, according to local publication TechCentral.
Explain like I’m new here. Unlike MTN and Vodacom, Cell C no longer operates its own radio network. Instead, it relies on infrastructure-sharing agreements with both companies to provide nationwide coverage. Under its arrangement with MTN, Cell C gets access to network infrastructure, while MTN gets access to some of Cell C’s licensed spectrum, the radio frequencies used to carry mobile signals.
Here’s where it gets interesting: Cell C has built a growing business serving mobile virtual network operators (MVNOs), companies such as Capitec Connect that sell mobile services without operating their own networks. In its FY2026 results, Cell C estimated that it hosts 80–85% of South Africa’s MVNO market. Its wholesale revenue grew 20% to R1.76 billion ($107.2 million) in the year to May, supporting 5.71 million MVNO lines.
But MTN wants a bigger slice of that market. It wants to become South Africa’s leading MVNO wholesaler and is introducing new wholesale pricing arrangements to compete for customers.
Between the lines: MTN is both Cell C’s infrastructure partner and a direct competitor for wholesale customers. That creates an uncomfortable relationship between the two operators. Cell C needs access to MTN’s infrastructure to serve its customers, while MTN earns revenue from that arrangement even as it competes for the same business.
Neither company has disclosed the exact reason for the disagreement.
Zoom out: Cell C’s strategy of relying on other operators’ networks has reduced infrastructure development and maintenance costs, letting it focus on acquiring customers and growing its wholesale business. But the model also makes the terms of its network agreements critical to its profitability.
For now, both companies say customers won’t experience service disruptions. But Cell C has to answer questions about how it can protect its fast-growing wholesale business as the company supplying its network competes more aggressively for the customers it serves.
Funding
South Africa’s Yoco secures $100 million credit facility
Yoco, a South African fintech, has secured a $100 million credit facility from US investment firm Victory Park Capital to expand Yoco Capital, its merchant cash advance business. The facility gives the company greater control over how it finances merchants, including pricing advances and managing the associated risks.
Here’s what Yoco does: Yoco Capital uses payment data to assess merchants for financing. Eligible merchants receive offers through the Yoco app based on their sales history. Advances range from R2,000 ($121.8) to R1.5 million ($91,360), with no collateral required. Repayments are automatically deducted from daily sales,
Explain like I’m new here: South Africa’s small-business financing gap is estimated at R350 billion ($21.3 billion), according to the 2025 Finfind and African Bank MSME Access to Finance Report. SMEs receive just 13% of national bank lending, compared with 51% for large corporations. Yoco is betting that its existing relationship with merchants gives it an advantage in serving some of that unmet demand.
Yoco wants to do more: Since launching Yoco Capital in 2018, the company has advanced more than R6.5 billion ($395 million) to over 40,000 merchants. It now wants to extend the service to more of the 200,000-plus businesses on its platform. It has expanded its point-of-sale software, acquired Dyner AI, a software business, in May, and is developing an AI-powered platform for small businesses. With the new facility, Yoco is betting that the payment data it has collected over the years can become a bigger business than processing transactions alone.

articles.title: Running AV Reasoning Models Within Onboard Compute and Latency Limits | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Autonomous vehicle (AV) developers need reasoning models that can operate within the compute and latency constraints of an onboard system. Larger models provide a foundation for developing these capabilities, but moving them into a vehicle requires additional work to reduce model size, preserve useful reasoning, and validate performance on the target hardware.
NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge addresses this need with an adaptive reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) model designed for real-time operation on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor. Built on the 2B Nemotron-based reasoning backbone of NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge and paired with a diffusion action expert, it leverages surround-camera observations, temporal context, and navigation inputs to generate Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning and future driving trajectories. It reasons adaptively, generating reasoning only when needed, reducing unnecessary token generation and conserving inference compute during routine driving.
Alpamayo 2 Edge is post-trained with closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL) in NVIDIA AlpaGym, improving closed-loop driving performance by 48.9% on top of the best-performing checkpoint without closed-loop RL. Together, these capabilities give developers a strong, edge-ready foundation for bringing reasoning-based driving into an onboard stack.
Making a reasoning model compact enough for onboard deployment introduces a key challenge: preserving the quality of its reasoning and driving behavior as model size is reduced. This requires a way to measure reasoning quality and use that feedback to improve the model. NVIDIA AlpaJudge is the human-calibrated evaluation and reward model used in Alpamayo 2 Edge development to evaluate reasoning traces, select higher-value training data, and provide RL rewards.
This post introduces Alpamayo 2 Edge, explains its inference optimization on DRIVE AGX Thor, and explores three ways to use AlpaJudge in AV development workflows:
- Run AlpaJudge-RB and AlpaJudge-RF on a PhysicalAI-AV sample, inspect their scores, and adapt the evaluation to policy-generated reasoning
- Select training examples that expose useful learning opportunities
- Use human-aligned reasoning scores as rewards for post-training
Together, these workflows connect an edge-oriented driving model with a repeatable process for measuring and improving it.
Bring reasoning-based driving to the edge
An onboard driving model must interpret a changing scene and produce a useful trajectory within the system’s inference budget. The key question is how much driving and reasoning capability a model retains under that constraint.
To balance model capacity and efficiency, Alpamayo 2 Edge leverages multiple new features:
- A 2B-parameter Nemotron-based reasoning backbone, sized for onboard inference
- Adaptive reasoning, reducing unnecessary token generation and conserving inference compute during routine driving
- Offline distillation, training with CoC reasoning autolabels generated by Alpamayo 2 Super
- Closed-loop reinforcement learning post-training in AlpaGym, in which the model learns from the consequences of its actions end-to-end in simulation
- Multi-resolution inputs to efficiently encode surround-view observations online
- Speculative decoding with DFlash2 to accelerate online reasoning without sacrificing quality
- Recipes for quantization and inference acceleration with NVIDIA TensorRT and NVIDIA TensorRT-Edge-LLM
Figure 2, below, shows how these choices translate into capability, comparing Alpamayo 2 Edge with Qwen-Drive-1.0 across closed-loop driving, open-loop trajectory prediction, and scene understanding and reasoning.
Early partner feedback also highlights Alpamayo 2 Edge’s driving performance and inference speed:
“Within days of getting early access to Alpamayo 2 Edge, we had it running closed-loop in NuRec reconstructions of our own London street recordings. In our early simulation tests, Edge kept its lane in more than twice as many runs as Alpamayo 1.5, recovered from lane offsets about 40% more often, and out of the box planned roughly twice as fast as our hand-tuned Alpamayo 1.5 server on the same GPU.” —Matas Simonavicius, CTO, PORT
“Alpamayo 2 Edge demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities, reducing displacement error (minADE) by 13.6% and lateral prediction error (RMSE) at 3 seconds by 46.1% compared to Alpamayo 2 Super in our zero-shot evaluation, despite substantial differences in sensor configurations. Fine-tuning on our own driving data delivered a further 44.2% reduction in displacement error compared to the Alpamayo 2 Edge baseline. Within just a few days, we went from receiving the model to running our first tests on a real vehicle.” — Luca Crotti, co-founder and motion planning lead, Niulinx
“In less than 48 hours, we made NVIDIA’s Alpamayo 2 Edge run at 10 Hz on AGX Thor for real-time planning.”— Hans Salomonsson, CEO and co-founder, Embedl
The Alpamayo 2 Edge repository’s inference script shows how the model operates: It takes in surround-view camera observations over time, navigation text, and historical ego-motion to produce CoC reasoning traces and future trajectories.
import torch
import transformers
from alpamayo2_edge.checkpoint import load_model
from alpamayo2_edge.load_physical_aiavdataset import load_physical_aiavdataset
from alpamayo2_edge.helper import prepare_model_inputs, to_device
from alpamayo2_edge.models.utils import fuse_traj_tokens
data = load_physical_aiavdataset(**clip)
model, loading_info = load_model("nvidia/Alpamayo2-Edge")
settings = dict(
    seed=43,
    top_p=0.98,
    top_k=None,
    temperature=0.6,
    num_traj_sets=1,
    num_traj_samples=1,
    max_generation_length=256,
    diffusion_kwargs={"inference_step": 10},
)
prepared = prepare_model_inputs(data, model.config, model.tokenizer)
prepared = to_device(prepared, device="cuda")
"""Seed text and diffusion sampling, then run the model on prepared inputs."""
torch.manual_seed(settings["seed"])
generator = torch.Generator(device="cuda").manual_seed(settings["seed"])
with (
    torch.inference_mode(),
    torch.autocast(
        device_type=torch.device("cuda").type,
        dtype=model.dtype,
        enabled=model.dtype != torch.float32,
    ),
):
    xyz, rot, _, extra = model.sample_trajectories_from_data(
        prepared,
        num_traj_sets=settings["num_traj_sets"],
        num_traj_samples=settings["num_traj_samples"],
        top_p=settings["top_p"],
        top_k=settings["top_k"],
        temperature=settings["temperature"],
        max_generation_length=settings["max_generation_length"],
        diffusion_kwargs={**settings["diffusion_kwargs"], "generator": generator},
        return_extra=True,
    )
In particular, note that the model will now produce special <NOMINAL> tokens instead of reasoning traces sometimes, indicating routine driving and conserving inference compute.
Retaining quality during deployment
When downloading the model from Hugging Face, by default, Alpamayo 2 Edge’s weights are represented in BF16 and it is directly runnable as a PyTorch model on any supported NVIDIA GPU. To run at real-time on DRIVE AGX Thor, however, Alpamayo 2 Edge must be further inference-optimized.
The Alpamayo Developer Hub includes the recipe for the DRIVE AGX Thor deployment workflow: stage the Alpamayo 2 Edge checkpoint and DFlash2 drafter, calibrate FP8 scales, export ONNX graphs, build TensorRT engines with TensorRT Edge-LLM plugins, and run the Python harness. The recipe’s reference configuration was measured on DRIVE AGX Thor-X with DRIVE OS 7.2.7.0, CUDA 13.4, and TensorRT 11.3.1.9.
After following the Alpamayo 2 Edge deployment recipe to stage the model, evaluation inputs, and engines, run the bundle with
python -m alpamayo2edge_edgellm.runtime.run \
  --engines "$WORK/engines" \
  --model "$MODEL" \
  --reference "$INPUTS" \
  --dflash2 \
  --rolling \
  --warmup 1 \
  --repeat 5 \
  --output "$WORK/results.json"
The recipe documents export, build, calibration provenance, board requirements, and per-stage measurements so developers can reproduce the latency and paired-quality check on their DRIVE AGX Thor configuration. For reference, the resulting optimized model has a pixel-to-trajectory inference latency of 160 ms to 190 ms depending on the amount of reasoning. The same recipe check compares optimized model outputs with a BF16 PyTorch reference built from identical inputs and seeded action noise.
Evaluate reasoning with AlpaJudge
Trajectory metrics describe how a model plans or drives. Reasoning evaluation adds another dimension: whether the model’s explanation identifies the relevant scene context and supports the decision it describes. AlpaJudge provides the human-calibrated critic for this aspect of Alpamayo 2 Edge development (as well as prior models). The following workflows describe how to conduct that evaluation and use it for model improvement.
Choose the judge for your available inputs
AlpaJudge provides two checkpoint variants. Choose the variant according to the evidence available for the example you want to evaluate.
| Variant | Required inputs | Returned assessment | 
| AlpaJudge-RB, reference-based | Question, reference answer, and candidate answer; no images | One alignment probability in [0, 1] | 
| AlpaJudge-RF, reference-free | Three front-wide and three front-tele frames, ego meta-action history and future, and a candidate rationale | Five rubric probabilities plus action, component, and overall scores | 
RB measures agreement with the supplied reference, rather than independently checking the scene. RF does not require a reference rationale, but it does require synchronized visual evidence and formatted meta-action context.
Workflow 1: Run AlpaJudge on a PhysicalAI-AV sample
The example notebook provides a useful starting point, visualizing the data, meta-action context, candidate rationale, and reference rationale tied to a PhysicalAI-AV sample. The same record can then be rescored with a policy-generated CoC trace. Preserve clip ID, timestamp, camera names, and action context in the output so a low score can be traced back to the scene.
In open-loop evaluation, the candidate explanation and trajectory can be compared with recorded annotations. In closed-loop evaluation, the explanation at each policy decision can be scored using the observation and action context from that rollout. A high reasoning score is evidence that a rationale matches the judge’s rubric, while collision, road-departure, close-encounter, and trajectory measures describe different aspects of driving behavior. Report them together.
Step 1: Set up the package and open the notebook
From the AlpaJudge repository root, install the locked environment, authenticate for the model and PhysicalAI-AV dataset, and open the example notebook:
uv sync --locked --dev
hf auth login
uv run jupyter lab examples/alpajudge_pai.ipynb
The notebook uses clip 030c760c-ae38-49aa-9ad8-f5650a545d26 at 5.1 s. It decodes front-wide and front-tele frames at −1.0, −0.5, and 0.0 s, oldest first. The example rationale and meta-action strings are manually authored; the dataset supplies the camera frames. Replace all text fields together when using a different moment.
Step 2: Download the two judge checkpoints
The notebook downloads nvidia/alpajudge once and selects the reference-based/ and reference-free/ subfolders. These are separate checkpoints with separate loaders. Its snapshot call filters to those two folders; set ALPAJUDGE_MODEL_REVISION to an immutable revision for a reproducible run. A model load needs a CUDA GPU and roughly 5 GB for weights before activations.
checkpoint_root = snapshot_download(
    repo_id="nvidia/alpajudge",
    revision=MODEL_REVISION,
    allow_patterns=["reference-based/*", "reference-free/*"],
)
Step 3: Score the sample and inspect both outputs
Run the notebook’s fixed construction-zone sample first. With its recorded checkpoint and inputs, the smoke test reports RB alignment 0.999 and RF overall 0.842. The five RF subscores assess action/reference agreement, action safety, component grounding, component completeness, and causal consistency. The RF model defines action = p_match × (1 + p_safe)/2 and component = mean(p_grounded, p_complete, p_causal), then combines them overall = 0.6 × action + 0.4 × component.
Core notebook calls:
rb_model, rb_tokenizer = load_reference_based(
    str(checkpoint_root),
    subfolder="reference-based",
    device="cuda",
)
rb = score_reference_based(
    rb_model,
    rb_tokenizer,
    [{
        "question": QUESTION,
        "answer": REFERENCE_RATIONALE,
        "student": CANDIDATE_RATIONALE,
    }],
)[0].item()
rf_model, rf_processor = load_reference_free(
    str(checkpoint_root),
    subfolder="reference-free",
    device="cuda",
)
rf = score_reference_free(
    rf_model,
    rf_processor,
    front_wide_frames=front_wide_frames,
    front_tele_frames=front_tele_frames,
    meta_action_history=META_ACTION_HISTORY,
    meta_action_future=META_ACTION_FUTURE,
    rationale=CANDIDATE_RATIONALE,
)
print(rb, rf.overall, rf.subscores)
To evaluate Alpamayo 2 Edge itself, run its inference script on the selected clip and inspect the generated rationale in output.json under text.cot. Use that same clip and decision time when loading AlpaJudge-RF’s six frames, and replace the notebook’s hand-authored rationale with the generated string. Provide meta-action history and future that match this decision rather than copying the notebook’s construction-scene example. If an expert reference CoC trace is available, pass it to RB as answer and the Edge CoC as student. 
Workflow 2: Select higher-value training examples
AlpaJudge’s score is useful for training data selection because the highest and lowest scoring examples often serve different purposes. A very low reference-based score can indicate a mismatched label, a failed rollout, or a genuinely difficult case. Review these cases before discarding them; a blanket removal of low-scoring clips would also remove rare failures the policy needs to learn. Very high scores can identify scenes the current model already explains consistently and is not learning much from anymore. The middle range often contains data that is highly informative for further training.
Applying this to your own dataset begins with candidate CoC rollouts per clip and a fixed AlpaJudge checkpoint. Score each candidate against the paired reference (if using AlpaJudge-RB), record the score, clip ID, and any scenario metadata, then review low-scoring and safety-critical examples manually. Set selection thresholds on a development split, stratify the retained set by scene type and maneuver, and keep the held-out evaluation split untouched. Resample informative clips for further training and compare the new checkpoint with the same baseline set.
Workflow 3: Use reasoning scores for post-training
The public Alpamayo RL recipe offers a concrete pattern for adding a reasoning reward to open-loop GRPO training. It generates groups of policy rollouts, decodes each CoC and trajectory, computes trajectory error and comfort, then calls a pluggable reasoning grader before combining the terms into one scalar reward. AlpaJudge-RB can be that grader when each sample has a reference reasoning trace: pass the fixed driving question, reference as answer, and sampled CoC as student, then use the returned alignment probability as the reasoning signal.
An adapter can implement the recipe’s BaseReasoningGrader.score(predictions, references) -> Tensor[N] contract by batching the text pairs through score_reference_based. Register that adapter in GRADER_REGISTRY and point the reasoning reward config to the corresponding checkpoint. The reward function should keep its trajectory gate and log both component scores, so the policy is less likely to earn a high total reward from a fluent but wrong driving explanation.
Get started with Alpamayo 2 Edge and AlpaJudge
These workflows form a repeatable development loop: run the edge model, score its reasoning next to trajectory and safety metrics, select informative clips, and compare the next candidate against the initial baseline. For teams that also train policies with RL, AlpaJudge can provide a reasoning reward through an adapter such as the one described above.
Explore Alpamayo 2 Edge and AlpaJudge on Hugging Face. For discussions and developer questions, visit the Alpamayo developer forum. Check out the following for more information on:
- Alpamayo Open Platform and its latest releases.
- State-of-the-art research informing Alpamayo’s development.

The much-anticipated CISO Forum Virtual Summit 2026 kicks off today, November 10, and runs through tomorrow, November 11. Designed exclusively for senior-level cybersecurity leaders, this immersive two-day virtual event is your premier destination to discuss, share, and learn the most innovative risk management and defense strategies defining the modern enterprise.
If you haven’t secured your virtual seat yet, there’s still time to register and join thousands of enterprise security executives navigating the complexities of the AI-driven threat landscape at virtual.cisoforum.com.
Value of the Summit
This year’s agenda tackles the most pressing challenges facing CISOs. The integration of artificial intelligence into enterprise environments has shifted from a novelty to load-bearing infrastructure, bringing incredible new capabilities alongside unprecedented vulnerabilities. The summit’s sessions are laser-focused on actionable strategies, cutting through the hype to deliver practical frameworks for AI governance, third-party risk management, and vital team resilience.

- Managing Cyber Risk at Machine Speed (1:30 PM ET) – Maril Vernon, Principal Technical Evangelist at Horizon3, will share strategies for providing evidence-based metrics for executive and boardroom decisions.
- Burnout Is a Security Risk (2:00 PM ET) – Patrick Kelley, CISO & Founder of Critical Path Security, will provide a vital playbook for measuring and mitigating team fatigue before it leads to a security incident.

Engage, Learn, and Lead

articles.title: Samsung prepara una revolución en sus Galaxy más baratos: la pantalla se verá mejor que nunca
articles.text:
Samsung podría llevar las pantallas OLED a sus Galaxy más baratos. Según ZDNet Korea, varios fabricantes de paneles están considerando desarrollar pantallas OLED con resolución HD para dispositivos de bajo coste. De confirmarse el rumor, este movimiento podría significar el principio del fin para el LCD, una tecnología que ha acompañado a estos dispositivos durante años.
Si bien la industria de los móviles es en donde vemos una adopción mayor del OLED, la realidad es que estas pantallas están reservadas para ciertos terminales. En modelos de gama media o alta es común encontrarlos, pero en la gama de entrada no se integran bien, a veces por el coste o por la resolución. Un ejemplo es el Galaxy A18, uno de los móviles más asequibles con OLED y pantalla FullHD+, algo que no se ve en el Galaxy A07 con panel LCD y resolución HD+.
El nuevo planteamiento consistiría en desarrollar paneles OLED más sencillos que sean compatibles con resoluciones HD (720p), lo cual ayudaría a reducir costes. Según el reporte, fabricantes como Oppo y Vivo ya están en conversaciones con algunos proveedores para sustituir las pantallas LCD por OLED con características similares. Aunque esto suena atractivo, el principal desafío es el precio, puesto que desarrollar un panel OLED que pueda competir con el coste de los LCD actuales todavía no es posible.
El OLED es común en casi todos los móviles, excepto en la gama de entrada
Si los fabricantes y los proveedores logran un acuerdo, el impacto de esta implementación podría ser más grande de lo que pensábamos. Según los analistas, unos 100 millones de móviles con pantalla LCD podrían adoptar el OLED en el futuro. Los usuarios que tienen un presupuesto ajustado no tendrían que sufrir con una pantalla de baja calidad, con negros que parecen grises y con un consumo mayor de la batería.
Samsung, Oppo, Vivo y otras empresas consideran los nuevos paneles OLED HD como una forma de activar las líneas de producción, reduciendo la presión de costes fijos. La firma de análisis Omidia estima que los envíos mundiales caerán un 12% este año, lo que ha obligado a toda la cadena de suministro a buscar nuevas oportunidades de negocio. Contar con una móvil con pantalla OLED podría ayudar a revertir la caída y generar más ingresos por la venta de dispositivos de entrada.
Por el momento no existe una confirmación oficial sobre la fecha en la que podríamos ver estos móviles. Compañías como Apple dieron el salto al OLED en sus iPhones más baratos, pero en Android las cosas son distintas. Todavía existen líneas muy básicas en las que se venden teléfonos con pantalla LCD, como el Redmi A5 o el Moto G 2026, incluyendo sus variantes Play y Power.

articles.title: Float appoints former BDC Capital partner Jack Fraser as FinTech’s first CFO
articles.text:
Toronto-based Float Financial has recruited experienced growth-stage technology operator-turned-investor Jack Fraser as the FinTech firm’s first chief financial officer (CFO).
Fraser began his career in banking before moving into tech operations. He previously held CFO and COO roles at Toronto’s itravel2000 and its parent Travelzest, and guided scaling Montréal-based luxury e-commerce platform Ssense as CFO from 2016 until 2020. Fraser spent the last seven years at the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) serving as a partner at BDC Capital’s Growth Venture Fund, where he backed and advised some of the country’s most valuable tech companies, from Cohere to Koho Financial, Hopper, and Super.com.
“My experience in hyper growth operations [at] technology companies lends very well to where Float is today, and going to for tomorrow.”
Jack Fraser, Float
Float helps Canadian small- and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) manage their spending through cards, software, and other products. Fraser joins the firm months after leading BDC Capital’s investment in Float’s $85-million CAD Series C round, raised in part to support the company’s push into AI. He said he officially left BDC two weeks ago to take on this CFO role, which he assumed last week. He described the position as “a very elegant fit” given his background.
“I believe that my experience in hyper growth operations [at] technology companies lends very well to where Float is today, and going to for tomorrow … I’m excited to be in a company that’s revolutionizing financial operations with AI,” Fraser told BetaKit in an exclusive interview.
Founded in 2019, Float got its start helping Canadian SMBs that felt underserved by traditional banks simplify their spending through corporate cards and expense management software. It has since moved into other areas, from bill payments to business accounts and credit, as it works to help these SMBs automate and improve their financial operations.
The fast-growing FinTech company now employs 190 people and serves 10,000 active Canadian businesses, up from around 7,500 this June when it announced its Series C financing. Its clients include Cohere, Clutch, Knix, and Impact Kitchen.
“We’d been looking for a CFO for a while, and the right answer turned out to be someone we already knew well … [Jack has] seen Float up close: the hard calls, the bets that paid off, and where we’re going next,” Float co-founder and CEO Rob Khazzam told BetaKit over email. Khazzam cited Fraser’s long track record of backing Canadian founders and belief in the importance of SMBs as among the factors that made him the right choice for the job.
RELATED: Float announces $85-million Series C round to support AI push
Fraser said he was attracted to Float’s mission of helping Canadian SMBs, and said that the AI and automation layer the company has been building remains in its “early days” in terms of market penetration. “There is so much more that Float Intelligence is capable of doing and will be doing for businesses,” he added.
Float is gearing up for expansion as American business expense management tech peer Ramp sets its sights on the Canadian market, and fellow Toronto FinTech platform Wealthsimple moves into serving businesses. Fraser said he is confident in Float’s ability to compete with both. He said he thinks more competition will lead to better services for Canadians, and he views Float’s focus exclusively on the Canadian market and businesses, respectively, as differentiators.
During his time with itravel2000, Fraser said the online travel company faced off against Expedia, which was expanding in Canada. “We competed head-on with them, and we survived and succeeded,” he claimed.
“Many times, we’ve seen American or other foreign competitors come to Canada and underestimate the uniqueness of Canadians … Those are mistakes we won’t make,” Fraser said.
Feature image courtesy Float Financial.

A newly disclosed flaw involving OpenSSH and musl, dubbed “*sshole,” allows attackers to log in to certain Alpine Linux and other musl-based Linux accounts configured to block password authentication simply by entering an oversized password.
“Oversized” means longer than 256 bytes. Details.

articles.title: After challenging Google's Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Almost a decade after Cyanogen shut down its Android operating-system business following a years-long, unsuccessful effort to loosen Google’s dominance, its co-founder, Kirt McMaster, is now targeting Microsoft’s Windows with a new operating system designed for people who rely heavily on artificial intelligence in their everyday work.
McMaster’s company, Kora Systems, on Tuesday unveiled a Linux-based desktop operating system that integrates AI models and autonomous agents directly into the computing experience, allowing them to work across applications, access files, and retain context between tasks. The software is expected to launch in 2027 as a free-to-use desktop operating system, with support for existing Intel- and AMD-powered PCs as well as machines running Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips.
Kora is developing the eponymous operating system with a team of about 50 engineers, relying on AI coding tools, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. McMaster told TechCrunch that these tools have accelerated development by at least fivefold, with most of the gains coming over the past six months.
Microsoft has long dominated the PC operating-system market, making it hard for newer players to establish a foothold. Windows held about 77% of the worldwide desktop operating-system market in October, compared with nearly 10% for Apple’s OS X, according to Statcounter’s web traffic data.
However, McMaster believes Kora does not need to compete for Windows’ entire user base. Rather, he is targeting people who use AI extensively and are willing to pay for access to powerful models and services.
“Microsoft can keep its billion users,” McMaster said, estimating that 45 million to 50 million people currently account for much of AI usage and revenue. He expects that market to exceed 200 million users by 2033.
McMaster told TechCrunch that his experience at Cyanogen, where he spent over five years, taught him the dangers of relying on the very company he was trying to challenge. Cyanogen remained heavily dependent on Google Mobile Services despite offering features beyond Google’s version of Android. That ultimately restricted its ability to build an independent ecosystem.
“If you are trying to compete with an incumbent but are still reliant on them, you have no chance,” he said.
Kora, McMaster said, builds on an idea he pursued toward the end of his time at Cyanogen, when he began exploring ways to integrate third-party services directly into the operating system. With Kora, he wants AI models and agents to work across applications and access files without being confined to individual apps.
Previously known as Playtron, a gaming operating-system company led by McMaster, the Palo Alto-based company rebranded as Kora in July 2025 as it shifted its focus to AI. The decision came as early companies, including Perplexity and OpenAI, were moving into AI-powered web browsers, McMaster said. He believed browsers would not give AI agents enough access to a computer to carry out more complex tasks, making an operating system a better starting point.
The shift also allowed Kora to build on nearly three years of work developing Playtron’s Linux-based gaming operating system, called GameOS, instead of starting from scratch.
Kora is designed to let users work with different AI models and agents across applications, while keeping track of conversations, documents, and other information. It also allows AI agents to operate in separate workspaces with restricted access to files and other resources.
While McMaster has drawn on his experience at Cyanogen, none of Kora’s engineers worked there. Instead, the company recruited heavily from the Linux gaming community, he told TechCrunch.
Kora’s software is built on Linux and uses Nix. It replaces the Fedora Silverblue foundation of Playtron’s earlier GameOS.
While Linux and Nix are open source, McMaster said Kora’s own technology, including its Cortex AI engine and desktop interface, remains proprietary. The company, he said, intends to support AI models and services from different providers, although it has not committed to making its own software open source.
Gaming also remains part of Kora’s plans. McMaster said the company intends to introduce AI-powered tools that would allow developers to create, publish, and play games directly within the operating system. He added that support for Android apps is also on its roadmap.
McMaster told TechCrunch that Kora’s team has worked closely with Qualcomm’s engineers for nearly a year to optimize the operating system specifically for Snapdragon-powered PCs. The collaboration includes support for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite chips.
Alongside Qualcomm, Kora is working with Saudi Arabia’s AI company Humain on an enterprise version of the operating system, called Humain OS, which is expected to run on Snapdragon-powered laptops in 2027. Kora also plans to announce partnerships with PC manufacturers at a later date, though McMaster did not identify any companies or provide a specific timeline.
Kora plans to generate revenue through subscriptions that bundle access to AI models and agentic services. Moreover, its Cortex engine is designed to run AI tasks locally when possible and use cloud-based models for work requiring more computing power.
Kora’s investors include Samsung Next, Square Enix, Alumni Ventures, Polychain, VanEck, and Circle, all of which previously backed Playtron. The company, McMaster said, has raised additional funding since shifting its focus to AI. However, he declined to disclose the total amount raised or its valuation. Kora has enough funding to operate for several years, he said.

articles.title: Digital Fairness Act: So will die EU Verbraucher besser vor Online-Tricks schützen
articles.text:
Digital Fairness Act: EU plant strengere Regeln gegen Abofallen und manipulative Online-Tricks
Die EU plant klarere Regeln, um problematische Online-Verkaufstaktiken, irreführende Werbeversprechen oder manipulatives Design durch „Dark Patterns“ einzugrenzen. Dazu wird die EU-Kommission voraussichtlich am Mittwoch einen Entwurf für den „Digital Fairness Act“ (DFA) vorstellen.
Bereits vor der offiziellen Vorstellung berichtet Euronews über die wichtigsten Eckpunkte des Vorschlags. Demnach listet der Vorschlag detailliert sogenannte „Dark Patterns“ auf, also manipulative Designelemente, die Nutzer:innen oft unbemerkt zu bestimmten Entscheidungen motivieren.
Dazu gehört etwa ein Webdesign, das es leicht macht, einen Vertrag abzuschließen, den Weg zur Kündigung aber erschwert. Ebenso zählt dazu, Preise und Bedingungen zur automatischen Vertragsverlängerung absichtlich so zu platzieren, dass sie nur schwer zu finden sind.
Auch das wiederholte Nachfragen zu einer getroffenen Wahl oder verwirrende Formulierungen, etwa doppelte Verneinungen, können die bewusste Entscheidung von Verbraucher:innen ins Wanken bringen. Zu den manipulativen Designs zählt der Entwurf außerdem falsche Knappheitshinweise während des Checkouts, falsche Angaben zur Beliebtheit eines Produkts oder einen künstlich erzeugten Zeit- und Kaufdruck.
Mehr Kontrolle über Abos und Preise
Abofallen und süchtig machendes Design werden damit als unlautere Geschäftspraktiken gebrandmarkt. Künftig dürften etwa Gratisphasen bei einem Abo nur noch mit aktiver Zustimmung in ein Bezahlabo übergehen. Vor einer automatischen Verlängerung müssten Kund:innen erinnert werden und hätten das Recht, den Vertrag jederzeit kurzfristig zu kündigen.
Dynamische Preise, etwa bei Konzerttickets, deren Preis sich in Echtzeit nach der Nachfrage richtet, müssten künftig transparenter dargestellt werden.
Außerdem soll es für Nutzer:innen möglich sein, Funktionen zu deaktivieren, die potenziell süchtig machen oder zu zwanghaftem und übermäßigem Konsum verleiten. Dazu gehören etwa die Wiedergabe von Videos im Autoplay-Modus, Belohnungssysteme für tägliche Serien oder Streaks oder Chatbot-Funktionen, die persönliche Beziehungen vorgaukeln.
Mehr Schutz für Kinder und Jugendliche
Der Entwurf sieht ein Verbot personalisierter Werbung vor, die sich an Kinder und Jugendliche wendet. Für Minderjährige sollen in Videospielen auch Lootboxen und Pay-to-Win-Spielmechaniken verboten werden. Virtuelle In-Game-Währungen sollen außerdem standardmäßig deaktiviert sein und den tatsächlichen Geldwert anzeigen, sodass Minderjährige nicht über die wahren Kosten getäuscht werden.
Auch Influencer:innen, die für Produkte oder Dienste werben, sollen das künftig klarer kennzeichnen müssen. Verboten wäre Werbung für jugendgefährdende oder gesundheitlich bedenkliche Produkte.
Der DFA soll die EU-Richtlinie über unlautere Geschäftspraktiken aus dem Jahr 2005 durch eine Verordnung ersetzen, wodurch die Regeln unmittelbar in allen 27 EU-Mitgliedstaaten gelten würden. Über den Vorschlag der Kommission wird jetzt aber noch im Parlament und im Rat verhandelt. Kommt es dann zu einer Einigung, könnte der DFA spätestens ab dem Jahr 2030 für Unternehmen und Händler:innen verbindlich sein.
Die neuen Regeln wären eine Ergänzung zum Digital Services Act (DSA), der bereits Maßstäbe für Online-Plattformen im Umgang mit Desinformation oder illegalen Inhalten setzt. Viele Online-Shops, Apps und Online-Games fallen aber nicht unter den DSA. Außerdem ergänzt der Entwurf den Digital Markets Act (DMA), der Regeln für große Plattformen wie App-Stores und Suchmaschinen schafft.

articles.title: One of our favorite multi-filament 3D printers is $100 off
articles.text:
If you’re tired of filament jams and clogged nozzles, perhaps it’s time for a new 3D printer. Through December 1st, the Bambu Lab P2S Combo, currently one of the best models that’s easy to use, is discounted. It’s $649 at Best Buy, as well as directly from Bambu Lab. That’s $100 off the list price for the bundle, which includes the Bambu P2S printer and the AMS 2 Pro multi-filament handler for multicolor prints.
One of our favorite multi-filament 3D printers is $100 off
Bambu’s P2S prints quickly and consistently, and automatically swaps between up to four filament colors out of the box.
Bambu Lab P2S Combo
Bambu Lab’s P2S Combo is a 3D printer that can print in multiple colors and automatically dry its materials to help improve print quality. It also features a 5-inch touchscreen, a built-in camera for monitoring prints remotely, and AI-powered tools that can detect printing problems.
My colleague Sean Hollister praised the P2S printer for its consistency and hands-off approach to 3D printing. Automatic bed leveling, including a warning if you forget to reinstall the plate, and a bevy of sensors helps ensure every print goes smoothly. There’s a live camera feed, too, so you can check in on your prints or share a timelapse. On its own, the P2S printer is usually $549, but is also currently $100 off.
The AMS 2 Pro’s filament handler’s fully enclosed setup saves your filament from absorbing moisture and clogging the nozzle or tubes. As a result, you can go weeks between prints and fire one off from your computer without checking on colors or manually swapping filaments. The AMS 2 Pro itself is typically $299, but is currently on sale for $229, and the P2S printer supports up to four AMS 2 Pro units simultaneously.

articles.title: La Switch 2 est trop chère ? Pour 179 €, E.Leclerc propose la première Switch avec Mario Kart 8 Deluxe
articles.text:
La Switch 2 est sortie en juin 2025, mais la première Nintendo Switch est toujours dans les rayons. À l’approche de Noël, beaucoup de parents la regardent encore. Il faut dire qu’elle convient parfaitement pour un enfant qui découvrirait les jeux vidéos, et qui n’a pas besoin des dernières nouveautés. Surtout, elle coûte moins cher que sa remplaçante et donne accès à des années de jeux déjà sortis.
E.Leclerc proposera le pack Nintendo Switch + Mario Kart 8 Deluxe à 179 € dans le cadre de son opération Black Friday, du 20 au 29 novembre 2026. Au moment où nous écrivons ces lignes, la fiche produit affiche encore un prix de 199 €. La réduction n’est donc pas encore effective. Il faudra surveiller l’offre de près à partir du 20 novembre pour profiter du tarif annoncé.
Que vaut encore la Nintendo Switch de première génération ?
La Nintendo Switch mise sur sa polyvalence et se connecter au téléviseur grâce à son dock, être installée sur une table avec sa béquille ou être utilisée directement en mode portable. Son écran tactile de 6,2 pouces propose une définition de 720p en déplacement, contre 1080p sur un téléviseur. Côté autonomie, comptez entre 4 h 30 et 9 heures selon les jeux utilisés. La console est également livrée avec deux manettes Joy-Con amovibles qui peuvent être utilisées séparément pour jouer à deux sur une même console. Pratique pour lancer une partie à plusieurs sans avoir besoin d’acheter une seconde manette.
Le pack inclut une version physique de Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, l’un des meilleurs épisodes de la célèbre série de courses de Nintendo. Avec ses 48 circuits (96 circuits avec le DLC), son casting généreux de personnages et ses objets capables de transformer une course en véritable champ de bataille, le jeu est aussi accessible que terriblement addictif. On peut y jouer seul, en ligne ou jusqu’à quatre sur la même console. Classé PEGI 3, il s’adresse à tous les publics et constitue un excellent jeu pour partager quelques parties en famille, même si les carapaces bleues risquent de provoquer quelques tensions autour du canapé.
Gardez en tête que la console montre toutefois ses limites face aux standards actuels. Avec des composants qui remontent à 2017, elle commence à accuser son âge. Elle ne peut notamment pas faire tourner les jeux exclusivement conçus pour la Switch 2. Si vous souhaitez profiter des prochaines grandes sorties de Nintendo, mieux vaut donc vous tourner vers la nouvelle génération.
À ce prix, la Nintendo Switch est-elle une bonne affaire ?
À 179 €, l’offre vaut clairement le coup. Vous repartez avec une console complète et Mario Kart, un jeu convivial qui peut réunir toute la famille dès le premier soir. Pour offrir une première console à un enfant ou ajouter une machine au salon, difficile de trouver un meilleur rapport entre le prix et le plaisir de jeu. La Switch première du nom a beau avoir quelques années au compteur, elle dispose encore d’un immense catalogue et reste parfaitement adaptée à cet usage.
D’autant que l’offre tombe au bon moment, juste avant Noël, période où les consoles ont naturellement leur place sous le sapin. Attention toutefois : le tarif n’est pas encore affiché en ligne et dépend des magasins E.Leclerc participants. Pensez donc à vérifier le prix et les stocks au lancement de l’opération.
En résumé, si votre objectif est de jouer à Mario Kart en famille sans dépenser une fortune, cette Switch à 179 € est une très bonne affaire. La Switch 2 s’impose si vous souhaitez aussi profiter des prochaines grosses exclusivités de Nintendo et investir dans une console faite pour durer plusieurs années.
Black Friday 2026 : tout ce qu’il faut savoir
Depuis une dizaine d’années, le Black Friday s’est infiltré dans le calendrier commercial des grandes marques et enseignes françaises. Avec l’expérience, on peut vous dire que cet événement fait partie des meilleurs moments pour faire de bonnes affaires.
Les dates du Black Friday
Bien qu’il porte encore le nom du vendredi noir, le Black Friday s’étend désormais sur un mois chez de nombreux revendeurs. Un format moins typique qui lui retire un peu son petit côté FOMO. On dirait presque les soldes, finalement. Mais c’est aussi moins le rush, ce qui est une bonne chose pour ceux qui veulent faire des achats plus raisonnés. Globalement, on peut résumer ce Black Friday en quatre temps forts :
- Début novembre : les avant-premières Black Friday.
- Autour du 20 novembre, selon les enseignes : la Black Week commence généralement plusieurs jours avant le jour J.
- 27 novembre : la date du Black Friday, même si les offres commencent généralement avant et se prolongent le week-end des 28 et 29 novembre.
- 30 novembre : le Cyber Monday.

articles.title: Buying an EV through your ABN? Here is what the lender actually checks - Tech Guide
articles.text:
By Nick Lim, Founder, Switchboard Finance
A lot of business owners are now looking at an electric vehicle as their next work car. The spec sheets get all the attention: range, charging speed, the screen in the middle of the dash. The finance gets about five minutes at the end, usually at the dealer, usually under pressure.
That is backwards. The car is the easy part. Whether a lender will fund it, on what terms and against which paperwork, is where self-employed buyers get caught out. Here is how it looks from the other side of the desk.
The first thing a lender looks at is not the car. It is the business.
How long the ABN has been active matters more than most people expect. Many lenders want to see at least two years, some will go to one, and a handful will go lower with a bigger deposit or a stronger file. GST registration matters too, partly because it signals turnover and partly because it affects how the deal can be structured.
Then comes income. A salaried employee hands over two payslips and is done. A sole trader or company director is asked for tax returns, financial statements and sometimes an accountant’s letter. If the latest return is late, shows a loss because of a one-off write-off, or simply does not reflect how the business is trading now, that is where applications stall.
This is the part the technology has actually changed. A growing share of lenders will now assess income from business bank statements instead of tax returns, using software that reads and categorises months of transactions in minutes. If that is your situation, it is worth understanding how low doc car loans for ABN holders work before you walk into a showroom, because the documents you bring decide which lenders are even in the conversation.
The software reads everything. Deposits, the ATO payment plan, the personal spending that runs through the business account, the direct debit that bounced three months ago. It does not get tired on page nine. So the practical advice is simple: read your own statements before the lender does, and be ready to explain anything that looks odd.
Only after the business is assessed does the lender turn to the vehicle, and an EV raises a few questions a petrol ute does not.
The first is resale value. A lender is not only financing a car, it is holding security over it. EV prices have moved around as new models arrive and manufacturers cut prices, and a lender wants to be confident the car is worth comfortably more than the loan for most of its term. That is why some lenders are more conservative on older or less common electric models, and why the deposit or balloon a lender will accept can differ from an equivalent combustion car.
The second is battery health on a used EV. A five-year-old petrol car with a full service history is a known quantity. A five-year-old EV depends heavily on its battery, and not every lender has a settled view on how to assess that. Buying used from a dealer, with a battery health report, makes life easier than a private sale with no paperwork.
The third works in your favour. A number of lenders price electric and low-emission vehicles more sharply than equivalent petrol cars. The discount is not always large, and it is not universal, but it is worth asking for.
Then there is structure, which is where business owners leave the most on the table. Broadly, an ABN holder buying a work vehicle chooses between a chattel mortgage, where the business owns the car from day one and the lender takes security over it, a lease arrangement, or a consumer loan in their own name. Each treats GST, depreciation and interest differently, and the right answer depends on how the business is set up and how much the car is used for work. Your accountant should have the final say, and the finance should be built around their answer, not the other way around.
A few things are worth doing before you start shopping.
Pull your own credit file. Every lender will read it, and a forgotten buy now pay later account or an old phone bill can cost you a better rate.
Get your last six to twelve months of business bank statements in order. If you are relying on statements rather than tax returns, they are your income evidence.
Decide on the structure with your accountant first. Chattel mortgage, lease or consumer loan is a tax question before it is a finance question.
Ask about the green discount, and ask what deposit or balloon the lender will accept on the specific model you want, not EVs in general.
And treat dealer finance as one quote, not the only quote. It may be competitive. It may not. You only find out by comparing.
The technology in the car gets better every year. The technology in the lending process is catching up, and for self-employed buyers that is mostly good news, because it means a lender can now see how your business really trades. The catch is that it sees everything. Get ahead of what it will find, and the EV becomes the easy decision it should be.
Nick Lim is the founder of Switchboard Finance, a Melbourne non-bank finance brokerage for self-employed and SME borrowers. He is an FBAA accredited finance broker and Credit Representative 576702 of LMG Broker Services Pty Ltd (Australian Credit Licence 517192). This article is general information only and is not credit or tax advice.

articles.title: WhiteMatter Raises $20 Million in Series A Funding
articles.text:
Cybersecurity startup WhiteMatter on Tuesday announced raising $20 million in a Series A funding round that brings the total raised by the company to $24 million.
The investment round was led by Blumberg Capital, with additional support from previous investors Crew Capital and Sprout & Oak.
Founded in 2024 and previously known as QuilrAI, WhiteMatter has built a platform that helps organizations secure and govern every AI agent running in their environments.
According to WhiteMatter, enterprises can run every AI agent through its platform and gain visibility into where agents are built and used: across endpoints, cloud, SaaS, and code.
The solution deploys and governs every agent, model, and MCP server, observes and secures each action, and optimizes traffic through a single gateway.
WhiteMatter can deploy a dedicated guardian agent for every agent running in the environment, scaling if agents multiply autonomously, to ensure continuous policy-driven control.
The cybersecurity startup will use the new investment to accelerate research and development and expand its go-to-market organization. It will also build its executive team.
“Despite all the discussion about pausing AI development, enterprises are doing the opposite. AI technology is too powerful, the opportunity is too significant, and the competitive pressure is too real to put it back in the box,” said WhiteMatter founder and CEO Vidit Arora.
“Companies that slow down AI adoption risk being overtaken by competitors that move fast, stay secure, and scale AI with confidence, which is exactly why we built WhiteMatter,” Arora added.
WhiteMatter has headquarters in San Francisco and Austin.
