articles.title: iPad verschenken: Welches Modell sich an Weihnachten am besten für dein Kind eignet
articles.text:
iPad zu Weihnachten verschenken: So findest du das passende Modell für dein Kind
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Bei vielen Schüler:innen hat sich der Wunsch nach einem eigenen Tablet schon erfüllt: Laut Bitkom besaßen 54 Prozent der Sechs- bis 18-Jährigen schon im Jahr 2024 ein eigenes Gerät. In Haushalten, in denen schon ein iPhone oder Macbook vorhanden ist, kann ein iPad besonders praktisch sein, weil es sich nahtlos ins Apple-Ökosystem einfügt. Außerdem bietet es zahlreiche Funktionen, um die Nutzung durch dein Kind im Auge zu behalten. So kannst du unter anderem einen Kinder-Account anlegen, das iPad in die Familienfreigabe aufnehmen, Bildschirmzeiten festlegen und den App- und Webzugriff begrenzen. Wir erklären dir, welches iPad am besten zu deinem Kind passt und mit welchen Kosten du vor Weihnachten rechnen musst.
Unter den Pioneers Picks stellen wir dir regelmäßig weitere praktische Tools und Gadgets vor.
iPad von Apple: Wann das Standardmodell ausreicht
Das Standard-iPad ist ein klassisches Einstiegsmodell und ideal für den Schulalltag. Es verfügt über ein 11 Zoll großes Display. Die Rückkamera mit zwölf Megapixeln filmt in 4K-Qualität. Die Frontkamera bietet ebenfalls zwölf Megapixel. Hinzu kommen Stereo-Lautsprecher und zwei Mikrofone. Die Leistung reicht für Lern-Apps, Notizen und Präsentationen in der Regel aus. Darüber hinaus eignet sich das Apple-Tablet für die meisten Spiele und Entertainment-Apps wie Youtube. Insbesondere für Grundschulkinder und alle, die ihr erstes Tablet bekommen, ist das Standardmodell somit eine gute Wahl.
Das iPad ist mit 128, 256 oder 512 Gigabyte Speicher und einem A16-Chip erhältlich. Laut Hersteller hält der Akku beim Surfen oder Streamen über WLAN bis zu zehn Stunden durch. Es unterstützt den WLAN-Standard 6 und ist optional als SIM-fähige Variante erhältlich. Zubehör wie der Apple Pencil und das Magic Keyboard Folio sind kompatibel. Apple bietet das iPad in Blau, Pink, Gelb und Silber an. Im Apple-Store kostet es Modell 499 Euro in der Basisvariante. Bei Amazon ist das iPad in allen Farben aktuell schon ab 444 Euro erhältlich.
Das zukunftssichere iPad Air für Schule und Studium
Das iPad Air die beste Wahl, wenn du eine leistungsfähige und möglichst langfristige Lösung suchst. Der M4-Chip, der auch in manchen Mac(book)s verbaut ist, bietet mehr Leistung als der A16 im Einstiegsmodell. Das Modell ist mit dieser Ausstattung erst seit März 2026 auf dem Markt und deshalb deutlich zukunftssicherer. Am besten eignet es sich für ältere Kinder in der Mittel- oder Oberstufe. Das iPad Air kann nicht nur bei Hausaufgaben in der Schule unterstützen, sondern dein Kind auch noch beim Start an der Uni begleiten.
Das Tablet ist mit Elf- und 13-Zoll-Display erhältlich. Die Rück- und Frontkamera entsprechen dem Standard-iPad, ebenso die Stereo-Lautsprecher und Mikrofone. Das iPad Air unterstützt allerdings den schnelleren WLAN-Standard 7 und ist als 5G-Mobilfunkversion erhältlich. Zur Auswahl steht es in Dunkelgrau, Türkis, Violett und Gold. Der interne Speicher beträgt maximal ein Terabyte. Laut Hersteller hält der Akku über WLAN bis zu zehn Stunden. Im Apple Store kostet das iPad Air ab 799 Euro. Bei Amazon startet der Preis schon bei 684,81 Euro. Dieser kann je nach Farbe variieren.
iPad kaufen: Was du bei der Auswahl beachten solltest
Apple hat noch weitere Modelle im Portfolio. Das iPad Pro ist auf rechenintensive Workflows wie Video- und Fotobearbeitung oder Grafikdesign zugeschnitten. Für die Schule reicht deshalb meist ein günstigeres Modell aus. Auch das iPad Mini ist für Hausaufgaben und Lernen weniger gut geeignet: Es ist das kompakteste Apple-Tablet und deshalb ideal für unterwegs. Gerade fürs Lesen ist der kleine Bildschirm aber weniger praktisch. Zudem liegt der Preis höher als beim Standardmodell. Als Weihnachtsgeschenk solltest du dich daher zwischen dem „normalen“ iPad und dem iPad Air entscheiden.
Außerdem kann es sich lohnen, mit dem Kauf noch etwas zu warten. Die Angebote von Amazon liegen derzeit zwar deutlich unter der unverbindlichen Preisempfehlung von Apple. Rund um den Black Friday am 27. November sind viele Elektronikartikel aber noch einmal reduziert. Solche Angebote lohnen sich besonders, da Apple aufgrund der anhaltenden Speicherkrise die Preise für einige Produkte deutlich erhöht hat. So kostet das iPad jetzt oft rund 100 Euro mehr als noch vor einigen Monaten. Wer noch mehr sparen möchte, greift zu einem gebrauchten Modell. Auch Kratzer oder Stürze sind hier leichter zu verschmerzen.

articles.title: Firefox’s free built-in VPN uncaps data limit through January 2027 | The Mozilla Blog
articles.text:
Firefox’s free built-in VPN uncaps data limit through January 2027
Whether you’re heading home to see family this winter or taking a well-earned break before the year wraps up, we want you to browse with a little more peace of mind. That’s why, as our gift to you, everyone using Firefox’s free built-in VPN gets unlimited data starting today, November 10, through January 31, 2027. Sign in with a Mozilla account and unlock extra privacy for all that shopping, travel planning, and everyday browsing, no gift receipt required.
Using Firefox’s free built-in VPN makes it harder for websites to use your IP address to determine where you are, or connect your visits across the web. Most importantly, you’re not trading your browsing data for that protection: Firefox doesn’t sell your browsing data, interrupt you with ads, or keep a record of the websites you visit.
You can use VPN to:
- Keep the sites you visit private on shared Wi-Fi. You might use café Wi-Fi to check your itinerary, or look up something you’d prefer to keep to yourself while at a relative’s house. Turning on VPN helps hide the sites you’re visiting from whoever runs those Wi-Fi networks so your browsing habits stay your own.
- Change your browsing location. Firefox’s built-in VPN lets you change where your connection appears to come from, making it easy to check news from home while abroad.
Two things to remember:
- VPN doesn’t make you anonymous online or hide browsing history on your device. Websites can recognize you through cookies or when you sign into an account. Use Private Window to browse without logging new visits in your Firefox history.
- Firefox’s built-in VPN only covers browsing within Firefox. For protection across other apps on your device, check out Mozilla VPN (a separate, paid subscription service).
Firefox’s free built-in VPN is available to people using Firefox on desktop and Android (iOS is coming soon!). To start using the service:
- Sign up for a Mozilla account if you don’t yet have one.
- Select the VPN icon in Firefox’s toolbar on desktop or open the three-dot menu and go to Settings > VPN on your Android device.
- Follow the setup prompts, turn on VPN, and start browsing.
You can check for availability in your region and review full instructions for using VPN on desktop and Android in our Help Center.
Download Firefox to try it out today.

articles.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
articles.text:
Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.
The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.
Vulnerabilities in Git
CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones
Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.
An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks. When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone.
The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.
[Advisory]
CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD
When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.
A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.
Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.
[Advisory]
CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures
When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.
This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.
The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.
[Advisory]
CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches
Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.
Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.
Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.
[Advisory]
CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges
Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.
The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.
The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.
[Advisory]
CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams
git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.
Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.
These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.
[Advisory]
Additional hardening
Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.
Protecting GitHub users
- We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.
- Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible.
- We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git.
- GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git.
Update Git
Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.
If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.
	
		Written by	
					
				
					
				
Elijah Newren is a Staff Software Engineer at GitHub. He is the designer and implementer of merge-ort, Git's default merge strategy since 2.34, author of git-filter-repo—the history rewriting tool the Git project officially recommends—and a driving force behind sparse-checkout.

articles.title: The AI Security Gap Hiding in Routine Maintenance
articles.text:
The AI Security Gap Hiding in Routine Maintenance
Abby Kearns | 10 November 2026
This blog was first published on November 9, 2026 at https://openssf.org/blog/2026/11/09/the-ai-security-gap-hiding-in-routine-maintenance/ and repurposed here with consent from the author.
Ask a security team what worries them about AI and you'll probably hear about supply chain attacks or prompt injection first. The Linux Foundation's new report, State of AI Impact on Software Security and Cybersecurity 2026, backs that up, with 93% of the security experts it surveyed concerned about supply chain attacks and 90% about prompt injection. Some of the report's most important findings, though, are about something a lot less dramatic: the everyday work of keeping software up to date.
LF Research surveyed 308 people working on security in companies and open source projects this summer, in research sponsored by OpenSSF, LF AI & Data, and ActiveState, where I'm CEO. Coming at it as an operator, I wasn't surprised by what they found, because every dependency a team adds comes with years of upkeep, and that work almost never gets staffed the way new features do.
Where teams feel least prepared
The survey asked practitioners how concerned they are about a long list of AI-related threats and how prepared they feel for each one, and for every single threat, concern came out ahead. The biggest gap was around automated exploit generation, which isn't surprising for such a new kind of threat. Right behind it, though, was something much more familiar, which is keeping up with component updates. 83% of practitioners said they're concerned about the extra maintenance that comes with a high volume of updates, but only 44% said they feel prepared for it, and 43% are already dealing with it today.
AI is adding to the pile
Part of the reason is that AI coding tools are adding dependencies. 60% of the organizations and projects in the survey said these tools have increased the number of external dependencies in their code (only 16% said the opposite), and teams review transitive dependencies, the packages your dependencies bring in with them, only about half the time. Meanwhile, 58% say they're shipping code faster than security review can keep up. I think AI is signing teams up for upkeep faster than most of them can hire for it, and these numbers are what that looks like in practice.
Why fixes wait
The report also asked why fixes get pushed back, and the top answer was the risk of breaking something (28%), followed by not having the time (22%). In my experience, that's exactly how backlogs build up. A team knows about the vulnerability and knows a fix exists, but the update might break something in production, so it waits for a better moment, and that moment can take a while to arrive.
Having someone own the problem helps. Among teams without a dedicated security team or role for AI threats, only 23% fix most new alerts right away, compared with 43% of teams that have one, and only 30% of teams have that kind of role at all. Everyone else is triaging, getting to the most severe alerts and leaving the rest to pile up into what the report calls security debt.
A question worth asking
If you're a CEO or engineering leader, here's a question worth bringing to your next security review: how much of our backlog is there because patching feels risky, and not because a fix doesn't exist? If the answer is a lot, more scanning won't help much, and you probably need a better way to keep components current.
The report has some good suggestions for where to start. Decide who owns AI security on your team, since teams with a dedicated role or a formal AI security policy felt better prepared for every threat in the survey (the report is careful to note that's a correlation, not proof). Cut the dependencies you don't really need, because, as the report puts it, "One less dependency means one less factor beyond the purview of the security team." And pull the ones you keep from a vetted, policy-governed source, so known-vulnerable code never makes it into the backlog in the first place.
The report's foreword asks readers to take one question back to their teams: "where is software development outpacing review, and who is responsible for closing that gap?" For a lot of teams, I suspect the answer starts with maintenance.
Continue the conversation at KubeCon
Visit ActiveState at booth (#277) to discuss practical approaches to managing open source dependencies and strengthening software security in the AI era.
About the Author:
Abby Kearns is CEO of ActiveState. She was previously CEO of the Cloud Foundry Foundation and CTO at Puppet.

articles.title: NVIDIA Expands Open Source Commitment With OpenShell Donation and New AI Infrastructure
articles.text:
Kubernetes, the open source system that manages how applications run across thousands of AI factories, has become the foundation for AI, and the demands on it are only growing.
To help meet them, NVIDIA is deepening its commitment to open source at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon, the flagship conference for the Kubernetes and cloud-native communities.
NVIDIA is contributing NVIDIA OpenShell, an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), a nonprofit that is part of the Linux Foundation and the host of KubeCon. As a CNCF Sandbox project, OpenShell will be governed by the organizations building it into their products and strengthened by the expertise of security professionals worldwide.
NVIDIA is also contributing to Agent Substrate, an open source Google-led framework for operating long-running agent workloads at scale on Kubernetes that has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox.
Additionally, NVIDIA announced new components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform: NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine, NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes and NVIDIA Snapshot. These tools help teams deploy, manage and scale GPU infrastructure on Kubernetes for AI factories.
Together, these advancements mark a step forward in making Kubernetes the leading foundation for AI workloads at scale — empowering developers to build safer, more efficient AI infrastructure for the future.
Securing AI Agents in the Open
NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF puts security infrastructure for autonomous agents in the community’s hands to build, inspect and improve — accelerating development and hardening its safeguards.
“The cloud-native community has a new infrastructure challenge: giving agents secure environments in which to operate,” said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation. “NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF gives developers a shared foundation to build on and an opportunity to shape how agent security evolves. Bringing this work into the community enables broader collaboration on infrastructure that will be critical to the next generation of cloud-native applications.”
OpenShell gives organizations control over what AI agents can do. It applies deterministic controls to agent activity, so teams can enforce policies as agents use tools, access inference services and execute workloads. Its extensible architecture lets teams connect their own compute, inference providers, credential storage and monitoring tools. This allows organizations to apply governance across different deployment environments while integrating OpenShell with their existing enterprise systems.
Hundreds of organizations have put OpenShell to use, and the project has received tens of thousands of contributions in less than a year since launch.
Scaling Agent Execution on Kubernetes
Governing agents is only part of the challenge. Organizations also need to deploy them at scale.
NVIDIA is contributing to Agent Substrate, a Google-originated project in the CNCF Sandbox, and ensuring it works with NVIDIA Dynamo for model inference and KAI Scheduler for shared cluster resource allocation. This effort brings together agent execution, inference serving and resource scheduling on Kubernetes.
Agent Substrate preserves agent environments between tasks while releasing compute when agents are idle. By suspending and resuming those environments across a shared pool of agents, it lets teams scale agent workloads without keeping dedicated compute running for every session.
NVIDIA and Google are also collaborating on an integration of OpenShell and Agent Substrate, so enterprises can secure and govern agents across clouds and on-premises systems.
Building an Open Foundation for AI Factories
AI factories need to offer customers managed Kubernetes services while retaining control of their infrastructure, software and customer experience. Three new open source projects extend the DSX AI Factory Platform to make Kubernetes easier to run and inference faster to scale.
NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) — now available in public preview — provide open source building blocks for delivering managed Kubernetes services on GPU infrastructure. They automate cluster lifecycle management and provide signed, version-pinned images.
NVKE and NVKR are launching with ecosystem support that extends their reach across AI infrastructure platforms and cloud services. Mirantis, Netris, OpenNebula Systems, Rafay, Spectro Cloud and vCluster, together with Firmus and SK Telecom, have aligned with NVIDIA on integration plans to bring NVKE and NVKR capabilities into their offerings.
NVIDIA Snapshot addresses the challenge of bringing additional inference capacity online quickly. Loading models and warming up workloads can delay scaling and recovery. The open source, modular component restores checkpointed replicas in seconds, without model reload or warmup, supporting faster startup, recovery and elasticity for inference and agentic workloads on Kubernetes.
Design partners Crusoe and Saturn Cloud have evaluated Snapshot on their own workloads using NVIDIA HGX B300 systems. Crusoe, an upstream contributor to Snapshot, tested GLM-5.3 on Crusoe Cloud and reduced the time for the workload to become ready from roughly eight minutes to 31 seconds. Saturn Cloud, a token factory platform, benchmarked Snapshot for scale-from-zero inference and reduced vLLM startup times from between two and 8.5 minutes to six and 34 seconds.
Learn more by joining NVIDIA at KubeCon.
